en: The Commentary on the Brahma-Sūtras (Brahmasūtrabhāṣya)
Composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda. Om.

That which is to be inquired into; which bestows birth, protection, abode, destiny, supreme inward knowledge, and liberation; which is accessible through the scriptures and primarily denoted by the words contained in the Vedas;
which is accompanied by the daughters of Bhīṣma and Satyā; whose body possesses manifold virtues; and which is far beyond fear and the ocean—[I bow to that].
I meditate upon Veṇukṛṣṇa, who is inconceivable through devotion, scripture, and so forth, and who is the supreme goal for those devoted to worship. // 1 //
I bow to that Lord of the World who, having approached the mango tree and struck Tāmratuṇḍa, became a lion-man (Nṛkesarī) and, being compassionate, seized him as he was submissive. 2.
I worship that Nṛsiṃhārka, who removes the darkness of obstacles, by whose grace one may master the Mahābhāṣya without having previously studied it.
I pay homage to the gurus Pūrṇabodha, the venerable Jayārya, the teacher Vyāsa, the noble guru Rāmacandra, and also the guru Lakṣmīkānta. // 4 //
By him, the purport of the Madhu, Guru, and Sadbhāṣya-Prakāśa was determined; the host of opposing philosophical systems was shattered; the ocean of his teacher’s teachings was bound together;
both types of wealth were bestowed upon his disciples; and the seat of learning was attained.
May this venerable Śrī Raghunātha Tīrtha, the sovereign of gurus, effect the purification of my mind.
Following the commentary composed by Jayārya,
this *Bhāṣyadīpikā* is being composed according to my own understanding by the ascetic named Jagannātha.
In some places, even the meaning of the *ṭīkā* is analyzed by means of an exposition of the *bhāṣya*, following the path set forth in works such as the *Tattvapradīpa* and the *Tātparyacandrikā*. (7)
Having bowed to Nārāyaṇa, who is exalted by all virtues and free from defects,
and also to the objects of knowledge, the goal, and the teachers, the meaning of the Sūtra is now stated.

In order to bring about the destruction of the bondage caused by beginningless ignorance, desire, karma, and so forth, for the sake of the individual soul— which is itself of the nature of consciousness and bliss as a reflection of the Supreme Self which consists of supreme bliss and the like— one must understand the Supreme Person as being, in ultimate reality, absolutely distinct from the entire phenomenal world composed of both sentient and insentient entities, and as being exalted by all auspicious qualities and devoid of every defect.
The truth is that the activity of all the authentic scriptures is directed toward this:
as they have said—"Everything else is non-suffering; it is only living beings who suffer."
This scripture is set forth for the sake of abandoning their suffering.
Thus,
"it proceeds" means that it establishes the Supreme Self as the means for the abandonment of suffering.
And for the sake of determining their meaning, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa composed the Brahma-sūtras.

These, however, have been explained otherwise by others—those whose eyes are covered by the film of ignorance, as described by the term "eyes covered by a film"—just as one with eyes covered by a film cannot see objects as they truly are.
Desiring to explain them correctly, the venerable teacher Ānanda-tīrtha, because an auspicious beginning alone ensures success, [proceeds] with the commentary he intends to compose...

Performing the auspicious invocation in the form of salutation to Nārāyaṇa for the sake of establishing the means to all fruits beginning with liberation (kaivalya), and for the sake of completing [the work] without obstacles and so forth,
he composes the following for the instruction of his disciples and declares what he intends to do: "Nārāyaṇa," and "exalted by all qualities."
"Exalted" means supreme;
"free from defects" means devoid of faults.
‘Jñeyam’ means that which is to be made the object of both types of knowledge, namely the indirect and the direct;
‘gamyam’ means that which is to be attained.
In both cases, the word “by the virtuous” is to be understood as the ellipsis.
"Having bowed to Nārāyaṇa and the gurus"— here, the meaning of the particle *ca* (and) is conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Thus, having bowed to the gurus as well, having prostrated with the eight limbs (*sāṣṭāṅga*), [he states] "the meaning of the Sūtra."

The construction is as follows: "I shall state the meaning of the Brahmasūtras—that which is the essence of the entire mass of words consisting of the Vedas along with their supplements, such as the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, known as Nārāyaṇa"—it is thus being commented upon (*bhāṣyate*).
Here, by the phrase "exalted by its qualities" (*guṇair udīrṇam*), [the subject matter] of the first chapter [is indicated].

It should be understood that the meaning of the second chapter has been summarized first by the phrase "free from defects," the meaning of the third chapter by "that which is to be known," and the meaning of the fourth chapter by "that which is to be attained," for the benefit of the students.

By these very four qualifiers, the word *Nārāyaṇa*, which denotes the qualified object, is not conventional like the word *Ḍittha* and so forth; rather, it means either "the abode of *nārās*," where *arās* are defects and *nārās* are virtues opposed to them,
or "one who does not become the abode of *aras*."

Alternatively, by virtue of being the object [of knowledge], he is the substratum of the cognition associated with a particular person (Nara), or, through yoga, he is the substratum of those liberated from the "ara" [of worldly existence]; thus, it is stated that he is a designator of preeminent qualities.
By this, it is demonstrated that Nārāyaṇa alone is the meaning of the scripture.

By these very four adjectives, the qualities that constitute the grounds for being worthy of worship—namely, possessing manifold virtues, being free from defects, being knowable through the scriptures, and being accessible through the scriptures—are stated.

Alternatively, here, by the five terms beginning with "Nārāyaṇa," the five forms known as Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are expressed; these are endowed with the five causes consisting of: (1) lying upon the ocean, (2) excellence, (3) sport, (4) knowledge, and so forth, which signify His loftiness; (5) the complete removal of defects; (6) the possession of supreme splendor; and (7) being unimpeded in reaching those who possess knowledge.
This is because these [works] are intended to be explained in the chapters (adhyāyas) and sections (pādas) of this treatise.

Accordingly, the interpretation stated in the *Tattvapradīpikā*—beginning with "Having bowed to Nārāyaṇa, who is exalted by qualities; having bowed to him who is free from defects"—should be observed.
Because of the statement, "A disciple should not utter the name of his guru, nor should a wife [utter] that of her husband," the teacher did not mention the guru's name;
nor did he speak of the gurus— who are denoted by the word Nārāyaṇa— using the word Nārāyaṇa itself.
It should not be said that this contradicts the *Tattvapradīpikā*, which states, "He alone is indeed Vyāsa, distinguished on all sides";
for that [statement] is consistent with the intention to express the actual non-difference between the Guru and the Deity.
This was stated thus because of the intention to express the uncommon names such as Yoga, Rūḍha, Vyāsa, and Kṛṣṇa;

or, the use of the plural number is for the sake of great respect, due to the multiplicity of aspects—namely, being the source of the scripture based on his gravity, being the initiator of the scriptural tradition, and being the direct instructor—or because of his "guru-hood" (gaurava).
Even though [Vyāsa] is the Guru...
Since he is also one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), there is no difference between the two; nevertheless, there is a separate salutation for the sake of receiving special grace.
Thus, the word "api" (also) is intended to indicate a lack of preference for a distinction between one's own guru and the deity.
And likewise: "api" (even);
the meaning is "even though there is no difference between the Guru and the deity.
However, the author of the *Tattvapradīpa* says that by the word "api," the author of the Sūtras is also included.
The intention is that there is a separate salutation for the sake of bestowing a special favor upon him as well;
or else, the word "api" (also) serves to include another qualification, and the phrase "the explanation of this is as follows," and so forth, is its clarification.

Thus, according to the method stated by Sudhākara, the word "api" (also) serves to include other unmentioned qualifiers—such as being the cause of the birth of the universe and so forth—which establish His fullness of attributes (*guṇapūrṇatva*).

By this very verse, the subject matter (*viṣaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), and relationship (*sambandha*)—which constitute the prerequisites for the listener’s engagement—are also indicated for the sake of instructing the disciples.

In the Dvāpara age, when all knowledge had become confused, the Lord Nārāyaṇa descended as Vyāsa at the request of Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and others, in order to provide a definitive determination of that knowledge.
Indeed, it is only when the *Brahmasūtras* possess authority that they are to be adopted by discerning persons, for such adoption is generally contingent upon their authority;
and only when that authority exists can they be correctly explained by dispelling any merely apparent meanings.

Anticipating the objection, "How indeed is its authority established?", and intending to offer the resolution that it is "by virtue of being rooted in a trustworthy source" (*āptimūlatva*) and so forth, he states the sequence of the Sūtras—beginning with the words "In the Dvāpara"—in order to demonstrate how it is rooted in a trustworthy source by way of the absence of defects in the speaker and the listener. [He explains: "In which Yuga, only two feet of Dharma remain... and so on.

"In two ages" means either in a subsequent or later age; or, within the Vaivasvata Manvantara, during the Mahāyugas, it refers to the age named Dvāpara—the twenty-eighth with respect to the first Dvāpara—because it is endowed with two quarters of Dharma.
"Everywhere" means among humans, sages, and gods.

According to the statement in the *Tattvapradīpa*, "By 'the world' (loka), virtuous people (sajjana) are intended," and according to the statement in the *Prameyadīpa*, "when the knowledge"— that is, the correct knowledge— of all virtuous beings, including gods, sages, and others, has become "confused" (*ākulībhūta*).

When it has been established that [the inquiry] concerns the object of doubt produced by conflicting views— namely, whether right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is the cognition of having attributes (*saguṇatva*) and so forth, or the cognition of being devoid of attributes (*nirguṇatva*) and so forth— and that it is indeed the cognition of being devoid of attributes and so forth, and not the other, which thus becomes the object of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*); and when there exists the doubt as to whether the reality (*tattva*) is the possession of attributes and so forth, which is the object of that [false] knowledge, or something else— and likewise when such a misconception (*viparyaya*) exists.
‘For the sake of determining that’:
for the purpose of ascertaining the correctness of that knowledge of [Brahman] as possessing attributes (saguṇatva) and so forth;
that is to say, for the purpose of ascertaining its validity regarding the object [of the teaching], namely, that “this alone is the reality and nothing else.”
"By Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the other gods"— the word "gods" is to be supplied as the subject.
"Entreated" means requested with a vow.

The qualification "by the gods, [namely] Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and so forth," which refers to other entities, is intended to demonstrate that this task is impossible even for those of well-known power who are other than the Blessed One.

"Bhagavān" means one endowed with all qualities such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*); "Nārāyaṇa" refers to Him; and "in the form of Vyāsa" is for the purpose of determining His identity.
"In the form of Vyāsa," meaning in the form of Vyāsa described as having "the color of an auspicious emerald," he "descended," that is,
he manifested.
The construction [of the sentence] is by repeating the phrase "for the sake of its determination" (*tannirṇayāya*).

Thus, Rudra was requested by Indra and the others for the sake of that determination; then, the Lord was approached by all of them—those who were qualified as the highest—and requested with the understanding that he was the Supreme One through discernment (*viveka*).

Now, for those who desire the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired, but do not know the means to achieve that, he manifested the lost Veda and divided it into four parts in order to make that [means] known.
[The Lord appeared] in twenty-four ways, one hundred and one ways, one thousand ways, and twelve ways.
To the question, "What follows from this in the present context?", he says: "Now" (*atha*).

This means: therefore, because [the Lord] has descended for the sake of that definitive determination, immediately after his descent, without creating any interruption by heterogeneous activities unfavorable to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Nor does it mean "without depending on the instruction of another.
Regarding the phrase "those who desire the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired":
this refers to those who desire both the attainment of what is wished for and the avoidance of what is not wished for.
Or, according to the system of the *Tattvapradīpa*, it means "of those who possess the desire for the attainment of unobtained happiness and the avoidance of suffering.

This was stated in this way both to establish that liberation (*mokṣa*) is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*)—since there are conflicting views among disputants on this point—and to define its essential nature;
otherwise, he would have simply said "of those desiring liberation" (*mumukṣūṇām*).
This much alone is not sufficient; it must be supplemented with the word "ultimate.
"Not knowing their yoga" means not knowing the specific means (upāya-viśeṣa) consisting of the knowledge of the higher and lower principles regarding the dharma of cessation (nivṛtti).

"For the sake of making known that [truth] to virtuous people who do not know it" means for the sake of making known the means for attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired. "'The Veda, which had perished'": [perished] means obscured by faulty readings and the like; "divided into four parts."
The phrase "he divided" is repeated;
[it implies that] "therefore, it was already divided even before that."
Thus, the phrase "and again, each one" is the remainder [of the sentence].
And so, prior even to the intermediate division of the Vedas, from that which was already divided fourfold by itself into the forms of the Ṛgveda and the others—
Having manifested the Vedas—consisting of the *ṛc*, *nigada*, and so forth—which were divided fourfold from the root Veda, by means of teaching;
and having thus manifested them, he divided them fourfold such that one part came from each [of the four].
Having extracted and manifested the *ṛcs* from the *ṛcs*, he [established] the *Ṛgveda*.
The meaning is that he composed the Yajurveda from the Nigadas, the Sāmaveda from the Sāmans, and the Atharvaveda from the Ātharvaṇas.

Furthermore, observing the limited capacity of students, he divided each individual Veda—each of the sub-divisions such as the Ṛgveda and so forth—into twenty-four parts, one hundred and four ways, one thousand ways, and twelve ways; this is the meaning.
As it has been stated in the Ṛgbhāṣya:
Having extracted the Ṛcas from the Ṛcas, the Lord composed the Ṛgveda;
likewise, he drew forth the Yajus from the Nigadas and the Sāmans from the Sāman.

The meaning is that, by means of such passages, he extracted and manifested the secondary Vedas (upavedas) in the form of the Ṛgveda and others from the root Veda—which is itself divided into four parts—and from those [secondary Vedas], he composed the intermediate branches such as the Ṛgveda.

Here, the prior mention of the *dvāpara* age is for the purpose of supporting the confusion regarding all knowledge; for confusion arises both from the division [of the Vedas] over time and from the lack of full comprehension of their respective branches (*śākhās*) before such a division. This explains how the secondary Veda extracted from the Great Veda functions as an intermediate Veda, and how the intermediate Veda is further divided into twenty-four parts and so forth.
As it has been said: "In the wheel of the tree of the Vedas," and so forth;
[referring to] those of "small intellect," whose knowledge has become confused.
The phrase "for the purpose of preventing that" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Although it is said:
"In the Kṛta age, there was indeed one Veda; in the Tretā, it became threefold;
and reaching the Dvāpara age, that very same [Veda] became fivefold."
When the Veda had almost entirely perished, having encountered the Kali age in its entirety, [he recovered it].

Thus, since the Smṛti cited in the Atharvaṇabhāṣya states that in the Kṛta age there was oneness of the Veda, in the Tretā age there was merely a threefold division, and in the Dvāpara age there were five divisions,
and likewise states that the disappearance of the entire Veda occurs only in the Kali age,
whereas here [the text says] "the Veda has disappeared";

Thus, a contradiction appears because of the statement that the fourfold division occurred in the Tretā Yuga and its disappearance in the Dvāpara Yuga itself. Nevertheless, since the unity of the Vedas can be maintained in view of the undifferentiated root-mass, and because the mention of a threefold division in the Tretā Yuga is intended to emphasize that [the other Vedas] were predominantly the means for the worship of the Lord, there is no denial of the actual existence of another mode known as the Atharvaṇa; thus, there is room for yet another division.
In the Dvāpara age, although the Veda is fourfold, it is possible for it to be fivefold when including human-authored works such as the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;

furthermore, even though the Veda undergoes destruction through all its various forms in the Kali age due to its great abundance, since [the Veda] existed prior to the incarnation of Vyāsa, there is no contradiction in the fact that destruction in the form of corrupt readings and the like could also occur in the Dvāpara age.
To determine the meaning of that [Veda], he composed the Brahma-sūtras.
Having thus stated the introduction, he speaks of the subject at hand: "for the determination of their meaning.

This means for the purpose of determining the meaning of all those [scriptures] by means of reasoning based on the introductory context (*upakrama*) and so forth. "[The Brahma-sūtras]"—this refers to the aphorisms concerning Brahman.
"Brahman" means the Veda, or its object, the Supreme Brahman; "aphorisms" (sūtra) means those which determine its essential nature— this is the meaning.
However, in the *Gītā-bhāṣya*, this is already resolved by the statement that the author Vyāsa is an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa, ending with the words "he composed the Brahma-sūtras"; furthermore,
by stating that Brahmā and others were the seekers, the absence of defects in the listeners and the absence of deception on the part of the speaker caused by such defects have been asserted.

By the statement, "When knowledge has become confused, for the sake of its determination," since the removal of ignorance is thus occasioned, the absence of the fault of *prasaṅga* (irrelevance) and, by that very fact, the absence of being subject to ridicule are stated; thereby, the foundation in authoritative tradition (*āptimūlatā*) is demonstrated.
[This refers to] the "Brahma-sūtras."

By this, it is indicated that [the *Brahma-sūtras*] are rooted in scripture (*śruti*) because they consist of an exposition of the Vedic texts concerning Brahman, and that they are rooted in reasoning (*yukti*) because they establish logical principles (*nyāya*).
Thus, the intended meaning is that the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the *Brahma-sūtras* is established.
And that has been stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Knowledge originating from Nārāyaṇa remained intact in the Kṛta Yuga;
it became slightly altered in the Tretā Yuga, and entirely so in the Dvāpara."
He establishes the very point already stated by means of a proof: "And that" (*tacca*).
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "only" (*eva*).
And thus—what was [stated] by us regarding the "Dvāpara" period...

The meaning is that what was stated by [the words] beginning with "ityādi" is indeed what was stated in the Skanda Purāṇa. The word "ca" (and) is used either for the purpose of conjunction—to indicate that this has been stated not only by us but also in the Skanda—or to indicate that it has been stated in such a manner in the Tattvapradīpa: "Even though the teacher himself is the authority regarding his own stated subject matter,"
"Because [the Buddha] is omniscient and non-deceptive;
nevertheless, he makes this bold assertion (prauḍhavāda) that it is also stated in the Skanda-purāṇa:
'Not only by us...'"
To the question, "What is stated even in the *Prameyadīpa*? he recites that [verse]: "From Nārāyaṇa.
The meaning is "due to his instruction.
The words "through Brahmā and others" are to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

Alternatively—since knowledge is included within the eightfold [category] beginning with origination, its being produced by Nārāyaṇa is established. The word "niṣpannam" (accomplished) means "utpannam" (arisen); and "akhilam" (entire) is also connected here, meaning it has all things, such as possessing qualities, as its object.
"Knowledge" means right knowledge; "established" means that it remains exactly as it has arisen, unassailed by doubt and the like.
The word "among the virtuous" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The implied meaning is that there was no doubt or the like regarding the object of knowledge. In the *tretā* age, "that" knowledge was "to some extent."
"In the object, 'born otherwise' (anyathājātam)";

the meaning is that it has attained the status of being an object of the aforementioned doubt—namely, "is this or that?"—and the status of being an object of false knowledge, namely, "it is something else entirely.
In this context, the twenty-eighth [Dvāpara] should be understood as including the Tretā and other ages as well.

In the Dvāpara age, everything pertaining to all subjects arose in a contrary manner; this is the grammatical connection. When knowledge had turned into ignorance due to the curse of the sage Gautama, the gods, led by Brahmā and Rudra, became possessed of confused intellects.
They went for refuge to Nārāyaṇa, the source of refuge and free from all affliction.

Now, if it is argued that since alteration is caused by time, it would be logical for the alteration to affect only two parts during the Dvāpara age and not the whole, [the author] states the specific cause: "of Gautama.
The word "but" (tu) has the sense of "and" (ca), indicating either that the curse was the specific cause or that there was correctness in his knowledge.

And likewise, when [the knowledge] has become an object of the notion that it is "ignorance"— that is, a cognition characterized by the mode "this is not the knowledge of reality" (tattvajñāna), being distinct from the knowledge of reality— due to the curse of the sage Gautama,
and having reached a state of doubt; in other words,
when the object of knowledge has become an object of doubt or error, which are contrary to right knowledge (samyagjñāna).
"Those headed by Brahmā and Rudra";
"the gods" beginning with them;
"those of confused intellect."

For those possessing knowledge mixed with ignorance and the like, regarding an object for which knowledge has arisen, they subsequently possess ignorance, doubt, and so forth concerning the various modes pertaining to that same object; [they approach Him who is] "śaraṇyaṃ"—excellent therein, foremost among protectors in providing refuge—and "anāmayaṃ.
According to the method stated in the commentary on the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa*, here the word *āmaya* denotes disease and is indicative of other defects (*doṣa*).

And thus, having described [Him] as ‘Nārāyaṇa,’ they ‘went for refuge’ in the manner stated in such passages as, “With the prior realization of His supreme excellence, their minds are always fixed upon Him”; the meaning is that they have gone for refuge.
It should be understood that he requested him and also made known his own purpose.

In this context, the "confusion" (*saṅkīrṇatva*) of the intellects of Brahmā and the others refers solely to their being endowed with compassion toward virtuous beings who possess confused intellects;
it does not mean being mixed with ignorance and so forth, as is the case with the intellects of others.
Alternatively, it refers to having ignorance, doubt, and so forth as its objects.

This is because the concealment described by the term "overpowering" (abhibhava), which was caused by the occasion of Gautama’s curse directed specifically at the person who slaughtered his own cow, is impossible among the gods.

As for the world other than the gods beginning with Brahmā—who were not the ones who slaughtered Gautama’s cow—it should be understood that ignorance arose there due to the absence of anyone to transmit the tradition and due to the lapse of time.

The manner in which Gautama’s curse was incurred is as follows: Formerly, during a twelve-year drought, the sages, afflicted by it, took up residence in Gautama’s hermitage, which was well-supplied with food. There they remained for a long time, honored by him and performing their respective prescribed duties. Then, when the drought had subsided, a desire arose in them to return to their own respective hermitages.
For that purpose, they requested permission from Gautama;
nevertheless, out of a desire not to leave his hermitage empty, he did not grant them permission.
At that very moment—
Thinking that the celestial river (Gaṅgā) residing on Hara’s head was her rival, Pārvatī sent Vināyaka, who approached those sages in disguise, wearing the garb of a religious student (brahmacārin),
and said: "O venerable ones, for what purpose do you dwell in this hermitage?"
"By eating the food of another for so long a time, your ascetic merit will perish.
Therefore, go each to your own hermitage,
and there listen to the means being described by me."
By the power of your knowledge and asceticism, create a golden cow made of illusion;
then cause her to enter into the crops that have been nourished by the rain falling from the clouds drawn forth by the power of Gautama’s asceticism.
Then Gautama will strive to drive away that cow which is devouring the crops.

Then, by the mere touch of the water from that water-pot, she will suddenly fall down. At that time, O Brāhmaṇas, you must reply to him: "As long as you do not raise up this cow, our mother, who is now completely lifeless, we shall not eat food. Then, having said to that repentant one, "Bring down the celestial river situated upon the head of Hara, and having sprinkled her with that water, restore her to life," Heramba [departed] toward Ambikā.
Then, having approached the means for departure as it was proclaimed by their leader, they carried it out;
by that very means they set forth.
Thereupon Gautama, having propitiated Tryambaka through austerity and brought the Mandākinī, consecrated Surabhi with that water.
Thereupon the sage rose up, liberated from the sin of that slaughter;
for this very reason, the name Godāvarī was given to her.
Then, perceiving the deed of Vināyaka, he became enraged at the sages.

And Gautama cursed him, saying: "May that knowledge by which these [cows] were driven away on account of the power of my knowledge derived from our food perish! Then, having been informed of this matter by them, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, the Great Yogin, descended through Parāśara upon Satyavatī.
The Blessed Lord Hari himself recovered the lost Vedas;
he divided them into four parts, and then again into twenty-four,
as well as into one hundred, one, and likewise into one thousand parts.
Regarding the question of what the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa did when requested by the gods in twelve ways, the author says: "By them" (taiḥ).
The word "but" (tu) is used for emphasis.
‘Mahāyogī’ refers to one who has the form of a sage or possesses great power; ‘Puruṣottama’ refers to the Blessed Lord, who is superior to both the perishable and the imperishable consciousness.
Nārāyaṇa, "by them"—

meaning by those very gods who had attained refuge in him— "having his purpose intimated," refers to one whose task (kārya) in the form of an incarnation and so forth was proposed and carried out as requested.
The grammatical construction is as follows: "Mahāyogī" by form (appearance), and "Kṛṣṇa" by name, who descended from Parāśara upon Satyavatī.
He states the purpose for the interval between incarnations with the words "those who have perished.
"Himself" means directly; "Hari" refers to the Blessed Lord (Bhagavān).
Vyāsa, endowed with qualities such as knowledge, [recovered] the "Vedas," which were "lost"— that is, obscured by erroneous readings and the like—
"by himself."
"Without another's instruction, he 'ujjahāra'";
that is, he made them manifest through vocalization.
And those Vedas, which had already been divided into four parts, he "again divided into four."
He divided [the Veda] into four parts;
and each single part he further divided the Ṛgveda into twenty-four ways, in the form of twenty-four branches (śākhās) and so forth.
The Yajurveda in "one hundred and one ways," that is, by way of the single division known as the one hundred and one [recensions],
and the Sāmaveda in "a thousand ways."
The meaning is that he divided the Atharvaveda into twelve parts;
he is called "Bhagavān" in order to indicate the preeminence of his status as a Lord.
Thus, there is repetition.
The words "eva" (indeed/only) serve to exclude any additional modes.
The words "ca" (and) serve to conjoin the various modes with one another.
Furthermore, in order to explain its meaning,
he states the subject at hand with the word "again" (*punah*);
its syntactical connection is with what precedes it.
Alternatively, there is also a connection with what follows;
the meaning is "immediately after the division of the Veda.
"Of that" refers to the Veda; "for the sake of knowing its meaning."
For the sake of knowing the meaning:

although the Vedas are many, because their meaning is one, it is not improper to refer to those Vedas—which were indicated by the plural "those Vedas"—by the singular "of that" (*tasya*), when one intends to express that [single] meaning; for the word "of that" (*tasya*) functions as a singular denoting the whole.
Because it is always dependent [on another word], the compound "arthavittaye" is correct. Furthermore, the word "punaḥ" has the sense of immediate succession, as in the rule "punaraprathame bhede."
This is established by the statement of Amara, "one should practice once again" (*punareva samabhyaset*),

where "again" (*punaḥ*) means immediately after the departure of sleep according to Sudhākara; and by the statement of Viśveśatīrtha, "and again in the third [period]," where "again" means after the three watches of the night.

In the phrase "cakāra," the word "Kṛṣṇo Vyāsaḥ" is also to be supplied by ellipsis. Now, one might raise the objection that since the determination of the meaning of the Vedas is possible through other sūtras alone, what is the purpose of the Brahma-sūtras? To dispel this suspicion of redundancy, he says: "Of those... (yeṣām).
"Sūtratvam" means the ground for applying the word "sūtra"; "añjasā" means primarily; the meaning is that it exists [there] in the primary sense.
It "made them" (cakāra) its own.
Thus, there is a connection either with the preceding phrase "of such a kind" or with the subsequent one;
[it is] concise in syllables, free from ambiguity, substantial, and comprehensive in its scope.

Those who know the Sūtras understand a Sūtra to be that which is free from superfluous additions (astobha) and irreproachable (anavadya). What is this quality of being a "Sūtra" (*sūtratva*) that constitutes the directness of the *Brahmasūtras*? To this he says: "Brief" (*alpa*). That is to say, it is devoid of more syllables than are necessary to establish the intended meaning through both the literal word and its underlying purport (*śruti-artha*), provided no other restrictive factor exists; for as long as the intended meaning cannot be established without a certain number of syllables, it consists of exactly that many syllables. Thus, it is free from any excess of syllables.

Some, however, say that between a synonym consisting of few syllables and one consisting of many syllables, "having few syllables" means being endowed with a word of few syllables; that is inconsistent with the commentary. And thus, "unambiguous" (*asaṃdigdha*) refers to the meaning not being something that has to be stated [by implication] as "it ought to be so."

"Of unambiguous meaning" means "of determined meaning," according to the statement in the *Tattvapradīpa*. "Substantial" (*sāravat*) means endowed with the supreme meaning that cannot be obtained from any other source.
It is called "viśvatomukha" (facing all directions) because it determines the meaning of words and sentences found across many branches [of the Veda].
In the *Tattvapradīpa*, however, it is stated that it is "viśvatomukha" because it explains the entirety of the required subject matter for each single purpose.
It is called "astobha" because it is devoid of those syllables used for other purposes, such as filling out the portions of the chant, which would be impossible without knowledge of the meaning.
"Flawless" means free from defects in word and meaning;
that which possesses these aforementioned qualifications is precisely what the "experts in sūtras" call a "sūtra."
Those who know the characteristics of the Sūtras "know" [it];
the meaning is that they accept it.

In this context, even though it does not convey a specific doctrinal meaning, there are statements such as those concerning the determination of the Bhāṣya, words spoken by authoritative persons, worldly reports, and so forth, including the name-mantra of the Blessed One and the like.

The purpose of the words [of the definition] is to be understood as they are stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*: the qualifiers are intended, respectively, to exclude the *stobha* syllables found in the *Sāmaveda* which complete the portions of the chant not pervaded by the syllables of the *Ṛgveda*, as well as such sentences that are accompanied by corrupt words (*apaśabda*).

Here, although the discussion concerns the substratum (*dharmin*) in all cases, the cause for the application of the words of the aphorism (*sūtra*) is also stated by way of that [substratum]; thus, there is no inconsistency. Furthermore, for this reason, the *Brahmasūtra* possesses the status of being an aphorism even without further qualification.

Just as the single Kṛṣṇa is designated by various names such as Vyāsa due to his specific attributes, one might ask: "But how is it that these [texts] are straightforwardly called the *Brahmasūtras*? To this, he says: "unqualified" (*nirviśeṣita*).
[This refers to] "of the *Brahmasūtra*."
Thus, this is a singular term for the collective whole.
The particle *ca* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and also in the sense of "since" (*yataḥ*).
The word *api* serves to include [this work] as a primary sūtra.
And likewise, because the *Brahma-sūtras* possess the status of being the primary sūtras, they are called "unqualified sūtras" (*nirviśeṣita-sūtratva*).

That from which distinctions (*viśeṣāḥ*) have departed is "without distinction" (*nirviśeṣam*); that which is so described is "unqualified" (*nirviśeṣitam*). The state of having such sūtra-words is what is meant.
Alternatively, "distinction" (*viśeṣaḥ*) means a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇam*).

The non-existence of that [qualification] has arisen for this; that is, the state of being such a word "sūtra" belongs to it, which is the state of being a *sūtra* without qualification (*nirviśeṣita-sūtratva*).
The fact that it is denotable by the mere word *sūtra* devoid of qualifications is stated in the Purāṇas and other texts.
Otherwise, that would not be the case.
The meaning is that there is a necessary rule (niyama) that when the pervader (vyāpaka) is absent, the pervaded (vyāpya) is also absent.
Here, in the first position, the word *tathākhyātam* is formed with the suffix *kta* in the passive sense (*karmani*) from the causative root (*ṇyanta*) meaning "to be so described" (*tathākhyāta*).
The distinction is that in the second [case], it is a secondary derivative (taddhita) ending in "itac.
By this, the reason— that [the Brahmasūtras] are primary sūtras because they are denotable by an unqualified word— is stated.

Having raised the objection that the reason (hetu) here is inconclusive, he seeks to refute it by means of a statement on pervasion (vyāpti). First, with reference to the positive concomitance (anvaya-vyāpti)—namely, "whatever is not qualified by [the specific nature of] food is not primary in that regard"—he states an example for that: "just as" (yathā).
The word "even" (eva) is understood to carry over from the previous context.
By this, the pervasiveness of the primary status of the meaning of the word "one" (eka) is obtained.

And thus, just as for Kṛṣṇa Vedavyāsa—who, though being one, possesses the state of being Vyāsa, that is, the state of being denoted by the unqualified term "Vyāsa"—so too, because they are unqualified, the *Brahmasūtras* possess the status of being the primary *Sūtras*; such is the completion of the sentence.

Now, intending to show the negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*)—that those which are not primary are not denotable by terms devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*), but rather are denotable by terms possessing attributes (*saviśeṣa*)—he provides an example therein with the word "others" (*anye*).
The word "just as" (*yathā*) is understood to follow from the previous context.
Since the word "one" (*eka*) was heard previously, it is understood here that these are "not primary."
The word "Vyāsas" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
And thus— as from Kṛṣṇa, those others such as the son of Droṇa (Aśvatthāman) who are secondary are [included] because of the absence of qualification.
The Vyāsas [are so called] only in dependence upon this very qualification, not independently of it;

or, the ablative case (pañcamī) is used in the sense of the instrumental (tṛtīyārthe), and the construction is to be understood as: "they are indeed denoted by the word 'Vyāsa' only when accompanied by the qualification."
For the learned know that there are indeed other sūtras with specific qualifications.
Now, let it be granted that the Brahmasūtras possess primacy;
nevertheless, others also possess it.
Anticipating the objection that this does not apply to those [others] alone because there is no reason for the others to be non-primary,

he states an inference— characterized by positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*) which was previously established through a statement of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) as an illustration, and now supported by the reason of "being unspecified" (*nirviśeṣitatva*) which functions as a co-extensive (*samavyāpti*) pervasion— as the determining factor in that regard.
Regarding the term "saviśeṣaṇa" (with qualifications): the word "ataḥ" (hence) is understood to carry over [from the previous context], and the word "aparāṇi" (others) is also repeated.
The word "hi" signifies reason;
and thus— since "others," that is,
other sūtras besides the Brahma-sūtras, are "others."

For this very reason, the "non-primary" [sūtras] are those "knowing ones" (*vidaḥ*)— the wise— who regard them as "secondary," namely, the sūtras containing qualifying attributes (*saviśeṣaṇasūtrāṇi*).
They "know"— that is, they understand— that these are expressed by the words of the sūtras together with their qualifiers;
and thus, because other sūtras possess qualifiers, they are indeed secondary.
The intended meaning is that it does not possess primacy (*mukhyatva*).
[This is because: "A word [denotes] the primary [object] without qualification, while [it denotes] others with qualification.

Thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the states of being unqualified and primary on one hand, and being qualified and non-primary on the other, has been established by means of an illustrative example.

In the case of the example, there is a possibility that the primary and secondary status [of the Vedas] are caused by other factors, such as being the author of the extensive texts that divide the Vedas or possessing similarity to them; therefore, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished. To dispel this doubt, he proves it by means of a valid instrument (*pramāṇa*) with the words: "Of the primary one. This is to be understood as restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇam*).
The same applies to the phrase "of others.
By this, the pervasion of both primary and non-primary [denotative capacity] is established.
The meaning of the genitive case is denotative capacity (*vācakatva*).
And thus, since there exists a "denotative word" for the primary [reality] itself— meaning that there is a word denoting it as "without distinction," that is, by the absence of qualifiers.
‘Of others’; that is, of those who are not primary, ‘specifically,’ either with reference to a qualification or by means of a qualification.
"Sound" (*śabda*) means that which expresses;
that is to say, it is the state of being expressible by a word accompanied by its qualifiers.
Thus say the knowers of the Veda, who understand the true nature of the reality of sound.

"In this manner," those who know the true meaning of words— those who understand the reality of sound as it truly is— and who are knowers of the Vedas, the elders who understand the meaning of the Vedas, "have said."

The meaning is that they say this. Regarding this, there is the statement: "Therefore, among these, the status of being a *sūtra* belongs directly to [only some]"; and: "Other *sūtras* that possess qualifiers are secondary (*amukhya*)."
The phrase "thus stated" is connected with the remainder of the sentence as "this is logical.
There is a variant reading, "viśeṣitaḥ" (qualified), in some places; its meaning is "having attained qualification."

And thus, since it has been stated that for both the primary and the secondary meanings, the Veda and the usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) are the authorities regarding their being denoted by words with or without qualifiers, no other cause for those two should be suspected; this is the sense.
As for the aphorisms (*sūtra*) in which all determinations have been set forth—let this quality of being a *sūtra* properly belong to the *Brahma-sūtras*.

Nevertheless, since the determination of the meaning of the Vedas is possible through other sūtras alone, one might ask: "What is the purpose of the Brahma-sūtras? To show how the objection is answered by the phrase "of those who" (*yeṣām*), he explains what is stated in that sentence with the words "in the sūtras" (*sūtreṣu*).
This is a locative case used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta-saptamī*).
The particle *api* denotes pervasion (*abhivyāpti*) and serves to preclude limitation.
The "universality" (*sarvatva*) of the determination (*nirṇaya*) is to be understood through its object, and that [universality of the object] in turn through the word [itself].

Thus, from whichever sūtras all determinations—that is, determinations of the meaning of all Vedic branches (*sarva-śākhā-artha-nirṇaya*)—are proclaimed as being to be accomplished, [from those very sūtras this work is derived].

The meaning is that they are said to be the determiners of all branches (*sarvaśākhā*) in terms of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Alternatively, "determiners" (*nirṇaya*) refers to those things to be determined (*nirṇetavyārtha*).
The meaning is as follows: in the statement "of those [sūtras]," it was first stated that the status of being a *sūtra* belongs directly and primarily to the Brahma-sūtras themselves.
This being the case, the quality of being "all-pervasive" (viśvatoṇusvatva), which is mentioned as a characteristic of a *sūtra*, also belongs directly and primarily to those very [Brahma-sūtras].

And when this is so, it follows that they (the Brahma-sūtras) are declared to be the determiners of all branches without exception, for if they were determiners of only a few branches, their directness [of authority] would be untenable. Since this is the case, it is appropriate [to say] "for the sake of knowing its meaning," because the Brahma-sūtras, which determine the meaning of all Vedic branches, possess a superior power of determination compared to other sūtras that do not determine everything.
"He composed the Brahma-sūtras";
this statement containing the word "that" (tat) is a declaration of the composition of the sūtras for that purpose (tādarthyena), and thus it serves as a resolution to the doubt. [Furthermore:
"That which is the authoritative determination of the entire collection of words..."
Since these [works] determine the meaning of only two or three branches, how can it be said that they alone determine all branches?
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of their being useless.

Thus, in order to resolve the doubt that "in some respects the subject matter has already been covered," he states another point indicated by the word "naturally" (añjasā): "'of the entire collection of words'."
The meaning is "of that which consists of the Pūrvamīmāṃsā and so forth.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Sudhā*: "Indeed, it is recited in the Purāṇa that 'it (the Vedānta) subsists upon this Mīmāṃsā' regarding the entire collection of words.
This genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), not in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*).
For this very reason, the instrumental case is used in the *Ṭīkā* in the phrase "by means of collections of words" (*śabdasamūhaiḥ*).
And agency [on the part of the Veda] arises through its being the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) that has become an instrument;
and its status as a procedure occurs because it provides assistance by way of the *Mīmāṃsā*.

Some maintain that the genitive case here denotes a relationship (*sambandha-ṣaṣṭhī*) with the intention that the word *śabdajāta* refers exclusively to verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*); and they hold that this relationship is one of producer and produced (*janya-janaka-bhāva*).
That of which a particular means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is the source is described as such.
The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of conjunction and also serves to carry over [the implication of] the term "samudāhṛtaḥ" (stated).
The word "iti" is to be supplied [in the text].

Thus, even though others may determine the meaning of two or three branches [of the Veda], it remains the case that the Brahmasūtras alone possess the status of determining all branches without dependence on anything else or with their scope restricted;

for the determination of the meaning of two or three branches by other authors is based upon the Brahmasūtras and depends upon the determinations produced by them, as those others are merely commentaries on the Śruti.

The sense is that just as there is no futility for a Smṛti rooted in Śruti, so too, since its utility is established, the root [Śruti] does not become futile because of the root-possessor [Smṛti]. [Regarding the phrase] "having composed such Sūtras," [it refers to] Vyāsa of great fame.
"Such" means of this kind.
The meaning is that they are directly endowed with qualities such as facing all directions (*viśvatomukhatva*).
Since this [statement] serves as a conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*), there is no tautology with the phrase "he made them."
“Among the gods such as Brahmā and Rudra, and among humans, ancestors, and birds”—

by the word "gods" (deveṣu), those gods and gandharvas born of karma or by birth are also included. The term "humans" (manuṣya) refers to [the rule] "the *nivīta* [mode] is for humans" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.11).
In such passages as these, [the term] refers to sages whose nature is reflection (*manana*).
"Pāḥ" means those who protect, namely universal monarchs (*cakravartin*). "Kṣī" is a form of the root *kṣi* in the sense of destruction, denoting the best of men.
Because their lifespan is extremely short in comparison to others;
this also serves as an indicator for human *gandharvas*.
The analysis of the compound is: humans (*manuṣya*), ancestors (*pitṛ*), and those who have perished (*kṣaya*).
By this [verse], all five types mentioned in the phrase "gods, sages, ancestors, humans, and birds" are included as being fit for liberation.
Regarding the term *pakṣin* (bird), if it is taken as an indivisible whole (*akhaṇḍa*), the word *pakṣin* refers to animals such as the *jaritāri* and others who are fit [for liberation].
"Having established knowledge, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, sports," and so forth.
"Knowledge" refers to right knowledge or specific knowledge; "having established" means having produced or having made firm.
"Consolidation" (dṛḍhīkaraṇa) means the removal of doubt and error regarding the object of knowledge.

And thus, the Supreme Person, the highly illustrious Blessed Vyāsa of excellent renown, in those sūtras wherein all definitive conclusions have been proclaimed and whose status as the determiners of all Vedic branches has been stated—

Likewise, the determination of the intermediate purport (*avāntaratātparya*) of a portion of the Veda regarding the Creator of the world— which is being effected by all collections of words consisting of the sūtras of Jaimini and others, as well as by the determinative Smṛtis and so forth— is rooted in that [determination of the Great Purport of all Vedas] and dependent upon it; for, as has been stated in the verse beginning with "yeṣām," liberation as the fruit cannot be established merely through the knowledge of the intermediate purport without that [knowledge of the Great Purport].

Thus, in the preceding statement regarding the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it should be understood that the phrase "the Supreme Lord plays" (*krīḍate parameśvaraḥ*)— referring to how He plays after having composed such *sūtras* of this kind and established knowledge among the gods beginning with Brahmā and Rudra, as well as among humans, ancestors, and birds—
is stated to dispel any suspicion of incapacity in composing such *sūtras*. This refers specifically to His sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

In this context, "the establishment of knowledge among Brahmā and others" refers to the strengthening of knowledge already present through specific reasoning and other means, as well as the attainment of something previously unattained;
for it is stated in a passage cited in the *Gītātātparya*: "Even though they already know, [they act] for the sake of knowing the specific meaning or for the sake of its stabilization."

Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the *Bhāratatātparyanirṇaya*, which states: "Neither the gods nor the sages have thus attained such knowledge again," because the word "again" (*punaḥ*) here indicates that all the gods and others have attained the knowledge of an object previously unknown or forgotten.
This is because his purpose has already been stated. Alternatively, what is being said here is that others besides Viriñca obtain knowledge of meanings that were previously concealed;
for the Teachers have stated in the *Gītātātparya*: "For Brahmā, however, there is generally nothing that does not manifest [to him]."
The phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*) is connected with the words "and that has been stated" (*taccoktam*).
This reference contains an elided case-ending (*luptavibhaktika*).
Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman (athāto brahmajijñāsā).

Since there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the existence of a Brahman distinct from the consciousness of the living individual (jīva), and since the living individual, being self-luminous, is not an object of doubt; [therefore, the inquiry is not justified].

And thus, since there is no object [for inquiry], even though Brahman—which is of the nature of immediate presence—is perceived as "I," liberation is not attained; and because there is consequently no purpose, and for that very reason no qualified seeker (adhikārī) bound by that [purpose], it follows that the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) need not be undertaken.
To this, the venerable author of the Sūtras has established the final position (*siddhānta*): *om*.
Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman. Om.
This is one sūtra, constituting one topical section (adhikaraṇa).

An *adhikaraṇa* (topic for discussion) is a collection of five components consisting of: the subject matter (*viṣaya*), the doubt (*saṃśaya*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), and the purpose (*prayojana*).

For example, in this very *jijñāsā-adhikaraṇa*, the subject matter is the inquiry into [Brahman]—consisting of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth—as enjoined by the sentence "Let one desire to know That" (*tadvijijñāsasva*).
The doubt is whether [this inquiry] ought to be performed or not.
"It should not be performed" is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
In this position, the result is the determination that the treatise (*śāstra*) need not be commenced.
"It should be performed" is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
And in that context, the determination of whether [the inquiry] ought to be undertaken is the result;

for if the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), which consists of the investigation of principles, were not to be performed, it would necessarily follow that the Mīmāṃsā treatise, which consists of the systematic arrangement of those principles, should not be undertaken.
This applies elsewhere as well.
There are five types of connection for a single topic (adhikaraṇa), namely:
connection with the treatise (śāstra-saṅgati) and connection with the chapter (adhyāya-saṅgati).
It consists of such forms as connection with the [preceding] quarter, connection with the preceding section, and connection with the scriptural passage concerning that subject.
Connection (*saṅgati*) is also generally twofold: in the form of inclusion (*antarbhāva*) and characterized by immediate succession (*ānantarya*).
Among these, the connection in the form of inclusion pertains to the treatise (*śāstra*), the chapters (*adhyāya*), and the sections (*pāda*).
However, by means of the preceding *adhikaraṇa* and its subject matter (*viṣayavākya*), there is a connection consisting of immediate succession (*ānantarya*).
That too is manifold in form, such as being introductory (*ākṣepikī*), analogical (*ātideśikī*), incidental (*aupodghātikī*), exceptional (*āpavādikī*), or relevant (*prāsaṅgikī*).
Among these, up until the fifth *adhikaraṇa*, there is merely a general connection with the treatise (*śāstra-saṅgati*).
There is no connection with the chapter or the section (*pāda*).

Even though there is a connection with the chapter for both the sections on "Harmony" (*samanvaya*) and "Investigation" (*īkṣati*), there is no such connection with the section; thus, the absence of these two connections is common to all five topics (*adhikaraṇa*).
Likewise, neither the connection with the preceding topic nor the connection with its subject matter applies to this present topic.
This is because it is the very first section (*adhikaraṇa*) and because the investigation of the Śruti has not yet been commenced;
however, it should be understood that [the syllable *oṃ*] applies to the other four [sections].

In this Sūtra, the syllable *oṃ* is to be pronounced at both the beginning and the end. Of these, the one at the beginning serves both seen (*dṛṣṭa*) and unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) purposes; for this very reason, it is pronounced separately rather than in saṃhitā form so that it may persist throughout all the Sūtras as a part of them.
Alternatively—at the beginning, there are two *oṃ* syllables, one for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) and one for a seen purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*);
however, at the end, in both cases, there is only a single *oṃ* syllable for an unseen purpose.
Being "for an unseen purpose" means that its function is solely to prevent defects such as the leaking or the dispersal [of the mantra].
"Having a visible purpose," however, means the capacity to convey the meaning of the word to be connected [with it].
In that regard, the indeclinable "Oṃ," which constitutes a part of the opening sūtra, is a qualifier of the word "Brahman" and signifies its fullness of qualities.
The word *brahman* also denotes Viṣṇu through established usage among the learned (*vidvadrūḍhi*) and through great yogic power (*mahāyoga*).
The word *atha* signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*), [following] from the context (*adhikāra*) according to its suitability.
Thus it is connected; "should be performed" is the ellipsis. And so [it begins with] "Now" (atha).

Following the qualification consisting of study, tranquility, self-control, and so forth, the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is used because [the scripture] possesses the fruit called liberation, which arises from the grace produced by the knowledge of one's own birth; and "Oṃ" refers to Brahman, who is full of all attributes.
The meaning of the aphorism is that an inquiry (*jijñāsā*)— in the form of reflection (*vicāra*) consisting of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth— into Viṣṇu must be undertaken.
The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) means "by the grace of Viṣṇu."
The word "śabda" has a different meaning [from "brahman"].
The connection is with the remainder of the sentence: "there may be for this [word] the effect of being an object of inquiry (*jijñāsā*) and so forth.

Although both the words *oṃ* and *brahman* are etymological (*yaugika*), there is no redundancy of either, because the connection is accepted by relying on one being conventional (*rūḍha*) and thus denoting the substantive (*viśeṣya*), while the other is etymological and thus denotes the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

The use of both [terms] is for the purpose of including numerous scriptural passages such as: “One should meditate on this syllable ‘Om’ as the Udgītha,” “Desire to know that; that is Brahman,” and so forth. Furthermore, the word *atha* (now/then) serves the purpose of indicating auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) and the commencement of a new topic (*adhikārāntarya*).
The word *ataḥ* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
Since the performance of an auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) at the beginning of a work is mandatory, he explains the word *atha* as being the cause of that auspiciousness—namely, "atha.

Its purpose (*artha*), meaning its objective, consists of the recitation of the word *atha*, which takes the form of the remembrance of Viṣṇu—a practice to be performed as the uncommon cause for the removal of obstacles.
Likewise, it is so described because its subject matter is Viṣṇu—who is auspicious by nature and whose form is to be practiced as praiseworthy—or his qualities.
As for the fact that the word *atha* (now/then) has the fruit of being auspicious, [it is said]:
"In ancient times, these two, the syllable *Oṃ* and the word *atha*, were born from Brahmā..."
Having pierced the throat, both of them emerged; therefore, they are both auspicious.
Thus it is established by the *Manusmṛti*.

Regarding the word *atha*, which is employed with the intent of refuting the engagement of anyone seeking liberation alone in the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), he states its expressed meaning as "qualification" (*adhikāra*).
The word *ca* (and) is used in a conjunctive sense, intending to express the literal meaning of both what is to be performed and what is not to be performed.
The word "ca" (and) does not merely indicate that [the word "atha"] serves as an auspicious marker, but also indicates immediate succession; or it may signify a conjunction of objects.
Alternatively, the word "ca" is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
By this, the purposes of performing an auspicious rite, commencing an undertaking, posing a question, or expressing totality are excluded.
The specific nature of that [meaning] has been stated in the *Candrikā*.
Thus, it is described as "having as its denoted meaning the sequence following the qualification" (*adhikārānantarya*).
Even though the word *atha* has the sense of mere sequence (*ānantarya*), such a description is used because of the connection with the word *adhikāra* through its fitness [to be construed with it].
By this, the engagement in the inquiry into Brahman by one who lacks qualification but merely desires liberation is refuted.
He explains the word "ataḥ" (therefore) as serving to remove the doubt that the inquiry into Brahman is devoid of purpose and cause, stating:
"'Ataḥ' means 'for this reason' [as a statement of the cause]."
It is so called because its cause (*hetu*) is its mark (*liṅga*), or because its cause— namely, the cause known as "clarity" (*prasāda*)— is its object (*artha*).
Thus it is described.
And it is stated in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:

"Now, as for the question—what is the purpose of the sūtras being preceded by the word 'atha' (now) and so forth? [Is it not possible] even by the utterance of another word, such as 'maṅgalaṃ tataḥ' (then there is auspiciousness), which serves to remove obstacles?"—the author dispels this doubt by means of a Purāṇic statement itself, saying: "'And it is stated.'"
The meaning is that what was stated [in our text] beginning with "Now, the word 'atha'... has indeed been stated in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa* as well.
The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of conjunction, implying not only by us, but also in the *Garuḍa*.
Now, therefore, all the aphorisms indeed begin with the word "atha" (now/then) by necessity alone; what, then, is the regulating factor here?
To state what was said, he recites: "Now" (atha).
To ward off the suspicion that [the arrangement] might be arbitrary—a synonym for lack of necessity—he says: "by necessity alone" (niyatyaiva).
The word "all" (nikhilāni) refers to the "aphorisms" (sūtrāṇi).
This is the qualification that prevents its restriction; the word "api" (also/even) signifies pervasion;
the particle "eva" (only/exclusively) is for the purpose of excluding non-restriction.
Or rather, the word order is inverted;
thus: "O ignorant one! [and] "O Brahman, first poet!"
"O Four-faced One,
even all [the sūtras]," meaning all the original sūtras composed by Vyāsa, Jaimini, and others,
"by necessity alone," that is, by rule, even in another kalpa, "begin with the words 'atha' and 'ataḥ'."
Now, the authors of the Sūtras begin with those very works in which the two words "atha" and "ataḥ" are to be employed first.
Regarding this necessity of being employed first, there must be some regulating factor for their mandatory initial employment.
The construction of the interrogative sentence is: "What is the regulator of those two? [Objection:
"O learned one, what is the meaning of those two, and how is their superiority?

Surely, the necessity of having a meaning that must necessarily be stated, or the excellence of their essential nature, or a preponderance in terms of meaning will serve as the regulator. Anticipating this, he asks regarding the first alternative: "And what [is the meaning]? (*kaśca*).
The particle *ca* is used for the purpose of joining questions or for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
The second [particle], however, expresses the specific quality of the meaning (*artha*) as being something that must necessarily be stated; this is the sense of the word *tu*.
The inclusion of the word "tu" (but/however) is natural;
for it means: "Of those two"—namely, the words *atha* and *ataḥ—what is that necessary meaning [of *atha*] by which its primacy is established?"
He raises the second [objection] with the word "how" (*katham*). "Superiority" (*uttamatā*) means excellence by way of its own nature.
The meaning is: "not in any way whatsoever."
Thus, having accepted that the word *katham* has the sense of an inquiry, this term *katham* should also be construed as an inquiry regarding the third alternative;
the words "in meaning" (*arthataḥ*) are to be supplied.
And so, it is the superiority—that is, the preeminence—of those two words, *atha* and *ataḥ*, in terms of their meaning.
The meaning is "how so?

In this regard, it should be understood that regarding the first and third positions, because one observes in common usage among other words both the necessity of stating a further meaning and the presence or absence of such an excess of meaning, there is doubt concerning the words *atha* and *ataḥ*, and thus [the sūtra] is merely a question; however, in the second position, because one does not observe an excess of intrinsic form (*svarūpa*) in other words, it is merely a censure (*ākṣepa*).

In this regard, it should be understood that the syllable *oṃ* is not the subject of questions and so forth because it lacks the status of being a constituent part of the aphorisms (*sūtra*) of all the scriptures; furthermore,

this is established by the Śruti text "it flows away" (*sravati*) and by Smṛti texts such as "of Him desiring to create" (*sisṛkṣoḥ*), which demonstrate that it is primarily the beginning of this specific scripture alone.
"O Brahman, explain this to me so that I may understand it according to reality.
Being thus addressed by Nārada, Brahmā, the most excellent one, replied:
"'This' refers to the regulating principle which has become the subject of your inquiry; [I shall explain] 'it according to reality.'"
"Tell me, as it truly is, so that I may understand it; tell it to me."
"Brūhi" means "thus addressed by Nārada";
"pṛṣṭaḥ" means questioned; "ākṣiptaḥ" means challenged; "sattamaḥ" means the best among the living beings; "brahmā" [is the one so addressed].
The meaning is that he replied.
Regarding the phrase "immediately following" (*ānantarya*) and "likewise for the sake of auspiciousness" (*maṅgalārthe tathaiva ca*):

since the introduction of the inquiry (*jijñāsādhikāra*) must necessarily be stated, it follows that its immediate succession—which establishes the causal relationship—and the cause of the inquiry itself, as well as the reason for its necessity, must also necessarily be stated; therefore, those two [terms] have that purpose.

Intending the resolution that it refers to the first application (*prathamaprayoga*), he demonstrates the necessity of stating the meaning of the words *atha* and *ataḥ* with the phrase "in the sense of immediate succession" (*ānantarye*).
Furthermore, the two particles *tathā* and *ca* signify mutual conjunction.
The particle *eva* is displaced [from its usual position]; by it, other possible meanings are excluded.
And thus, the word *atha* in the Sūtra signifies "immediacy following a topic."

The meaning is that the word *atha* was "uttered" by the authors of the Sūtras with the intention of denoting only that specific sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*) determined by the context (*adhikāra*), and not as a word signifying auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) and so forth.

Furthermore, he demonstrates the authority for his own position—that the word *atha* signifies auspiciousness—on the grounds that it is employed first because its purpose is necessarily to be performed, stating: "for the sake of auspiciousness."
Thus [it is said].
This is either a locative case used in the sense of the dative, or it is an indeclinable.
The word *artha* denotes purpose.

And thus—the meaning is that the word *atha* was uttered by the authors of the Sūtras for the purpose of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) as well. The sense is that the auspicious act consisting in the utterance of the word *atha*, which contains the syllable *a* denoting Viṣṇu, is accomplished thereby; [the locative case] is used here in the sense of "for the sake of," just as in the expression "in the case of auspiciousness" (*maṅgale*).
The statement "artha" (object/purpose), rather than saying "iti" (thus),
is intended to indicate that difference.
As for the deviation from the sequence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in his own sentence, it was done because the auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) is to be performed first.
The word *atha* is indeed declared to have the sense of a reason (*hetvartha*) by means of the word *ataḥ*.

Having thus demonstrated that the word *atha* has as its defining characteristic the necessity of expressing what must first be stated, he shows the same for the word *ataḥ* as well: "The word *ataḥ*, however, is for the sake of a reason.
Here, the word "however" (*tu*) is used for the purpose of distinction.

The meaning is as follows: "cause" (hetu), "mark" (liṅga), and "reason" (kāraṇa) are that very object and the thing to be expressed; thus, it has been "proclaimed by the authors of the Sūtras" with respect to that subject, by virtue of being its designator.

However, in the *Gurvarthadīpikā*, it is stated: "In the phrase 'in the sense of cause' (*hetvarthe*), the reference is primarily to the abstract state (bhāva-pradhāna), following the subsequent sentence: 'stating its causality' (*taddhetutvaṃ vadan*) with respect to his own statement and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
That [explanation] is fruitless;
we shall explain it accordingly.

By not stating "in the cause" (*hetau*) and instead employing the word "meaning" (*artha*), according to the maxim that "the addition of a word implies an addition of meaning," it serves to state the meanings of both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*): namely, that "cause" is the meaning of the base, while "the state of being a cause" is the meaning of the suffix.

Alternatively, since the word *artha* is heard in both places, it should be understood that it is to be supplied (*anuṣañjanīya*) in the preceding case as well; thus, one should consider that only its referent (*tadartha*) differs. Or, it may mean "by the grace of the Supreme Brahman, Viṣṇu."
In this context, he states another necessary meaning for the word *ataḥ* with the words "of the other" (*parasya*).
The word *vā* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*).
For it has been stated in the *Prameyadīpa*: "The word *vā* has the sense of *ca* (and)."
For it has been stated in the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇayaṭīkā*: "Regarding the phrase ‘whether [there is] difference or the differentiated,’ the word ‘or’ (*vā*) has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Likewise, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, regarding the passage “in deep sleep or in liberation,” it is said: “the word ‘or’ has the sense of conjunction.”
By this [explanation], the word "ataḥ" (from this) is derived from the base "a-", ending in the suffix -tasil; its etymological meaning (prakṛtyartha) is Viṣṇu.
The word "prasādāt" (by grace) is a statement of what has already been established; it is meant to express that [grace] is the cause, as the meaning of the suffix.
The word "parasya" (of the Supreme) is used for the purpose of excluding others.
By using the term "Supreme Brahman," he indicates the scriptural authority: "‘A’ is Brahman" (Ai. Ā. 2.3.8.7).
To explain the word "Brahman" as it occurs therein, he states "of Viṣṇu" by way of restating "of the Supreme Brahman."
The ellipsis [to be supplied] after "prasādāt" (from grace) is that the effect, consisting of the desire to know that [Brahman] and so forth, [arises].
The word "ataḥ" (therefore) is also connected with the sense of the word "bhavet" (it would be).
As for how the result, which is the primary meaning of the stem of the word "ataḥ," serves as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the necessity of performing the desire to know:

It is not so for the clarity regarding that object; rather, the separate mention is made with the intention that [the clarity] connects as a cause for the desire to know what is to be done (*kartavyajijñāsā*), for knowledge and liberation (*jñāna-mokṣa*), and for the study and so forth which constitute the meaning of the word *atha*.
Although this meaning could indeed be obtained by the phrase "in the sense of a cause" (*hetvarthe*) alone, [it is stated separately].
This is because the word *hetu* has both the meanings of "logical mark" (*liṅga*) and "cause" (*kāraṇa*);
nevertheless, there is no fault here, as this [term] is used for the sake of being understood by means of a word derived from a non-universal base (*asarvanāma-prakṛtika*).
For he (the Self) is indeed proclaimed to be the impeller of all mental modifications (*manovṛtti*).

[Objection: But for the sake of inquiry (*jijñāsā*) and so forth, what is the need for the grace of the Lord (*bhagavatprasāda*), by virtue of which this [grace] would become a necessarily explicable matter? To this, he says: "For that" (*sa hi*).
"For" (*hi*) means because; "that" (*saḥ*) refers to the grace of Viṣṇu—that is, Viṣṇu being pleased—which is "the impeller of all mental modifications."
For all qualified aspirants, that which is "proclaimed" by authoritative persons as the impeller of the mental function toward the complete Viṣṇu in every respect is the cause of its inclination;
the desire to know (jijñāsā) as well is precisely this inclination of the mental function, whether directly or through the means of valid cognition.
For it is stated in the *Sudhā* commentary: “The desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is also that very same [desire].

Thus, it should also be explained that He is the impeller and the accomplisher of all mental modifications (*manovṛtti*), their various subdivisions—including those comprised by the word ‘and so forth’ (*ādi*) in the *Ṭīkā* such as knowledge, study, and the like—as well as liberation and other goals achievable through mental modification.
Therefore, the word ‘therefore’ (*ataḥ*) may also have that as its referent; this is the connection with what precedes.
From Viṣṇu, who desired to create, two things first emerged: the syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha*. Therefore, these two are the first [terms] according to their sequence.

Now, one might ask: since the performance of auspicious rites and so forth can occur even through other words—such as the expression "then there is auspiciousness" (*maṅgalaṃ tataḥ*)—why is this [the use of *oṃ* and *atha*] restricted to such employment?

Since the question has been raised as to what the resolution is, [the author] states their "superiority in essential nature" (*svarūpādhikya*) as an answer to the query "How is there superiority? with the words "of one desiring to create" (*sisṛkṣoḥ*), intending to show that the initial employment of the words *atha* and *ataḥ* is not merely because their meaning must necessarily be stated, but also because of their superior essential nature.
In the case of the conjunction of words, the first *ca* [particle] is used;
in the case of the conjunction of causes, the second. The phrase "the best of its own form" (*svarūpottama*) is the remainder [of the definition].
The word "therefore" (tasmāt) is repeated [from the previous verse]. And thus, because [the Lord], desiring to create (*sisṛkṣoḥ*), that is, wishing to emit [the world], [is] "supreme" (*paramāt*).
From Viṣṇu, the Supreme of All;
from His mouth, first—
prior to the production of any other sound of its own class— the syllable Oṃ and the word atha emerged, having burst through the throat.
They have emerged;
therefore, they are supreme by their very nature; and because they are supreme by their very nature, they are "the first."
The construction is that "these two are to be employed first.

Here, it should be understood that even though the syllable *Oṃ* is not the subject of the [immediate] objection, its excellence in terms of its own nature is stated with the intention of showing its primary and secondary status within the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā* system alone, following what is to be said later in the words, "all these."
Now, one might object that it is contradictory for two things to have the same kind of primacy; therefore, it is said, "in succession" (*kramāt*).
This means "by way of the sequence of beginning, middle, and end.
In that regard, the syllable *oṃ* possesses primary primacy.
It should be understood that because the word *atha* occurs second, it is primary.
Furthermore, the third [word] is cited as expressing its causality (*taddhetutvam*).
Having explained the identity and the additional nature of the word *atha* together with the syllable *oṃ*, he now states the same for the word *ataḥ* by using the term "that" (*tat*).
The phrase "stating its being the cause" is a restatement of the expression "in the sense of a cause."

And that [word "ataḥ"] is stated as the third [member] for the purpose of enjoining [the suffixes] such as *tṛtīyā* by way of making known the word-referentiality (*śabdaparatva*) of the term "ataḥ" which presents the subject (*uddeśya*); otherwise, there would be an inconsistency in the context of stating the addition of its own form (*svarūpa*).
Although, following the preceding statement (*purovāda*), it could easily be said that "[it] expresses its being the cause of that"; [nevertheless, the present formulation is intended as explained].

Nevertheless, in the view that the word *hetu* signifies the logical mark (*liṅga*), its essential nature is explained; whereas in the view that it signifies the cause (*kāraṇa*), its effect and the meaning of the suffix *-tas* are demonstrated by the phrase "stating its causality" (*taddhetutvaṃ vadan*).
Here, the word *ataḥ* recurs more than once.
Among them, one is devoted to Śiva,
another to Hara, and another to Viṣṇu.

In this context, the word *api*, which has the sense of conjunction, is connected with the word *ataḥ* (which follows the word *śabda*), while *ca* is used in the sense of *yataḥ* (because). "The third [case] has been illustrated."
Thus there is a repetition of these two;
the term "the first two" is to be supplied by transposing the word order.
The word "third" (tṛtīya) has the abstract state as its primary meaning, and there is a shift in case endings;
thus, it is not only the syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha*.
However, by stating "taddhetutvam" (the state of being the cause of that),

which expresses through the suffix -tas the causality of Viṣṇu— who is denoted by the form "prasanna" (gracious)— in relation to that inquiry and so forth, [the author] indicates, by the very nature of the base word, the mark (liṅga) consisting in the fact that such inquiry and so forth are causes of liberation;
thus [he says] "ataḥ" (therefore).

The word *ataḥ* also has as its base both pronouns and non-pronouns; since it is "cited" (*udāhṛtaḥ*)— that is, uttered— as the third [case-form] of Viṣṇu, namely as "third" (*tṛtīyaḥ*), therefore it too is the "supreme by its own nature" (*svarūpottama*).
