Since this is so, the construction is as follows: for that very reason, the word *atha* is also cited first by way of being the third [term].

And thus, even though the auspicious word (*maṅgala-śabda*) expresses auspiciousness, it does not have its meaning already covered by that [word], because its specific nature is not stated there; furthermore, unlike the two words *atha* and *ataḥ*, it does not state the subject matter (*adhikāra*) and the purpose (*prayojana*), and these two must necessarily be required for the indication of the subject matter and the purpose.

For this very reason, although the word "etc. (ādi) in the phrase "of the utterance of auspiciousness, etc. (*maṅgaloktyādeḥ*) in the *Ṭīkā* indicates—by means of the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*)—the cause, immediate succession, the correlative, and the topic (*adhikāra*), it is not appropriate to include it in the opening sūtra; the point is that it does not state any additional nature (*svarūpa*) for that [auspiciousness]. The letter *A*, which is the soul of all speech, denotes the Supreme Brahman.
The first use of the words *atha* and *ataḥ* is not only because their meaning must necessarily be stated, nor merely because of the superiority of their own forms;
rather, it is also on account of the meaning of their constituent parts (*avayavārtha*).
With the intention that it is for this reason as well that they are used first, he provides an answer to the third question—"How?"—by means of another perspective, stating: "The letter *a*."
The word "of those two" (tayoḥ) is understood to carry over.
And thus: the letter *a* is related to the words "atha" and "ataḥ," because it is the soul of all speech.
"Therefore, the letter 'A' expresses all the qualities of Lord Viṣṇu.
According to this direction from the *Aitareya-bhāṣya*, [the syllable 'Om'] denotes that fullness which is the meaning of all speech;
hence, it denotes the Supreme Brahman, because the Supreme Brahman is precisely that whose attribute is the fullness of all qualities.
The intended meaning is that this is because there is no difference between the property (*dharma*) and the possessor of the property (*dharmī*).
Likewise, they are said to consist of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and to be the ordainers of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and stability (*sthiti*);
thus, for those two, [the term] "likewise" (*tathā*) [applies].

The two phonemes *ta* and *tha* are "of the nature of breath" (*aprāṇātmaka*); [this is] like [the expression] "breath" (*prāṇau*) [being used for] "that which consists of the humors" (*doṣātmakaḥ doṣaḥ*).
The two qualifiers are to be construed with each [phoneme] individually.

The word *prāṇa* denotes both Vāyu and Viṣṇu; as in the expression “from the Great One, the Four-faced [Brahmā],” it refers to both the presiding deity (*abhimānin*) and the object of that presiding (*abhimanyamāna*). Likewise, [it is said]: “This world is indeed the first *Mahānāmī*.”
Thus, there is the designation of identity between the denoted and the denoter through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
The word "consisting of" (*ātmaka*) is used to indicate that this [identity] is well-established.
By the phrase "as stated," he asserts the authoritative validity of both being the denoted and having the conceit of being the denoter.
The alteration of the sequence, however, has been made in accordance with the order of the groups (vargas) and for the sake of brevity in pronunciation.
And he states that its denotation of the Supreme Self is by way of its qualities, saying "pervasion" (vyāpti); the word "of it" (tasya) is to be supplied as the remainder.
And thus—the meaning is that these two express the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the abiding (*sthiti*) of that Supreme Brahman denoted by the letter *A*.
This should be applied to those two in this sequence:
here, the meaning of the letter *A* is the pervasion of the qualities (*guṇavyāpti*).
The meaning of the letter *ta* is the pervasion of space and time, whereas the meaning of the letter *tha* is abiding without change; thus, the difference in their meanings should be understood.
However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, it is stated: "The letters *ta* and *tha* signify that [the two] have attained the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)."
Thus, accepting this variant reading, it has been explained that [the two words] refer to Viṣṇu— who is of the nature of breath and the leader of breath— as the denoter [of the term].

Although such an explanation of the meaning of the individual parts is not appropriate for the word *ataḥ*, which enters into the sūtra as a pronoun (*sarvanāma*), it is indeed appropriate for the word *parasya*, which is not derived from a pronoun.

By this very [statement], superiority in meaning has already been expressed. Nevertheless, since the superiority in meaning of the word *atha* has not yet been explicitly stated, there is no fault in this [verse] being an expression of a distinct, superior meaning that does not enter into the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha)—namely, the phonemes contained within that [word] and the phonemes contained within the word *ataḥ*, which is not derived from a pronominal base (*asarvanāmaprakṛtika*). And for this reason, all these [phonemes] are considered by the wise to be those which should be pronounced first.
"Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "And therefore (ataśca).
Here, the particle *ca* serves both to emphasize (*avadhāraṇa*) and to connect (*samuccaya*).
In this context, regarding the words *atha* and *ataḥ*, it signifies a connection (*samuccaya*).
It should be understood that the restrictive particle (*eva*) in the phrase "but in the case of the syllable *oṃ*" is intended to mean "precisely because of its superiority by nature.
Furthermore, the word "all" (*sarve*) is an elaboration of the word "these" (*ete*),
meaning "the words *om* and *atha*."
The word "ataḥ" (from this) is connected by repetition to both "pūrvam" (before) and "kramāt" (in sequence), meaning "at the beginning of this treatise" and "in due order," respectively.
The word "uccāryāḥ" means "approved by" (sammatā) "satām," that is, by virtuous people;
or alternatively, [it may mean] "of the virtuous" (satām).
The meaning is "in the first sūtra" among the principal Brahma-sūtras.

Nor does this contradict the *Sudhā*, which states, "because all the authors of the Sūtras have employed [the term] in exactly this way," for that statement refers exclusively to the words *atha* and *ataḥ*.

For this very reason, having previously stated "these two," all the authors of the Sūtras have declared it to be exactly thus; the meaning is that they did so at the very beginning, without adopting any other sequence.
The words "by the author of the Sūtra" are to be supplied after the word *atha*.
"Now, having thus understood in truth the power of the two words *atha* and *ataḥ*, those of great wisdom employ them at the very beginning of their sūtras.
Thus [the author] concludes the answer to the question "What is the purpose here? with the word "atha."
The word *tu* (but/then) is used for emphasis and distinction.

"In this way" (*evam*) means by the manner already described; "vigor" (*vīrya*) refers to the majesty consisting of the excellence of its essential nature and so forth; "having understood" (*ājñāya*).
Having understood in reality that, in all the sūtras as well as in the treatises on inquiry and so forth,
it is precisely those two words "atha" and "ataḥ" that occur at the beginning, and no other.
"From the very beginning they employ"; the meaning is that they perform the application.
"Those of great wisdom."
By this, the author of the Sūtra precludes the [objection] that there is an incapacity for knowing the reality of the self-nature of words.
The particle *eva* (only) serves to exclude the syllable *oṃ* from the intended meaning of the Sūtra and all other treatises.
For this very reason, he says: "And therefore."
Thus, although all three [words] are under discussion, the words "atha" and "ataḥ" alone are mentioned in order to indicate their distinction from the word "oṃ".
For this very reason, regarding the scope of the words "atha" and "ataḥ," there are references to "all the sūtras" in the introduction and "in the sūtras" in the conclusion.
Thus it is stated in all the sūtras;
however, regarding the syllable *oṃ*, there is no such mention.
Furthermore, although the word *atha* is recited together with *oṃ*, it is not universal [in its application].
Because of the contradiction between the introduction and the conclusion;
the word "iti" (thus) is connected with the word "uktam" (stated).
Furthermore, the qualification has been stated in the *Bhāgavata-tantra*:
It has been stated that the word *atha* expresses immediate succession to a qualification (*adhikāra*).
To the question, "What is that qualification for the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), and of how many kinds is it?", he says: "The qualification."
The word "ca" (and) serves not only as a heading (*adhikāra*), but also as a conjunction (*samuccaya*) indicating that its classification is also stated in the work known as the *Bhāgavata-tantra*.

Here, although the heading is mentioned as the authoritative source, there is no inconsistency, because by virtue of being its qualification, the heading is also described in terms of the nature of the deity (*devatva*) and so forth.
Indeed, the qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*) are of three kinds: inferior, middling, and superior.
To the question "How so?", he recites that statement: "'Manda'.
The word *tvaḥ* is connected with each [term].
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe*).
The word *hi* indicates well-known fact. Regarding the phrase "Among them, those who are considered the highest class among men":

"among them" means among the three types; "those who are considered the highest class among men" refers to those who, within the category of those qualified for liberation, are the practitioners of the lowest capacity (*manda-adhikārī*). This should be understood as the relationship between the subject and the predicate.
The same applies hereafter.
By the word "group" (*gaṇa*), the three types of superior humans mentioned in the system of human goals (*puruṣārtha*) are included.
Among them, the middling are the sages (*ṛṣi*), the gandharvas, and the gods; these are considered the superior ones.
"Ṛṣis and Gandharvas" [is] "ṛṣigandharvāḥ. The plural number is used in the sense of "et cetera" (ādi). By this, the Pitṛs and others are included.
"In that regard" means "among the three.
Furthermore, regarding the word "therein," it refers to "such as these."
Because this is of the nature of a conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*), there is no tautology.
Alternatively, the meaning of the first occurrence of the word "therein" (*tatra*) is "in the inquiry into Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsāyām*).
Therefore, it has been stated in the *Ṭīkā*: "In the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*).
And likewise: "In that regard"—that is, in the inquiry into Brahman—there are three kinds of qualified persons (*adhikārin*).

The word "therein" (*tatra*) is to be construed with the three types [of persons]. Alternatively, according to the method of the *Tattvodyota-ṭīkā*, which states that "the word *iti* is connected to each [term], and for this very reason there is a double mention," the expression "therein" at the beginning and the end is intended to indicate the inclusion (*anuṣaṅga*) within the middle [category].
"In that regard" means among those qualified persons.
Thus, there is a distinction based on caste (*jāti*), as well as another based on qualities (*guṇa*). "Thus" means in this manner; "based on caste" refers to the distinction produced by birth.
The meaning is that "non-difference" (abheda)— whether caused by the commonality of form such as being human, a seer, or a deity, or caused by birth in a particular family—
is to be understood as either an internal sub-division or a mutual absence (anyonyābhāva).
By this, what is intended is the general definition of one who is fit for liberation and qualified for Vedic knowledge of Brahman.
But is this definition not over-extensive (*ativyāpta*), as it would include virtuous Śūdras and others?

Nor should it be argued that there is no over-extension because virtuous Śūdras and others possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) in another body, such as that of a Brāhmaṇa; for even if the qualification exists in another body, it is of no use for activity in the present life.
However, because of the certainty of its absence in one who has not yet produced the immediate realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) of Brahman, delimited by that very body;
and thus, because this qualification is common to, or prevalent among, virtuous *śūdras* and others;
and for this very reason it is absent in this body; and for this very reason it is unobservable.

Furthermore, since this fitness for liberation (*mokṣayogyatva*) exists even in the state [prior to realization] as its very nature (*svarūpa*), and because its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is therefore constant, there is no lack of eligibility; thus, he states the nature of the eligible person by means of another method, beginning with "tathā" (likewise).
This word has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

The word "another" means that there is a distinction based on birth; "preceded by qualities" means there is a distinction caused by auspicious dharmas such as devotion (*bhakti*), study, and so forth—this is the remainder [of the sense].
One who is devoted to the Supreme Viṣṇu and who possesses the study [of the scriptures]...
The lowest is one endowed with tranquility (*śama*) and so forth; the middling is thus described.
He demonstrates that very point by saying "the devoted one" (*bhaktimān*).
Although there was a plural designation in the previous summary statement, here it says "the person" (*naraḥ*).
Thus, the use of the singular number in such expressions is not untenable,
because this is a definitional statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*);

for even though the enumerative statement (*uddeśavākya*) uses the plural form "the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāni*), the definition is stated in the singular as "the instrument of valid knowledge is the means of valid cognition" (*pramākaraṇaṃ pramāṇam*).

In this regard: "Indeed, even in the Veda, there is no qualification for one who is not a Vaiṣṇava, nor for one devoid of devotion to the guru, nor for one lacking tranquility and the other [virtues]."

Because of this statement, devotion to Viṣṇu and qualities such as tranquility (śama), even when acquired through study, are mentioned separately for the purpose of excluding the study and tranquility performed by those who are non-devotees and lack qualification.
By the word "etc. (ādi), those [qualities] mentioned in the passage "tranquil, self-controlled" are included.
Furthermore, the two words beginning with "api" (even/also) indicate both essence and constant conjunction.
The word "iti" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
The word "naraḥ" (the person) refers to the devotee;
it is to be connected with everything [that follows].
And likewise: "The authoritative teachers have declared that the man who possesses devotion to the Supreme Viṣṇu and is engaged in Vedic study is the lowest qualified candidate (adhikārī).
The man who is endowed with tranquility (śama) and other virtues is said to be the middling one.
[From] the Brahma down to a blade of grass, [the world] is essence-less and impermanent.

That which is "from Brahmā down to a blade of grass," meaning the entire multitude of living beings starting from the four-faced Brahmā and ending with the smallest of grass-insects, is "insubstantial," that is,
not the most excellent of all.

The term *asārapada* refers to that which is "impermanent" (*anityaka*), meaning inferior to the supreme state of liberation; it is called "impermanent" because, although the bodies of living beings such as Brahmā and others perish, there is no destruction of their essential nature (*svarūpa*), hence the suffix *kap*.
However, the Supreme Brahman is the essence of all things and is eternal in every respect.

"Having realized," meaning being possessed of knowledge—that is, possessing the discrimination between essential and non-essential matters, and between eternal and non-eternal entities—one who has thereby "arisen to dispassion"; and who, from that discrimination, has become dispassionate; having Viṣṇu’s feet as his sole refuge.
"Having understood thus, [he becomes] one in whom dispassion has arisen," or alternatively:
"He whose sole refuge is the foot of Viṣṇu"— that is,
he who possesses the knowledge that the foot of Viṣṇu alone is his primary, principal refuge and shelter.
"He would be the most excellent candidate, having renounced all ritual actions. Thus [it is said].
And he who "possesses all actions renounced"—
meaning he who possesses all desireless action that has been renounced, or surrendered to the Blessed Lord—
"he" is the "supreme qualified person."
The construction is "it may be so.

Here, what is called *saṃnyāsa* (renunciation) is the relinquishing of actions into the Lord— after having understood that the Lord performs all actions and that all actions are of the nature of worship of the Lord— of those actions which were previously known through delusion to have the individual soul (*jīva*) as their agent.
As stated in the *Gītābhāṣya*: "The Blessed Lord alone performs all actions," and so forth;
by this [it is meant] "one who possesses devotion toward the supreme Viṣṇu," and "one who has renounced all actions."

By this final statement, it is meant that all those qualifications of the three types of eligible persons (adhikārins) mentioned together constitute the general definition (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) of an eligible person.

Nor should it be argued that [this definition] is impossible because each of the three combined is absent in any one of them individually, or that if they were present [in each], it would result in over-extension (ativyāpti) of the definition— characterized by being neither too narrow nor too broad— to the middle and other classes.

Because there is no impossibility [in this system], as everything exists everywhere through the attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*) of the preceding [quality] into the subsequent statement and of the subsequent [quality] into the preceding statement; for it is accepted that all [qualities] exist in all [stages].

If it is objected: "But since the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the unmixed [qualities] have not been stated, a threefold division is untenable,"—to this some reply by relying on the meaning of the *Ṭīkā* passage, "because of the lack of abundance (*aprācuryeṇa*) of those qualities stated for the subsequent [stages]," interpreting it as follows:
"The qualities stated for the two subsequent types of practitioners (*adhikārin*) are present only in a state of non-abundance in the first, inferior [stage]."

They state that there is no confusion [of categories] as follows: possessing the three qualities of study and so forth in the highest degree constitutes superiority; possessing the three qualities of study and so forth in a greater degree constitutes mediocrity; and possessing the three qualities of study and so forth exclusively, while being distinct from both of those [other degrees], constitutes inferiority.

They state another interpretation: that those very qualities which are summarized later and carried forward from the previous sections—namely, those mentioned in the subsequent passages such as "one who is devoted to them" (*bhaktimān*) and so forth—are present there in greater abundance compared to the qualities as they appear in their original, literal form in the root text.

However, in the *Candrikā*, relying on the meaning of the commentary (*ṭīkā*) that [the qualities] are present in greater abundance in each subsequent stage than in each preceding one, it is understood that among the co-occurring qualities—such as the attainment of study, tranquility, self-restraint, and exclusive refuge at the feet of Viṣṇu—he who possesses abundant study is intended.
But those for whom the others are not abundant—he is the inferior (adhamā) qualified person (adhikārī).
He who possesses abundant study, tranquility (śama), and so forth, while possessing only one other [quality] in a non-abundant measure—he is the middling (madhyama).

He who possesses abundant refuge in the feet of Viṣṇu alone and so forth, while the others are not abundant—he is the superior (uttama) qualified person. Thus, it has been stated that the threefold classification is established based on the distinction of these characteristics.
The word "iti" is connected with the phrase "in the Bhāgavata-tantra.
[And: "For one who possesses merely the study [of the Veda], [there is no entitlement], because there is no distinction. (1)
And so it is stated further on (Brahma Sūtra 3.4.12–13):
"Study [of the Veda] constitutes eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman.

Why is this so? Because in the cited authority, the phrase "in the knowledge of Brahman" is not explicitly mentioned; and furthermore, why is there a threefold eligibility therein? To answer this, he says: "study."
The word *mātra* signifies entirety.
Thus, the meaning of the sūtra is that one who has studied all the Vedas according to his capacity possesses the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
There is another sūtra: "Not so, because there is no distinction."

The meaning is that the eligibility of gods and others for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) does not arise from their general commonality without distinction, but rather solely from their relative gradation (tāratamya).
"Above"; in the third [chapter], eligibility will be explained according to this gradation.
The word "Sūtrakṛt" (the author of the Sūtras) is to be understood as the subject [of the statement].

The sense is that since it is stated in the Smṛti intended by him— namely, in the passage "in the knowledge of Brahman declared in the Veda"— that the threefold eligibility for knowledge is also mentioned in the scriptural citation provided there, the aforementioned doubt is thereby resolved.
The word *ca* (and) [is used] in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* [in the sense of] "one who possesses Vedic study.
“Having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, one should see the Self in oneself alone” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.23).

Regarding the fact that tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities also constitute the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), he cites the Kaṇva recension of the Śruti (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.23): "Tranquil" (*śānta*).
Here, by the mention of "in the Self" (*ātmani*), the person of middling qualification is indicated.
"Because of the Vedic scripture (Caturvedaśikhā): 'The Ṛṣis have internal illumination,' and 'The Gandharvas are the intermediate [beings]';"
And because it is so stated:
"Peaceful" means one whose intellect is fixed on the Blessed Lord, as the *Bhāgavata* says: "Peace is the fixing of the intellect on Me.
In the *Tattvapradīpa*, however, it is concluded that peace (*śama*) is defined as not wavering from the Vaiṣṇava doctrine.
‘Self-controlled’ (dāntaḥ) means one whose intoxication has been restrained, that is to say, one who possesses restraint over the senses;
‘withdrawn’ (uparataḥ) means one who has ceased the desire for sense objects.
According to the *Bṛhadbhāṣya*: "Contented" (*santuṣṭaḥ*) means one who is satisfied with Viṣṇu, who resides near [him] within one's own heart.

"Patient" (*titikṣuḥ*) means one who endures the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat. "Concentrated" (*samāhitaḥ*) means one whose mental fluctuations are directed toward Hari, who is equal and the abode of bliss.

Alternatively, according to the statement: "Knowledge that accords with the object as it is is called 'equal' (sama) because of its correspondence [to the object]," he is so described because his placement—the mental modification in the form of knowledge and desire—is equal, meaning it is placed in accordance with reality;
thus, the meaning is that he possesses knowledge and so forth that correspond to the actual state of things.
The word "having become" (bhūtvā) is connected with each [term];
"is established" (sthitam) is the ellipsis.
And thus—previously, "in this way" (evam);
By the word "vic," one who knows Hari as the liberator from saṃsāra and possesses tranquility and other qualities is indicated; having become such,
[he perceives] the "Self" situated within the "self," that is, in his own heart.
"One should see" (paśyet) the Supreme Self means one should know it;
"one should investigate" (vicārayet) is the figurative meaning.

By the statement, "Having become tranquil and so forth, one should know the Self," it is stated that tranquility and the rest serve the purpose of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), just as the initiation (*upanayana*) serves the purpose of Vedic study.

Although the reading of the scripture is *paśyati* ("he sees"), nevertheless, according to the principle stated in the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā*: "In some places the reading is *sa tathā cakāra*; this should be understood as belonging to a similar recensional branch (*śākhāntara*), and the same applies elsewhere," there is no fault here either—whether this [reading] belongs to a similar branch or is a restatement of the meaning of *paśyati*.
"Having examined the worlds acquired through action, let the brāhmaṇa attain detachment,
for there is nothing uncreated to be gained by what is created.

By this, [the author] cites the Atharvaṇa Śruti (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12) to show that even the dispassion born from the constant discrimination between the essential and the non-essential qualifies one specifically for the knowledge of Brahman.
—‘Having examined’; thus:
a ‘Brāhmaṇa’ is one fit for the knowledge of Brahman; ‘worlds’ refers to those other than the world of Viṣṇu, which are ‘accumulated by karma’.
Having "examined"— that is, having discerned— that those [results] accomplished through rites performed for desire are indeed insubstantial and impermanent,
one should "attain," or reach, "dispassion"— that is, detachment— from both the ritual action for desire and its fruit, by means of that discernment.
Since liberation consists in the manifestation of the bliss of one’s own true nature (*svarūpānanda*), it is "uncreated" (*akṛta*)—
being the nature of the eternal human goal—
and therefore "does not exist" through "what is created" (*kṛtena*), that is, through ritual action determined to have a fruit characterized by origination and destruction.
But [this is attained] through knowledge:
for the sake of realizing that, one should approach a teacher alone,
carrying fuel in his hand, a learned scholar (śrotriya) who is firmly established in Brahman.
"Therefore" (*tat*); for that reason, "he" (*saḥ*),
being dispassionate toward anything other than liberation, [approaches the teacher] "for the sake of higher knowledge" (*vijñānārtham*).
For the sake of Brahmā’s specific knowledge:
‘*samitpāṇiḥ*’ means one whose hands (*pāṇī*) are joined with fuel-sticks (*samidh*).
Alternatively: he whose hands are joined together in the *sampuṭa* gesture or held open (*ariktaka*) at the time of approaching;
being thus constituted, he should "approach" a teacher who is a *śrotriya*—one who has studied the Veda—and who is firmly established in Brahman.
The meaning is "he should approach.
Alternatively, the word *eva* (only) is to be construed as "the guru alone and not another.
However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, it says: "accumulated by karma."

Having "examined"— that is, having scrutinized from all sides— the perishable palaces and other such things of this world accumulated through action, and likewise having examined as perishable even the worlds such as heaven, which are the opposite of those (being accumulated through actions for the sake of the next world),
one should attain "non-despair" toward them. [One should seek] the "Uncreated" Lord, who is dear to the wise, "through what is created."
It is not attained by mere action;
therefore,
for the sake of knowing Him— Viṣṇu, who is dear to the wise— one should approach a guru.
Thus the meaning of the scriptural passage has been stated.
Here too, by the word "vijñāna" (higher knowledge) and the term "supreme brāhmaṇa," the person of the highest qualification is indicated;
for it is said: "The knowledge of that [Brahman] belonging to the gods and others is celebrated as vijñāna."

This is because of the statement in the *Gītā-bhāṣya*: "Thus it is said," and because of the statement regarding its purport: "Those who have not attained the vision of Brahman have not truly reached the state of the gods."
"He is attainable by him alone whom He chooses"—
this [text] shows through the Kaṭha Śruti that devotion to Viṣṇu is also a qualification for the knowledge of Brahman. This is likewise recited in the Atharvaṇa.
"This Self," whose nature is will, is Viṣṇu; "whom" He chooses as a qualified candidate.
One grasps [it] "by means of that"; it is "attainable," meaning it is to be reached;
he becomes pleased with that.
To him, this Self reveals its own body.
And therefore,
"this" [refers] to "him," the qualified seeker.
The meaning is that the serene Self reveals its own body; that is, it makes its form manifest.

In this context, according to the method stated in the *Prameyadīpa*—"and it is well known that he chooses [him] as a devotee alone"—the word "chooses" (*vṛṇute*) indicates the state of being a devotee (*bhaktatva*).
However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, [it is explained as]: "whomever he... [and so forth].
The Supreme Self "chooses" [the devotee] by granting devotion; He accepts him "by that" [devotion],
since he alone is the one to be attained as His "own body."
It has been stated that [the scripture] "makes manifest.

Regarding this, the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (6.23) provides scriptural authority for the meaning that: "He whose supreme devotion is directed toward the Lord, and who regards the Guru as he does the Lord—that devotion is most excellent when directed toward Viṣṇu, and even when directed toward others, it is useful for the knowledge of Brahman in accordance with their fitness."
He demonstrates this with the words "of whom. The word "just as" is repeated; the word "so" is used in the sense of conjunction.
The division is twofold: "those who have been taught" and "those who have not been taught";
the ellipsis [to be supplied] is "by the teacher through the former Vedas and so forth."
And thus: "of whom," i.e., of the qualified seeker, "in the god"— that is, in Viṣṇu, who possesses qualities such as luminosity— "supreme."
"Devotion is the highest of all;
it exists thus toward the Divine."
Just as there is devotion toward the other gods, such as Brahmā and others, according to their respective fitness,
so too is it toward the Guru.
And there is appropriate devotion toward others and those superior to oneself.

"To him these meanings, when declared, indeed become manifest"— here, the genitive case *tasya* (of him) is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) with respect to the "Great-Souled One" (*mahātmanaḥ*).
These "meanings" were previously "not told" by that qualified person, or by the Veda and so forth, or by the Guru; they have now been "spoken."
The meaning is that those which consist of the nature of the higher and lower principles are "revealed," that is, they are known.
Alternatively, these "objects" (arthāḥ) consist of tranquility (śama) and so forth.
"In that, the qualities are manifested"; the meaning is that they are perceived.
Alternatively, [the word] "unspoken" (akathitāḥ).
"Objects not taught by the gurus are indeed revealed to him through the power of his devotion."
The meaning is "well-known.
In the reading "prakāśante" (they shine/are manifested),
the meaning is that they become the agents of the measurement conducive to the knowledge produced by that [agent].
And from such scriptural passages as these;
and in the Vyomasaṃhitā:
"And from such scriptural passages as these."
The phrase "thus his qualification has been stated" is to be construed with this [statement]; not only by the aforementioned scriptural citations, but also by [the Lord's own words]:
"But by undivided devotion alone, O Arjuna, am I thus to be known and seen" (Bhagavad Gītā 11.54).
The meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and from such Smṛtis as... is that [the qualification for knowledge of Brahman arises] from these sources as well.

Now, an objection is raised: if the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman belongs only to those who have studied the Vedas, then others than the three castes (the *trivarṇa*), lacking such study, would not possess that qualification.
And then, fearing that there would be an absence of liberation for them due to the absence of knowledge of Brahman, he refutes this doubt by means of a Smṛti text, stating: "And in the Vyomasaṃhitā.
The phrase "preceded by the removal of the aforementioned doubt" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The word "and" (ca) serves to connect with the preceding text.
"For him too, the qualification has been stated"—
this is the syntactical connection.
"Even those of the lowest caste who are devotees are qualified for the knowledge of the Name."
Those who are born among the final states of existence are "antyajas," meaning those excluded from the three [upper] varṇas.

And this meaning was indicated by the *Nyāyadīpikā* in its commentary on the passage beginning with "There is no fire, nor sacrifice, for a Śūdra," by way of an introduction to the statement: "The study of the names of Viṣṇu is for the antyas."

The term "devotees" (bhaktāḥ) is a statement explaining the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman as described by the phrase "possessing devotion" (bhaktimān). The same applies to the term "of those possessing devotion" (bhaktimatām); both of these are connected [to the preceding context].

And thus— it is not only the members of the three [higher] castes; rather, even those who are outcastes (antyaja), excluded from the three castes, such as Śūdras and others down to the Pulkasas, although they lack the qualification for Vedic knowledge of Brahman, nevertheless, because they are devotees, they possess the qualification for knowledge through the Name— that is, they possess the qualification for the knowledge of Viṣṇu’s Name and its study.
Therefore, the construction is that they are qualified for the knowledge of Brahman and liberation.
[However,] women, Śūdras, and those who are mere nominal Brahmins (brahmabandhu) have no qualification for the knowledge of Tantra.

He states something other than what was previously mentioned regarding certain individuals among the three varṇas who are ineligible for the Vedas, as well as certain devoted persons among the low-born (antyajas): "Of women, śūdras, and those who are mere nominal brahmins."
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "women, Śūdras, and those who are mere Brahmins in name (brahmabandhus)—that is, those who only appear to be Brāhmaṇas.
"Tantra" refers to the Pañcarātra and similar systems; "in the knowledge of that" means in the knowledge of the meaning taught therein.
The phrase "in the case of the knowledge of Brahman arising from the Tantras" is what is intended.
The word "api" (even/also) is to be connected here as well;
thus, the sense is that for them, liberation is possible even by means of that [Tantric] knowledge.
However, when only a single portion has been taught and not preceded by the full text,
there is no entitlement to the entire tantra,
but rather only to that single portion.
In that regard as well, it is "not preceded by a formal treatise";
there is no qualification for undertaking a treatise on its own authority, but rather [it concerns] "what has been stated by another."
He says "only" (*eva*)—namely, "one part"—to show that when another person has stated it for the sake of another, [the meaning] has indeed already been commenced.
The word *tu* is used for emphasis. He states what is excluded by that [emphasis] with the words "but not" (*na tu*).
The meaning is that those [women and others] have no entitlement to the tantric texts and so forth that are accessible merely by virtue of being women and the like.
By this, it is stated that one should not even undertake the teaching of Purāṇas and other such texts solely on the basis of being a woman, a Śūdra, or the like.
The second occurrence of the word "tu" (but/however) is to be construed with what follows.
For those of the three castes who possess perfect devotion toward Hari as declared in the Vedas.
In that case, who has the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman arising from the Vedas?
If it is by process of elimination the members of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), does everyone among them have the qualification?
No; rather, it belongs to only some of them, as he says: "of the members of the three higher castes."

Regarding the phrase "from the Vedic injunction": it means that while the knowledge of Brahman arising from the Vedas is for those of the three castes who possess perfect devotion to Hari alone, the eligibility for [the knowledge of] Brahman other than what was mentioned belongs to the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
The word "but" (tu) indicates that the qualification [of eligibility] applies not only to the knowledge of names and so forth, but also to this meaning.
They say: "There is indeed eligibility for the highest women in the Vedic [rites]:
'May I surpass my co-wife; make my husband mine alone.'"

Since it is observed that even women have the qualification for the Vedas in passages such as *maṃ-pra-16-2*, how can it be said that they lack qualification? To this, he states an exception to what was previously mentioned with the words "they say" (*āhuḥ*).
The particle *tu* has the sense of *api* (even).
The word "Vedic" (*vaidike*) is to be repeated by modification [of its case ending].
The term "uttamastrīṇām" (of the highest women) is a *tatpuruṣa* and a *karmadhāraya* compound.

Thus, it is not only that there is eligibility for the knowledge of the names and so forth of the highest female deities; rather, the followers of the Veda declare that there is eligibility even for Vedic knowledge—that is, even for the Brahma-vidyā arising from the Vedas.
The interpretation:
"Just as Urvaśī and Yamī, as well as Śacī and others."
He illustrates them with the word "yathā" (as follows):
"eva" (thus) refers to Yamī, the dark-complexioned wife of Yama.
The word "ca" (and) is used for the inclusion of what has already been mentioned;
by the word "ādi" (etcetera), Umā, Rati, and so forth are included.
The second "ca" is for the inclusion of what has not been mentioned.
By this, the divine women born into human and other lineages are included.
The word "tathā" (likewise) is used either for comparison or for the conjunction of what has been stated.
"Others" refers to those different from the excellent women, namely the wives of debtors.
Or "inferior" (*avarāḥ*), because the wives of the middle *ṛṣis* are inferior in comparison to the women of the highest gods;
thus it is stated in the *Vyomasaṃhitā*.
Thus, the word *iti* is connected [to the preceding].
Since there is no liberation without the grace of Nārāyaṇa, and there is no excessive grace without knowledge.
Therefore, the inquiry into Brahman must be undertaken.

Thus, having explained the word *atha* both briefly and in detail by way of elucidating the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and the subject matter (*adhikāra*) through the presentation of the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), [the author] shows that the word "to be performed" (*kartavyā*) in the aphorism serves to present that which is referred to by the word *ataḥ*, and that words such as "since" (*yataḥ*) must be supplied; he states: "The word *ataḥ* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*)."
He clarifies the meaning stated in brief with the words "yataḥ" (since).
The word "yataḥ" is repeated.

Thus: since liberation is universally desired by everyone in the sense that "may there be happiness for me alone, and may there not be even the slightest suffering," [it follows that the self exists].
The correct [attainment] does not exist without the grace of Nārāyaṇa;
and that grace is "excessive" (*atyartha*),
meaning it is an exceeding grace, which in turn does not exist without direct realization (*aparokṣajñāna*).
And that [attainment] does not occur without the desire to know Brahman; therefore, the meaning is: "Hence, the inquiry into Brahman must be undertaken.
For it has been stated in the *Tattvapradīpa* under the section on the Word (Śabdādhikaraṇa): "Because liberation alone is the supreme human goal, and because of that..."

"Because [the goal] is unobtainable without Viṣṇu’s grace, and because that [grace], being of the highest degree, is to be accomplished through immediate intuition (aparokṣajñāna), and because that immediate intuition depends upon the desire to know (jijñāsā), it has been stated that Viṣṇu alone is the object of inquiry.
This statement also implies that the connection with the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) is intended.
Therefore, because it is referred to by the word "ataḥ" (hence), there is no inconsistency; by this [sūtra], it is shown that since liberation does not occur without the grace of Nārāyaṇa,
but rather through grace alone, [the Lord is the cause].
Furthermore, there is no excessive clarity without knowledge;
rather, it occurs through knowledge alone, and there is no knowledge without the desire to know (jijñāsā).

However, by way of demonstrating the logical connection that "therefore, the inquiry into Brahman (brahmajijñāsā) must be undertaken" precisely because of [the Lord's] grace, it is explained that the meaning of the word *ataḥ* is the reason: "because [grace] is the means for the knowledge which is itself the means for the attainment of liberation.

Furthermore, by interpreting the construction as "since there is neither knowledge nor inquiry without the grace of Nārāyaṇa, but rather [they arise] through grace alone," another meaning of the word *ataḥ* is also explained.
By the employment of the word *nārāyaṇa*, the word *brahman* from the Sūtra is also explained. Where there is no other occasion, the term is established there.
Or rather, "one should speak"—this is the conduct of the virtuous; however, that [conduct] does not apply when there is an opportunity [to act].
(Thus, in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā:

But why is it that only the word "not to be performed" (*akartavyā*) is supplied as an ellipsis in the Sūtra? For since the supplying of ellipses (*adhyāhāra*) is unrestricted, [one might supply] "it is not to be performed" (*na kartavyā*).
To the objection, "Why should there not be an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the very sentence [itself]? he says: "'yatra'.
Here, the words "yatra" and "tatra" are repeated, as is the word "vākya."
The word "vinīya" (having disciplined) is supplied [from the context].
And thus, in the subordinate clause, that which is the "word" (*pada*)— namely, "yatra" (wherein)— [is connected].
"Without" means "elsewhere"; "lack of occasion" means "in another sense"; "impossibility" means "therein."
In a sentence, that very word alone becomes "established"— that is, attained— and nothing else; such is the rule for the wise.

In a sentence where there is scope for another meaning—that is, when it is capable of being construed with a different sense—that very word would not necessarily be firmly established [in its primary sense].

Likewise, in a case where a subordinate sentence within a great sentence (mahāvākya) has no other occasion for application except therein, that very sentence is firmly established within that great sentence; whereas in a great sentence where there is scope [for the subordinate sentence], that subordinate sentence would not necessarily be firmly established. This is the meaning.

Since it is stated in the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā* that "in whatever sentence a word or a sentence is required, there is no occasion for another elsewhere," the word "to be performed" (*kartavyā*) must necessarily be supplied;
thus, its connection is with the remainder of the sentence.

The sense is that if one were to supply the word "not to be done" (*na kartavyā*), then the meaning of the words *atha* and *ataḥ*, as well as the introduction (*adhikāra*) and so forth, would be incompatible with the context here. Thus, according to the method stated in the *Candrikā*, [the word is] "where" (*yatra*).
Thus, this verse beginning with "from which [it arises]" (*ayataḥ*) should also be explained as being intended to justify the supply of such words as "from which.
"Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here in this world."
"No other path is found for this journey" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12).
As it has been said: "From which [comes] the grace of Nārāyaṇa."
By this, [it is shown that] serenity (*prasāda*) is the means to liberation. To the question "Why is that so?", he cites scripture as authority therein with the word "him" (*tam*).
"Here" (*iha*) refers to the class of qualified aspirants; "him" (*tam*) refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) designated by the term "the Person" (*puruṣa*) under discussion; "thus" (*evam*)—

In this world, the "wise one"— who, by means of the method described through the "thousand-headed" [hymn] and so forth, knows [the Self] directly through the mediation of indirect knowledge— becomes "immortal" at the end.
One becomes liberated;
for there is no other path than the knowledge of the Supreme Person for the sake of liberation, which consists in attaining that state through the way leading to Nārāyaṇa.
"No means exists";
the meaning is that there is none.
Here, the fact that knowledge is the direct means to liberation is made known.

However, the fact that *prasāda* (divine grace) is the means to liberation is established solely through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*), according to the method explained in the *Ṭīkā-sudhā*— namely, that liberation does not occur by mere immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) indicated by the word "Vidvat," in the absence of *prasāda*— and not directly.
It should be understood that this is an indication of the effect (*naimittika*) by its cause (*nimitta*).
"For I am exceedingly dear to the knower, and he is dear to Me" (Bhagavad Gītā 7.17);
"and there is no [attainment] without knowledge."

Since it has been stated that [devotion] is the means for the grace of immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), from what source does this follow? To address this, he cites the traditional authority of the *Gītā*: "For I am exceedingly dear" (*priyo hi*). "I am exceedingly (*atyantam*) dear" to the man of knowledge (*jñānin*).
The word "hi" means "well-known.
The meaning is: "And he too, the possessor of immediate knowledge, is dear to me.
This is a statement of Kṛṣṇa.
“He is to be attained by him alone whom He chooses” (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.23);
“The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6).
That grace is the means to liberation is understood not merely from the explicit statement, but also by implication.
However, with the intention that this is also supported by Śruti, he cites the Kaṭha-Śruti there, beginning with "yaṃ" (this).
Here, the particle *eva* (only/itself) is to be construed out of its normal position;
thus, it refers to "eṣaḥ" (this one).
The Supreme Self— this one— being gracious in the form of His own will, "chooses" this qualified aspirant.
The meaning is that he is "attainable" (labhyaḥ)— that is, reachable— by that [knowledge] alone, and not by any other action.

For this very reason, in the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇayaṭīkā*, the meaning of the entire passage was stated in accordance with the present context as follows: "This is the Supreme Self who is to be attained only by him whom He chooses and upon whom He is gracious. How so? Because He reveals His own body—that is, He makes it manifest—and consequently, He reveals His own body, which means He manifests His true nature that had been veiled by ignorance."
Regarding that which was previously stated—that inquiry is the means for attaining immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*)—he cites scripture as the authority for this: "The Self" (*ātma*).
The reading is *vā ara*, with the words separated;
the word *vā* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*).
"'Are'—this is Yājñavalkya's address to Maitreyī.
And thus: 'O Maitreyī,' if immortality is desired, then [one must seek] the 'Self'."
"The Supreme Self is to be seen by you"; the meaning is that He is to be made an object of vision.
To the inquiry "By what means would there be such vision?", he says: "He is to be heard," and so forth.
For the sake of direct realization (*darśana*), one must meditate upon [the Self] (*nididhyāsitavya*).
For that purpose, one must "listen" (*śrotavya*);

that is, by means of the teacher's instruction, one must take as an object through hearing (*śravaṇa*) the grasping of the meaning of the Upaniṣadic sentences, in the form of understanding: "This is the meaning of this sentence."
"Thus it should be reflected upon" (tathā 'mantavyaḥ');
the meaning is that it should be made an object of reflection in the form of an investigation through reasoning (*yukti*).
By this [statement], [the necessity of] the inquiry consisting of hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative cultivation (*nididhyāsana*) [is established].

It is stated that the limbs (*aṅga*), which possess their own specific forms, serve as the means for attaining knowledge; this is established by such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*) as "by the *śruti* and *smṛti*" (*śrutismṛtibhyaḥ*).
The analysis of the compound is "from those which are the Śrutis and Smṛtis.
The syntactical connection is that what was stated in [the passage] beginning with "From whom, Nārāyaṇa" is established by this.
But it is said that the lowest [form of] grace is attained through action, while [the highest] is through hearing and so forth.
Is it not stated: "That action which pleases Hari" (Bhagavad Gītā 18.68) and "He who [teaches] this supreme secret"? (Bhagavad Gītā 18.68).
An objection is raised: since the grace of the Lord can be accomplished even through ritual action (*karman*) and other means, what is the use of knowledge (*jñāna*)?

Furthermore, in the statement "For [the devotee] is dear" (*priyo hi*), there is no exclusion of other means—as there is in passages such as "Knowing him thus" (*tamevaṃ vidvān*) and "He chooses him alone" (*yamevaiṣa vṛṇute*), which teach that grace is the sole means to liberation. To dispel this doubt, he cites a Smṛti text:
"By action" (*karmaṇā*).
That is to say, by means of action that is either desirable, undesirable, or both;
and thus, the "favor" (*prasāda*) which is produced "by action" (*karmaṇā*).
"He is declared to be the lowest" by those who accept authoritative means of knowledge.
Thus,
the clarity that arises through hearing and so forth is considered middling; however, the clarity resulting from the perfection of knowledge is regarded as supreme.
That is the "middling" [type]. It is the "serenity" (*prasāda*) produced by the "perfection of knowledge," that is, by the maturation of direct realization (*aparokṣajñāna*).
"He alone is considered the highest" (*uttamo mataḥ*);
the meaning is that he is measured as being superior.
The double use of the particle *tu*, which serves the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), is for the sake of indicating its connection with all three [verses].
"From the grace of Viṣṇu, the world of heaven is proclaimed.
To the question, "What follows from this if it is so?", he says: "'From the grace' (prasādāt).
The particle *tu* indicates a distinction.

And thus, the meaning is: "From the lower Viṣṇu, through His grace"— that is, from that [Viṣṇu] who is to be attained by means of rites performed for specific desires— the "world of heaven" has been proclaimed as the goal to be realized by the elders.

This [verse] is indicative of the fruits of desire alone, according to the Śruti passage, "Having examined the worlds" (MuU 1.2.12). It should be understood that there is also utility for rites performed for specific desires in liberation, by way of generating dispassion.

Likewise, it should be understood that liberation occurs through the purification of the internal organ and other means, resulting from the lower grace (prasāda) achieved through non-desirous (akāmya) karma.
Nor should it be asked how Duryodhana and others—who were devoid of faith in the Dharma and excessively hateful—attained heaven;
for although it is stated that such attainment does not occur for those who lack the Bhāgavata teachers, it is possible for those who possess them.
As it is said in the *Gītātātparya*:
But by the power of the teachers,
they go swiftly to heaven from there, and then they fall into the blinding darkness.
And others than those do not attain heaven at all.

Thus, by the mention of "the heavenly world" (*svargaloka*), that which was described in that very context as "the wish-born heaven (*sāṅkalpika-svarga*)— the fruit of becoming a *bhūta* and so forth in succession"— which is imagined as a substitute for heaven and attained by those eternal transmigrators who are *rājasarājasa* and *rājasatāmisa*, namely the world of the lords of the Daityas, is not intended here.
However, it is indicated that among the seven worlds, only the heavenly world (svargaloka) is attainable by those characterized by the quality of goodness (sāttvika),
while the intermediate worlds such as Janaloka and others grant liberation only to the most excellent.

Regarding the term "janalokādiḥ," it should be understood that the word "loka" is employed here for the purpose of conveying the world specifically named "jana," by means of abandoning [the specific name] "jana.
In the expression "janalokādiḥ," both a *tatpuruṣa* and a *bahuvrīhi* compound are intended.
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of specification.
And thus, by the grace of Viṣṇu from the "middle" [state], Maharloka— the beginning of Janaloka— or indeed Janaloka, Tapoloka, and so forth, are attained, but not liberation.
The construction is as follows: "the giver of liberation" is proclaimed by the elders to be the highest grace alone,
and not the other two.

And thus, even though the grace of the Lord may be accomplished through ritual action (*karman*) and other means, because that [grace] is not supreme—since only that which is accomplished through knowledge is supreme—and because liberation is not attained even when heaven and the like are achieved by means of that which is not supreme, knowledge is required for the sake of attaining the grace that accomplishes [liberation]; this is the intended meaning.
Nor should one fear a contradiction here with the statement: "By action they go to the three worlds; by knowledge alone, those beyond them."
Because Maharloka is the domain of the unconditioned portion,
whereas this [world] is the domain of the portion subject to return,
it is said that "the worlds are seen through commonality."

Thus, by the force of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) has as its object an immediate [cognition] distinct from that which is capable of having its own reflection as its object— such as the descent of universals (*sāmānya-avatāra*) and so forth— or else because, in the phrase "by hearing and so forth" (*śravaṇādibhiḥ*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes other means; or else, according to the method stated in the *Nyāyāmṛta*, because the words "through the medium of knowledge" (*jñānadvārā*) are to be supplied as a remainder.
Alternatively, there is no contradiction because the particle *eva* has the sense of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). [Objection:
"Hearing, reflection, meditation, and likewise devotion—surely these are required for knowledge in order to attain supreme grace."

Nevertheless, one might raise the objection that since it is said, "One spreads knowledge through action" (*karmaṇā jñānam ātanoti*), knowledge can also arise through ritual action and the like; therefore, the inquiry (*jijñāsā*) need not be undertaken for its sake, as there is no negation of other means in the statement "the Self" (*ātman*). He dispels this doubt by means of the remainder of the present authority with the word: "'Śravaṇam' (hearing)."
Here, the double use of the particle *eva* is for the purpose of making known its connection with every [term].

Furthermore, these [terms] exclude the association of hearing and the other [means] with anything else in the accomplishment of the result, and they also serve to exclude undesired objects such as ritual actions (*karman*), just as in the expression “Nara and Nārāyaṇa alone.”
The word *ca* occurs twice for the purpose of conjunction;
the word *tathā* signifies comparison;
and likewise, *tathaiva ca*.
Or rather, it is a collection of particles (*nipāta*).
The mention of "devotion" (*bhakti*) is either for the sake of a relevant context or for the purpose of an illustration:
"In the attainment of knowledge, the means (*sādhana*) is held to be the primary factor, and nothing else."
And likewise, regarding "the perfection of knowledge":

upon the attainment of direct realization (aparokṣajñāna), just as there is devotion, so too hearing and the other [limbs of yoga] alone are the means, and not anything else such as ritual action; this is the meaning.
What, then, is the status of such statements as "one expands knowledge through action"? To this he says: "The primary";
that is, hearing and so forth are the primary means, while "the other" is accepted as the non-primary.

The construction is as follows: that [the agent is the primary factor] is accepted by those who uphold authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), but it is not the case that other means of proof do not exist at all.
The intention is that the mention of "object" (*karman*) and so forth refers to the domain of secondary means of proof.
And without these, no one has ever attained knowledge from any source whatsoever.
Thus it is stated in the Nāradīya.
To the objection, "Why might it not be the reverse?", he says: "And not" (*na ca*).
The word *ca* has the sense of *api* (also/even).
And thus: "these."
Without hearing and the other [means], no one at all— regardless of their qualification— attains knowledge from any existing source such as ritual action and the like.
Thus, the construction is as follows: even if these [means] such as hearing exist, knowledge does not depart from them without [the removal of] karma and so forth; nor does it [depart] otherwise.

And so, by means of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) that are independent [of other factors], hearing and the rest alone are the primary, direct means (*sākṣāt-sādhana*) for knowledge, whereas karma and the like are indirect means (*pāramparya-sādhana*) due to the absence of those [direct means]. Therefore, there is no reversal [of the relationship between cause and effect]; this is the intended meaning.
"In the *Nāradīya*"; the words "since it is said" (*yata uktaṃ*) are to be supplied.
This connects with the supplemented sentence: "Therefore, what was stated [in the verse] beginning with ‘From whom Nārāyaṇa... is logical."

By the phrase "from whom [comes] Nārāyaṇa," it is explained that the word *brahman* used in the Sūtra— which was employed to dispel the doubt that the inquiry [into Brahman] might be devoid of an object— refers specifically to Nārāyaṇa;
and the word *brahman* applies to Viṣṇu alone.
Now, if it be argued that there is no liberation without the grace of Nārāyaṇa, then one should investigate Him alone, and not "the inquiry into Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsā*);

nor should it be said that the author of the Sūtras intended by the word "Brahman" is specifically Nārāyaṇa, because since the word "Brahman" has many meanings, the specific intention of the author of the Sūtras is difficult to ascertain—to this he says: "Brahman."
The word "mukhya" (primary) is to be supplied as the ellipsis; and the particle "ca" (and) is used in the sense of "also," as in the phrase "the word *brahman* has many meanings."
The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of "because.

Thus, even though the word *brahman* has multiple meanings, since it is primarily applied to Viṣṇu alone, and because between the primary and secondary senses the primary one must be accepted, the construction is as follows: it is understood that He alone is intended by the author of the Sūtras.

Here, by abandoning other words and employing the word "Viṣṇu," and by drawing lines representing the number of the letters *ṇa*, *ṣa*, and *va*—which correspond to the fifth, sixth, and fourth consonants of that word's class—the number of the aphorisms (*sūtras*) is stated to be five hundred and sixty-four. Alternatively:
"By way of place, time, qualities, and also by way of completion..."
This name "Brahman" applies primarily to Viṣṇu and not at all elsewhere.

The term *Viṣṇu* is employed here in order to explain the word *Brahman*—which, as stated in the *Aitareya-bhāṣya*, signifies the threefold perfection consisting of being unlimited by space, time, and qualities.

However, in the *Ṭīkā*, it is noted that by the inclusion of *Viṣṇu* here, [the author] refers to the very commencement of the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā* immediately following the composition of the two successive sūtras: "He is Viṣṇu, for so it is said" (*saviṣṇurāha hi*) and "They call Him Brahman" (*taṃ brahmetyācakṣate*).

Another purpose is stated: because it was commenced by Vyāsa, this [work] indicates that Nārāyaṇa alone is the subject matter as Brahman in the final two sūtras of the immediately preceding *Devatāmīmāṃsā*.

This very point is also stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "And he who was declared at the end of the *Devatāmīmāṃsā* as the supreme among all deities by the statement, 'For Viṣṇu alone is that [Brahman], for so says the Śruti; they call him Brahman,' is [the subject] as Brahman."

"That very [Self] is referred to by the word *brahman* as the subject of inquiry in the Uttara-mīmāṃsā," it is stated with a variation in the reading. "That which the sages perceive within the ocean, in that supreme Imperishable (akṣara), all beings [dwell]."

Since the word *brahman* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) elsewhere as well, and since conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) constitutes the primary mode of signification (*mukhyavṛtti*), one might ask: why is this [word] primary only with respect to Viṣṇu? To this, he says: "Him.
The phrase "And the word *brahman*... and so forth is also to be connected here.
The phrase "co yadyapi" (even though) is used in the sense of "although";
the word "hi" is used in the sense of "since" or "because";
and the words "śrutir āha" (the scripture says) are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
And thus, although the word *brahman* is conventionally established in other senses,
nevertheless, according to the view of the seers (*kavayaḥ*), that very [reality] is the supreme *brahman*, because of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) beginning with "Him whom... and so forth.
The phrase "thus they say" expresses a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) characterized by frequent application;
therefore, the meaning is that the word *brahman* is most primarily (*parama-mukhya*) applied to Viṣṇu alone.
The underlying intention is that while there is a conventional usage among the ignorant (*ajña-rūḍhi*) regarding other things, the usage among the learned (*vidvat-rūḍhi*) is more primary.
Regarding the statement "within the inner ocean":

since He has entered men, cattle, and all beings, both moving and stationary, through the medicinal herbs (*oṣadhī*), there is nothing else more subtle than this; for He is higher than the high, greater than the great.
That which is one, unmanifest, of infinite forms, the ancient universe, beyond darkness.
This has been explained along with the [relevant] statement in the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇayaṭīkā*. For it is said:
"The wise ones [know Him] who is within the ocean";
here, the *avyayībhāva* compound is used in the sense of the locative case, meaning "situated within the ocean. "The wise ones" (*kavayaḥ*)...
The wise "understand" it; they know it only slightly—
that which is "in that Imperishable."

In that which is characterized by the aforementioned qualification of being "unintelligible," and which is established as the indestructible "Supreme," all creatures are dependent. From whom [the Supreme] the progenitor of the world was born, he emitted living beings upon the earth with water.
‘The source of the world’;
‘source’ means the progenitor, the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), Lakṣmī; ‘from whom’ means from which she was produced or born.
Or, it may mean that [the water] became oriented toward creation;
and whatever substance was [present], by means of the "water"— that is, by the karma of living beings or by its own inherent potency— [it was transformed].
Or, by means of the elements indicated by the word "water" (toya),
he "emitted living beings" (*jīvān vyasasarja*)— that is, he created them diversely— upon the "earth," meaning in the worlds such as the earth and so forth.
Having stated this and so forth, [the text continues]: "That alone is the eternal, that they call the truth; that alone is the supreme Brahman of the seers" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 1), and also:
"by means of herbs..."
He entered into men, animals, and all moving and non-moving beings for the sake of impelling them;
[namely,] "all moving and non-moving beings."
Although this [meaning] is already established by the fact that they are limbs of the sacrifice (*yajñāṅga*) and so forth, there is a further statement in order to include specific grains and herbs.
"Therefore" (*ataḥ*): because of that, "higher" (*param*), meaning "exceedingly different" (*atiśayenānyat*).
The reality is "subtler than the subtle," for there is nothing subtler,
and it is that which is "higher than the high."
"Greater than the great" means greater even than that which is of great magnitude;
"that which is one" means the absolute "Unmanifest."
Without his grace, that very *ṛta*— the universe which is beyond the senses, full of darkness,
or situated "beyond" (*parastāt*) due to ignorance of *prakṛti*—
remains [unrealized].
"That" which consists of knowledge of reality as it is, that alone is "truth";
and like action preceded by knowledge, that alone belongs to the "seers."
They say that "supreme" means primary, and "Brahman" means the ultimate reality.
In this context, the reading of the scripture is "tadakṣare" (in that imperishable); however,
where the reading is "yadakṣare" (in which imperishable), one should not supply the word "yasmin" (in which).
The common reading of the scripture is "vyasasarja";
[another version reads] "vyacasarja".
Thus they read in some places as well.
Here, the substitution of *ca* for *sa* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Even in the first alternative, the analysis is *vi ā sasṛje*; therein, the shortening of the vowel in the prefix (*aṅga*) is Vedic due to the frequent application (*bahulagrahaṇa*) [of rules].
The statement of Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya is that just as in the Vedic scripture *indrā varuṇa vām aham*, the vowel following the letter *ṇ* becomes short, so it is here;

the statement in the *Prameyadīpa*, "He emitted (*vyasasarja*), he emitted (*visasarja*), because of the frequentative inclusion (*bahulagrahaṇāt*)," also intends a short vowel. However, some explain the meaning of the *Prameyadīpa* to be that the augment *aṭ* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) is Vedic due to the frequentative inclusion.
This is a different position from that stated by the Noble One (Ārya).
However, in the *Nyāyaratnāvalī*, which is a commentary on the *Tattvanirṇaya* composed by Padmanābha Tīrtha, the text is divided as follows: "vayanti" and then "tadakṣare."
And having recited thus:

"The sages weave that Person who is within the ocean; they desire that Imperishable (akṣara) in which [all things abide]. In that Imperishable, which is devoid of destruction, in the Supreme, the creatures stand supported by Him.

The Source of the world (jagataḥ prasūtī)—Nature (prakṛti), the progenitor of the world—from which, having been produced and manifested, she [the world] exists through water mixed with the other [elements]."

In the *Tattvamañjarī* composed by Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitārya, it is also stated: "She emitted (*vyasasarja*) the living beings (*jīvān*) as possessing bodies. By this single syntactical connection, the meaning is expressed as follows: "That alone is the *ṛta* because it is the object of the intended purport; that alone is the *satya* because its form is uncontradicted; that alone is the supreme Brahman desired by the seers (*kavīnām*). [And further: "'In that Imperishable' (*tadakṣare*)."

Having recited this, the meaning is stated through the following syntactic connection (*anvaya*): "In whatever syllable they utter and understand, in that very syllable all creatures exist; from which [syllable] they were born, having attained a state dependent on another, Śrī [the Goddess of Fortune] scattered forth living beings upon the earth—upon the primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—by means of water and ritual action (*karman*).
Furthermore, it is said: "That alone is *ṛta*, eternally of one kind, the Truth (*satya*), the Good, and full of qualities."
For thus says the Śruti:
"May Viṣṇu grant us that" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 3.16).
Because of this statement, it is indeed Viṣṇu who is spoken of there.
But one might ask: in the sentence "That very [thing]," how is Viṣṇu determined by the word "that"?

If it is argued that [the Lord] is Viṣṇu because of the mark of residing in the ocean—no, for that [mark] can somehow exist even in Rudra and others; therefore, he says "that is not so," meaning [the Lord is Viṣṇu] solely on account of the unambiguous scriptural statement regarding Viṣṇu.
"By this declaration, Viṣṇu alone [is meant]."
In that context,
the meaning is that it is determined [by the scripture] that "that very [thing]" is expressed by the word *tat* in the Vedic text.
The word *hi* indicates well-known tradition (*prasiddhi*).
Here, by taking the partial expression "that [is] for us" (*tan naḥ*), [it refers to the full mantra]: "We know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva."
"May that Viṣṇu impel us"—thus the entire sentence is taken [as the mantra].
The two forms ending in the dative case are used in the sense of the accusative.
And so, because we "know" Nārāyaṇa;
We know that because we meditate upon— that is, we contemplate— that Vāsudeva;
therefore, "for us" (tat naḥ).
The meaning of the Vedic text is: "May Viṣṇu impel us toward that auspicious [state]."
If that [Brahman] were not obtained from the other word,
then— given that Viṣṇu alone is spoken of as the Brahman here because the word "Viṣṇu" is heard in the subsequent sentence—
the mantra would have been "tanno rudraḥ" (may Rudra protect us).
Since the word "other" (*itara*) is heard in such passages, it might follow that even Rudra and others possess the status of the primary Brahman; therefore, he says: "And not [so].
The word "and" (*ca*) is used in a conjunctive sense.
And thus, [the reason is] "because of the word 'other'."
The meaning is: "There is no attainment of that status of being the primary Brahman for Rudra and others by virtue of words denoting Rudra and so forth.

[Objection: Since there are no names in the world that do not apply to him when he has manifested, everything belongs to Anṛta (the Unreal). To this, the author provides a supplementary reason—namely, that the words which establish that status have their primary application (*mukhyatva*) to Viṣṇu alone—and intending to avoid the charge of that [reason] being unestablished, he cites scripture regarding Viṣṇu’s being primarily denotable by all names.

Regarding the word "nāmāni," there is in some places a reading with the ablative case ending, "śruteḥ. In the reading with the nominative case ending, the words "yato 'taḥ" (from which, therefore) are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
This [word] connects with the phrase "and not" (*na ca*).
"Since" (*yat*); because of the "unreal" (*anṛtasya*)—that is, of the world or universe other than Viṣṇu, which is distinct from *ṛta*—"all" (*sarvam*).
The ground for the application of names appeared;
it came into being. Therefore, because it possesses the grounds for the application [of names], it is "Viśvā"; "Viśvāni" means all names.
"In the world" means in the universe beginning with Rudra; "preeminently" means primarily by way of denotation; "they do not exist"—this is the meaning.
They declare that he into whom all names enter is indeed Viṣṇu, the supreme.
If one asks, "In what then are those [names] primary?", he says: "Names.
The word *vai* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
The term *paramam* is a qualifying attribute containing a reason (*hetugarbha*).
And thus, "all names" enter "Him" primarily by way of denotation.
The meaning is that the wise call Him "Viṣṇu," who is the supreme, whose ground for application (pravṛttinimitta) is not delimited by space or time.
But in the Tattvapradīpa it says: "In the world, there are no names whatsoever that exist on all sides [other than those belonging to Him]."
Primarily they do not exist; primarily there are no worldly designations [for them],
because from which Person everything— the birth, dissolution, and so forth of the world other than Viṣṇu— manifested as "unreality" (anṛta).
And that which they enter from all sides as names by virtue of its denotative power— him, indeed, they call Viṣṇu.

The meaning "they speak the highest" has been stated. In this view, there is a repetition of the word *yat* (which); the second and following three quarters of the verse serve as the provision of the reason (*hetu*).
In both cases, the word *viṣṇu* has its position shifted [in the compound].
Thus says the Bhāllaveya Śruti:
"He who is the giver of names to the gods—to him alone do all other worlds go for this inquiry."
By the word "only" (*eva*), other [deities] do not possess the status of being the "all-name" (*sarvanāmatā*).

Now, one might object: "Just as the status of Brahman stated here for Viṣṇu is established because his status as the 'all-name' is proven by another scriptural passage (*śruti*), why should the status of Brahman stated here not likewise belong to Rudra and others, since they too are denoted by words such as 'Viṣṇu'? To this, he says: "'Yaḥ' (He who...)."
"From the word *eva* in the phrase *ity eva*"; that is, from the word *eva* in the sentence *iti*, there follows the "universality" (*sarvanāmatā*) of "others," namely Rudra and the rest.
The meaning is that [the Supreme Being] is not denotable by all words such as "Viṣṇu" and so forth.

Immediately after the phrase "by all pronouns," the remainder of the sentence is: "Since this is so, therefore in passages such as 'May Viṣṇu protect us' (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 3.16), there is no application to others; for this very reason, they do not possess the nature of Brahman."
"The Blessed One alone is the bearer of the name among the gods," such as Brahmā and others—
this term "bearer of the name" (*nāmadhāḥ*) is used like the word *viśvapā* (the protector of all)— meaning he is the one who holds that name, and not others; [ask] him "that question."
"To the questioner," [he says];
"other," meaning other "worlds" (*bhuvanā*), that is, worlds (*lokāḥ*); "they come together."
The meaning of the Vedic scripture is that they go toward liberation and [dissolution] at the time of cosmic dissolution.
For the passage, "In the navel of the Unborn, one [thing] was placed; upon it all the worlds rested," is indeed a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of Viṣṇu.

But here too, why [is it] Viṣṇu by virtue of the word *yat*? Because of the force of the scriptural statement "Viśvakarman," this context known as a *sūkta* refers to Viśvakarman and others; therefore, it is appropriate that the word *yat* occurring therein also refers to them. To this he says: "'of the Unborn' (*ajasya*); 'for' (*hi*); because (*yasmāt*)"—in this sentence, there is the "mark of Viṣṇu" (*liṅga*).

The uncommon attribute known as "having a lotus-navel" (padmanābhatva) has been heard [in scripture]; therefore, the syntactical connection is that Viṣṇu alone is denoted by the word "yat. The sense is that although, as a general rule, direct statement (śruti) is stronger than indicative mark (liṅga), the sublation of the scriptural mention of Viśvakarman—which has room for another interpretation—is possible by means of the indicative mark which admits of no other application. As for the meaning of the direct statement: "of the Unborn" (ajasya).
In the navel of the unborn Puruṣa, one thing has been "placed," that is, manifested—
that in which all worlds reside.
"All fourteen worlds stood over [it]";
that is, they were presided over.
And no other meaning is appropriate without a well-known meaning.
To the question, "Could there not be something other than the lotus placed upon the navel? he says: "And not" (*na ca*).
The word *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction. Without the object known as the lotus, which is well-known for its location on Viṣṇu’s navel, no other object is tenable.
The meaning is that [the opponent's position] is sublated by common consensus (*prasiddhi*).
To the objection—"Why might even the mark (*liṅga*) of having a lotus-navel (*padmanābha*) not belong to another, just as in the case of the *Viśvakarman-śruti*?"—he says "And not" (*na ca*).
Apart from the Blessed Lord, who is the well-known referent for the term "having a lotus-navel," there is no "other."

The meaning is that [the term] *padmanābha* (Lotus-navelled) is not tenable because it is contradicted by common usage (*prasiddhi*). [However, it is established otherwise: "In the navel of the Unborn (*aja*), from whose navel arose the lotus—the essence of the world—according to the Veda.
It is not merely by the force of common usage that this lotus and Hari as *padmanābha* are determined; rather, it is so understood from what is stated in the Śruti.

However, because of the scriptural statement "of the unborn" (ajasya), which conveys both [meanings], and because it is supported by Smṛti, he says "of the unborn" (ajasya). The grammatical connection is with the words "because of the scriptural statement" (iti śruteḥ).
And likewise, from the Vedic text "in the navel of the Unborn," [there arises] the "lotus" (*puṣkara*), which is the essence of the worlds and the support of the worlds.
It is known that "the lotus came into being.
Homage to that Viṣṇu, the creator of the world, who is the manifestation of the universe both individually and collectively.
And thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"To Him, the one for whom the manifestations of the universe are both distributed and unified.

The manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) of the universe—that is, the world—consist of the eightfold acts beginning with creation; they are "distributed" (*vyasta*), meaning expanded, within the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth, and "unified" (*samasta*), meaning condensed, within the insentient (*jaḍa*) and so forth.
