He by whom these manifestations of the universe are thus possessed is "the one for whom the manifestations of the universe are both distributed and unified," and to Him [is the salutation].
The meaning is: "Salutation to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the world.

However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, it is explained in two ways: "He by whom the manifold manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) of the entire universe have been distributed [in various forms] is the one whose universal manifestations are both distributed and unified"; or alternatively, "He by whom the universal manifestations, whether distributed or unified, [are manifested]"—thus it is interpreted in two ways.
In that regard, the second [point] has been explained in the commentary (*ṭīkā*).
Since there is an absence of words denoting Viṣṇu in the first half [of the verse], the example is given from the second half:
"Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa."
And the word "iti" (thus), by means of a displaced word order, is connected with the supplied word "uktaṃ" (it has been said).
Since this is so, therefore [the term] "of the unborn" (*ajasya*).
Thus, it has been stated that [the word] "padma" refers specifically to the lotus,
and the ellipsis of the sentence is that "Padmanābha" refers specifically to Hari; the meaning is also that this is not merely because of a contradiction with common usage.
In the scriptural passage known as the *samākhyā*, it says: "Beyond heaven, beyond this earth" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 10.82.5).

With the thought, "If even a mere indicative mark (*liṅga*) that leaves no room for another interpretation can sublate a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), then what need is there to mention one accompanied by a name (*samākhyā*)?", he says: "'para'.
This [word] recurs, and the phrase beginning with "Viṣṇu alone" is also connected here.

And likewise, because in the *Viśvakarmasūkta* there is the statement and expression, "That which is beyond heaven, beyond this earth, beyond the gods and the asuras," and because that same [expression]— namely, "beyond heaven"—
exists in the form of a Vedic revelation (*śruti*) in the *Āmbhṛṇīsūkta*, for this reason also, it is Viṣṇu alone.
The meaning is that he is proclaimed in the *Viśvakarman-sūkta*.
Having stated: "Whomever I desire, him I make fierce; him I make a Brahmin, him a seer (*ṛṣi*), him one of excellent wisdom" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 10.125.5).

Now, one might ask: even when there is an explicit scriptural mention (*samākhyā-śruti*), why should Viṣṇu be the one denoted? To this he says: "Him" (*yam*). After the word "iti," the words "by the sentence" (*vākyena*) are to be supplied as a supplement in both places.
Furthermore, the entire phrase "beyond heaven" (*paro divā*) should also be construed with this [word "him"].

In this context, the phrase "in the scriptural mention of the name" (*samākhyā-śrutau*) constitutes a single compound word. Thus, because there is the scriptural mention of the name "beyond heaven" (*paro divā*), that which is accompanied by the name "death" (*meti*) is the "name-accompanied" (*samākhyā*). As the Mādhyandina Śruti states: "Prakṛti is indeed both the same and the different. (*prakṛtir vāva samāsamā*)

Since the Śruti states that they are equal in status (*samāmatva*), by the maxim of "a part [standing for] the whole" (*nāmaikadeśe*), the word *samā* refers to Lakṣmī who is the subject under discussion. Having stated through the passage beginning with "Him" (*yam*) that Brahmā and the others are under her control, she [the Śruti] then refers to Viṣṇu—whom it was previously said is "beyond heaven" (*paro divā*)—by means of the passage: "My womb is within the waters, in the ocean."
He states this by way of being its own cause and by way of residing within the ocean;
therefore, the meaning is that Viṣṇu alone is what is established by the scriptural designation (*samākhyā-śruti*).
By the word "having stated," any doubt as to whether the cause of Lakṣmī might be one of the others, such as Brahmā, is dispelled.
In the Śruti passage beginning with "divā," the third case ending is used in the sense of the fifth;
thus, it means "divaḥ" (from day).
"Of Fortune"; "Supreme";
"this."
And "higher" than this ground means "supreme";
[the terms] "by the gods," "to the gods," and "by the asuras."
And he is "higher than the Asuras," meaning superior;
what more need be said— he is higher than even "whatever exists," that is, higher than all of it.
That Viṣṇu is beyond heaven and earth; but I, by my greatness— that is, by my majesty—
am "as great as this."
She became limited;
the meaning of the Vedic text is that "I am only this much," meaning she is of the magnitude described and not greater than that in her majesty.
By the word "I" (*aham*), which has been attained [as a term], Lakṣmī is denoted.
Because the daughter of Ambhr̥ṇa (Āmbhṛṇī), who is the originator of this hymn, is the very form of Lakṣmī;
and thus—she [says]: "Whichever" living being "I" deem worthy of the state of Rudra, "the fierce one" (ugram)...
"I desire" (kāmaye) means I wish to make "Rudra"; "that and that" (taṃ tam) I make or perform as "Ugra."
Thus, for each respective station, he appointed whoever was suitable— be it a "Brahmā," an "Ṛṣi," or one of "excellent intelligence."
The meaning is: "I desire to make him wise, and I act accordingly.
The full sense of this statement will be explained in the section on Brahmasūtra 2.2.37, *Patyurasāmañjasyāt*.
"He says, 'My womb is within the waters, in the ocean' (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.125.7).
Nevertheless, he says 'my' to indicate that even so, there is no independence on my part."
‘Mine’; ‘the womb’ means the cause; ‘in the ocean, in the waters’; he ‘stands within the waters.
The purpose of the accentuation (kampa-svara) is to indicate his preeminence.
With the intention that his own name should not be grasped, he did not say "Nārāyaṇa" directly, but spoke thus in order to make its meaning understood:
"Ugra" is Rudra;
within the ocean is Nārāyaṇa.
Because this meaning is well-known and has been indicated [in other texts], one might ask:

"Could Rudra not be the one staying in the ocean here, given the statement in the *Mahābhārata*, 'to him who was performing austerities in the water'? Furthermore, there would be no contradiction with the statement regarding his subordination to Ramā (Lakṣmī).
Since it might be possible to understand "Ugra" as referring to some cruel being, he says: "'Ugra'.
The word "might be" (bhavet) is to be supplied in both instances.
Thus, in this context, that which is called "Ugra" must indeed be Rudra.
Thus, the meaning of the two propositions is that Nārāyaṇa alone must be situated within the ocean;
regarding this, he states the reason: "because it is well-known."
Regarding the phrase "of this meaning":
because the meaning consisting in Rudra’s being denotable by the word *ugra* is well-known,
as it is established in lexicons such as [the Amarakośa], which states, “*Ugraḥ kapardī*,” and so forth.
The meaning is that by the word *ugra*, the cruelty (*kraurya*) denoted by the word *rudra* is made known;
the intention is that *rudra*, *raudra*, and *ugra* have a single identical meaning.
Likewise, the meaning consisting in "lying upon the ocean" is well-known from the *Viṣṇusahasranāma*, such as in the passage: "He who lies upon the great ocean, the Ender (*antaka*)."

The meaning is: "And because, by the statement that [the Lord] resides within the ocean, the meaning of the word *Nārāyaṇa*—which consists in being the substratum of the waters denoted by the word *nārāḥ*, as established by the Smṛti text ‘āpo nārāḥ’ (the waters are *nārāḥ*)—is also indicated.
Furthermore, when there is no contradiction, a well-known meaning is not to be abandoned.

And by the logic already stated, the Śrutis declare this very [Brahman]. Now, one might ask: even though there is the existence of common consensus and so forth, what is the obstacle to abandoning that and accepting something else? To this he says: "Nor... Here, the word "of the object" (arthasya) is to be connected by transposition.
And thus, since this meaning is "well-known," it is therefore "not abandoned" when there is "no contradiction," that is,
in the absence of contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The meaning is that it is not abandoned; for a well-established meaning can only be set aside by contradiction, otherwise it would result in the subversion of common consensus— this is the intended sense.
“They arise from space alone” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.1);
“Born indeed from Viṣṇu” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 9.97.5);
“O Indra, there is none superior to you” (Ṛgveda 4.30.1).
In such cases, the term "non-contradiction" (*avirodha*) is used to exclude the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Now, one might object that the absence of contradiction is unestablished;

for if Rudra were here denoted by the word "Ugra" as being dependent on Lakṣmī, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as "Rudra is superior to the universe. Therefore, it is appropriate to set that aside here. To this, he says:
—It is said:
"The *nyāya* is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through the etymological derivation based on the instrument (*karaṇa*-vyutpatti).
And thus: 'From whom [proceed] all names' (Bhāllaveya Śruti)."
By means of the aforementioned scriptures (*āgama*),
by the inference based on the possession of origins and causes of activity as stated therein,
and by the proofs to be mentioned later— such as "in the Veda and in the Rāmāyaṇa"— which are conjoined by the word "and" (*ca*), [the term] "the Śrutis" [is established].
Scriptural passages such as "Rudra is superior to the universe" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 10.3) either rely on the fact that words like "Rudra" denote Viṣṇu,
or they rely on the meaning "He from whom the universe— meaning Vāyu— is superior," thus [referring to] "this very one."
The phrase "they speak of Viṣṇu alone" is understood to mean that they make him known as the primary subject through the intended purport (*tātparya*).
Therefore, the construction is that there is no contradiction with such scriptural passages as "He who transcends the universe."

Regarding the fact that the Vedas refer exclusively to Viṣṇu, he cites the Smṛti in the verse beginning with "In the Veda": "In the Veda, in the Rāmāyaṇa, in the Purāṇa, and likewise in the Mahābhārata, [it is] Viṣṇu alone.
Thus, it is Viṣṇu who is the subject in the Veda, the Rāmāyaṇa, the Purāṇa, and the Mahābhārata.
Viṣṇu is celebrated everywhere—in the beginning, in the end, and in the middle; what need is there for more? He is "celebrated everywhere," that is, in all scriptures.
It is explained that even among those [stages], it does not occur in parts,
but rather at the beginning, middle, and end.

The meaning is that [the Supreme Reality] is primarily propounded throughout all three sections beginning with *karma*, in the introductions and conclusions, and in the intermediate sub-sections— in every sentence, every word, and every syllable.
Thus it is stated in the *Harivaṃśa*.
There is no contradiction with other texts;

for the statement "the Veda" is intended to indicate that [the *Bhāgavata*] exists within all three parts of the *Harivaṃśa* known as the *Khila*, the *Akhila*, and the *Pārijāta*. Therefore, it says "in the *Harivaṃśas*."
This is the plural form.
Following the word "in the Harivaṃśas," the phrase "that which was said" is to be understood as the ellipsis;
therefore, there is no contradiction with that.
The connection [of the words] is either "by the logic stated in the *Harivaṃśa*" or "in the manner described.
Now, it may be argued that the absence of contradiction with the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is unestablished;
for even in the absence of contradiction with the Śruti, there exists contradiction with scriptures such as the *Pāśupata*.

In that regard, since it has been stated that Rudra and the others possess the state of being supreme over all and the state of being the cause of all, he says: "And not" (*na ca*). The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "also": not only is there an absence of contradiction with the Śruti, but there is also no contradiction with other [authorities].
The phrase "of this matter" (asyārthasya) is understood [from the preceding context].
"I shall quickly create this delusion which will bewilder people."

Why is this so? With the intention of supplying the reason—that it was created for the purpose of deluding them—he refutes its lack of proof by citing an authoritative example, beginning with the word "This" (*eṣa*).
This is a statement of Viṣṇu addressed to Rudra.
That by which people are deluded is called "delusion" (*moha*).
"Naṭana" means deception or delusion;

"moha" refers to the cause of delusion, which consists of the beginningless latencies of karma— this is the meaning even according to the *Tattvapradīpikā*, and it is also supported by the statement of Vyāsatīrtha that it is a "delusive scripture."
Nor should it be suspected that Viṣṇu is not the teacher of this "treatise against delusion," for the Śruti declares: "Of the unborn, whose mind is not crooked" (KaU 5.1).

Thus, the contradiction with the *Tattvapradīpa* is to be suspected only in reference to the wicked; for "acting" (*naṭanam*) consists in concealing an existing form and displaying a non-existent form,
while "deceiving" (*vañcanam*) consists in speaking what is non-existent.
From the use of the first-person verb "I create" (*sṛjāmi*), the agent is understood as "I.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to conjoin the action and the agent.
Furthermore, the relative pronoun *yat*, heard later, is the qualifier for the demonstrative pronoun *etat*, which was heard earlier.
According to the statement in the *Nyāyadīpa*, the construction is: "He who is this [one].
Thus, I am the one who says, "I create delusion," meaning "I do it. And "he who is this" delusion "will delude people."
It will bring about ignorance, false knowledge, and so forth.
And you, O Rudra, O mighty-armed one, compose treatises of delusion;
for "arm" (*bāhu*) refers to a limb of a living being, [and you shall be] a tormentor of others.
"One whose arms are great" is *mahābāhu*; the vocative form of that is "O *mahābāho*," meaning "O *Rudra*, you who possess limbs capable of afflicting enemies."
"And you, create delusion and cause delusive scriptures to be made; that is, compose them."
And have it performed by Dadhīci and others.
O "Mahābhuja"—
O great devourer, or O Greatly Crooked one— O Rudra!
"O mighty-armed one, show those things that are unreal and false"—
the word "in them" (teṣu) is the ellipsis; thus,
it refers to "in those delusive scriptures," [those things] which are "unreal."
"Those things which do not exist anywhere—such as the search for the base of the *liṅga* and so forth—are 'unreal' (*avitathya*);

those which exist in a different locus, or which reside in Viṣṇu or Vāyu, yet are spoken of as residing in Rudra and others, such as [his] being the supreme of all, his absolute independence, and his swallowing of poison—'show' (*darśayasva*) these;
that is to say, establish them."
"Make yourself manifest and make me unmanifest";
in the phrase "me as myself," the word "me" (mām) is in the accusative case as the object of the purpose.
The two words "ca" (and) signify mutual conjunction;
and thus, in the worlds, with reference to "ātmānam," that is, one's own self, [it becomes] "prakāśam" (manifest).
"Make [this] famous";
not only this much, but also "with reference to me," "in secret."
The meaning is that one should effect its non-establishment (*aprasiddhi*).

However, some explain it by relying on the suffix *-ac* (in the sense of "possessing") as in *prakāśa*—meaning "that which has light"—and thus, without resorting to the accusative case for the object of the designation, they interpret it as "the well-known" (*prakāśaṃ prasiddham*), based on the statement from the *Vārāha-purāṇa*:
"Thus [says] the *Vārāha*."
And in the *Śaiva-skānda*:
"Because it is understood from the words of Vārāha that [the teaching] was made for the purpose of deluding others"— thus, by way of a reason, [it is stated] "not others."
Thus is the connection with the statement of the proposition (*pratijñāvākya*).

As for the discourse on the investigation of the basis of the *liṅga*: previously, there was a dispute between Viṣṇu and Viriñca regarding the status of being the creator of the world, each saying, "I alone am the creator of the world; none other than me.
In the meantime, in order to destroy their pride, a certain *liṅga* appeared between them.
Having seen that, in the presence of all the gods, the two made a mutual agreement.
Thereupon Brahmā said to Viṣṇu: "Between us two, whoever reaches the end and the beginning of this *liṅga*, he shall be superior in the world;
he shall be the creator of the world and the Lord."
"Therefore, O Viṣṇu, you go downward to search for the root of the Liṅga, while I shall go upward to search for its end.
Having thus made this agreement, the two of them set out searching.
Thereupon, Viṣṇu went downward in the form of a boar to search for it,
while the son of Vāṇī (Brahmā) went upward in the form of a swan.
Then Viṣṇu, having returned to his own place, spoke the truth in the presence of all the gods, saying, "I saw the beginning of the Liṅga."
Brahmā also approached and spoke a falsehood under a pretext, saying, "I saw the end.
Then Maheśvara, in the form of a *liṅga*, having heard their words, said: "O Viṣṇu, since you have spoken the truth, therefore in your world there shall be worship equal to mine;
but for Brahmā, it shall not be so."
Then Brahmā said, "O Rudra, you must forgive me for the offense committed by my speaking a falsehood.
Thereupon Rudra replied, "My word shall not become false;
nevertheless, go to Mount Gandhamādana in order to avoid the fault incurred by your speaking a lie."
"In that regard, perform sacrifices; thereby, honor shall come to you through the very performance of Śrauta and Smārta rites,
but not in temples and such places"— having spoken thus, [the deity] vanished, as described in the Skanda Purāṇa.

[Objection: But even so, there would be a contradiction with this meaning [of yours] by Purāṇas such as the Skanda and Brahmavaivarta, because those have as their subject matter the supremacy of Śiva, Brahmā, and others. To this, he says: "And in the Śaiva [Purāṇa].
The word *ca* has the sense of *api* (also) and serves as a conjunction (*samuccaya*).

The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "even though" and so forth; it also indicates the ellipsis of the phrase "because of the statement in the *Skānda*," namely, "even in the *Śaiva* [Purāṇa], which is intent upon the excellence of Śiva."
The same applies to what follows:
"Even the gods, such as Brahmā, Īśāna, and others, become more wretched than even a dog-cooker (outcaste) at that very moment, O Acyuta, when you turn your face away."
O Acyuta; "at that very time"; and if you indeed remain entirely "not turning away" and bestow your grace, "then."

The meaning is as follows: "Then [those such as] Brahmā, Īśāna, and other gods—even from a *śvapaca* (an outcaste who cooks dogs), there is a state of being more wretched (*kaṣṭatvam*), that is, a state of being beset by affliction (*kleśayuktatvam*) or suffering (*kaṣṭam*); they certainly undergo this."

Since this is a form of reasoning (*tarka*), when it reaches its conclusion through the process of elimination (*viparyayaparyavasāna*), it establishes that Brahmā and the others are dependent on Viṣṇu and are recipients of His absolute grace; thus, there is no contradiction with authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
The word "iti" is to be construed as "thus [it is stated] in the Skanda Purāṇa."
And in the *Brahma* and *Brahmavaivarta* [Purāṇas]:
"Neither I, nor Śiva, nor others possess even a single fraction of His power;
just as a child plays with toys, so does Acyuta play with us. Thus it is said.
"In the Brahma[-state]" means regarding Brahman. Here, "I" refers to the four-faced one (Brahmā). Because of the hearing [of the word] "just as," it follows "in that same way."
Thus it is obtained.
The two words "ca" (and) have the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Regarding the phrase "by us" (*asmābhiḥ*), there is an *ekaśeṣa* compound meaning "Śiva and others and I—we, by them."

And thus, although we do not "partake of even a single portion of His power"— that is, we do not partake of even a single portion of that power or capability belonging to Acyuta— nevertheless, "just as," for example, "a child [plays] with toys."
He plays with objects that are the means for play;
"in that same way," so too does Acyuta.
Hari also "plays" with "us," meaning that He performs the play of creation and so forth by means of us as His instruments.
The statement "not again" (punarna ca) refers to the intended meaning; or [it means] "no person" (na puruṣa).
The word "iti" connects with the phrase "thus in the Brahmavaivarta."
By means of the two words "from the statement" (*vacanāt*) following the phrases "in the Skanda" and "in the Brahmavaivarta," there is no contradiction with other texts.
This is the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
Thus, even though they belong to the Śaiva and other traditions, there is no contradiction;
for since those texts also state that Viṣṇu is supreme and so forth, they lack authority regarding the exaltation of Śiva and others, as that would involve internal inconsistency.
Nor should it be asked, "Why might this not be the reverse?

For the excellence of Śiva and others is established exclusively and uniquely within the Śaiva and other Purāṇas; therefore, since the certainty regarding their authority is restricted to that very [text] where Viṣṇu’s excellence is stated, while there is a lack of authority regarding the excellence of Śiva and others, a reversal of this situation is impossible.

Therefore, the sense is that the sequence of the superiority of Śiva and others as postulated by the Pāśupatas and other schools is presented within them using the terminology of their own philosophical systems (darśana), and thus there is no contradiction. Furthermore, this is not the case among the Vaiṣṇavas; and that has been stated [by the Lord] in the words, "This is my illusion."
Thus concludes the section on the inquiry [into Brahman].
Nevertheless, since there is a contradiction with Vaiṣṇava texts regarding Viṣṇu’s superiority and Rudra’s inferiority, he says: "And not" (*na ca*).
The word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of conjunction.
And thus: "Among the Vaiṣṇavas."
Even in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa and other such texts,
it is likewise stated that there is no one superior to Viṣṇu;
for this very reason, it is "likewise."

The meaning is that there is no contradiction regarding the matter of being supreme or inferior, as in the case of the Śaivas; the point is that such a contradiction within itself would result in invalidity regarding its own subject matter.
[Objection: "In that case, how is it that among the Vaiṣṇavas, praises of Śiva performed by Viṣṇu—such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa—are spoken? To this, he says: "And that... (tac ca).
The meaning of the word *ca* is "and.
The term "because of the statement" (*vacanāt*) is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*).
There is a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the word *tat*.

And thus— since that which is stated in the Vaiṣṇava texts regarding the praise of Śiva and so forth is "spoken" with the intent of delusion, as known from the statement "This is delusion," it has been answered and resolved.
The meaning is that this has been stated.
Its connection is with the supplied phrase: "Therefore, there is no contradiction with that."
Thus concludes the section on the inquiry [into Brahman].
// 2. The Section on Birth //
He states the definition of Brahman:
"From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this.
[This means: from which proceed creation, maintenance, dissolution, governance, knowledge, ignorance, bondage, and liberation.

He shows what is to be established in this section with the word "of Brahman. Since, by the force of unimpeded conventional usage, it might be concluded that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is this Brahman, and since that [identity] is beyond doubt, there would be no need for it to be an object of inquiry; in order to refute this, he states the definition of the Brahman to be inquired into as taught in the Śruti, which serves as a sublation to the notion that the word "Brahman" refers to the individual soul.
The meaning is "the author of the Sūtras.

By the commentary (*ṭīkā*) stating, "He states the definition as declared by the Śruti," and by the *Tattvapradīpa* stating, "That Taittirīya Śruti which prescribes Viṣṇu’s status as Brahman and states His definitions— those [definitions] the Blessed One has stated by means of this Sūtra," the meaning of the Bhāṣya is explained through the ellipsis of the word "that" (*tat*).
Therefore, it should be understood that the term "definition" (*lakṣaṇam*) is used in the singular to denote the collective whole.

By this, since the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises here by way of challenging the previously intended inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), the "introductory connection" (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*) with the preceding section is stated. Furthermore, the connection with the scripture (*śāstra*) as a whole is already established, because [this inquiry] has Brahman as its subject matter.
Although it has been stated by the phrase "and the word *brahman* applies primarily to Viṣṇu alone" that the term *brahman* is used in its primary sense for Viṣṇu,

nevertheless, because this was not explicitly stated by the author of the Sūtras despite having been stated by the authors of the Bhāṣya, the doubt remains as to whether *brahman* refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) or to Viṣṇu.
He recites the Sūtra: "Birth";
the ellipsis is that by the statement "from which," the subject under discussion, namely Brahman, is established.
Alternatively, the completion of the sentence is: "It is heard in the Sūtra, 'From which [comes] the birth and so forth of this [world]'."
Thus, according to the statement of Sudhā, the ellipsis is "it was heard.

The term *janmādi* is a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* compound, meaning that for the collection beginning with birth—namely, the group consisting of creation and so forth—"birth" is included as a subordinate member (*guṇa*) of the referent of the compound.
This is because "birth" is understood as a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) of that which constitutes a part of the compound's meaning.
And likewise, having in mind the meaning of the Sūtra— "That from which the birth and so forth of this known world proceed,
as heard in the Śruti, is Brahman"— [the author] intends that "of this" refers to the birth of this world, and so on, as indicated by the word "ādi" (and so forth).
To prevent the misconception that Brahman is merely that from which [the world] originates, persists, and dissolves, the author explains the Sūtra "sṛṣṭi" etc., exactly as it is: "sṛṣṭi".

Here, by means of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), the words "creation," "destruction," and "regulation"—which denote the activity of an agent—convey the activities of the object (*prayojya-vyāpāra*), namely the birth, destruction, and state of being regulated residing in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
Regarding this, the statement in the *Candrikā* is that the purpose of the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is to demonstrate that Brahman is not the material cause (*upādāna*).
Furthermore, each of the eight [characteristics] beginning with creation (sṛṣṭi) possesses the status of a definition individually, and not as a collective whole,
because there is no occurrence of over-extension (ativyāpti) or other such fallacies.
And this characteristic also implies the state of being filled with infinite qualities.
Although it is possible to indicate [the Lord] by means of a single one, the mention of all eight is purposeful because they are to be known by those seeking liberation (mumukṣu).
As it has been stated in the *Śrīman Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya*:
Having understood emanation, preservation, withdrawal, knowledge, necessity, ignorance, bondage, and liberation from Viṣṇu itself, there is liberation; and not otherwise.
Thus; after the word "yataḥ," the remainder of the sentence is either "śrutāḥ" (are heard) or "bhavanti" (exist).
The connection is with the phrase "His is that Brahman," which has been supplied.
From whom [proceed] creation, maintenance, and destruction, destiny, knowledge, concealment, bondage, and liberation— He is Hari, the sole sovereign.
Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.

Now, if the status of being the creator of the birth of the world and so forth were restricted to Viṣṇu alone, then the apprehension of the individual soul (jīva) by the word "Brahman" would constitute a contradiction;
but how is it known that this [creatorship] is restricted to Viṣṇu alone? To this he says: "From the origin," etc. "From whom" this world [originates].
From the Puruṣa arise origination, maintenance, and dissolution; "niyati" is the regulation, and "āvṛti" is knowledge.
And because from Him come "bondage and liberation," and because He is "the sole sovereign," Hari is independent.
This is the meaning. The term "sole sovereign" (*ekarāṭ*) is used to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to Viriñca and others.
Following the phrase "in the Skanda Purāṇa," it continues: "From this statement, it is clear that Hari alone is the creator of the universe and so forth."
This is the completion of the sentence. [As it is said:
"From which indeed these beings are born; by which, once born, they live..."
"That into which they enter when they depart—desire to know that; that is Brahman."

In the inference that "Brahma, who is to be known, must be Viṣṇu alone because He is the agent of birth and so forth," [the author] sets forth the definition of the world as the cause in order to refute the non-establishment of the reason or the impossibility resulting from the non-perception of the definition of Brahma—who is to be known—therein. (Tai.U. 3.1)
He states that this was mentioned in the preceding sentence, "Desire to know That," by using the word "yataḥ" (from which).
The word *vai* indicates well-known fact.

The word *bhūta*—based on the statement from the *Gītātātparyanirṇaya*, "From all living beings, because they exist (*bhūta-nāmabhyaḥ*)"—denotes the individual soul (*jīva*), and by implication, refers to the entire universe characterized by that soul.
And thus: "From which these beings are born, by which, once born, they live," that is,
they sustain their life-force.
And that into which they "enter" at the time of dissolution; and that toward which they "approach" by their own will, entering it perfectly.
In liberation, that alone is "Brahman" and nothing else;
primarily, for the sake of knowing that which constitutes the meaning of the Veda, [the text says]: "Seek to know That."
The meaning is: "Perform an inquiry concerning that.
The word *iti* is present in the scripture itself; it belongs to the phrase: "'Thus Varuṇa spoke to Bhṛgu.'"
Thus is the connection with the verb.
He who alone has supported the threefold earth and the sky, and all the worlds.
With ninety-four names at once, he has spun out [the hymn] like a revolving wheel.

In order to dispel the suspicion that the definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpti*) or the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the aforementioned inference, [the author] first cites a Smṛti because its meaning is clear; he now [argues]: since even each individual act such as creation resides solely in Viṣṇu, how much more so the case when all [acts] are considered together?
Regarding the fact that the agency of sustaining the world resides in Viṣṇu alone by virtue of his nature, he cites the scripture beginning with "He who" (*yaḥ*).
The word *u* has the sense of *eva* (indeed/only); *tridhātu* is a single compound word.
The word *uta* signifies conjunction;
and thus— He who is Viṣṇu is "one" alone, "threefold."
The sustainer of primordial nature, the person, and time [upholds] the "earth," the "sky," and all "prosperity."
And he "sustained" (*dādhāra*) all "beings" (*viśvāni bhuvanāni*); the meaning is that he held them fast.
Regarding the fact that Viṣṇu alone is the agent of even the restriction [of time], he cites the Śruti: "With four";
the word "sa" (he) is to be supplied as the subject, and the particle "na" has the sense of "iva" (as).
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "only" (mātra).
Thus: that Viṣṇu, who possesses a vast body and is the primordial form, [is designated] by "names";
that is, by mere names devoid of any difference in essential nature, "four."
"Along with Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, [he conquered] ninety"—that is, those numbering ninety—"transcendent ones" (*vyatīn*);
this word is used in its etymological sense among the gods—meaning "those who are especially superior" (*viśeṣeṇādhikān*)—let alone others; "his wheel has not ceased."
Like a wheel, it "caused to roll" (avīvipat) simultaneously; the root *vṛt* means "to turn around," thus the sense is that it caused [them] to revolve.
The eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, the eleven Ādityas excluding Viṣṇu, the ten lords of progeny together with Hiraṇyagarbha, and the fifty Maruts along with Pradhāna—thus there are ninety.
However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, after first stating the meaning as explained in the commentary, it says:
"The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and also the two Aśvins..."
Bṛhaspati, Kāma, Manu, Dakṣa, Vināyaka,
Bhṛgu, Aniruddha, Dharma, and Nirṛti— these gods,
together with Kubera, are proclaimed to be ninety in number.
Ananta, Garuḍa, Vāyu, and the four [guardians] together with Brahmā.
Thus, according to the authoritative sources, ninety-four [names] have been stated by way of another classification;
in that very context, it is also explained as "those possessing names" and "those possessing fame. O you who have grown beyond measure with your body, others do not equal your greatness.
Neither being born nor already born, O Viṣṇu, has anyone reached the furthest limit of your divine greatness.

Although the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of these characteristics has been implicitly avoided by the statement that they reside exclusively in Viṣṇu and by Smṛti, [the author] now refutes it directly by means of Śruti which establishes their absence elsewhere, stating: "The Supreme" (*paraḥ*).
The word "in Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇau*) is to be supplied from the context.
According to the method stated in the *Tattvodyota-ṭīkā*, the remainder is that they are both liberated and unliberated;
for this very reason, it is said "who" (*ka*) in the commentary.
And thus: "by the body";
"O Viṣṇu, who art increasing by Your own form and not by fame alone; O unconditioned one, You who are beyond all measure (mātrā) because You transcend all measurement."
"You are unique; you are immeasurable," and so forth.
Therefore, "your greatness"—the majesty consisting of the creation of the world and so on—"in accordance with" such a being as you...
"Even some who are liberated and some who are not do not attain"—the meaning is that they do not reach [it]. Or alternatively: "do not attain."
The meaning is that they do not experience [it].

Because of the negation of the present tense in the phrase "they do not attain" (nāśnuvanti), one might think it could occur later; therefore, he says "no. The word "attains" (prāpnoti) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
And thus: "O Viṣṇu,
the supreme limit of the greatness of the gods," that is, of the greatness of Ramā and the others.
"His greatness"— that is, his majesty which constitutes the ultimate limit of the gradations of magnitude—
"being born," does not reach.
The meaning is "born, he shall not perish.
This is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), and it should be understood that "being about to be born, he shall not attain [destruction].
For this very reason, in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "O Supreme One, increasing with a body by means of measure..."
They do not reach the full extent of your greatness;
we know both your realms upon the earth, O Viṣṇu, yet you alone know the supreme divinity of the highest.
Neither one being born nor one already born has reached the furthest limit of your divine majesty, O Viṣṇu.
"You propped up the lofty, vast sky; you established the eastern peak of the earth"—this pair of verses has been explained in exactly this manner.

For instance: "Beyond measure" means exceeding all dimensions; "increasing in body" means growing in body, being full in form—the instrumental case here denotes the state of being—meaning he is full in the form of a body.
Since the body of Viṣṇu is non-different from [Him] and consists of consciousness, bliss, and so forth,

they do not experience nor attain His greatness— that is, His majesty. We, however, know both merit and demerit— the two products of the quality of *rajas*— belonging to Your earth, which is *prakṛti*.
For by the *rajas* of *prakṛti*, merit and demerit are produced;
yet you alone know the greatness of that Supreme One.

You alone have reached the end of greatness—the totality of all majesty—whether that of Brahman or Śrī; for the greatness of Viṣṇu surpasses all others, and no one has ever attained the ultimate limit of your greatness.
That which has no suffering (*naka*) is *nāka*.
It is lofty (*ṛṣva*), having the nature of light;
it is vast (*bṛhant*), the full world. You propped it up (*udastabhnāḥ*); you raised it aloft.

By the establishment of Indra, you have supported the eastern quarter of the earth—that is, the eastern direction of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) which consists of earth; this serves as an illustration for supporting everything. He who is our father, our progenitor, and the ordainer, he who knows all abodes and dwellings.
And so forth, as in (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.82.3). //2//
And the scripture shows that Brahman’s status as the cause of the world is not by way of being subject to modification, but rather solely by way of being the instrumental cause, like a father,
in the passage beginning with "He who" (*yaḥ*). "He who" (*yaḥ*) is indeed "the one" (*eka eva*) "of us" (*naḥ*).
For all of us, beginning with ourselves, He is the ‘progenitor’; that is, the actual father— not merely a protective father, like one who adopts a son.

Alternatively, according to the direction of the Aitareya Bhāṣya—"He alone, being established as the father, is named 'father' (pitṛ) because he is a protector"—and based on the statement in the Tattvapradīpa that "a father (pitā) is a protector (pātā)," the meaning is: 'janitā' means the progenitor;
'pitā' means the progenitor and also the protector.
‘Yo vidhātā’: He is the specific sustainer and nourisher;

for it is stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*, "And the nourishment of the liberated consists in the granting of knowledge and liberation. It is also stated in the *Prameyadīpa*, "The Vidhātṛ is the creator (*kartā*)."
The sense is: "of its holding and nourishing.
He who "knows" all the worlds (*viśvā bhuvanāni*)—that is, all the abodes (*dhāmāni*) situated therein—and the essential natures of living beings and so forth; he is "aviśvā."
The meaning is "he knows.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth," the ellipsis is "this statement is the authoritative proof (pramāṇa) for the stated meaning.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), other scriptural passages of this kind, such as "generating heaven and earth," are included. // 2 //
Thus concludes the section on birth.
3. The Section on Scripture Being the Source [of Brahman] (Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa)
The others are not to be postulated on the basis of inference,
because [the Veda] is the source of the Śāstra (śāstrayonitvāt).

In this section, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding the cause of the world is stated in order to avoid the over-extension (ativyāpti) of the previously mentioned definition of Brahman— characterized as the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe— to Rudra and others.
Having refined the formal proposition of the established doctrine (siddhānta-pratijñā), he demonstrates it with the words "by means of inference" (anumānataḥ).
The phrase "as the cause" (kāraṇatvena) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

Thus, through such inferences as "Śiva is the agent of the world's birth and so forth, because he is omniscient; for if it were otherwise, he would be like Yajñadatta," [it follows that] Viṣṇu is "other" [than Śiva].
Even Rudra and others are not to be postulated as the cause of the world; the meaning is that they are not to be suspected [of being so].
Why? In response to this expectation for a reason, he presents the aphorism: "Because [Brahman] has the scripture as its source" (Śāstrayonitvāt).
The word "of the cause of the world" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

Just as there is an ellipsis (adhyāhāra) in the middle of that [passage] because of the statement in the *Sudhā* commentary on the phrase "or its established reasoning" (*tannirdhāritayukti*) in the *Anuvyākhyāna*: "After the word 'established' (*nirdhārita*), the word 'pervasion' (*vyāpti*) is to be supplied";

or just as there is an ellipsis in the middle of that [passage] because of the statement in the *Prameyadīpa* on the *Gītā-bhāṣya*: "The meaning beginning with 'being devoid of all sense organs' (*sarvendriyavivarjitatva*) has been stated"—where it says: "After the word 'beginning' (*ādi*), the word 'word' (*śabda*) is to be supplied."

Or, just as in the Mahābhāṣya sentence, "in the case of words such as *puruṣa*, *vadha*, *vikāra*, *samūha*, and *tena*-kṛta," there is the insertion (*adhyāhāra*) of the word *tena* in the middle of the compound, so too here the word *eka* is to be inserted after the word *śāstra*, and the word *jñapti* before the word *yoni*. Thus, the meaning of the sūtra is: that which is the state (*tattva*) of that reality for which the Veda—consisting of the Ṛgveda and so forth—is both the single, unaided scripture (*śāstra*) and the source of its cognition (*jñaptiyoni*), i.e., the cause of its knowledge.
By this, it is stated that the cause of the world is not inferable, because—like *dharma* and so forth—it is to be understood solely through scripture (*śāstra*).
Furthermore, there is no deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example;
for the ascertainment of *dharma* and the like does not occur by means of inference.

And thus—the sense is that since it is improper to establish the causality of the world for others through inference, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to them. [As stated in the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* (3.12.9): "One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One, the Self who experiences all, in the hereafter."
And from such scriptural passages as, "The person known through the Upaniṣads" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26), [it follows that the Cause is known solely through scripture].
To the question, "Why is it that the Cause is to be known through scripture alone?", he says: "Not [by other means]."
This is a passage from the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad].
Here, the reading is the short vowel *u* (*au*).
[The term is] "aupaniṣadaḥ."

Thus says another Śruti passage. Here, the nasalization (āṅ) must be applied as a prefix; by the word "etc. (ādi), [the following is included]: "That state which all the Vedas... (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.15).

The statement from the Bhāllaveya, “For the Vedas indeed [know him],” and the passage from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (5.9.26), “I ask you about that person who is known through the Upaniṣads,” are also taken into account.
"That" refers to the previously mentioned "Great One," who is full and "experiences everything";
he is called the "experiencer of all" (sarvānubhū) because he experiences everything— that is, the omniscient one.
Alternatively: "the all-experiencer" (*sarvānubhūḥ*) refers to that Self who is the creator of the entire world or the master of all, because He experiences everything.
Regarding the term *sāmparāye*: "samparāya" is the attainment (*āya*) of the supreme state (*para*) in a complete manner (*sam*); it is the same as *sāmparāya*.
The locative case here is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*).

And likewise, for the sake of liberation, the term "one who does not know the Veda" (*avedavid*)— according to the method stated in the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā*— refers here to the true scriptures (*sadāgama*). Thus, one who lacks knowledge of the true scriptures and their meaning, or one whose knowledge is contrary to the Veda, "does not reflect" (*na manute*), that is, he does not truly know.

The meaning of the first scriptural passage is that nothing other than the Veda establishes a creator of the world; rather, only one who knows the Veda knows [it], for the Veda itself is the means of establishing it. The meaning of the other scriptural passage is that the Person who is the creator of the world is "derived from the Upaniṣads" (*aupaniṣada*), meaning he is to be understood solely through the Upaniṣads.
The state of being cognizable (gamyatva) is the state of being graspable (grāhyatva), which is the meaning of the secondary derivative suffix;
the plural form "from the scriptures" (śrutibhyaḥ) is used in reference to the various scriptures implied by the word "etc. (ādi).
The word "ca" (and) is used to include the probandum that has been supplied,
or to include what has been stated by [the author] himself;
it is to be construed with the phrase "because this [Brahman] has the scripture as its source."
The word "of the cause" (*kāraṇasya*) is to be supplied [to the compound].
Thus, the sense is that since it is understood from such scriptural passages as these that the cause has the scripture alone as its source (*śāstraikayonitva*), there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*).
By citing a scriptural passage containing two negative particles (*nañ*), it is indicated that the word "alone" (*eka*) is to be supplied in the Sūtra.
Nor is inference invariably authoritative;
for an inference devoid of the assistance of scripture cannot establish an object with certainty,
nor can it serve as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) on its own.
To the objection that the cause taught in the Upaniṣads might also be established by means of inference, he says: "And not" (*na ca*).
The word "and" (*ca*) is used for emphasis.
And thus: "of inference" (*anumānasya*).
"Inference alone lacks validity";
the meaning is that it does not establish the cognition of supersensible objects.
And thus, the implication is that it is not proper to use it to prove the creatorship of another [the Lord] over the world.

[Objection: But how can this be so? For in the section [sūtra 2.1.38], "And because all dharmas are possible," it is accepted that Viṣṇu’s perfection and other qualities are established by reasons such as his independence (*svātantrya*). To this, it is said: "restricted" (*niyata*).
And this word, meaning independence, is a qualifier of the sense of the root *pra-mā*, which functions as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The phrase "of inference" contains a reason (*hetugarbha*).
And thus: precisely because it is an inference, it does not independently determine an unperceived object, since there is the possibility of counter-arguments and so forth.
However, [the validity] depends on independence (*svātantrya*).
Independence, moreover, consists in being devoid of assistance.

And that [independence] does not exist in the case of a cause such as self-reliance (*svātantrya*); for since it lacks the assistance of scripture (*śruti*), it is not independent, and thus its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not established—this is the intended meaning.
To the question, "Why is there no fixed validity for inference? he says: "Scripture" (*śruti*).
This term also implies *smṛti* (tradition).
Here, the word "aid" (*sahāya*) signifies the root source.
Therefore, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of the base itself;
"scripture" (*śruti*) and "its assistance" (*tatsāhāyyam*) form a *karmadhāraya* compound, and [the phrase] "devoid of that" (*tena rahitam*) forms a *tatpuruṣa* compound with the former.
This means "devoid of being supported by scripture";
the word *ca* (and) functions as a conjunction;
the word *eva* (only/just) is displaced in its position [in the compound].
And likewise: "In some cases"—that is, regarding an object revealed in scripture that is not perceived by people such as ourselves—there is inference devoid of the assistance of scripture;
for example, the inferential mark (liṅga) such as "God is not independent because he is conscious," and so forth.
Likewise, the inference that sacrificial violence is dharma is "not another means of valid cognition" (apramāṇāntara), meaning it is other than inference;
and perception—which perceives defects such as those of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa and perceives their humanity—is "due to certainty" (niścayāt) [of their being free from faults];
thus, [perception] "would not establish" (na sādhayet) a supersensuous object clearly—this is the construction.
Alternatively, the meaning is that one should not fail to accomplish the goal through certainty;

indeed, it is said in the *Gītā-bhāṣya*: "It must be practiced with certainty; the meaning is that it must certainly be practiced by one who desires to attain [liberation]. For it is stated in the *Prameya-dīpikā*: "The word 'certainty' (niścaya) serves to exclude non-yoga.
This is the supreme other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which is supported by *śruti* and *smṛti*.
It shall attain the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); no deliberation need be made on this point.
If one asks, "Then, of what kind [of perception, etc. is there the capacity to determine an unseen object (*adṛṣṭārtha*)?", he says: "Scripture" (*śruti*).
This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

And thus: that other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) which is conjoined with the auxiliary factors consisting of Śruti and Smṛti—namely, the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of Yaśodā and others—is "supreme" (*uttama*). Therefore, it [attains] the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇapadavīm*).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "one should go" means one should attain the method (*paddhati*) consisting in being the instrument of valid cognition (*pramākaraṇatva*) for subsequent valid knowledge (*anupramāṇa*).
Even with the reading *tat*, the construction is exactly the same.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: that reasoning (*tarka*) which is assisted by *śruti* and *smṛti*—namely, the inference of equal pervasion (*samavyāpti*) stating "Viṣṇu is independent because he is complete"—that too shall attain the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Regarding this matter, there is "no doubt" (*avicāraṇā*).
The meaning is that [this] must be done; by the phrase "not here," the suspicion of invalidity regarding his own stated point is refuted.

Reasoning (*tarka*) consists of such deliberation as, "What could be the intended meaning here so as not to contradict what precedes and follows? However, one should avoid "dry reasoning" (*śuṣkatarka*).
Thus it is stated in the *Mahākaurma-purāṇa*.
To dispel misconceptions such as that the term "tarka" (reasoning) refers to the superimposition of a pervader (*vyāpyāropa*), he states the true nature of *tarka* with the words "pūrva";
[and] "atra," meaning "in this disputed statement, what meaning is intended?"
"It should be the object of the intended meaning," and so forth;

preceded by such a deliberation, [one should determine it] "without contradiction between the preceding and the following"—that is, without contradiction between the introduction (*upakrama*) and the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*), and through their uniformity. This also indicates other indicative marks (*liṅga*); and thus, by means of the indicative marks of intention such as the introduction and so on, the object of the intended meaning here is precisely this.

That which is the first [type of] "reasoning" (ūhana), beginning with "it might be," and that inferential mark (liṅga) which is the means for attaining valid knowledge— that alone is intended here as "tarka" (hypothetical reasoning).

"Dry reasoning" (*śuṣkatarka*) means reasoning that lacks the support of *śruti* and *smṛti* and is independent of them, such as reasoning based on [the mere fact of] being conscious (*caitanyatva*); one should avoid this, meaning that the determination of supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha*) must not be made by means of it.
However, some, relying on the dual meaning of the word *ka*, maintain that the verse "Who among the meters? (Ṛgveda 10.115.9) is what is referred to by the word "here" (*atra*).
For this very reason, they say that the phrase "thus beginning" is also appropriate;
after the word "in the Kūrma," the words "since it is stated in the Purāṇa" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.

This [phrase] is connected with the word "and not" (*na ca*). Furthermore, because inference is possible everywhere, there is not only the presence of evidence for the lack of validity of an inference that is devoid of association with scripture and the like; rather—
Moreover, he states that there is also a subverting argument against accepting its validity: "Because it is possible" (*śakyatvāt*).
The word "to employ" (*prayoktum*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
In the term "of inference" (*anumānām*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*).

The word "ca" (and) has the sense of a conjunction of what has been stated, namely "not only. And thus: for "inferences"—that is, for mere reasons such as "sentience" or "being a real entity"—which are devoid of the accompaniment of scripture and so forth, "everywhere";

The construction is as follows: since it is impossible to employ [the reason] even when the probandum—such as the absence of being the cause of the world in the case of Rudra and others, or the possession of horns in the case of a rabbit and others—is to be established, inference does not possess invariably certain validity. For everywhere, an inference can indeed be made without recourse to scripture (āgama).
"Therefore, it is not capable of being observed without scripture," so it is said in the *Vārāha*.
Regarding this very point, he states the authority: "everywhere";
for [the word] "hi" means "because [without scripture]."
Inference dependent on that [scripture] applies "everywhere," such as in the case of the absence of God as a cause and so forth; it is "to be performed."
"It is not possible to employ [it];
therefore,
inference must wait for scripture."
"To cause to look up" means "to make known," with "the meaning" being the understood object; "capable" means "endowed with the power [to do so]," and not otherwise.
This applies to both the word "in the Vārāha" and "in the Kūrma."
Such is the logical sequence.
Therefore, since mere inference is not determinative, it is established that the determination of authorship occurs through the scripture alone. [The examples are:
semen, a drop of water, and the perfuming of ghee by smoke.
Recollection of past births, the magnet, the sun-gem, subsisting on water,
the dissolution of the elements after death, the propitiation of deities, and the cessation of karma upon death— these are established as authoritative means of knowledge; such is the certainty.
Thus, according to the words of the Mokṣadharma, the doctrine of nihilism is not tenable.

[Objection: "But since there is no means of knowledge other than perception for objects beyond the senses (*atīndriya-artha*), how can God be established through scripture (*śāstra*)? Thus, he refutes this nihilistic argument by means of a statement from the *Mokṣadharma*:
‘Semen... [The word] ‘semen’ (*retaḥ*) and so forth—each of these words ending in the nominative singular—is to be construed individually with the word ‘means of knowledge’ (*pramāṇam*).
The phrase ‘in this matter’ (*atra-arthe*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

And thus: "In this context, the *retodhātvādi* [passage] is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—that is, the prover (*pramāpaka*)—regarding the existence of supersensuous objects and the validity of inference and other means of knowledge.

The construction of the second occurrence of the word "thus" (*tathā ca*) in the Commentary is as follows: by these reasons understood from the statements in the *Mokṣadharma*, the doctrine of nihilism (*nāstikyavāda*) is not tenable.
Nāstikya is either the nihilist himself or the collection of nihilists;
and thus: "There is no other world."
The meaning is that the discourse proceeds with the thought that "there is no dharma" and "there is no adharma.

Alternatively, according to the method stated in the *Nyāyadīpikā*, it refers to the state of mind or cognition (*bhāva-buddhi*) characterized by *āstikya*— the sense that there is a purpose served by [the practice of] dharma and so forth.
The meaning is that discourse preceded by that [belief] is [orthodox], whereas any other is a doctrine of nihilism (*nāstikyavāda*).

The manner in which the seminal essence (*retas*) and so forth serve as inferential marks (*anumāpaka*) is as follows: the causal relationship between the body and the final constituent (*dhātu*) denoted by the word "semen" is not perceptible (*pratyakṣa*).

However, its validity is established by the fact that it is cognizable through inference known as *anvaya* (positive concomitance) and *vyatireka* (negative concomitance). The proof of the existence of the individual soul (*jīva*) follows from the observation that semen poured into a dead body does not take on the form of a body; whereas semen poured into a body presided over [by a soul] transforms into the nature of a body.

The proof of the Lord’s unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) follows from the observation that semen poured into all bodies such as those of barren women is incapable of producing an effect, whereas semen impelled by that [unseen merit] is capable of producing an effect.
From that very fact, the validity of the scripture that teaches it is established.
Likewise, the elements such as wind and bile undergo transformation only in a living body due to unwholesome food and other causes,
and not in a dead body.
Nor does it exist in all bodies while they are alive;
therefore, there is no establishment of a living soul (jīva), a Lord (īśvara), the authority of the scriptures that reveal them, and so forth.
It is well known that a banyan tree arises from a banyan seed, as stated in the phrase "from the banyan-germ" (vaṭakaṇikā).
Nor [is it produced] from that [grain] which has been roasted, nor from all those that have not been roasted; thus, the existence of an unseen force (adṛṣṭa) in a directing Lord is established.
Furthermore, corpulence arises only in a living body through the consumption of ghee.

"Perfuming with smoke" (*adhūmādhivāsana*)— which is for the sake of the excellence of flowers and other qualities— is not performed by throwing [smoke] onto a dead body, nor even upon all bodies while they are still living; rather, it is the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of a tree by means of smoke.
Therefore, the abundance of flowers and so forth occurs only on trees that are not yet dry,
neither on those that are dry, nor on all those that are not dry.
By these two marks as well, the existence of the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), and the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) is established.
For some, due to a particular means, there occurs "recollection of birth" (jātismṛti)—that is, memory of a previous life—such as: "By this very merit, heaven was experienced in such a way."
"By this evil, such a hell was experienced"— and that [experience] belongs only to someone, not to everyone.
Since that [activity] is not logical in the absence of volition and so forth, for this reason as well, the existence of volition, unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), and so on, is established.
A piece of iron moves because of a particular kind of stone called a magnet; yet, it is never observed that an insentient thing possesses the capacity to cause motion.
Nor can it be established that a Lord who impels all volitions exists on the grounds that fire is produced from a specific stone called the sun-gem (*sūryakānta*);
for such power is not logically possible in an insentient thing.
For this reason as well, there is no establishment of a motivating God, unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), or the like; for by drinking water, thirst is quenched only in a living body,
and it does not cook when that [water] is placed in a dead body or in another vessel.

Nor does it exist in all bodies while they are alive; therefore, neither the individual soul (jīva) nor the Lord (īśvara) and so forth are established [as its substratum]. After the word "pretya" (having departed), the word "sthitasya" (of that which remains) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
‘Pretya’ means having abandoned the living soul; ‘bhūtāpyayaḥ’ refers to the dissolution (laya) of the body into the elements (bhūtas).
Thus, through death, the dissolution of the body occurs within the five elements, such as earth and the rest.
Nor is it by the will of a living being; therefore, from this [fact] as well, there is no proof of a creator God (Īśvara) or the like who determines such things.
Likewise, through the propitiation of deities, prosperity and so forth occur for only some individuals.
Thus, when the body has died, activity ceases; it does not cease prior to death nor by its own will.
From this as well, the existence of the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa), and so forth, is established.
And because the fruits of austerity and so forth are observed.
He refutes the doctrine of nihilism by means of another argument as well: "and because [the fruits] are observed. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to collect the arguments.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), sin (*pāpa*) is included.

Thus, the meaning is that since the results of extremely intense austerities (*tapas*)—such as Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) and celibacy (*brahmacarya*)—in the form of radiance (*tejassvitva*) and so forth, are indeed perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣa*), the doctrine of nihilism (*nāstikyavāda*) is not tenable.

The underlying point is that one must accept both the supersensible entities known as merit and demerit (*puṇya-pāpa*) and the validity of the inference and scripture (*anumāna-āgama*) that establish them.
The Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, the Bhārata, the Pañcarātra,
and the Mūla-Rāmāyaṇa are designated as the Śāstra.

Now, if it is argued that since inference is not determinative, the status of being the cause of the world is established solely through scripture, then it would follow that the Pāśupata and other scriptures would establish Rudra and others as the cause of the world; to this, he says: "The Ṛg...
This word *Atharvan* ends in the vowel *a*.
The *Ṛk*, *Yajus*, *Sāman*, and *Atharvan* are what have been so described; the word "only" (*eva*) is to be connected with "the *Ṛk* and so forth," meaning "only the *Ṛk* and so forth.
By the phrase "only the original *Rāmāyaṇa*," there is the exclusion of the intermediate *Rāmāyaṇas*.
Thus says the *Sudhokti*.
The two words "ca" (and) are used in the sense of conjunction.
And that which is favorable to this [work] is proclaimed as the *śāstra*.
Therefore, any other extensive composition is not a treatise at all; it is a false path.
Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
To the objection that [if this were so] the Mānava and other śāstras would [likewise] be [authoritative], he says: "And that which...
The word "and" (ca) is used for emphasis.
The second [term] also has the sense of "in this matter"; and thus, "of this" refers to the Ṛgveda and so forth, and "that which" [refers to its fruit].
Whatever is "conducive"— that is,
that which explains non-contradictory meanings, such as the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra] or the *Purāṇas* and so forth—
all that is "proclaimed to be scripture" (*śāstra*).
By those who accept authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), "from this"— that is,
from this Veda and that which is concordant with it— "another"— meaning that which is contradictory or indifferent— refers to whatever expansion of texts there may be.
The extensive textual elaborations such as the Pāśupata and others are "not scripture at all," but rather a "bad path" (kuvartma), meaning a contemptible way.
The term *amāna* means a contemptible means of knowledge, like a "pseudo-path" (*mārga-iva-mārgaḥ*).
The sense is that the particle *eva* (in the phrase *ṛgādikam eva*) serves to exclude objects that are contradictory and so forth.
The grammatical construction is: "it is stated thus in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The meaning of the word "thus" (iti) is that the Pāśupata and other such systems are false paths. [As it is said:
"Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pāśupata, and likewise Vaitāraṇyaka..."

Beginning with these words, and with the intention of demonstrating the identity between the Veda and the Pañcarātra, the authority of the Pañcarātra alone is asserted in the Mokṣadharmas after showing that the others represent divergent views.
For this reason as well, he states that the Pāśupata and other such systems are false paths, saying "Sāṅkhya" and so forth.
The construction here is as follows: not only in the Skanda Purāṇa, but also in the Mokṣadharma section [of the Mahābhārata].
"Starting from the passage: 'Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pāśupata, and likewise the Vedic Āraṇyaka,' it was studied by beginning [with those words]."
Nārāyaṇa himself is the speaker of the entire Pañcarātra;
O king of kings, among all these systems of knowledge, this one indeed excels.

By this subsequent statement, even though the Sāṅkhya and other systems have been introduced, their exclusion is used to state the superiority of the Pañcarātra alone in terms of its authoritative status; therefore, the Pāśupata and other such paths are indeed non-authoritative. [An objection is raised: "But by this, would not only the authority of the Pañcarātra be established, while the non-authority of others is not? To this, he says: "of the others. This means: of the Sāṅkhya and others, distinct from the Veda and the Pañcarātra.

"Having demonstrated" (*pradarśya*) "the state of having different views on reality" (*bhinnamatattvam*), that is, having shown it to be a state of holding contradictory perspectives, meaning having established it.
Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pāśupata, and the Vedic Āraṇyaka—these systems of knowledge are distinct; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
The phrase "by the remainder of the sentence" is the implied sense.
The connection is that by the words "having shown," it is stated that the authority belongs to the Pañcarātra alone;
the underlying intention is that when mutually contradictory [texts] are declared to have a single authority, the lack of authority for the others follows as a matter of course.
In that case, it might follow that even the *Vedāraṇyaka* would lack authority; therefore, he says "vedā...
[etc.]. The phrase "with the intention of unity" means with the intention of the relationship of root and branch, which consists in having a single purpose.

And thus, since the authority of the Pañcarātra is stated on the grounds that it possesses a meaning equal to the Veda, the implication is that the authority of the Veda itself has been stated; therefore, its lack of authority cannot be maintained.
Nor should it be asked from what basis the intention of identity [between the two] is inferred;

for if the human-authored Pañcarātra, which deals with transcendental matters, were rootless, it would be non-authoritative, and consequently, the statement regarding its superiority would be inconsistent.
"Sāṅkhya" refers to the scripture taught by Kapila other than the incarnations of Īśvara. Kapila, known as Vāsudeva, indeed proclaimed the Sāṅkhya system;
however, another Kapila proclaimed a [different] Sāṅkhya that is contrary to all the scriptures.
Because it has been stated thus:
"Yoga" refers to that taught by Hiraṇyagarbha and that of Patañjali;
"Pāśupata" is that proclaimed by Paśupati.

Because it is to be studied in a forest, in a secluded place, it is called the *Āraṇyaka*; thus the *Upaniṣad* is so designated. The Vedas and the *Āraṇyakas*—the collective term for these is *Vedāraṇyaka*.
Alternatively, it is a dual compound treated as a singular (*dvandvaikavadbhāva*).

Or, because of the multiplicity of the dharmas to be expounded—such as the duties of the castes (*varṇa*), stages of life (*āśrama*), kings, and giving—or because of the diversity of the *mokṣadharma*s (dharmas leading to liberation), the plural form "in the *mokṣadharma*s" (*mokṣadharmeṣu*) is used.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "The plural form 'in the *mokṣadharma*s' is due to the distinction between the dharmas."
For it is said in the Mokṣadharma:
"Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pāśupata, and the Vedāraṇyaka—these systems of knowledge are distinct; or rather, are they not? Let this be declared."
Thus there is the reply spoken by Vaiśampāyana;
and these [accounts] concern Yudhiṣṭhira and Bhīṣma as the agents.
The Lord’s various forms of knowledge and the means to that knowledge are distinct, representing different philosophical views.

Since it is impossible for all conflicting doctrines to possess validity— given that a single entity cannot possess multiple forms— it must be stated that among them, only one is valid while the others are invalid.
Regarding this, Bhīṣma and Vaiśampāyana provide the answer to the heartfelt questions of Yudhiṣṭhira and Janamejaya as to which one is valid and which is invalid.

Beginning with “Kapila is the proponent of Sāṅkhya” and ending with “of the entire Pañcarātra,” [the text] establishes that among all forms of knowledge and the means for attaining knowledge, this Pañcarātra is preeminent.
The intention is as follows: since the Pañcarātra was composed by Nārāyaṇa, the most supremely authoritative being, its validity is first established;
furthermore, when contradictory systems cannot both be valid, the validity of one necessitates the invalidity of the others.

This [interpretation] is possible only by accepting that the term *vedāraṇyaka* in the first sentence indicates the Pañcarātra rooted in the Vedas, and the term *pañcarātra* in the subsequent sentence indicates the foundational *vedāraṇyaka*, thereby establishing a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) between the two;
otherwise, since the Pañcarātra has not been previously introduced, there would result an inconsistency between the preceding and following sentences.
Furthermore, when one accepts the indicative sense (*upalakṣaṇa*) and acknowledges the syntactic unity [of the two texts], it is established that only the Veda and the Pañcarātra possess authority;
those systems such as the Pāśupata which contradict them lack authority. Thus, they are indeed invalid.
"Śāstrayoni" means that the scripture (*śāstra*) is its source (*yoni*) or means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (Sūtra 1.3)

Having thus explained the Sūtra, the author—intending to show that the claim made by another, namely that the Śāstra is the "source" (yoni), is incorrect—presents his own intended meaning with the words "The Śāstra.

With the intention that the word *yoni*, in its sense of "cause," appropriately relates to "cognition" (*jñapti*) and thus results in the meaning "the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), he has explained it as: "The source is the means of valid cognition."
Regarding the phrase "of this [Brahman], which is the cause of the world, [it is known] from the scripture" (*iti śāstrayoni*), the word *tu* (but/however) must be supplied after it.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Gītā-bhāṣya*: "But thus [is established] its having the scripture as its source" (*iti tu śāstrayonitvam*).
The meaning is precisely this:
thus, "that whose source is the scripture" (śāstrayoni) means that Brahman is the one for whom the scripture is the source—that is, the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa).
This is the meaning of the compound *śāstrayoni*, and not the meaning "the source of the scripture."
Furthermore, the interpretation by others has been refuted in the commentary itself as being both irrelevant to what was stated and logically untenable. // 3 //
Thus concludes the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with "Because [Brahman] has the scripture as its source" (Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa).
4. The Section on Endowment (Samanvayādhikaraṇa)
Even though it is perceived by those lacking knowledge, the fact that the scripture is its source does not apply to others.
Why?
Because "that [Brahman] is established through the harmony [of the texts]. (1.1.4)

In this section, by way of resolving the objection raised against the result of the preceding section—that the definition [of Brahman] suffers from over-extension because the cause of the world is known through scripture—it is established that Viṣṇu alone, and no others, is the cause of the world as accessible through scripture, thereby proving that He indeed possesses the status of being defined by that definition.
Stating the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) first, he declares the final conclusion (siddhānta): "Of the ignorant... (ajñānām).
This is a genitive in the sense of the agent;
"of the others" expresses a relationship. The particle *api*, having the sense of conjunction, is to be construed with both [terms].
Or it is characterized by traditional scripture based on [reasoning].
And thus— it is not only that which is stated by the Pāśupatas and others,
but rather [it applies to] "the ignorant."

The meaning is that the status of being the source of the scriptures— that is, being knowable through the scriptures as the cause of the world— belongs not only to Viṣṇu, but also to "others," such as Rudra and so forth, even though this may be superficially understood by those who do not know the intended meaning of the Vedas.
This is not the case.

One might ask: "Since [the world] originates from perception and so forth, which are rooted in ignorance, what is the reason for not accepting the Vedas as the source [of knowledge], while instead regarding other things as its causes? Thus he asks, "Whence?
This question connects with the phrase "even though it is being perceived.
To state the reason for that, he introduces the aphorism: "tat tu... (But that...).
In the passage beginning with "yataḥ," the term *grāhyam* (to be understood) is to be supplied.
*Anvaya* (concomitance) refers to the logical mark (*liṅga*) such as consistency (*upapatti*). He explains the words of the sūtra: "anvaya" and so forth.

*Anvaya* means that by which a scripture or a word is followed—that is, connected with its own meaning and understood as being directed toward it; the sense is that it refers to the indicative marks of *tātparya*, such as logical consistency (*upapatti*) and so forth.
The singular number is used in accordance with the Sūtra and intends the collection [of these marks] as a whole.
By this, he indicates that there is sometimes no contradiction among the [six marks], such as the introductory statement (*upakrama*), and the rest.
The term "and so forth" (*ādipada*) includes *śruti*, *liṅga*, *vākya*, *prakaraṇa*, *sthāna*, and *samākhyā* as well;
for it is stated in the *Ṭīkā* that "the group of six beginning with *śruti* is to be understood here.
Indeed, the meaning of that [statement] is that even the group of six beginning with *śruti* is to be understood by the word "and so forth" (*ādipadena*) in this sentence.

However, since the *śruti* and other criteria lack the capacity to grasp the intended meaning (*tātparya*)—unlike the *upakrama* and other indicators—and serve merely to determine the literal sense of the scripture, there is no statement here of the evidence that points toward them.
For this very reason, it will be stated later: "The *śruti*, the *liṅga*, the *samākhyā*, the *vākya*, and likewise the *prakaraṇa*..."
In determining the arrival [of a rule], each preceding one shall be stronger than the following.
He will state the authority for this point as well.

For it has been stated in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa-ṭīkā*: "The division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) is intended to indicate the distinction that while [factors] such as the opening statement (*upakrama*) serve as indicators of the purport (*tātparya*), these [others] are the purport itself.

Nor should it be argued that the statement in the *ṭīkā*—"here the group of six beginning with direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is also to be included"—is incorrect, as it would imply they are subsumed under the indicators of purport.

The meaning of the word *samanvaya* in the phrase "since [the word] here" is precisely this [meaning of "connection"], and not [the meaning of] "those which apprehend the purport," as in the cases of "Ākāśa [is Brahman], because of its characteristic mark" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.22) and "[Brahman is] known from the Word alone" (Brahma-sūtra 1.3.24).

In passages such as these, since we observe the determination of the meaning of scripture through direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth, it is appropriate that these [criteria] constitute the meaning of the word *anvaya*—based on the etymology "that by which the collection of words is known as possessing a relationship in the form of potency. Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the *Sudhā* (the commentary) on the *Jñānapāda*, which states: "Direct statement, indicative mark, syntactical connection, context, position, and name are the marks of intended meaning (*tātparya-liṅga*), along with the six criteria of beginning, conclusion, repetition, novelty, fruit, explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), and consistency (*upapatti*). This is because [the *Sudhā*] refers to those [six criteria] as marks of intended meaning in the context of determining the primary sense of a passage, whereas the present discussion concerns the relationship between words and their meanings.

In this context, because there is also a connection through *śakti* (denotative power), it is stated in the *Candrikā* that "samanvaya" is the relationship characterized by *śakti* and *tātparya* (intentional meaning), which is established by the means of proof such as the opening statement (*upakrama*).
Here, the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes *śruti* (direct assertion) and the other criteria as well.
The connection [of the words] is by way of transposition.
By this, it is indicated that the citation from the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā* here serves as an illustration for the statement to be made later, namely, "the Veda is the indicative mark" (*śrutir liṅgam*).
And it has been stated in the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā*:
The opening, the conclusion, repetition, novelty, the fruit,
the explanatory praise, and the logical justification are the marks for determining the intended meaning [of a text].
Thus [it is said].

To the question, "What are those [reasons] such as logical proof (upapatti), and where are the signs? he says: "And it has been stated. The phrase "logical proof and so forth" is to be supplied [from the previous context].
The meaning is that not only have the logical arguments (*upapatti*) and so forth been stated and indicated, but their implied significance (*tajjñāpya*) has also been explained;
or alternatively, that the logical arguments and other signs (*liṅga*) stated by us are also mentioned in the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā*.
