To address the question "What was said?", he recites the verse beginning with "upakrama" (the opening).
"Upakrama" refers to the introduction, such as the context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth; "upasaṃhāra" refers to the conclusion (*tadanta*).
Both the opening and the conclusion are expressed by those two terms respectively.

In this context, since the characteristics of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are stated as "commencement (*upakrama*), conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*), uniformity thereof (*tadaikarūpya*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), novelty (*apūrvatā*), fruit (*phala*), and explanatory praise (*arthavāda*"),

one should consider that the commencement and conclusion are distinct when intended individually, yet they form a single indicator of purport (*tātparya*) when considered as a collective— either characterized by non-contradiction between the two or characterized by a single unified meaning (*ekārthatva*).
This uniformity (*tadaikarūpya*) must also be understood as a separate indicator of purport.
For this very reason, there is the use of the dual number. Repetition (*abhyāsa*) is the repeated utterance of the same form.
Novelty (*apūrvatā*) is the capacity to convey a meaning not established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), occurring with abundance.
The "fruit" (phala) is that which conveys a meaningful result;
"praise" (stuti), "censure" (nindā), and "the account of another's deed" (parakṛti), which consists of a narrative concerning a single agent;
The *purākalpa* (ancient account), which consists of narratives concerning multiple agents,
is also an *arthavāda* (explanatory passage).
*Upapatti* is logical reasoning (*yukti*).
In the phrase "in the determination of the purport," the meaning is that it is the "mark" (liṅga), that is, the means, for ascertaining the purport of the sentence.
Alternatively, the meaning is that when the intended purport (*tātparya*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), it is "not a mark" (*aliṅga*); that is, it is not a logical reason (*hetu*).
The term *liṅga* is to be connected individually with each of the words beginning with "introductory statement" (*upakrama*), as appropriate.

Although *smṛti* is mentioned first among the criteria such as *upakrama*, the *Bhāṣya* reverses the order by stating "reasoning (*upapatti*) and so forth" in order to indicate that each subsequent criterion possesses greater authority when there is a conflict.
Furthermore, reasoning is mentioned separately from *upakrama* and the others because of its relationship as a general principle to the specific ones.

Alternatively, although this [set of criteria] beginning with *upakrama* consists of words directed toward their own primary meanings, it is here intended to refer to the [ultimate] reality; for, provided there is no sublation, it is due to the presence of these [criteria] such as *upakrama*.
In such a form, [the consistency of the meaning] also serves as an indicator (*liṅga*) for the intended purport (*tātparya*) of the sentence.

As for the logical justification (*upapatti*), just as [the meaning] exists in its actual form as fire and so forth, so too regarding the purport, [one reasons]: "This is the object of this purport, because it is logically consistent (*upapanna*). It is mentioned separately as being of the nature of an indicator (*liṅga*) in this manner.
When [the purport] is correctly determined by the indicators of purport such as the introduction (*upakrama*) and so forth, that very [purport] is what is to be understood from the scripture.
He applies the sūtra: "from the beginning" (*upakramāt*) and so forth;
the word "in the treatise" (*śāstre*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
The meaning of *sam* is "correctly" (*samyak*).
It should also be understood that this applies to "everything.
By the phrase "when being examined," the connection of the meaning of the prefix *sam-* with the supplied verb is demonstrated.
The meaning of the word "tu" (but) is precisely this:
the meaning of the connected term "śāstrayoni" (having scripture as its source) is "to be known through scripture."

And thus, since here— in this entire scripture consisting of the Ṛgveda and so forth— when it is being examined through the investigation of relative strength and weakness by means of the indicators of power and intentionality, namely direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), name (*samākhyā*), and the beginning (*upakrama*) which are termed "concordant" (*anvaya*), [the conclusion is reached that] "it is *saṃ*," meaning "perfectly" (*samyak*).

When investigated as having a single meaning, and being understood as possessing the pervading attributes consisting of power (*śakti*) and intentionality (*tātparya*), it is recognized that "that alone"—
namely, Brahman called Viṣṇu— is "accessible through scripture," meaning it is known to have that [scripture] as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It is not [the case] for Rudra and others;
therefore, the construction is that although it is perceived by the ignorant, the status of having the scripture as its source does not belong to others.

By the use of the instrumental case in "liṅgaiḥ" (by means of marks) and the locative case in "nirūpyamāṇe" (when being determined), it is indicated that the introductory passages and so forth are the grounds for the intended meaning (*tātparya*).

And it is indicated that the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is the reason for the scripture being the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The meaning of the word "concordance" (*samanvaya*) is not merely logical consistency and so forth;

rather, it is that which is caused by such [consistency], consisting in being the object of the valid cognition produced by the scripture, and serving as the reason for the scripture's status as the source [of knowledge].
This is because of the statement in the *Sudhā*: "The relationship of being intent upon that [the Supreme] also...

By this [sūtra], "on account of harmony" (*samanvayāt*), [the author] establishes the priority of determining relative strength through criteria such as having scope (*sāvakāśatva*) or lacking scope (*niravakāśatva*), and through the sublation of one or the other; thus, from the introductory passage (*upakrama*) which is characterized by correctness—consisting of a thorough investigation in the form of a reflection on the meaning of the sentence—[the conclusion is established].

Because of the "harmonious correlation" (*samanvaya*), that is, because it is understood through the connection known as "power" (*śakti*) and "purport" (*tātparya*)—by means of the proper application of words—that the entire scripture, through its power and purport, relates to the Blessed Lord alone;

therefore, Brahman called Viṣṇu alone is the source of the scripture (*śāstrayoni*) by virtue of being the cause of the universe, and not Rudra or others. This is [the meaning of] "because of the harmonious correlation."
By repeating this [verse], the application of the sūtra has been demonstrated.
"I enjoin myself, I express myself, I am that which is conceptualized and that which is excluded"—the heart of this [truth] is known directly by me alone; no one else knows it.
Thus it is said in the Bhāgavata. // 4 //

One might raise the objection: "How can a scripture consisting of injunctions regarding ritual action (karma) have Brahman as its ultimate purport? He refutes this doubt with the words of the Lord: "Mām" (Me).
Although in the *Bhāgavata* the reading is "ityasyā hṛdayaṃ loke," a reading with the two halves of the verse transposed is also observed.
Nevertheless, there is no fault, as this belongs to another ritual manual according to the teacher's statement;
these words of Kṛṣṇa were spoken to Uddhava in the eleventh book [of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa].
Here, by the word "we" (asmat), Kṛṣṇa is meant.
And likewise, the Vedic scripture that enjoins ritual action, such as "In every spring," prescribes the rite specifically with reference to "me" as being my worship;
and the scripture that names Indra and others "names me."
It expresses my qualities, such as sovereignty and so forth: "I am to be conceptualized"; conceptualization (*kalpana*) means the act of fashioning (*vidhāna*), and thus—
"Four are the measured steps of speech; those Brahmins who are wise know them.
Three, hidden in the cave, do not stir; the fourth of speech, humans speak. (Ṛgveda 1.164.45).
According to this Śruti, Hari—who is called "speech" (vāk) because he is the speaker or the instrumental cause of speech—has "measured steps" (aparimitāni) in view of his various locations.
"The four defined quarters" refers to the forms of Vāsudeva and the others; only those wise ones who are Brāhmaṇas know them.
Among these, the three forms beginning with Vāsudeva are deposited within the cave of the heart of speech, while "human beings" [know] the remaining one.
The common [states] "do not stir"; they do not know.
But they "speak of the fourth," which is called the unceasing (aniruddha).
The meaning is that I alone am to be enjoined as a plurality, through various forms such as Vāsudeva and the others, characterized by the number four, in the form "I am indeed [the knower]."
In such statements as "I am to be avoided" and "One should not drink liquor" (Manu 11.94), the word "unpleasant" (*apriya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

And likewise, according to the statement in the *Bhāgavata-tātparya*, "That which is the object of the cognition of negation is indeed remembered as being displeasing to Hari," drinking liquor and so forth are prohibited because they are means for my displeasure;
thus, by way of being displeasing, it is I myself who am the object of prohibition in such injunctions as "One should not drink liquor. This is the meaning.

Alternatively—the meaning is that I am to be excluded from, or set aside from, that which is unpleasant to me, namely the drinking of *surā* (liquor) as designated [in scripture]; for, by reflecting that "the qualities of Hari may be my *surā*," one must exclude or prohibit that [liquor] in comparison to those [divine qualities].
As it has been stated in the *Bhāgavata-tātparya*: "Conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is the imagining [of something] in a positive form, such as 'Speech is fourfold,' and so on.
In that context, the word "speech" (*vāk*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
"In the portion concerning injunctions, it is the worship of Hari; in description, His qualities;
in the case of alternatives, their multiplicity; and in the case of negation (apoha), that which is displeasing to Him.
This is declared in all the Vedas, for He alone indeed knows them. Thus it is said. Furthermore—
"The contemplation, 'May those qualities of Hari, which are called *surā*, be mine'—this is declared to be the drinking of *surā*; one should never do that.
However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, it says: "'There are indeed two forms of Brahman'..."

Having thus reflected and conceptualized in various ways, the meaning stated is that "in that regard, he for whom there is a self" (*Talavakāra Brāhmaṇa*)— though [the self] is to be excluded as being defective, it is to be enjoined as being faultless; and that very [self] is I myself.
In this regard, according to the *Tattvapradīpa* position, there is the suffix *-lyap* in the word "vikalpya.

However, according to the *Ṭīkā* author's position, the distinction is whether the word "vikalpya" is contained within a compound or is used as a separate word (*vyasta*). And this [refers] to the Blessed One.
The method of syntactical connection (*vākyasamanvayarīti*) is as follows: the first occurrence of the word *iti* has the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*) and is connected with the word *hṛdayam*.
The second has the sense of "being of such a nature.

Thus, [the phrase] "of this scripture"—which is of such a nature, consisting of injunctions, prohibitions, and so forth, and which is perceived as having another primary intent—[is said to] "enjoin me."
In the manner described above, "the heart" means the intended meaning; "I alone know"— that is,
I understand— "no one other than me."
"Anyone" means that, for the most part, no one knows [it] specifically;

since it was stated immediately after the word "devotee of the Lord" (bhāgavata) that "that very thing is accessible through scripture," there is no room for the doubt "how [is this so]?"—this is the remainder of the sentence. // 4 //
Thus ends the section on Concordance (Samanvayādhikaraṇa).
// 5. The Section Concerning the Contemplation (Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa) //
Is it not said: "From which words turn back, together with the mind, failing to reach it"?
(Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1)
In this section, the expressibility denoted by the prefix *sam-* and its totality are raised as objections and then resolved.
He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "But surely" (*nanu*),
referring to such scriptural passages as "by these and other śrutis."
Thus, [the word] has the sense of the third and fifth cases.
The phrase "not" (na) and so forth is repeated;
and thus [it refers to] "that" (tat).

The cause spoken of in the previous sūtra—that which is denoted by the word "That" (tat), which is the object of the word "Brahman," and which is taught in the scriptures—is not [the primary meaning]. Why?
Because that which is the object of words is not the primary meaning of the scripture.
And why is that so?
Because it is not within the range of words and is inexpressible by words, yet there is no contradiction with its being visible, since that [invisibility] is unestablished.
Why? Because it is not the object of a cognition that does not have that as its range.
This means "it is unknowable.
Nor is there any lack of proof for its ineffability and unknowability,
as the construction [of the argument] is based on such scriptural passages as, "From which words turn back," and so forth.
The point is that in the statement "whence words turn back" (*yato vācaḥ*), its ineffability (*avācyatva*) is expressed, and in "without reaching [it] with the mind" (*aprāpya manasā saha*),
its unknowability (*ajñeyatva*) is stated. Furthermore,

because the word *gocara* is used here in the feminine gender to agree with its substantive in "the triple Veda is not within the range of hearing" (*trayī na śrutigocarā*), the form "not within the range of that word" (*na tacchabdagocaram*) is grammatically correct.

In the *Sudhā*, however, the correctness of the term *śabdagocara* has been explained by resorting to a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi*— namely, that in which there is the moving (*cara*), that is, the movement (*caraṇa*) or activity, of words (*śabda*) and cows (*go*), i.e., cognitions (*jñāna*)— and by treating it as ending in the possessive suffix *ac* (in the sense of "possessing"), namely, "that which has moving/coursing as its attribute. Thus, the form *śabdagocara* is established as grammatically valid.
The Taittirīya passage "yataḥ" means:
from whom [the Vedas]— that is, the Vedas and the organs of speech— and the mind,
along with the organ in the form of the mind, having failed to reach Him.
They cease [from fear] precisely because they do not know the knowledge of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) having that as its object.
The meaning is: "The knower of that bliss of Brahman does not fear.
This has been illustrated by relying on the non-difference between the quality and the possessor of the quality.
"That which is soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying, likewise tasteless, eternal, and odorless" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.15).
"Soundless"— this is the statement from the Kaṭha [Upaniṣad].
In all these cases, the word "yat" (that which) should be supplied.
That in which no sound, quality, or means of valid cognition exists is described as such.
The meaning is that it is devoid of the qualities of ordinary sound, is not an object of the means of valid cognition regarding sound, and is distinct from sound.
"Intangible" (*asparśam*) means devoid of the quality of touch; for that very reason, it is not an object of the mark of touch and is distinct from it.

"Formless" (*arūpam*) means devoid of color; for that very reason, it is not an object of visual perception and is distinct from it. "Tasteless" (*arasam*) means devoid of the quality of taste and distinct from taste.
This also serves as an indicator for "without odor" (*agandha*);
by this, its distinctness from the five elements is also stated.
It is "imperishable" (*avyaya*) and "eternal" (*nitya*).
Thus, by means of "light," its freedom from destruction is stated both in terms of its essential nature (*svarūpa*) and its physical form (*deha*).
By the expression "like that which has no odor" (*agandhavat*), its characteristic of being unlike the earth, which possesses odor, is stated.
By this illustration, its distinctness from the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*) is also implied.
Its connection is with the phrase: "Having realized Him, one is released from the jaws of death.
[And] "He spoke by means of silence alone."
(Bāṣkala Śruti):
"'By means of non-speaking'"; this is another scriptural statement.
"'By means of non-speaking'": even without the function of speech, the Guru taught Brahman through indication (lakṣaṇā).
The meaning [of the statement] "he taught it to his disciple" is according to the perspective of others.

Alternatively, by such scriptural passages as, "That which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed... that which one does not hear with the ear, but by which this ear is heard," it is not within the range of words.
The phrase "that which by speech" refers to another statement from the *Talavakāra*:
"by speech"—that is, by the sound to be uttered—"that which is unuttered," meaning that which has not been spoken;
that by which speech itself is "uttered," meaning by which it is made to speak.
The meaning is: "A person does not hear with the sense-organ of hearing;
know that by which this hearing is heard to be Brahman itself.
In this context, according to the method of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is a negation of the operation of speech.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādipadena*), scriptural passages of this kind are included.
He says: "No; because of seeing, [Brahman] is not that which is not based on scripture" (*īkṣater nāśabdam*). (BS 1.1.5)
"He beholds the Person dwelling in the city, who is higher than the highest mass of life" (Praśna 5.5);
"One should see the Self in the self alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.23);
"Having known [this], one should exercise wisdom" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.21).
Because it must be seen according to such statements as these, it is indeed expressible; thus, he introduces the aphorism that establishes the final conclusion: "No."
The word *iti* recurs [in the sūtra].

Thus, the meaning here is that the author of the Sūtras negates—by means of the word *na*—"not so"—the Brahman's inexpressibility as asserted by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), which was derived from a failure to understand the intended purport of the Śruti.
He recites the Sūtra: "Because of seeing" (*īkṣateḥ*).
Here, the word "that" (tat) is carried over [from the previous rule].
And that [word], which until the end of the chapter serves to present the thing to be enjoined, here serves to present the subject of the proposition (*uddeśya*).
That which has no expressive word is "non-verbal" (*aśabda*).
And thus, that Brahman is not "wordless," meaning it is not inexpressible by words.
But it must indeed be stated.
Why? Because of "seeing" (īkṣateḥ). This is a reference to a verbal root.
It is just as stated in the *Sudhā*:
nevertheless, since a mere word is not a proof, its meaning is indicated by it;
by that [indication], what is intended to be expressed is the state of being worthy of observation due to its suitability for the subject at hand.

And likewise, regarding the [sūtra] "Because of seeing" (*īkṣateḥ*), with the intention that it means "because of being worthy of being seen," i.e., because of being an object of knowledge, he explains the sūtra with the words "He" (*sa*). And this is the statement consisting of six questions.

In this regard, the preceding passage states: "Furthermore, he who meditates upon the Supreme Person by means of this very syllable *oṃ* consisting of three measures—he, having attained the sun, just as a snake is freed from its slough, is indeed freed from evil; he is led up by the Sāman chants to the world of Brahman. Thus, it refers to that which was introduced in the prior text as the *praṇava*, endowed with the three parts known as the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*.

Having meditated upon the Supreme Self and realized it directly, the individual soul who worships the Praṇava—freed from sin like a snake that has cast off its skin—is united with the Sun, which is of the nature of light; then, together with the deities presiding over the Sāman chants, he reaches the world of Brahmā known as Satya.
From "this," namely from the "mass of living beings" (jīvaghana)—the essence of individual souls and the most excellent of them—he [proceeds].
Through that instruction from the Four-faced One (Brahmā),
[he realized] the "Person" (Puruṣa) who is higher than the high, who dwells in the city (the body), and who resides within the entire body.
"He beholds" (īkṣate) Pūrṇa Vāsudeva, the Supreme Self;
the meaning is that he knows Him.
Although it is stated in the *Ṣaṭpraśnabhāṣya* that [one attains Him] "from Viriñca, who is a mass of individual souls (jīvaghana), by means of meditation upon Him,"...
"Furthermore, one whose knowledge has increased beholds [it];

and having beheld it, he attains it. From this statement, it is understood that the root *īkṣ* signifies immediate, direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*). Nevertheless, this scriptural passage is cited here in order to avoid the fallacy of the unestablished reason (*asiddhi*)—namely, that the object of the root *īkṣ* is merely general knowledge—as asserted in the original [Mīmāṃsā] text.

Because of the commentary’s statement, "by means of the instruction on Hiraṇyagarbha," and because it accords with the context here, *īkṣati* (the act of seeing) should be explained as having the sense of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*).
The other Kāṇva passage, "in the Self" (*ātmani*), has been explained in the *Jijñāsā-naya*;
the other Vājasaneya passage is "having known" (*vijñāya*).

The wise Brahmin, steadfast in Brahman, having "known" (vijñāya)— that is, having known through scripture or from a teacher— that very Supreme Self (tam) as the Transcendent (parokṣataḥ), [attains] wisdom (prajñām).
The meaning is that one should "perform" or accomplish the supreme knowledge born of discrimination (*apokṣajñāna*).
The phrase "and so forth" refers to this.

The meaning is "by such statements as these. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [statements such as] "Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5) and "The unborn, great, eternal Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.20) are included.
The passage beginning with "Having known that very [Self], the wise man" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.21) is taken [as the subject],
because it is something to be beheld.
This is an indicator of comprehension;
otherwise, there would be no logical connection (*anvaya*).
By this, the fault of being unestablished (*asiddhi*) is avoided.
The phrase "because it cannot be otherwise" (tadanyathānupapatteḥ) is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The expression "it must indeed be denotable" (vācyam eva) states the meaning obtained from the two negative particles in the sūtra;
the sense of the word "indeed" (eva) is that it is neither undenotable nor even suggestible (lakṣya).
The word "that" (tat) is connected with this [word "seeing"].
The statement in the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya reverses the order of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) in order to indicate that there is no fixed rule [regarding their sequence].
Because [the Self] is known through the Upaniṣads, it cannot be seen by means of verbal instruction alone.

[Objection: Let it be granted that Brahman is to be seen; nevertheless, its being denotable (vācyatva) cannot be established by the fact that otherwise [its being seen] would be inexplicable, because its being seen is possible even through perception and other means. To this, he says: "Because it is known through the Upaniṣads" (aupaniṣadatvāt).
The word "tat" (it) is to be understood as following here, having been modified [to "tasmāt"].
And thus, because that Brahman is "derived from the Upaniṣads"— that is, because it is to be understood solely through the Upaniṣads— it is [to be known] "without words."
The meaning is that "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) is not knowledge [attained] by means other than verbal testimony (*vacana*).

Thus, the sense is that the expressibility (*vācyatva*) of Brahman is indeed established through the otherwise inexplicability of its being an object of seeing characterized by its non-cognizability through perception and other means when devoid of the assistance of Śruti and Smṛti.

Alternatively, this may be explained by repeating it with the intent of establishing it through the remaining means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The construction [of the argument] is as follows: the "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) mentioned in the Vedic texts regarding Brahman must indeed occur through a means of valid cognition;
and among the means of valid cognition that have been proposed, [it cannot be established] "without a statement" (*avacanena*).

Observation by means other than verbal testimony is not possible because [the Self] is known through the Upaniṣads; its observation occurs only through verbal testimony and not without it, nor through other modes such as indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) which function differently from direct verbal expression.
Why? Because the term "without words" (*avacanena*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the predominant factor.
Since it is characterized by being "non-verbal" (*avacana*) and "inexpressible" (*avācya*), it follows by process of elimination that this very [state] establishes its expressibility (*vācyatva*).
Thus: "That state which all the Vedas seek, and which all austerities proclaim... (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.15).

Now, one might object: "How can the ineffability established by scripture (śruti) be refuted by mere reasoning regarding its being perceivable, given the statement that 'the authority of scripture alone is supreme'? To address this, with the intention that the reason stated in the Sūtra is indicative of scripture, [the author] cites Śruti and Smṛti concerning its expressibility: "All... [etc.].
This is the Śruti of the Kaṭhas:
"All the Vedas proclaim that state," which is the essential nature of Brahman.
All the Vedas and all the well-known ascetic practices, with their primary function and full intent,
declare that which is Brahman.
The meaning is that they indicate for what purpose [the rites] are to be performed;
or, according to the *Tattvapradīpa*, "austerities" (*atapāṃsi*) refers to arguments in the form of observations (*ālocana*).
"I alone am to be known by all the Vedas as the primary object of exposition;
I am the author of the Vedānta."
The meaning of the *Gītā-smṛti* is that the author of the *Brahmasūtra* is both a "knower of the Veda" (*vedavit*) and a "knower of the meaning of the Veda" (*vedārthajñānī*).
From the word "etc. (*ādi*), [it is understood that] the passage beginning with "Now, for what reason is it called... [is also included].
This is a summary of such passages as "all names" and "the supreme object of all speech."
And likewise, because the Śruti directly states that [Brahman] is denotable by saying "they declare," and the Smṛti says "I alone."

The sense is this: since it is necessary to intend "being the object of knowledge" (*vedyatva*) in its primary sense in order to justify the restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*), and since that [primary sense] is impossible without being denotable (*vācyatva*), and because secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by all words is impossible, it follows that denotability itself is established by these two [reasons].
The phrase "and from the Smṛtis" is to be construed with the words "it is indeed denotable."

The plural number is used with reference to the various Śruti and Smṛti texts implied by the word "ādi" (and so forth). The meaning of the particle "ca" (and) is that [I am to be known] not only for the reason of being worthy of contemplation. As it is said: "By all the Vedas, I alone am to be known; I am the author of the Vedānta and the knower of the Vedas."
This is also established by such scriptural and traditional texts as Bhagavadgītā 15.15;
furthermore, attributes such as "ineffability" are not applicable because they are unestablished.

Now, if expressibility (*vācyatva*) is thus established by reasoning and other means, what is the status of the cited scriptural passages such as "from which speech turns back" (*yato vāco nivartante*), which declare inexpressibility and unknowability?
To this, he says: "Inexpressibility and so forth.
The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes unknowability (*ajñeyatva*) and unthinkability (*atarkyatva*).
The word "tu" (but) serves to dispel doubt, or it indicates emphasis with a shifted word-order. Thus,

because [Brahman] is not established as an object in its entirety— that is, because it is beyond the range of the senses— it follows that Brahman possesses such qualities as "ineffability" based solely on that very reason.
The sense is that the designation of "ineffability" and so forth is appropriate, and thus there is no contradiction with that [scriptural statement].

By this, in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), since [the term] "without words" (*aśabda*) and so on is not well-known in its literal sense, the meaning is that it is entirely devoid of expressive words, and so forth.
Regarding the term "by means of non-utterance" (*avacanena*), its meaning is stated to be "without uttering [it] in its entirety.
"It should be known that it is not like this; it cannot be expressed, nor can it be conceptualized.
Even the wise, though looking, do not see the form of Meru."
As in the case of [the expression] "it is like this."

To the question, "Where has this designation such as 'ineffability' (avācyatva) been seen to be based on non-apprehension? he says: "Not that..."—because even when the wise (*vipaścit*), the knowers, behold the form of Meru, they do not perceive it as being "like this."
"In their entirety, they do not see"; that is, they do not know. By this, the reason of non-establishment (*aprasiddhatva*) is indicated.
Therefore, the form of Meru is not cognizable through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
It is not to be expressed by words;
the meaning is that it is "not reasoned" (tarkyate) and "not inferred" (anumīyate) by means of a logical mark (liṅga).
The phrase "itivad" means "as in the sentence.
Its connection with the preceding clause is: "[the fact that] this [Self] is inexpressible, and so forth."
And thus, the sense is that just as there are designations such as "inexpressible" based on the cause of non-recognition regarding the form of Mount Meru, so it is also with Brahman.
"It is inexpressible because it is not commonly known; it is expressible because it is taught in all the scriptures.
It is inconceivable yet conceivable, unknowable yet knowable—thus is the Supreme remembered."
Thus it is said in the Gāruḍa [Purāṇa].

The established conclusion— that the designations "unestablished," "unknowable," "inconceivable," and "inexpressible" are not based solely on the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the statement "they see," but rather that these terms are also established by tradition (smṛti)— is stated with this intention: "Because of its being unestablished."
That Brahman is "supreme" because it is full; therefore, because it is not known in its entirety, it is said to be "inexpressible.
Alternatively, because it is declared in all the true scriptures (sadāgama) and is thus well-known, it is also "expressible"—this is the meaning.

"Thus, by way of both non-establishment and establishment, that [reality] is remembered as being beyond reasoning and yet inferable, unknowable and yet knowable, and accessible through the direct perception of the wise;
the meaning is that this was stated by the authors of the Smṛtis.
The word 'in the Gāruḍa' is followed by the ellipsis 'it was stated.'"
The phrase "its [the word] also being inexpressible, etc. connects with this.
Furthermore, its lack of being a word is not established by anything else.

Thus, having explained the Sūtra— stating that Brahman is not inexpressible by words because other meanings [of the scriptural passages] are possible through the force of reasoning and so forth regarding such Śruti texts as "whence speech turns back"— he rejects the misinterpretation with the words "And not" (na ca).
The word "and" (ca) serves to include the negation "not" (na), even though its establishment is already evident.
And thus, the cause of the world is not the Pradhāna, which is "without scriptural authority"; why? Because that [Pradhāna] is indeed without scriptural authority.

"Non-audible" means that the *pradhāna* is not the cause; why? "Because of seeing"; for it is heard that the cause of the world is the agent of seeing, as in the text, "It thought," and since this is impossible for the *pradhāna* because it is insentient—thus, in the explanation intended to refute the Sāṅkhya position, regarding the first proposition...
"Being non-verbal" is made the reason;
"not being based on the Veda" is established by the other.
It is not established by any other Sāṅkhya school,
nor is it merely that; furthermore, it is not even established by its own [system].
This is because the Sāṅkhya system accepts its own Vedic character,
as the author of the Sūtras acknowledges that [the doctrine] is stated in such Śrutis as "The one unborn female" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.10.1).

Alternatively, according to the *Tattvapradīpa*, the argument based on "not being mentioned in the scriptures" (*aśabdatva*) put forward by the Māyāvādin against the Sāṅkhya is not established for the Sāṅkhya who is other than the Māyāvādin, nor is it established for the Māyāvādin who is other than the Sāṅkhya, precisely because of the reasons stated above;
thus, the meaning is that such an interpretation is not tenable, as it results in the fallacy of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*).
In this way, the fact that Brahman is "not mentioned in the scriptures"—that is, its lack of scriptural authority—is not established for the Māyāvādin who is other than the Sāṅkhya.
According to that view, [the Lord] is inexpressible; furthermore,
it should be explained that even the status of being a "Beholder" (īkṣitṛtva) is not established, because His essential nature is that of pure "Beholding" (īkṣati).

Thus, the sense is that since both reasons are contrary to one's own position, the interpretation of others is not tenable. However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, the commentary beginning with "And not" (*na ca*) explains that "established by the other" (*itarasiddham*) means that the quality of being non-verbal (*aśabdatvam*), as established by the Māyāvādin, is not the meaning of the scripture; for, according to the reasoning already stated, Brahman is indeed denotable (*vācyatvāt*).

Thus, having explained in two ways that "the state of being beyond words" (*aśabdatvam*)— that is, the ineffability of Brahman— is not established even for the other [proponent], the proponent of *māyā*, because it would entail the consequence of an absence of linguistic usage regarding Brahman, he has also provided an explanation intended to state the non-establishment of the reason put forward by the opponent, according to the method of the commentator (*ṭīkākāra*), in order to refute the interpretation offered by another.
"If it be argued that [the term 'Self'] is secondary, we say no, because of the word 'Self'.

(BS 1.1.6) This sūtra is intended to resolve the objection that the reason—being "worthy of being seen"—is unestablished due to a difference in substratum. Its meaning is as follows: "Because one should see the Self in the Self alone."

If it is argued that the Self described in such scriptural passages as "the Self is non-figurative" refers only to the individual soul (jīva) bound by qualities such as *sattva*, and therefore—since the [other] meaning would otherwise be untenable—that very soul must be the primary referent and not the qualityless Supreme Self; we say no. Why? Because [the scripture says]:
"One should see the Self."
"Thus, because the word 'Self' (ātman) is heard in reference to that which is to be seen.
[The masculine gender is used] "for the sake of grammatical coordination with the word 'Self'.
Nor is it logical to claim that the Self is figurative, visible, expressible, or devoid of attributes (nirguṇa).
From the word "self" (ātman). He explains the Sūtra: "And not... Here, [the phrase] "because it is invisible" (yato 'dṛśyaḥ) [is used].
In the scriptural passage concerning "seeing," the "Self" is described as being visible;

this refers only to the secondary (gauṇa) Self known as the individual soul (jīva). Therefore, by the very necessity of accounting for that [visibility], even the primary referent must be that same [individual soul] and not the "devoid of attributes" (nirguṇa) Viṣṇu who transcends all qualities. Thus, Viṣṇu is not the "visible" one.
The meaning is that [the Self] is described by the scriptural text concerning "seeing" (īkṣati),
because there is no subverting argument against taking it in its primary sense, nor is there any other indicator [to the contrary].
Therefore, the objection that "it cannot be so expressed" is not tenable.
Why? "Because of the word 'Self'";
for in the statement "in the Self alone," since the word 'Self' is heard in reference to that which is to be seen, the object of vision is indeed the one devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Therefore, the construction is that by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of "seeing," that very [Brahman] must also be the primary denotation (*vācya*).

Although in the *Sudhā* commentary the term "secondary" (*gauṇa*) was explained as referring to the qualified Brahman (*saguṇabrahman*) endowed with attributes such as sovereignty mixed with *māyā*, nevertheless, for the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), it is either the Brahman mixed with *māyā*, or the individual souls (*jīva*) bound by qualities, or the objects of perception (*dṛśya*) that are the primary denotations.

There is no contradiction, because the intention is that Brahman is not devoid of qualities in every respect. "That which is entirely destitute of qualities, yet free from defects, and devoid of both the rejectable and the acceptable— that is designated as the Self."
That which has a nature other than this [self] is "non-self"—this is the view of the wise;
however, the word "self" is applied to what is non-self only figuratively.
Thus it is stated in the Vāmana [Purāṇa].
Now, one might ask: "Even if the word 'Self' (ātman) exists [in this context], why is this [Self] devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and not figurative (gauṇa)? To this he says:
"He who..."—meaning he who, in every respect, [is distinct] from the qualities (guṇas).
That which is empty of existence and so forth, which is free from defects such as suffering and the like, and which is devoid of both the rejectable and the acceptable;
this [compound] has the abstract state (bhāva) as its primary meaning,
namely, being devoid of acceptability accompanied by rejectability.
The meaning is that [the Lord] is indeed to be accepted (*upādeya*).

Alternatively, according to the *Tattvapradīpa*, because He is free from natural defects and, being full of qualities, has all His desires fulfilled, He is "without anything to be rejected" (*upādeyarahita*).
Or, according to the *Tattvodyota-ṭīkā*, because of the absence of defects or the absence of a substrate (*dhātu*), He is "devoid of the state of being rejectable" (*heyatvarahita*).

Because of the absence of worldly qualities, or because of the absence of any other independent entity distinct from the grasper, it is devoid of the state of being an object to be grasped; because of the absence of anything undesirable, there is nothing to be abandoned; or because of the absence of any lack of fulfillment, it is said that for him there is nothing to be acquired. That which is thus characterized is designated as the "Self."
The meaning is that it is the established and accepted view of the wise that whatever possesses a nature contrary to this [definition] is "non-self" (anātman).

This is because, in certain instances— such as in the passage beginning "For this Self is in the heart"— the term "Self" (ātman) is applied even to that which has a nature other than this [true Self].
How is it that he is "not-self"? To this he says: "in what is not-self.

Regarding the phrase "in what is not-self" (*anātmani*): the word "self" (*ātma-śabda*) is used "metaphorically" (*sopacāraḥ*) for the living being (*jīva*), which is distinct from the primary meaning of the word "self."

"Metaphorical usage" (upacāra) means a secondary application of a word other than its primary sense, accompanied by that [primary sense]; the meaning is "possessing that mode of application. The word "but" (tu) is for the sake of distinction.
After the word "in Vāmana," the phrase "because he is stated to be solely devoted to the qualityless [Brahman]" is to be supplied as a complement.
This [Self] is neither perceptible nor expressible through qualities;
rather, it is connected with the phrase "indeed devoid of qualities" (nirguṇa eva).
"There are indeed two forms of Brahman: the Self (ātman) and the non-Self (anātman).
Of these, that which is the Self is eternal, pure, absolute, and devoid of qualities;
whereas that which is not like this is the non-Self."
Thus ends the Talavakāra Brāhmaṇa.
In this very context, he states another authority: "There are indeed two," etc. The "forms" (rūpe) of "Brahman"—that is, of the Supreme Brahman—are its two forms.

In this context, the first word "rūpa" refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*), while the second, derived from the etymology "that which is manifested or known as Brahman," refers to an image or representation (*pratimā*). The particle "vāva" is a collection of indeclinables used to indicate well-known fact. He shows those two forms with the word "ātman."
The meaning is that [the Self] is both the primary denotation of the word "ātman" and that which is not denoted by it.
In this context, between the two [meanings of] "ātman," the construction is: "He who... (sa yaḥ).
Otherwise, there would be redundancy;
and thus, "he" (*saḥ*) refers to what is well-known, while "this" (*ayaḥ*) refers to what is being pointed out.

The Self (ātman), which is the primary referent of the word "Self," is Viṣṇu; He is "eternal" (nitya), being devoid of the destruction of the body and so forth; "pure" (śuddha), being free from the taint of karma; and "absolute" (kevala).
"Mixed with the insentient" means "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇa*), that is to say, bound by the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva* and the rest;
the particle *ca* is used for the conjunction of qualifiers.

Having thus demonstrated the meaning of the term "Self" (ātman) as first introduced by way of its definition, he now shows the non-Self (anātman) by way of the exclusion of the aforementioned definition— beginning with the word "atha" (now).
Since the Self is of such a nature, "therefore, that which is not like this" [is the non-Self].

The meaning is that it is well-known among the wise that "that which is devoid of eternality and so forth is non-self. After the word "Brāhmaṇa," the ellipsis is to be supplied as: "because it declares that Viṣṇu alone, who is devoid of attributes, is the Self."
The syntactical connection here is also "in the case of the dwarf" (*vāmane*). And when the primary sense is possible, a secondary sense is not appropriate.

Now, one might object: "Since the word 'self' (ātman) is indeed used in a figurative sense through metaphorical application, why could that very self mentioned in the scripture not be the visible object? To this he says: "And not" (na ca). The meaning is: since the primary sense of the word 'self'—the attributeless reality which is presented by the scripture as the object of seeing—is possible, it is not appropriate to resort to a non-primary, figurative meaning.
Here, by the word "since" (sati), the reason known as "the possibility of the primary sense" is stated.

By the statement "it is not logical that [the Self] is non-primary," the thesis is established. The word *ca* (and) signifies either a conjunction of both [the two reasons] or a conjunction of the doubt and its refutation. // 6 // "Because liberation is taught for one who is intent upon That. (BBs 1.1.7)
But surely, why could the word *ātman* not primarily refer to a secondary self?

Nor is there a contradiction with the aforementioned Śruti and Smṛti, because it has not been stated that the word *ātman* is primary in reference to Viṣṇu, who is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), and secondary in reference to individual souls (*jīva*); for it is possible for both the words *ātman* and *anātman* to have sentient and insentient entities as their respective objects.
Furthermore: if the words "self" (ātman) and "non-self" (anātman) refer to the well-known sentient and insentient [respectively], there is straightforwardness (ārjava) for the Śruti,
because it does not abandon its well-known meanings and because one does not have to postulate multiple meanings for the word "form" (rūpa).

Nor is it the case that the soul (jīva) cannot be described as faultless; for since defects such as suffering are merely adventitious (aupādhika), scripture’s declaration of the soul’s faultlessness by its very nature (svabhāvataḥ) is shown to refer to its essential nature. To dispel this doubt, the author recites the Sūtra: "Om. For one who is established in That, [the previous statement] applies.
(Brahma-sūtra 4.1.3).

And thus— the meaning of the Sūtra is that because liberation is taught for one who is "devoted to That" (tanniṣṭhasya), this knower of the Self does not refer to the secondary [meaning] of the word "Self," but rather to its primary denotation.

For there is no liberation for one who is established in a secondary (gauṇa) self. Anticipating the objection as to why this self is not secondary even though liberation is taught for one established in it—thereby rendering the argument inconclusive—the author says: "For not...
Here, the word *hi* (for), used in conjunction with the term "secondary liberation," indicates the reason known as contradiction (*virodha*).

And thus: "For" (hi); because for one who is "established in the secondary self"—that is, for a knower of the individual soul bound by the qualities—liberation, which consists in the cessation of bondage to the qualities through that knowledge, is not possible.
Because of this contradiction, [the phrase] "for not" (na hi) is used;

the meaning is that one should not suspect the reason [of the argument] to be unestablished (*aprayojaka*). He whose Self has been perceived and awakened, having entered into this dense thicket of doubt—
"He is the maker of all, for he is the creator of everything; his is the world, and he indeed is the world" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.13);
thus, liberation is taught for one who is established in the Self.

In order to dispel the doubt regarding non-establishment— namely, what this instruction on liberation residing in the Self is— he shows it by means of the words "Of whom" (*yasya*). Here, the Śruti explains the word *u* used by itself as meaning "alone" (*eka*) or "the primary one" (*pradhāna*).
The word "tat" (that) refers to Viṣṇu and his knower;
and thus— "hi" means because "saḥ" (He),
Viṣṇu, is "the creator of all."
Therefore, he alone is the "creator of all," the maker of Vāyu, the "awakened," and by his own nature omniscient, within this collection [of doubts].

Or, because the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is gathered by means of it, or because it consists of the aggregate of cause and effect, or because it consists of the collection of elements, it is situated in the "dense" middle body named *sandoha*;
having entered the "deep" place of the cave of the heart (*hṛdayaguhā*),
that is the "Self" (*ātman*).
Viṣṇu is "of whom"; by which worshiper he is "known," that is, correctly understood; "of him."
The word "u" refers to the qualified person;
the meaning is that his very world— that which is the world of Viṣṇu— is his world, that is, his abode.
Even with the reading *saṃdoghe*, the meaning is the same; however, with the reading *saṃdehe*, the meaning is "in a state of confusion regarding multiple meanings.
In the *Tattvapradīpa*, however, it says: "He is the creator of the universe, one who has accomplished all that was to be done."
Why? Because it has been stated that when that Supreme Self is pleased, being omnipotent, He performs every task for this knower;
in this interpretation, the first occurrence of the word *tat* (He) ending in the nominative case refers to the knower of Viṣṇu, and the word *viśva* (all) refers to the tasks to be done.
The word "all" (sarva) refers to those who possess knowledge and perform their duties;
however, according to the commentator's view, the first [word] refers to Viṣṇu as the subject matter at hand,
while the word "universe" (viśva) refers to Vāyu.
The distinction is that the word "all" (sarva) refers to the entire world.
In both positions, the second and third [words] refer to Viṣṇu and His world.
Thus, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, regarding the phrase "of one established in the Self" (ātmaniṣṭhasya):
"From that [Self], the knowledge of which liberation is taught";
since this [Self] is taught as the source (yataḥ), it follows by connection with the subsequent proposition to be stated— that "therefore the Self is not secondary."
However, the connection with the preceding [argument] is that the word "self" (*ātman*) in the Sūtra is not used in a figurative sense.
By the phrase "as the self," it is stated that the pronoun *tat* in the Sūtra does not refer to the word "self," but rather, by implication, refers to the primary "Self."
"This Self is Brahman" (Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 1.2; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.19).

Regarding the fact that the word "Self" (ātman) is primary only for Viṣṇu and not for individual souls (jīvas), the proof is not only the inference stated in the passage beginning with "of one who is devoted to That," but also the clear Śruti and Smṛti texts intended by the author of the Sūtras; with this intention, he cites those various texts, beginning with "This... (ayam).

The connection with the preceding [phrase] is that "it is taught as ending with *brahma*. The meaning of the *Māṇḍūkya-śruti* is: "'This Self' (*ayam ātmā*)"—the Self who exists as the agent of taking up [the world] and so forth among Ramā, Brahmā, and others—is *Brahma*, that is, Viṣṇu alone.
“As this very Viṣṇu, who is always present as Ramā, Brahmā, Rudra, Ananta, and so forth,
is the Self because he is the agent of both taking up and not taking up,” as stated in the Māṇḍūkya-bhāṣya;
he is designated by the terms ‘Brahman,’ ‘Paramātman,’ and ‘Bhagavān.’
He gave [these] to Durvāsas, Soma, Ātman, Īśa, and Brahmā.
O Lord, the conscious principle is said to be twofold: as the individual soul (jīva) and as the Self (ātman).
Brahmā and the others are called jīvas, while Janārdana alone is the one Ātman.
In other cases, however, the word "self" (ātman) is used figuratively;
liberation is declared to result from the knowledge of that self which is devoid of qualities.
Others, however, have declared that there are deities possessing qualities (saguṇa), but one is not liberated by knowledge of them;
for Viṣṇu is the Supreme Person (puruṣa), and from Him liberation is traditionally taught to arise.
Thus it is stated in the Padma Purāṇa.
“The knowers of reality declare that reality is non-dual knowledge,
which is Brahman”— this is another statement from the *Bhāgavata*.
That reality which the wise describe as non-dual— meaning devoid of anything equal or superior— and whose nature is knowledge, exists [unchanged] throughout space, time, and so forth.

Because he is magnified and because he possesses qualities such as sovereignty through his state of being the inner ruler of all, he is "designated" by the terms "Brahman," "Paramātman," and "Bhagavān"; the meaning is that he is denoted by these words.
This also connects with what precedes it.
In that very same fourth *skandha*, there is another sentence: "Datta," and so forth.
And this [is stated in the verse]: "Anasūyā likewise bore to Atri sons free from stain."
This is to be connected with the first half-verse alone:
"Marīci’s wife, Sukalā, the daughter of Kardama,
gave birth to Kāśyapa and Pūrṇimāna, by whom the world was filled."
Thus, the word "tathā" (likewise) has the sense of conjunction with what precedes.
And so: Anasūyā, the wife of Atri, [obtained] from Atri those who were "born of Ātman, Īśa, and Brahmā";

that is, Ātman is Viṣṇu, Īśa is Rudra, and Brahmā is the four-faced one; they are thus called "Ātman, Īśa, and Brahmā," and those who exist together with them are "born of Ātman, Īśa, and Brahmā. [She obtained] those "who are free from blemish."
Durvāsas and Soma begot these sons—Apāpa, Datta, and others; that is, they brought them forth.
Alternatively, Anasūyā gave birth to Atri’s sons, beginning with Datta.
And the phrase "born from Ātman, Īśa, and Brahmā" is to be explained by means of transference (*vipariṇāma*).
Here, the word *sambhava* ("originated") is used in its primary sense with respect to Candra, who was born together with the entry of Brahmā.

However, it should be understood that in the case of Datta and Durvāsas—who were born from those [deities] as direct portions (*aṃśa*) of Viṣṇu and Rudra—the term is used in a secondary sense, according to the maxim of the umbrella-bearer (*chatrinyāya*).
Although the reading in the *Bhāgavata* is "Atri’s wife Anasūyā gave birth to three highly illustrious sons: Datta," nevertheless,
because it is read thus in the *Anuvyākhyāna* and explained accordingly in the *Sudhā*, there is no fault, as this must be a different reading belonging to another *kalpa*.
The phrase "of this too" is to be construed with the words "is taught.
"But the conscious one," however, is a separate sentence. "O Lord! is an address to someone.
The word "therein" (*tatra*) is understood as the ellipsis. The first particle *tu* has the sense of specification (*viśeṣa*), while the second is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
And thus: "The individual souls (jīvas) are said to be Brahmā and the others, but the Self (ātman) is Viṣṇu, Janārdana; He alone is the primary denotation of that word."
Thus it has been stated regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇas*).

Regarding "others," such as Brahmā and so forth, the term "Self" (*ātman*) is said by the knowers of reality to be "figurative" (*sopācāra*), meaning that in comparison to its primary and most direct application, it is endowed with a subordinate mode of operation. This is the sense.
To the question, "Why is that alone the Self and not others?", he says: "Of that.
Because, from the ignorance of "that"—the attributeless Self—there is liberation.
Because He is described as "He by whom [the earth] is known" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.31) and so forth,
this Self is indeed Viṣṇu, who is devoid of qualities, and none other.
Why? Because liberation can only be granted by that very Viṣṇu who is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), whereas it is impossible for others; this is the meaning.

Even if liberation is taught to come from knowledge of the Self, why is the status of being the Self not attributed to others as well, since it is possible for them too to grant liberation? To this he says: "They are possessed of qualities" (saguṇāḥ).
The word "tu" (but) is used for emphasis.
And thus: "others"—that is, Brahmā and the rest, who are different from Viṣṇu—are "possessed of qualities" (saguṇa).

The qualified person is bound precisely by qualities such as *sattva* and is not inherently devoid of them; therefore, the meaning is that he is "not at all liberated" from them through knowledge of them.
The sense is that liberation, which consists in the cessation of the bondage of the *guṇas*, arises from the realization of the Self as bound by the *guṇas*.
Now, one might object: "Even in the case of Viṣṇu, since he is devoid of *guṇas* (*nirguṇa*), the possibility of his being the bestower of liberation may exist;
but from what [source] does the certainty of this arise? To this, he says: "For he is supreme... (*paro hi*).
"Hi" means "because"; "viṣṇuparaḥ" means independent, or according to the *Tattvapradīpa*, one who is the supreme among all.
The term ‘puruṣa’ means ‘full’ (pūrṇa). Therefore, liberation from that [Viṣṇu] occurs; this is what is recorded as being stated in the Smṛti—this is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase “in the Padma,” its connection with the preceding clause is: “thus it is taught. // 7 //
And because there is no mention of [the Self] being something to be abandoned:
"Know that one alone as the Self; cast off other words;
this is the bridge to immortality" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.5).
Thus, because other [entities] are stated to be rejectable while this [Self] is stated not to be rejectable, the Self is not secondary.
By another argument, the author of the Sūtras states that [the word "Self"] is not figurative because of the term "Self" and so forth, beginning with the words *heyatva* (to be abandoned).
Here, "being something to be abandoned" means not being prescribed as the primary object of knowledge for the sake of liberation.
And thus, it is not only because liberation is taught for one who is established in That, but also...
However, because the scripture stating "that one alone" does not mention the self as something to be abandoned,
and on the contrary mentions its non-abandonability by saying "know [it]," [the self is not to be discarded].

And because it is stated that the individual soul (*jīva*) is to be abandoned by those seeking liberation in the words, "Abandon other speech," [the author], keeping in mind the commentary on the Sūtra, explains the Sūtra as follows: "O sages, 'him'— that is,
the Self, Viṣṇu— 'alone, indeed'..."
"Know the Pradhāna"— that is, know it;
"abandon other words"— words concerning the individual soul (jīva) and so forth— meaning you should relinquish them, for the sense is that you should not primarily know anything other than Viṣṇu.
The analysis of the phrase "know the Self" is intended to demonstrate that Viṣṇu is distinct from everything else;
the transposition of the verbal suffix, however, is a Vedic anomaly.

The singular number in "of the immortal" (*amṛtasya*) is used with the intention of referring to the group as a whole; and thus, "of the immortal" means "of the class of liberated beings," and "this" refers to him.
"Viṣṇu is the bridge";
the meaning is that He is the primary support.
"In this manner"—that is, in the Muṇḍaka Śruti—"of others... [the text continues].

By the phrase "because of the statement that living beings are to be abandoned," that which is to be conjoined by the word "and" (ca) has been shown. Intending an alternative construction by transposing the negative particle (nañ) from the sūtra, he states another thing to be conjoined: "because of this Viṣṇu’s non-abandonability."
The word *ca* (and) is used for conjunction.
He states the meaning of the phrase “the word ‘self’ is not secondary,” which is carried over from the previous sūtra: “no” (*na*).
That is to say, the word “self” does not have a secondary referent as its primary denotation.
However, the meaning is that Viṣṇu alone is devoid of attributes (nirguṇa).
And thus it is established that even though He is referred to by the word "Self" (ātman) in the Śruti passage concerning "He who sees" (īkṣati), He is indeed attributeless.
The sense is that His status as the primary denotable object (vācyatva) is established through the necessity of otherwise rendering the act of seeing (īkṣati) inexplicable. // 8 //
Because of [the state of] deep sleep:
"That is full, this is full; from the full, the full arises.
When the full is taken from the full, only the full remains. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.1.1)
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 7.1.1):
“Having extracted the Self from the self, he dissolves it into the Self alone; then he becomes the Self alone.
That divine Puruṣottama, though devoid of qualities, having become manifold, [remains] the Supreme Person.
"Having become one again, Hari, the original creator, lies there faultless. Thus [it is said].
He introduces the aphorism—*svāpyayāt*—which establishes by another argument that Viṣṇu, though devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), is expressible.
He explains the aphorism with the word *pūrṇam*:
"That" (*adaḥ*), meaning the primordial form (*mūlarūpa*), is "full" (*pūrṇam*).
And this form of the incarnation is "full";
the form of the incarnation is "full" from the "Full" at the time of creation.
"Is raised up" (*udacyate*) means it emerges from its original form.

According to the *Tattvapradīpa*, this [one] is raised up from that [many] merely by way of number; that is, the one alone becomes many in number, or rather, it does so precisely because of its specific nature.
At the time of dissolution, having assumed His own "full" primordial form, which is "complete," as well as His "full" incarnate forms;

"Having accepted [all] and become one, it remains as the 'Full' alone"; thus, while existing as that which has not dissolved elsewhere, it "remains itself"— this is the meaning of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad śruti.
The other scriptural passage is "sa" (he).
Its meaning is as follows: "sa" refers to Viṣṇu, and "ātmanaḥ" (of the self) [refers to him].

Having "extracted" His own essential nature as an incarnation from His own original form— having manifested it separately at the time of creation— and [having withdrawn it] into "Himself" at the time of dissolution;
He causes [them] to dissolve into Himself alone;
He unifies them.
Then, immediately thereafter, that Viṣṇu is indeed the Self.
"He exists as the primordial form";
"he remains"—
thus the Skanda-smṛti explains the meaning of that word as used in the Śruti.

"Deva," from roots such as *dyut* (to shine); "Nirguṇaḥ," meaning one who has emerged beyond the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* and so forth, and for that very reason, devoid of the defects that are effects of those qualities; "Puruṣottamaḥ," the supreme among conscious beings, both perishable and imperishable; "Ādikṛt," the primordial creator.
"He" is the creator of the origin of the universe or the primordial creator;
"Hari" is the one residing in Śvetadvīpa;
and at the initial creation, he became "manifold."
Having created many forms such as the Boar and others, and then,
at the time of dissolution, having become one— that is,
having brought them to a state of unity within his fundamental form— he "lies" upon the Lord of Serpents.

The meaning is that he enters into yogic sleep (*yoganidrā*). Regarding the word "iti" (thus), by supplying the phrase "and because it is so stated in the Śruti," it is to be connected with the ultimate conclusion (*paramasādhya*) "that [the Self] is indeed the object denoted."
Because it is stated that [the Self] dissolves even into itself;
for there can be no dissolution of one who is free from defects into a secondary self.
Even though this [Brahman] is declared by scripture to be "without qualities" (nirguṇa), why [is it so]?

One might ask: "Why should it not be merely figurative (gauṇa)? To address this, he applies the reason stated in the Sūtra by repeating the word "its own" (sva) with an emphatic particle: "of its own" (svasyaiva).
The particle *eva* is displaced [in its position].
The word *iti* is repeated and should be applied here as well.
The word "from the statement" (*vacanāt*) is also repeated.
The term "not figurative" (na gauṇaḥ) is understood from the preceding context; the word "this" (ayam) is to be supplied as the subject.
The phrase "the state of deep sleep" (svāpyayapada) is also indicative of fullness (pūrṇatva).
And thus, because the Śruti states "Full" (pūrṇam), indicating fullness characterized by the term "dissolution" (svāpyaya), and because it speaks of one's own dissolution into oneself;
and because even in the clear Śruti "He [is] That," it says "he dissolves into the Self alone," speaking of one's own dissolution into oneself;
and because his abiding in the qualityless Hari is stated in Smṛti—this [state] is indeed qualityless and not secondary; such is the construction.

Since the state of being dissolved (*svāpyaya*) is not a direct cause for [the attainment of Brahman] when it is taken as the literal meaning (*vācyatva*), there is no use of the word "and" (*ca*) in the Sūtra or the Bhāṣya. Even though, according to the view of the Commentator (*ṭīkākāra*) who intends this to be an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), the word "and" should be supplied from the previous context to conjoin the reason of "fullness" (*pūrṇatva*), nevertheless, because this [state of dissolution] is not a direct cause when taken as the literal meaning, the word "and" indicating another reason should not be supplied there. Nor is it the case that...
One might ask: "Since the word 'ca' (and) must necessarily occur when the reason 'because it is stated in the Śruti' is supplied as an ellipsis, how can its absence [in the sūtra] be maintained?
This must be answered by the intention that the word 'ca' is absent from the reason explicitly heard in the sūtra itself;
for this very reason, it is stated in the Ṭīkā: "tatra" (therein).
And thus is the meaning of this Sūtra: not only is Brahman, known as Viṣṇu and devoid of qualities, denotable because it is the object of "seeing" (īkṣaṇa), but also because it is so stated by Śruti.
Why is it that what is stated by Śruti is indeed the qualityless [Brahman] and not merely figurative?
Because of its fullness and because of its absorption within itself,
whereas the secondary [self] is not full and lacks absorption within itself due to its dissolution in something else;

thus, it is stated in the Bhāṣya that "because of the words of Śruti and Smṛti" in order to avoid the charge of unestablished premises regarding the fullness and absorption mentioned in Śruti, and to demonstrate the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of the probandum with the reason.
[Objection: But surely this [Self] must be secondary (gauṇa), since it possesses deep sleep and is not dissolved elsewhere;
for there exists another [Self] that is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). [Reply: No.
If this [Self] possessing deep sleep is secondary, then both this one and the qualityless one would remain without dissolution elsewhere at the time of cosmic dissolution (pralaya)?
Or does the dissolution of one thing occur within another? Not the first, because it contradicts such scriptural passages as, "O Agni, this was indeed nothing at all" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.2.9.1).
In this context, because only a second [entity] is negated at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*),
there is no merging of the secondary (*gauṇa*) into the qualityless (*nirguṇa*);
for it is accepted that the latter persists in its own state, like deep sleep (*svāpyaya*).
And likewise, the dissolution of the attributeless (nirguṇa) into the qualified (saguṇa) must be stated;
yet that is not possible, as he says with the words "for not" (na hi),
[referring to] "in the secondary self" (gauṇātmani).

The meaning is that the dissolution of Viṣṇu—who is "in the living soul" (*jīve*) and who is "faultless" (*anirdeṣasya*), that is, devoid of defects consisting in the bondage of qualities such as *sattva* and the like, and who is thus "without qualities" (*nirguṇasya*)—is not possible.
By the word "hi" (for), [the author refers to] the passage: "That toward which they go" (*yat prayanti*, Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1).
The reason "because of contradiction with such scriptural passages" has been indicated.

Therefore, since the dissolution of the attributeless [Self] must be stated as occurring within itself, this [Self] is indeed the attributeless one that does not dissolve into anything else; thus, its status as the object of expression is established because it alone is so declared by scripture—this is the intended meaning.

In this system, designations such as "secondary" (gauṇa) and so forth refer exclusively to the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman), based on their respective attributes consisting of the presence or absence of qualities such as *sattva*.

However, although one ought to have said "of the one devoid of qualities" (nirguṇasya) in order to indicate that this refers to an object lacking the qualities of the primary meaning—just as in the cases of "resorting to the secondary [meaning] when the primary is impossible" or "this is devoid of qualities"—the term "faultless" (nirdoṣasya) was used instead; nor is it stated otherwise in any of the Vedic branches (śākhās).
Because their goal is common:
all the Vedas, reasonings, and excellent means of knowledge proclaim only the one supreme Brahman-knowledge;
there is no contradiction anywhere in all the Vedas, nor likewise in the Itihāsas.
Thus, according to the Paiṅgi-śruti, there is indeed equality between the two types of knowledge.
Granted that it may be possible for the qualityless Viṣṇu to be denotable by words, and thus for his status as the cause to be accessible through scripture;
yet, since this is established by the force of the opening passages (*upakrama*) and other criteria, it results in his being taught as the cause only within those well-known recensions (*śākhā*).
However, in the case of the less well-known recensions, let some other [deity] also be spoken of as the cause.
Nor is it the case that they do not exist, for their number cannot be determined due to their infinity; therefore, he says: "And not..."
Whatever the meaning may be; and thus— in certain "unfamiliar recensions" (*aprasiddha-śākhāsu*)— "otherwise."
The one with attributes is "otherwise" than the one without attributes—
by virtue of being a cause (whereas the other is not), by being the primary denotation of the word "Self," and by being the object of the knowledge that produces liberation;
or else, the one without attributes is "otherwise."
The construction is as follows: "it is said because of being causeless and so forth";
let it be said; [the response is] "no";
"not otherwise."

By this [statement], it is indicated that the word "not" (na) from the preceding secondary sūtra is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) and that the word "otherwise" (*anyathā*) is to be supplied (*adhyāhāra*). The meaning is: "It is not as stated in the sūtra 'But that [is] equal' (*tat tu sam*).
To the question "Why not?", he introduces and explains the sūtra as the reason for that, beginning with the words "gatī" (motion).

Intending the construction [of the argument] based on the fact that the commonality of the goal (*gatisāmānya*) is heard [in scripture] through the attraction of the words of the subsequent sūtra— thereby being common to all qualified seekers— he states the scriptural authority indicated by that sūtra in order to avoid the charge of unestablished reason (*asiddhi*):
"All," which is an elaboration of the word "Vedas."
And thus: "all the Vedas";
likewise, "well-measured" (*supramāṇāḥ*);
those whose measure is excellent—that is, whose reasoning (*yuktayaḥ*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that stands after [the Vedas] as their fundamental basis.
The phrase "likewise in the Itihāsas" implies that the Itihāsas are also to be understood here, in accordance with what will be stated later; thus,
it means "and likewise the Itihāsas."
"Brahmic" means having Brahman as its sole object; "one" means being of a single kind because its object is the nature of bliss (rama); "supreme" means the highest; "knowledge."
"They are manifested" means they are produced,
but not in multiple forms.
Therefore, [it is found] "in all the Vedas," likewise "in the logical treatises," and "in some part of the Itihāsas."

The meaning is that there is no contradiction whatsoever, whether caused by the object (*viṣaya*) or by the mode (*prakāra*); or alternatively, [the texts] make known the single nature of Brahman, which is of the very form of knowledge (*jñāna*).
The ablative case in the word *śruteḥ* is used in the sense of the instrumental;
the word *gateḥ* is explained as *jñānasya*;
and regarding the sūtra-word *sāmānyāt*, he states its nominal stem meaning as *sāmyam*.
The meaning is that there is equality because the qualities of the objects are stated without any discrepancy.

This is based on the statement in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "For it is not the case that after describing knowledge, bliss, and so forth in one place, Brahman is described elsewhere as having the nature of ignorance and so forth"—the word "is said" (*kathyate*) is to be supplied.
Alternatively, the meaning of the word "only" (*eva*) is either that there is no inequality, or that [this is stated] directly by [the author] himself and not through another's mouth.

And thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: because it is directly understood from the Śruti text "All the Vedas" (*sarve vedāḥ*) that the knowledge produced by all the Śākhās is of one kind due to its commonality, it is not stated otherwise in any of the Śākhās.

Here, although the cognitions differ in their objects and modes, since there exists a similarity among them by virtue of being "cognition," the statement "due to similarity" (*sāmyāt*) does not establish an identity of object and mode; rather, it refers to their commonality (*sāmānyāt*), equality (*samānatvāt*), and uniformity (*ekavidhatvāt*).
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra.
It should be understood that this is precisely the meaning of the word *bhāṣya* as well. // 10 // [And because it is heard in scripture. (BBs 1.1.11)
"The one God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings,
the overseer of actions, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious, absolute, and devoid of qualities"—
thus is the word heard [in scripture].
And that which is unestablished should not be postulated, because it is illogical to apply figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to that which is inexpressible by any word. // 5 //
For this reason as well, the author of the Sūtras states that Brahman is to be denoted as devoid of qualities (nirguṇa): "And because it is so heard" (śrutatvācca).
The word "and" (ca) serves to aggregate reasons.
The phrase "that which is not denotable by words" (aśabdaṃ tat) is understood to carry over from the preceding context.

And thus, that which is called Viṣṇu is not only devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) on account of [the Sūtras] such as *Īkṣati* and others, nor is it "non-verbal" (*aśabda*)—meaning not denotable by words—but rather, because it is directly mentioned by its own name in the Śvetāśvatara Śruti as "the One" (*ekaḥ*), according to the Sūtra [Brahma Sūtra 1.3.14]: "And because it is heard [there]" (*śrutatvācca*). With this intention, he recites the scriptural passage cited in the Sūtra: "The One."

"Ekah" means the primary one, or that which is devoid of internal differentiation; "devaḥ" refers to the one who shines and so forth; "gūḍhaḥ sarvabhūteṣu" means abiding in a hidden manner within all living beings.
He does not merely abide within beings, but is also "all-pervading" (sarvavyāpī); the meaning is that He pervades everything in terms of space, time, and qualities.
It is not merely that He has an abiding presence within all beings.
But he is called the "inner self of all beings" (*sarvabhūtāntarātmā*) because,
dwelling within all living creatures, he is their complete controller and sustainer;
or else, he is so designated because he is the agent of taking [the breath] and other such functions.

"Karmādhyakṣaḥ" means the presiding lord of karma; for it is stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "He is the presiding lord (*adhyakṣa*) because his senses (*akṣāṇi*), that is, his faculties, operate with respect to karma."
"Sarvabhūtādhivāsaḥ" means the abode of all living beings;
"sākṣī" means one who directly observes or sees everything.
And he states that this seeing is not material, but rather has the nature of consciousness, by saying "the knower" (cetā), meaning one whose form is knowledge.

He is "alone" (kevalaḥ), meaning unmixed with the insentient, or devoid of anything equal or superior, as stated in the second purport [of the Upaniṣad]: "He is alone because of the absence of such [a second]."
Since even for a yogi established in asamprajñāta-samādhi there occurs a perception by means of pure consciousness alone, he says "nirguṇa" (devoid of qualities) in order to exclude that;
the meaning is "freed from the bondage of the qualities such as sattva," or "devoid of material (prākṛta) qualities."

The word *iti* connects with the sūtra "because it is heard [in scripture]" (*śrutatvāt*) through the ellipsis of the two words "in scripture" (*śrutau*) and "of the one devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇasya*). Following a certain reading of the commentary (*ṭīkā*), which states: "In this context, the sūtra, demonstrating that [Brahman] is expressible, recites the scriptural passage it has cited as an example—'One' (*ekaḥ*)"—the Bhāṣya, in some places, follows the recitation of the scripture immediately thereafter.
The reading of the Sūtra is observed;
however, it should be understood that in that case, the positive concomitance (anvaya) is indeed easily established.
To the objection—that even if [the word] is heard in the text, why should it not be non-verbal (aśabda), thus rendering the reason inconclusive—he says: "For not... (na hi).
For [it is] "without sound" (aśabda);
that is, the referent (padārtha) is inexpressible and is "not heard," meaning it is not denoted by the word of revelation (śruti).
Therefore, the remainder of the sentence is that the reason is not "inconclusive" (aprayojaka).

The word "hi" (for/indeed) also signifies the sense of "because of contradiction. Now, one might ask: why could even Brahman, though not directly denoted by words, not be considered "heard" (śruta) through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā)? To this, he says: "And not... (na ca).
‘Unestablished’ (aprasiddham):
the meaning is that the status of being a *lakṣya* (that which is indicated) cannot be postulated for Brahman, which is inexpressible (*avācya*).

Why? Because the status of being a *lakṣya* is unestablished for an object that is inexpressible; therefore, this [statement] should also be construed as being intended to establish a logical pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Now, one might ask: how can this be so?

For it is well known that even a riverbank (*tīra*), though denotable by the word "Ganges" (*gaṅgā*), is also the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) of that same word. To this, it is said: "of that which is not denotable by any word. That is to say, *sarvaśabdāvācyasya*.
