The meaning is that it is contrary to reason to claim that Brahman, which is characterized by being indicated by Vedic words, cannot be the object of indication; for the proposition "that which is disputed [as being Brahman] is not an object of indication because it is unexpressible by any word, like a riverbank (tīra)," is contradicted by logic.
Furthermore, we do not establish the absence of being an object of indication based on mere unexpressibility, such that a deviation (vyabhicāra) might be suspected in cases like a riverbank.
However, it is by virtue of being inexpressible by any word;
and that [reality] does not reside in the bank and so forth,
because those [banks] are expressible by words such as "bank."
But Brahman is not like that,
because it has been accepted by the opponent as being precisely inexpressible by any word;
therefore, there is no deviation [from the rule], and the meaning is that the contradiction with reasoning is difficult to avoid.
If it is argued that [the reason] is "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) because the reason is absent in things such as a flowing stream—which lack the status of being a "thing to be defined" (lakṣya)—we say no.

For if the meaning of the term "thing to be defined" were simply that which is unfit for definition, then since all things whatsoever are unfit for definition by some particular word, the probandum consisting of the absence of that [fitness] would be non-existent anywhere; consequently, there would be no similar instance (sapakṣa) at all. // 11 //
Thus concludes the section on "Iksati" (the one who sees).
6. The Section Concerning that Which Consists of Bliss (Ānandamayādhikaraṇa)
He reveals that very same point himself for the most part through the entire chapter beginning with "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of repetition" (*ānandamayo ’bhyāsāt*).

Now, one might ask: since this group of five topics (*pañcādhikaraṇya*), which serves as the pedestal (*pīṭha*) by way of being an introduction to the chapter and its sections, exhaustively defines the nature of Brahman, what is the purpose of the remaining portion of the chapter? To this, he says:
The phrase "even so" (*tathāpi*) and others should be applied at the beginning [of the subsequent section].
Furthermore, the word *samanvaya* (correspondence) is to be repeated with a change in grammatical form.
And thus: "even so, despite the absence of any other purpose for the remainder of the text called the chapter, [the Lord says] 'that very same' (*tameva*)."

By the [sūtra] "But that [Brahman], because of the harmony" (*tattu samanvayāt*), the author of the sūtras—treating it as already established in a general sense as the reason—now "manifests" (*prakaṭayati*) this "harmony" (*samanvaya*); that is, the fact that all scriptural statements are determined to refer to Hari through their primary mode of signification, a fact made known by the marks such as the opening passages (*upakrama*).

He elaborates upon this by taking up each individual statement and presenting the reasons for it, beginning with "The one consisting of bliss, because of repetition" (*ānandamayo 'bhyāsāt*) and so forth; such is the meaning of this first chapter.

Otherwise, if a mere thesis—namely, the simple presentation as an established fact that "that alone is the source of the scripture, because of its concordance" (*samanvayāt*)—were sufficient as a proof, then one might argue: "The source of the scripture is something other than Viṣṇu; why?
Because of concordance, that is, because [the scripture] has him as its proper object of purport."

The intention is that the opponent might also say: "In that case, the object of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) must be something else; why? Because of the indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as the opening statement (*upakrama*).

Just as the opening statement and so forth indicate that intended meaning, and that intended meaning is the referent of the term "harmonization" (*samanvaya*), so too has the *Bhāṣya* been applied accordingly below.

Although there is no need to cite the Sūtra here because it will be cited later as a pratīka (representative extract), nevertheless, if the Sūtra were not cited here, there would arise no suspicion as to what the prior connection (*pūrvasaṅgati*) might be for establishing that the one called Ānandamaya is Viṣṇu— due to a lack of full understanding of that subject— and consequently, no fundamental question (*tanmūlapraśna*) would arise; furthermore, in the absence of a full understanding of Ānandamaya, there could be no arising of a doubt in the form of an objection based on the perception of Brahman being a mere limb (*avayava*) of that [Ānandamaya].

And it should be understood that the citation of the Sūtra here is for the purpose of demonstrating the connection in the form of this objection and for raising a doubt regarding the connection of the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*), whereas in the subsequent [section], it is by way of a representative extract (*pratīka*).
The phrase "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) and so forth is intended to distinguish this from other chapters.

By using such wording instead of simply saying "by the first," it is indicated that the commencement of this chapter begins with this particular section (*adhikaraṇa*), whereas the group of five sections (*pañcādhikaraṇī*) does not fall within the scope of the chapter.

If one holds the position that the commencement of the chapter begins precisely with the *Samanvaya* section because this [chapter] is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of that, then there is no contradiction in interpreting "by the chapter" as meaning "by the remainder of the chapter.
As for the statement "by the whole," which was said to exclude the view of others that the fourth quarter (*pāda*) does not establish *samanvaya*,
it means "by the complete [chapter]."

In order to dispel the objection that the term "by the whole" (*samastena*) is untenable because the sections concerning the deities (*devatā*), animals (*paśu*), and Śūdras do not deal with *samanvaya* (harmonization), [the author uses] the word "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*),
meaning "in abundance" (*prācuryeṇa*). This word *prāya*, which ends in the vowel *a*, is a synonym for the indeclinable ending in *s* (*sakārānta*).
Therefore, by virtue of its inclusion in the group beginning with *prakṛti*, the third case ending occurs [after the word *prāya*], and thus the form *prāyeṇa* arises.
For this very reason, in the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā*, the word *api* was employed [in the commentary] to indicate that the indeclinable *aprāyaḥ* also exists in the sense of "abundance" (*bhūma*).
In the *Prameyadīpa* as well, it is stated that only that which has an end possesses immutability (*avyayatva*).
In this section (*pāda*), the application (*samanvaya*) of words generally well-known in other [contexts] to the Supreme Self is demonstrated;
otherwise, that would not be perceived.

If that is so, since the chapter has a single unified purpose, on what basis is there a division into sections (pādas)? To this, with the intention that there is an internal distinction even within the process of reconciliation (*samanvaya*) due to the distinction between the things to be reconciled, he shows the subject matter of the first section of the first chapter by saying "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*).
"In this" first quarter [of the verse], "mostly"—
that is, for the most part— "elsewhere," meaning other than Viṣṇu, [there are] "those well-known [names]."

The "harmonious convergence" (*samanvaya*) of those words consisting of names— which are perceived through scripture and so forth, through common worldly usage, and through established convention— as referring to the Supreme Self, Viṣṇu, has been explained.
‘Is demonstrated’ (*pradarśyate*); the meaning is ‘is explained in detail’ (*prapañcyate*).

Here too, because the concordance (*samanvaya*) with the mark of being situated within (*antaḥsthatva*) was established in the *Antaradhikaraṇa*, the word ‘generally’ (*prāyeṇa*) is used to exclude non-pervasion (*avyāpti*).
In the *Tattvapradīpa*, however, it is stated that the word "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*) occurs only once in the Bhāṣya;
with the intention that this very word is to be connected even to what follows, it says: "And there is a connection [of 'mostly'] with the phrase 'of words well-known elsewhere'.

Likewise, in the section on the *ānandamaya* (the one consisting of bliss), after an investigation of the indicative marks (*liṅga*), it is further stated that "that too" is what is excluded by the word "mostly."

Alternatively, even in the *Ṭīkā*, the citation of the pratīka was made with the intention of repetition (*āvṛtti*), in order to demonstrate the connection of that very same [term] again later on; thus, one should not assume a discrepancy in the text.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Candrikā* following the *Tattvapradīpa*: "In the *Ṭīkā*, the word 'of the name Ānandamaya' should be understood as referring to names such as 'Ānanda' and so forth.
Now, he refutes the meaning of the section (*pādārtha*) as stated by others with the word "no" (*na*).

Otherwise—the meaning is that the reconciliation (*samanvaya*) of words with clear marks of Brahman is taught in the first [pāda], while in the second and third [pādas] the reconciliation of words with indistinct marks of Brahman is taught;
however, the distinction between those two lies in their having as their objects [respectively] Brahman with attributes (*saviśeṣa*) and Brahman without attributes (*nirviśeṣa*).

But in the fourth pāda, the statement that the Pradhāna is not based on scripture (*aśābdatva*)—the meaning is that the subject matter of the pādas should not be stated in any manner other than what we have described.
To the question "Why not?", he says: "That" (*tat*).

The meaning is: because of the "non-perception" (*adṛṣṭeḥ*)—that is, the non-observation—in this chapter of the restriction of categories (*pādārthaniyama*) as stated by the opponent within the sections (*pāda*) contained in this chapter.
The sense is that there would be total confusion;
and this has been stated in the *Ṭīkā* and other works.
[It was] stated that "the inquiry into Brahman ought to be undertaken."
And that [is stated in] "Brahman is the tail, the support" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5.2).
Now, beginning from the section on the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), it is necessary to state the fivefold connection (saṅgati) for all the subsequent sections.

In this section, because words denoting the possessor of qualities— which are indicated by the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) and are well-known in common usage elsewhere than [in the Upanishads]— as well as words denoting qualities such as bliss, are shown to be consistently applicable to Brahman, its topical connection (*saṅgati*) consists in its inclusion within this scripture, this chapter, and this section.

Nevertheless, since there is no fixed rule that the connection must be stated with the immediately preceding section alone—given that one might ask what the prior connection is for establishing that the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is Viṣṇu—he first demonstrates its "suggestive" (ākṣepikī) connection, characterized by immediate succession, with the distant preceding section on the inquiry into Brahman (jijñāsādhikaraṇa) and its subject matter, by stating: "Brahman... and so forth.
The phrase "it was stated" refers to the *Jijñāsā-adhikaraṇa*;
the word "that" means that very Brahman which was proposed as the object of inquiry.
Alternatively, the word "ca" (and) serves to connect with the present context.
After the word "iti," the term "in the Śruti" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. [The phrase is:
"having the form of the limbs of the one consisting of bliss."
The meaning is that [Brahman] is perceived as being a constituent part called the "tail" belonging to something known as the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya).
Now, one might ask: even if Brahman is stated to be a constituent part, for what purpose is the identity of the "consisting of bliss" with Viṣṇu being established? To this, he says: "For not...
The word "hi" (for) indicates the reason.
The word "ataḥ" is repeated;
the section beginning with "tacca" and ending with "ityata āha" should be explained as being intended for both the connection [of the argument] and the purpose.

The phrase "for not" (na hi) serves as the justification for that [conclusion]. The construction [of the argument] is as follows: because in the scriptural passage, "Brahman is the tail, the support," Brahman—which was declared to be the object of inquiry—is perceived as being merely a constituent part of something called the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya).
It is said: because, even though it is to be known as a subordinate member (*anyāṅgatayā*),

Brahman does not have a separate status as an object of knowledge (*jñeyatā*) apart from the "whole" (*avayavin*), namely the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), as a mere "member" (*avayava*) or isolated part.
The state of being an object of inquiry is possible because [the primary sense] is not intended;
nor is the abandonment of the very desire to know appropriate.
“Desire to know That” (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1)— since [the inquiry] is thus enjoined by scripture, such a doubt arises. Therefore,

because there exists a connection in the form of this doubt— since, under the view that the *ānandamaya* is other than Viṣṇu, the inquiry into Brahman would be sublated, whereas under the view that it is Viṣṇu, that inquiry is established— thus, between the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), [the following applies].

And because of the existence of the fruit [of the inquiry], for the sake of establishing the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), he states that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is Viṣṇu, on the basis of repetition (*abhyāsāt*), in the sūtra: "Therefore, [the desire to know] Brahman" and "The one consisting of bliss, because of repetition."
The author of the Sūtra provides support [for this view]:
"Therefore, different from this self consisting of consciousness, there is another inner self consisting of bliss."
By that, this [body] is filled.
Indeed, it is of the very form of a person;
its nature is that of a person.
It is of the same nature as a person. Its dearness is the head;
its joy is the right wing.
“Joy is its eastern wing; bliss is its self; Brahman is the tail, the support” (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5.2).
This is the meaning of the Taittirīya passage:

"From that"— from Him denoted by the word *ātman*— "from this"— from Viṣṇu, who is designated by the term *vijñānamaya* because He is full of consciousness and resides within the bodies of individual souls— though non-different, [He] is called by another word as the *ānandamaya*.

Because he is full of bliss, the Self denoted by the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is Nārāyaṇa; he is the "inner one," situated within the "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya). By him—
By the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*),
this Vāsudeva, denoted by the term "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*), is "full"—
that is, filled due to being without any gaps.
The word "vai" (indeed) signifies well-known fact.
"He, this one consisting of bliss, is verily of the form of a person";
that is, he is indeed of the shape of a person.

Following (anu) the human form of that [self] consisting of bliss, which stands in the place of a body, this [self] consisting of consciousness, which also stands in the place of a body, is "of the form of a person" (puruṣavidha).
Therefore, it has manifested; the former [elements] are completely filled by the latter without any gaps.
All of them possess the form of a person, and the former arises from the latter.
This is according to the statement in the *Taittirīyabhāṣya*:
"Of Him"— meaning of Viṣṇu, who consists of bliss— "this supreme [state] is named 'Pleasure' (*priya*)," as stated in the commentary.
That happiness which is denoted by the word "dear" (*priya*) because it is attainable by other supreme deities is its "head.

That very thing, being the head of the body of the individual soul known as the *ānandamaya*, is named "dear" because it is attainable by others who act as benefactors; it is the head consisting of the so-called sensual pleasure produced by such assistance.

And that which resides therein—namely, the right arm, left arm, middle [body], and torso of Viṣṇu, who is designated as the *ānandamaya*—is [so called] by reason of their being joy (*moda*), extreme delight (*pramoda*), and bliss (*ānanda*).

Those named *pramoda* and *ānanda* are the names for the right and left wings of the living body (*jīva-śarīra*) called *ānandamaya*; they constitute the right arm, the left arm, and the middle part of the body.
*Moda* is caused by enjoyment, while *pramoda* arises from its particular excellence, according to the statement in the *Aitareya-bhāṣya*: "arising from a specific instance of that."
That happiness which arises from objects and emerges from superior objects is called *sukha*; that which is one's own essential nature is called *ānanda*.
And because it is stated in the *Bṛhadbhāṣya*:

"The names *moda*, *pramoda*, and *ānanda* reside in those [states] due to the causes of arising from objects that are inferior, arising from objects that are superior, and being the bliss of the soul's own nature (*jīvasvarūpa*), respectively.
Thus, there is the "tail" (*puccha*) of Viṣṇu, who is designated as the *ānandamaya*.

That which is designated by the word *pratiṣṭhā* (foundation) through the etymology "that by means of which the world stands and moves"—namely, the limb called the foot—is that very Brahman. According to the method stated in the Taittirīya-bhāṣya, "But by the creation of Brahman, [the world] should be made to grow," it is denoted by the word *Brahman* because it causes the increase of the qualities of the universe through activities such as creation.

That very Brahman is the "tail" (*puccha*)—the limb called the foot—of the body of the living being known as the *ānandamaya*; and it is within that which is established as Brahman [that the self rests].
It resides in the primary wind (*pradhānavāyu*).

By this it is stated that the reason the part of the sheath (*kośāvayava*) is denoted by the word "Brahman" is its being presided over (*adhiṣṭhāna*) by the primary wind which is itself denoted by the word "Brahman"; whereas the primary wind is denoted by the word "Brahman" because it is presided over by the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*).

By this, it is stated that there are two kinds of "pleasure" (*priya*) and so forth: those which are limbs of Viṣṇu—who is denoted by terms such as *ānandamaya*—and are non-different from Viṣṇu; and those which are limbs of the sheaths (*kośa*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), such as the *ānandamaya*, and are distinct in every body.

As it is said in the *Candrikā*: "Those 'pleasures' and so forth which are limbs of the sheaths beginning with the *ānandamaya*, which are identified with the individual soul (*jīva*), are distinct in every body."

Those [limbs] called Ānandamaya and so forth are not limbs of Viṣṇu; and those limbs of the Blessed One such as Priya (the Beloved) and others are not distinct in every body, but rather non-distinct. Thus, because bliss—which is the very nature of the individual soul—is situated within that which is called the heart, it is logically consistent that the "body within the sheath" is merely figurative, and that the body of the essential nature consists of non-insentient parts.

Although, by considering the statement "the head is Nārāyaṇa" which will be cited in the Bhāṣya, it appears that the one named Ānandamaya— namely Nārāyaṇa— is further divided fivefold into the forms of Nārāyaṇa and so forth, and exists as the self of the limbs beginning with the head, in the Taittirīya Bhāṣya, however, it is stated that "pleasure (priya) and the others are the limbs of the Ānandamaya."

Nevertheless, since it is possible for those very forms of Nārāyaṇa and others—which reside in the primary vital air (pradhāna-vāyu) called Brahman that sustains the body and bestows specific pleasures such as those of beloved ones—to constitute the limbs of Viṣṇu known as the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), it belongs to them alone.
This [sheath] is "the other," named *priya* (pleasure);
and the two named *moda* and *pramoda* arise from gladdening (*modana*) and exulting (*pramodana*).
"And one should cause Brahman, which resides within the wind of the body, to expand through creation.
According to the method stated in the *Taittirīyabhāṣya*, there is no contradiction, as it is also possible for [Brahman] to be denoted by words such as "the dear" (*priya*) and so forth.
However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, regarding the section on "having the dear as the head" (*priyaśirastva*), it is said: "The 'dear' arises from hearing..."
"The joy arising from seeing is *moda*, and the joy arising from enjoyment is *pramoda*"; thus another meaning for these three terms has been stated.
Likewise, in that same work: "'Non-existence [is the goal], says Bādari.'"

Thus it is stated: by the Sūtra [referring to] "the pleasant and the unpleasant" (*priyāpriye*; Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1), and because the word *priya* found in that Śruti is explained in the commentaries on the Taittirīya and Chāndogya Upaniṣads as "this Supreme One is named *Priya*," it is indicated that what is to be understood here is material happiness, which denotes the general category of pleasure attainable in the conditioned world (*para*).
This, however, must be understood: the body visible here is composed of food (annamaya);
within that is the body composed of vital breath (prāṇamaya); within that is the body composed of mind (manomaya);
and within that is the body composed of consciousness (vijñānamaya).
Within that, there exists the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*).

Among these five sheaths known as the body, forms in the shape of a person—designated by their respective names and consisting of the natures of Aniruddha, Pradyumna, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, and Nārāyaṇa—exist in the relationship of the body and the embodied;
thus, the form of the limbs of the *ānandamaya* is perceived.
For there can be no knowability of the mere parts without the whole; therefore, he says:
"The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of repetition" (BBs 1.1.12).
The one consisting of bliss is either Brahmā, the primordial nature (prakṛti), or Viṣṇu.
Having thus stated the connection and the fruit, he shows the subject matter and the doubt with the words: "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya).
The subject matter is indicated by the representative term "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*).
Regarding the compound *brahmādi*, the analysis is: "Brahmā is the first of the multitude of individual souls (*jīva*). Here, Brahmā is the four-faced one.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the gods headed by Rudra, Indra, and Bṛhaspati, as well as the individual souls (jīvas) residing in their respective bodies, are included. By the word "primordial nature" (prakṛti), the conscious primordial nature (cit-prakṛti) is meant.
The words "thus there is doubt" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

From the word "Brahman," there is the attainment of Hiraṇyagarbha, and by the name Śatānanda as well. Regarding this, he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) along with its reasoning: "From the word 'Brahman'... and so forth.
The meaning is: "from the word *brahman* heard in such passages as 'If one knows that there is Brahman' (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1), which refer to the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*).

Since the word *brahman* is used elsewhere as well, [the author] states another argument to show how the four-faced Brahmā's state of consisting of bliss is determined by that word: "by the hundred... and so forth.
The word *ca* is used here in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*):
"A hundred joys of Prajāpati constitute one joy of Brahmā" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8.4).
The meaning is that [it is attained] by one named Śatānanda, as indicated by the word "iti" through its sense;
or alternatively, it means by the name Śatānanda existing in Hiraṇyagarbha, which has the same meaning as the word *ānandamaya*.
The word "attainment" (*prāpti*) implies the attainment of the state of being *ānandamaya*; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
And thus—the logical connection (*anvaya*) is that there is the attainment of the state of being composed of bliss (*ānandamayatva*) for Hiraṇyagarbha.
Furthermore, because Rudra is said to possess eight forms (*aṣṭamūrtitva*) and because he is proclaimed [to reside] in the sun;
having thus stated one prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states another: "because of his possession of eight forms."

The word "ca" (and) is connected with "of Rudra. Alternatively, it serves to draw back the term "attainment" (*prāpti*); thus, [the question arises]: why is there an attainment of the state of consisting of bliss for Rudra?
Because it has been stated regarding the sun.

The meaning is that because it is stated [in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8.5], "And he who is in the sun," that the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) resides in the sun, and because Rudra has the sun and other [deities] as his eight bodies;
thus, since the linga of Rudra is heard of in the context of the one consisting of bliss, the implication is that the one consisting of bliss is indeed Rudra.
And Rudra’s state of having eight forms beginning with the Sun is as follows:
"The Sun, water, earth, fire, wind, space,
the initiated Brāhmaṇa, and the Moon— these are his bodies in sequence."
This is established by the statement from the Viṣṇupurāṇa.
In the same way, it applies to others as well.
He presents another prima facie argument with the word "evam" (thus).
The meaning is that for "others" than those already mentioned—

namely Indra, Bṛhaspati, and so forth— "in this way," i.e., by the aforementioned manner such as being presiding deities over their respective lower [levels] like the sun and so on, there is also the attainment of the state of consisting of bliss (*ānandamayatva*).
"From the word *brahman* in the passage, 'My womb is the great *brahman*' (Bhagavad Gītā 14.3), and because of the manifold nature of *prakṛti*."

He states another prima facie argument supported by reasoning: "mameti. The construction [of the argument] is as follows: the attainment of the state of consisting of bliss belongs to the conscious primordial nature (cit-prakṛti). Why? Because of the word "Brahman."

Regarding the word "Brahman" heard in the context of the *ānandamaya*, it is because of its usage for the conscious primordial nature (*citprakṛti*) in the *Gītā*: "My womb is the Great Brahman; in it I place the germ.
In the Smṛti, "the Great Brahman" (*mahad brahma*) are two distinct words.

And thus, the Great One, Lakṣmī—who is denoted by the word *brahman*—is my *yoni*, that is, my wife for the purpose of conception. In that *brahman*, which is *prakṛti*, I place the seed; the meaning is "I deposit.
This is a statement by Kṛṣṇa addressed to Arjuna.

How can the nature of the primordial matter (prakṛti) be determined as consisting of bliss by means of the term "Brahman," which is subject to other interpretations? To this, he states another reason: "because of its manifoldness" (bahubhāvāt), and "because of its multiformity" (bahurūpatvāt).
The word "ca" (and) serves to conjoin these reasons.
And likewise, from the passage "He desired:
'May I be many'" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.2), there is the "state of being many" for the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya).

The meaning is that because the nature of consciousness (cit-prakṛti) is heard to possess multiplicity and because it identifies with that [multiplicity], multiplicity is possible through the medium of the insentient modifications (vikāra-jaḍa) with which it identifies.

In this way, by relying on the interpretation of "of the prakṛti" as "of the insentient prakṛti," another prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) should also be seen. The construction [of the objection] is: "Or rather, the attainment of the state of being composed of bliss (ānandamayatva) belongs to the insentient prakṛti."
Why? Because, even without the presence of egoism (*abhimānitva*), there is a direct multiplicity [of forms] from [the word] itself.
In the passage beginning with "In *Bṛhat*, *Jāti*, *Jīva*, *Kamalāsana*, and *Śabdarāśi*," it is precisely from the word *brahman* that [the identity of all individual souls] is established.

And because of [the mention of] "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and so forth, he states another prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) supported by reasoning: "The great ones, etc. This implies that all individual souls (*jīva*) residing within those respective bodies would attain the state of consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*).
Why? Because of the word "Brahman" applied to the individual souls (jīvas).
The meaning is: because of the word "Brahman" which denotes the individual soul. The force of the word "eva" (only/itself) is that no separate reason need be sought for this.
To the question, "Whence does the word *brahman* have the sense of 'living being' (*jīva*)?", it is said: "Because [the root] *bṛh* means 'to be born'.
The meaning is that the verbal root *bṛh* occurs in the senses of birth and so forth.
After the word "iti," the phrase "because of the etymological explanation of the root" is to be supplied as the remainder.
Because the word "Brahman" is common to many things, it is non-conclusive; therefore, he says: "And because of being composed of food, etc.
This phrase is repeated, and in that context, the second part is modified.
The word "ādi" (etcetera) is displaced [in its position];
by it, breath and so forth are included.
And the word "ca" (and) is used in its respective order to indicate a collection of both stated and unstated reasons.
And thus— it is not only from the word "Brahman," but because [the self] of living beings is "consisting of the essence of food" (annarasamaya);

The construction is as follows: since it has been stated that [the self] consists of breath (*prāṇamaya*), and because it consists of food and so forth, and because it identifies with the body and other things which are modifications of food and so forth, the state of consisting of food (*annamayatva*) and the rest are established; therefore, by virtue of being mentioned in that same sequence, the state of consisting of bliss (*ānandamayatva*) is also established.
In this context, although Hiraṇyagarbha and others are individual souls (*jīva*), they are mentioned separately with the intention of referring to them as deities (*devatā*).
For this very reason, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, the analysis of the compound "brahmādi" is shown as "of which host of deities Brahmā is the first.
Even there, because Hiraṇyagarbha and Rudra are extremely well-known, they are mentioned separately according to the sequence to be described later.

Then, following the mention of the perishable deities (Indra and others) according to the order stated in the passage "Brahmā, Śiva, Sureśa, etc.," there follows the mention of the imperishable Prakṛti.
Now, it should be understood that this is because the living beings who identify with the visible body possess very limited intelligence.
Nevertheless, they are not denoted by the term "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*);
rather, it is Viṣṇu alone who is so designated.
"That alone is the supreme Brahman of the seers" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 1.3);
"They call this very one Brahman" (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 3.2.3.12). He establishes the final conclusion with the words "nevertheless" (tathāpi).

Although the attainment [of this state] occurs for others in this way, nevertheless, the meaning here is that those who are designated by the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) are not Hiraṇyagarbha and the like.
One raises the objection, "Who then? with the words "But rather... (kiṃ tu).
He states the answer: "Viṣṇu alone.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that "he who is spoken of is Viṣṇu alone.

By this, for the sake of establishing the consistency (*saṅgati*) and the logical connection (*anvaya*) of the portion of the Sūtra's proposition stating "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), the term "that indeed" (*tattu*)—which was cited under the Sūtra on Consistency (*samanvaya-sūtra*) and serves to present the predicate—is [connected].
Thus, the portion of the thesis has been explained. To the question, "Why is Ānandamaya Viṣṇu alone? he explains the scriptural reason (sūtra) that follows: "Tadeva" (That very same), etc.

In such sentences as these, the word *brahman*—which is well-known and used in its primary sense for that very Viṣṇu—is [applied] to that Ānandamaya, as in the passage cited concerning Ānandamaya: "Asat eva" (He is indeed non-existent).

In this verse, the word "from repeated practice" (abhyāsāt) means "from hearing [the scriptures] repeatedly. Immediately after "from repeated practice," the phrase "from understanding the intended meaning (tātparya) regarding Viṣṇu" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

To ward off the suspicion that [the term] is non-essential, and to make known that the word "Brahman" has no other scope [of application], it is stated: "well-known in that [sense]" and "indeed. By the word "etcetera," [passages such as] "The supreme, great Brahman" and "Higher than Vāsudeva" [are included].
The phrase "Who indeed could be designated by the word 'Brahman'? is taken [as the subject];
the meaning of that very scriptural passage has been set forth in the *Jijñāsā* method (the first chapter).
The meaning of the scriptural passage "this very [one]" will be explained in every section (*adhikaraṇa*). The word *brahman* is intended for the supreme Viṣṇu alone and not for anything else;
for other [entities] are incomplete, or [the term may be applied to them] only figuratively.
"He is designated as Brahman, as the Supreme Self (paramātman), and as the Blessed Lord (bhagavān);
[he is] Brahman whose essence is Vāsudeva," or "the ascetic [meditates on him] by means of the root-mantra"—
because in such passages, the word *brahman* is repeatedly used in reference to that very [Vāsudeva], it is well-established [that he is Brahman].
In the Smṛti passage "the word Brahman," the term "in the supreme" (pare) is a qualifying attribute containing a reason, meaning "in the full" (pūrṇe).

The word "vā" is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Thus, since Viṣṇu is the Supreme (*para*), the term "Brahman" is accepted as being used in its primary sense (*mukhyatayā*) with reference to Viṣṇu alone.
This is accepted by those who follow authoritative tradition;
however, it does not apply to Viṣṇu "elsewhere," meaning that it does not apply even to Hiraṇyagarbha and others.
Why is this? From this, he states the reason for their not possessing the primary sense of the word "Brahman": "Because others are incomplete" (*pare*).
If so, [one might ask about the scriptural statement]: "From that, this Brahman is born—name, form, and food" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.9).

Regarding the question of how the word *brahman* is intended to apply to them in such passages as "Two Brahmans are to be known" (*Maitrī Upaniṣad* 6.22) and "All individual souls (*jīvas*) are indeed Brahmans," the author says: in some other instances, even though the word *brahman* is accepted [in its primary sense], it is used [for the *jīvas*] "figuratively" (*upacāreṇa*).
It should exist by way of the primary sense for the supreme [Brahman] and by way of the secondary sense for others;
this is the meaning of the Bhāgavata Smṛti regarding the term "Brahman," as has already been stated.

Regarding the phrase "the cause for the common recollection associated with the word 'Self' in the middle," it is stated in the *Candrikā* that this indicates that the meaning should also be described as being due to the repetition of the word "Ātman" which denotes Brahman, as in passages such as "There is another inner Self" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.2.1). [The text continues:
"Consisting of Vāsudeva."

This statement from the Vyāsa-smṛti, however, is to be construed with the preceding sentence: "Without causing injury, one should worship with flowers or with the Praṇava. For it has been stated in the Nyāyadīpa that here, from the passage beginning "Brahman whose essence is Vāsudeva," the Blessed Lord is understood to be Brahman.

By the phrase "the ascetic (yatiḥ) should worship with his intellect (buddhyā)— that is, with his mind— the Brahman known as Kṛṣṇa, whose essence is Vāsudeva," mental worship (mānasapūjā) for ascetics is prescribed; by the phrase "or he should worship with flowers and so forth," physical worship (kāyikapūjā) is prescribed.
‘Non-violence’ (avihiṃsan) means not causing harm or injury to anyone; this is a statement of their general duty (sāmānyadharma).

By this, it is implied that for ascetics, the general duty characterized by non-violence is indeed stronger than the specific duty (vaiśeṣikadharma) arising from their Vaiṣṇava status, such as the gathering of *tulasī* flowers and the like.
As it is stated in the *Bṛhadbhāṣya*: "The general rule (*sāmānyadharma*) is stronger than the specific rule (*vaiśeṣikadharma*).

By the phrase "with the *praṇava*" (the syllable *oṃ*), "with the root mantra" (either the eight-syllabled mantra or another), or "one should worship," it should be understood that vocal worship (*vācikapūjā*) is being described.
If it be argued that [the suffix] *mayaṭ* is not [to be applied] because it denotes a modification (*vikāra*), we say no, because of abundance (*prācurya*).
The word *mayaṭ* is appropriate for primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the rest because they consist of modifications and because they possess identification with them;
however, let it not be thought that this is not so for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

It is "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) because of its abundance of bliss, but not because it is a modification of that [bliss]. Having raised an objection to what was stated, the Sūtra is recited; then, the author explains the portion containing the objection with the words: "vikāra... (modification).
And here, *ca* signifies a conjunction of reasons.
By the word *prakṛti*, both the conscious and unconscious primordial natures (*cidacit-prakṛtī*) are understood; by the word *ādi*, the individual souls (*jīvas*) are understood.
The word "prakṛti" and so forth is also modified; the negative particle *nañ* is repeated; thus, there exists the term "ānandamaya."
"But Viṣṇu," and so on. The word "but" (tu) has the sense of distinction and the sense of restriction.
And thus: the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is not Viṣṇu.
But [the term refers to] primordial matter (prakṛti) and the rest alone.
Why? Because here there is the word "non-modification" (avikāra).
The word *mayaṭ*, which has the sense of "modification," is employed;
and it is employed precisely by virtue of being either a modification or the conceit (*abhimāna*) of that [modification].
It proceeds;
therefore, it is logical that this applies only to primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the like.
Why? Because insentient primordial matter consists of transformations, whereas sentient primordial matter and the like possess the conceit of being the transformer.
"But not of the Supreme Self, because of its changelessness and lack of ego-identification"— this is the construction [of the sentence].
He explains the portion "if this is said" with the words "let it not be so."
The word "is called" (śaṅketi) is to be supplied.
To the question "Why?", he explains the scriptural reason that follows: "abounding in" (pracura-), etc.;
"the one consisting of bliss is spoken of" is to be supplied.
The word "hi" indicates a reason;
the word "tu" has the sense of restriction.
And thus, because [it is said] "hi," [it follows that he is] "ānandamayaḥ."

The meaning of the term is "because of abundant bliss" and "because of full bliss"; it is designated by the word *ānandamaya* solely on that account, and not because it is a modification (*vikāra*) of bliss.
The construction is intended to prevent the doubt that [the self] might be so called because it is a modification of bliss.

The meaning is that there is no contradiction because the suffix *mayaṭ* functions by depending on another sense, namely "abundance" (*prācurya*). Furthermore, the reason for this is that the fact that the suffix known as *mayaṭ* has "abundance" as its meaning is established by the statement: "The suffix *mayaṭ* is threefold: in the sense of identity (*tādātmya*), in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), and in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*).
This is also the intended meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed).

Although, for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the derivative term "ānandamaya" occurring in the Śruti and Sūtra, one should— consistent with that derivation— form the compound as "ānandapracuraḥ," meaning "that in which bliss abounds," and not its opposite, "pracurānandaḥ," meaning "that in which there is abundant bliss."

Nevertheless, regarding the expression *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss), if one were to explain it as a compound meaning "abounding in bliss" (*ānanda-pracura*)—which would not conform to the function of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*)—then, just as in the case of the phrase "a village abounding in Brahmins," the presence of non-bliss (*an-ānanda*) would also be implied.
To preclude this, the reverse compound *pracurānanda* (abundant bliss) has been employed.
However, some maintain that since the word "abundance" (*prācurya*) is explicitly stated in the Sūtra, the sense "of bliss" (*ānandasya*) is already obtained by implication.

They say that although, according to this statement, one ought to employ a compound expression as "because of the abundance of bliss" (*ānandapracuratvāt*), nevertheless, with the aforementioned purpose in mind, the compound in the Sūtra has been made contrary to the expanded form by saying "because of having abundant bliss" (*pracurānandatvāt*).

This is not correct, because it contradicts the commentary which states: "In the case of expressing [the meaning] as it stands, namely 'one who has an abundance of bliss' (*ānandapracura*)," and so forth.

Even though, according to the Śruti and the Sūtra, the term "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) expresses abundance as the predicate, there is no attainment of manifold bliss; for even when it is said, "the sun is abundant in light," no trace of darkness is perceived in the sun.

Therefore, it is more appropriate to explain it simply as "abundance of bliss," since abundance can be defined by the smallness of a similar entity belonging to a different substratum—namely, the limited bliss of individual souls (*jīva*).
Nevertheless, since even our opponents have accepted that abundance (*prācurya*) cannot be established as a qualifier because it would not exclude non-bliss,

whereas they have admitted that when it is the qualificand— as in "a village abounding in Brahmins"— it is indeed established because it is defined by the smallness of dissimilar things existing in the same locus,
the text must be explained in accordance with what is proven for both parties; it is with this intention [that the following is said].
"In the commentary (*bhāṣya*), it is explained that [the term *anna* refers to food] because of its abundance; this is stated in the *Candrikā*.
Furthermore, the abundance of food and so forth is precisely what is meant by the passage: 'It is eaten and it eats' (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.2)."
Thus, from this explanation, its abundance is also appropriate.
But surely this word "ānandamaya" does not denote an abundance of bliss;
rather, it has only the sense of a modification (*vikāra*).
Because they are recited together with the words "consisting of food" (annamaya) and so forth, which signify modifications of food and the like, he says: "And of food, etc. (annādīnāṃ ca).
And this [term] recurs;
the word "mayaṭ" also recurs.
Therefore, the word "ca" (and) is construed in the sense of conjunction.
There is a designation of non-difference between the signified and the signifier.
Thus, it is not only in the case of "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) that the suffix *mayaṭ* is used;
rather, even the suffix *mayaṭ* in connection with food and so forth expresses precisely the abundance of food and the rest—this is the meaning.
The word *eva* (indeed) is for the purpose of excluding the sense of modification (*vikāra*).
By the word *ādi* (and so forth), breath (*prāṇa*) and the rest are included. Previously, it was stated: "And because of [the mention of] consisting of food (*annamaya*), etc."

And here, by the mention of "food and so forth" (*annādīnām*)— referring to many items— it is indicated that the term *ānandamaya* in the Sūtra, through the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of not abandoning its own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārtha*), implies other terms that follow the same logical principle.
Now, one might object: how can the word *annamaya* here mean "abounding in food"?
For although an abundance of food produced from herbs may exist in earthly bodies that subsist on food, it is impossible in the case of Hari, who possesses a non-material form;
moreover, describing an abundance of food would result in [the Lord] being reduced to a state of extreme insignificance. To this, he says: "It is eaten" (*adyate*).
The word "by the sentence" completes the phrase "of the word *anna*. Immediately after "is appropriate," the term "the meaning of the word *annamaya*" is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
The word "of the Supreme Self" (paramātmanaḥ) exists [in the text].
Furthermore, the meaning is that there is not only an absence of contradiction with the co-occurrence [of the terms];
rather, the construction is as follows: "the abundance thereof" (tatprācuryam).
The meaning of the term *annamaya* as "abundance of food" is appropriate;
how so? Because it is offered (*yajyate*) to that Supreme Self.
Nor should it be argued: "How can it be applied to Hari, since, by having a limited meaning, it lacks the nature of greatness (*māhātmyarūpatva*)?"

Since, in this context, according to the method of the author of the *Sudhā*, the word "food" (*anna*)—being primarily expressive of a state (*bhāvapradhāna*)—is logically applicable only to these two meanings, namely, the state of being those respective elements and so forth, and the state of being their consumer; it is said that the commonly known food is not meant here.
How is this known?
This is because the word *anna* (food) is explained by the statement, "It is eaten (*adyate*) and it eats (*atti*) beings;
therefore it is called *anna*," since it is impossible for ordinary food to be a consumer of beings, and thus it cannot be what is intended here.
The meaning of the scriptural passage is as follows: because he is "eaten" (upajīvyate) by beings— that is, by living creatures— and because he "eats" (atti) beings,
he destroys them.
Therefore, that which is called Viṣṇu is declared in the Vedas to be "food" (anna).

Thus, since the words *prāṇa* and *manas* signify the state of being the agent of excellent activity and perfect consciousness respectively, any claim that they primarily denote the breath-air or the internal organ-intellect—which would be a limited meaning—must be avoided.
Being the very basis of subsistence (*upajīvyatva*) is what constitutes "primacy" (*ādyatva*).
Because of the commencement of another [topic] with the words, "This, indeed, is that" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.2).
But even so, how is the state of being abundant in elements and so forth intended for Brahman?
Since the state of being edible and so forth is inappropriate in that context, he states the meaning of the word "adyatva" (edibility) as "the state of being a means of subsistence."

In this context, following the *Anuvyākhyāna*’s reading "ato 'dyate" (therefore it is eaten), the word is divided as "adyatvam. Thus, according to the method explained in the *Sudhā*, what is intended by "being eaten" (*adyatva*) is, through a figurative sense (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*), precisely the state of being the source of subsistence (*upajīvyatva*).
But it does not possess the quality of being relished;
and that [quality] is not contradictory in the case of Brahman—this is the intended meaning.
However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, it says: "Nor is the food of others that which is the first-born of all beings..."
And that [primacy] does not belong to anyone else in a primary sense;
rather, Viṣṇu alone, residing within that [food], is the primary one because He bestows satisfaction and contentment which constitute the fruit of eating.
Therefore, primacy consists precisely in being the source of subsistence (*upajīvyatva*).
Because he is the self of all worlds, Hari is called "food" (anna);
and because he is that upon which all beings depend for life, Janārdana is food.
By this statement, it is shown that being the "basis of subsistence" (upajīvyatva) is indeed the primary meaning;
nor is there any contradiction, because, according to the method explained in the *Kampanādhikaraṇa*, the *Tattvapradīpa* proceeds with the intent of establishing systematic harmony (*samanvaya*).
In passages such as "like a vajra" (*vajravat*), the term *sudhā* (nectar) is employed with the intention that it refers to Brahman in some manner or other.
Now, one might ask: how is the word *annamaya* (consisting of food) appropriately used in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*)? [It is so because] "from herbs comes food."

Having first stated, "From food [comes] the person" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.2), referring to the body as a modification of well-known food, the text then says, "This very person, indeed, consists of the essence of food" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.3).
Since this is a restatement (anuvāda) identifying the person as consisting of the essence of food, it refers to the person as a modification of food.
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with that; therefore, he says: "He" (saḥ).
The word "non-contradiction" (avirodhaḥ) is drawn over from the previous context.
And by the phrase "tathā ca," because the ether and so forth were produced from this Self, he is this very Puruṣa, [not] "another's."
Because there is a "consideration" (parāmarśa) of a self other than the body, there is "no contradiction"; that is, there is no contradiction with the consideration.
To dispel the doubt as to why this [Brahman] is referred to again, he says "because of the commencement" (*prārambhāt*) instead of saying "because of the reference" (*parāmarśāt*).

Having previously stated that the Self is the cause of ether and the rest, he speaks of "commencement" once more in order to demonstrate that very same Self— by means of another purpose— that is, for the sake of other effects, possesses the fivefold form consisting of the one made of food (*annamaya*) and so forth.
The meaning is "because it has been introduced [in the context].
In the scriptural passage "He, indeed" (*sa vā*), the word *vai* signifies either emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) or well-knownness (*prasiddhi*).
The word *anna* (food) has the abstract state (*bhāva*) as its primary sense.
The state of being *rasa* is the state of being supreme, and that is a qualification of the nature of food (*anna*).
And thus, because from the Self— endowed with characteristics such as truthfulness and so forth— the ether and the rest were produced, "He" [is that Self].
He who is designated by the word "Self" is the creator of the elements and so forth; He is the "Person" (puruṣa) residing within the body of the individual soul;
the Blessed Lord, endowed with the six perfections in their fullness, dwelling in the city called the body, is "consisting of the essence of food" (annarasamaya).
The meaning is that [the self] is filled with the nature of the highest food (*uttamānna*).

However, in the *Taittirīya-bhāṣya*, it is explained by repeating the word "food" (*anna*) and transposing the order of the words, as follows: "Since Viṣṇu is the essential core (*sāra*) of the body composed of food (*annamaya*), which consists of the nature of being the eater of food and so forth, he is therefore 'consisting of the essence of food' (*annarasamaya*)."

From such scriptural passages as "those who meditate on food as Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.2), and because of its manifold forms, there is no contradiction in its not being a mere modification. Now,

since the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in both senses [of "abundance" and "modification"], and since defects are seen in both positions here as well, what is the determining factor that the meaning of the five instances of *mayaṭ* is only abundance and not modification?

Furthermore, if one were to accept that the five [sheaths] beginning with the "consisting of food" (annamaya) are Brahman, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as "One alone indeed... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1); therefore, he says: "Those who [say] 'Food is Brahman'... and so forth.
Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), [the following passages are included]: "Those who meditate on prāṇa as Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.3.1);
"Knowing bliss as Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1); and "If one knows vijñāna as Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5.1).
The collection of statements beginning with "If one knows that Brahman exists" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1) is taken here;
it means that [Brahman] exists and is of the nature of bliss.
The phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*) has its locative case ending elided;
"in the verses" (*ślokeṣu*) is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The word "brahma" (*brahmaśabda*) is indicative of hearing that [word].

When these two reasons have been thus demonstrated as being suitable for the logical connection (anvaya) through the introduction of further reasons, he states the probandum (sādhya) in sequence: "not being subject to modification" (*na vikāritvam*).
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "it is determined that this is the meaning of the suffix *mayaṭ*.
"Non-contradiction" (*avirodhaḥ*) means the absence of contradiction.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "api" (also).

Thus, the construction here is as follows: because of the word "Brahman" in the verses cited with reference to the "consisting of food" (annamaya) and so forth—such as "Those who [know] food as Brahman"—which have the "consisting of food" and the others as their subject matter.

Since the word *brahman* is heard [in proximity], and since its co-occurrence with that term can be established otherwise [than as a material cause], it is determined that for the suffix *-maya*, which is possible in both ways, the meaning is "abundance" (*prācurya*) alone and not "modification" (*vikāritva*).
Therefore, the objection regarding the need for a restrictive rule is not tenable;
thus, because the single Brahman itself possesses manifold forms.
Since it is logically consistent for a single entity alone to be described as having many forms, there is no contradiction with the Śruti statement "one alone" (ekameva).
This is because, previously, [the term] was established as referring to Brahman through the repeated use of the word "Brahman" in that very context.

Having stated this, the *Candrikā* explains that the purpose of mentioning only the word "Brahman" (*brahma-śabda*) here is precisely to state a reason common to all [the cases], namely: "Because the word 'Brahman' is not repeated in the other [contexts] as it is in the [contexts of] Bliss (*ānanda*) and the Consisting of Knowledge (*vijñāna-maya*), its application to those [others] would otherwise be unestablished; therefore, the mention of the word 'Brahman' serves to exclude such non-establishment.
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to assume separate [meanings] for each instance.
And its own nature is thus appropriate, just as one says, "The sun is abundant light.
Here, others maintain that the *ānandamaya* itself is Brahman,
and that the suffix *-maya-* in that context signifies abundance (*prācurya*).
It has been stated that the sheaths (kośas), such as the one consisting of food (annamaya) and so forth,
and the suffix *mayaṭ* applied to them, have the sense of "modification" (*vikāra*).
To this he says, "And not," [meaning] that this is incorrect.
Since the suffix *maya* is generally used in the sense of "consisting of," it is not reasonable to assume a dual meaning;
consequently, it is likewise not reasonable to assume that only one among the series beginning with *annamaya* is Brahman.
The meaning is that [the alternative view] is strained because it contradicts the context of the sequential reading (*prāyapāṭha*).

As for the proponent who asserts that all five—beginning with "consisting of food" (*annamaya*)—are not Brahman, he has already been made the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) by the author of the Sūtras themselves; therefore, the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) does not refute that position here.

In the *Tattvapradīpa*, however, it is stated: "The phrase 'na ca' does not imply a separate conception by a magician; rather, in the passages 'Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite' (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1) and 'From this very Self' (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.2), it is Brahman that is being spoken of."

The five sheaths, beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya), are mutually distinct; although they are designated by the word "Brahman," they are not Brahman. Only the final tail-end (puccha) is Brahman.
Liberation consists in the transcendence of the sheaths beginning with that of food.
The eye, ear, mind, and speech, which will be mentioned later, do not persist in the [sheaths] beginning with "consisting of food" (*annamaya*).
In passages such as "He understood that food is Brahman" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 3.2), the fifth element, bliss (*ānanda*), is the Brahman-hood.

The reasoning that the subsequent portion of the text beginning with "these worlds" (Tai.U. 3.10.5)— which forms a single syntactical unit with the preceding qualified description— is intended to set forth the fruit [of the meditation], distinct from the statement regarding the attributeless Brahman which transcends the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), is indeed appropriate.
This has been explained as being intended to refute the final position because it is utterly inconsistent with the reasons already stated.
Nor should it be said that there is no contradiction between this and the *Ṭīkā*,
for we accept the intention of the *Ṭīkā* to be that the author of the *Bhāṣya* did not specifically refute [that view] in detail.

But is it not the case that such usage as "there is no abundance of bliss in Brahman" is appropriate? For since Brahman has bliss and so forth as its very nature, [the expression] "rice with an abundance of ghee" [is likewise appropriate].
Since such usage occurs only in instances where there is a distinction [between the word and its meaning], he says: "And in the case of the essential nature (*svarūpa*)";
the word *ca* has the sense of *api* (also);
the word *iti* refers to the category of sound (*śabda*).
After "like the sun," the word "usage" (*vyavahāraḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Furthermore, there is a repetition of the phrase "and in its own nature" (*svarūpe ca*).
And likewise, even though the solar orb is of the nature of light, there is such conventional usage as "the sun is abundant light" due to the force of a specific attribute;

similarly, even though Hari is of the nature of bliss and so forth, it is entirely appropriate to employ such usage with respect to Him through His specific attributes. Thus, the meaning is that there is no inconsistency in that [usage]. "And because of the designation of Him as the cause. (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.14)
"For who indeed could breathe if this bliss were not in the ether? (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7). Thus, if the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) were Viṣṇu alone...

And presenting the sūtra that establishes the reason for the claim that the meaning of the suffix *mayaṭ* is indeed abundance (*prācurya*) in the form of another cause (*hetvantara*), he states: "taddhetu... (That-sūtra).

The words "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) and "that very thing" (tattviti) are carried over [from the previous sūtra]. There is a repetition of the word "that" (tat); furthermore, it may be analyzed as "that which is the cause" (sa cāsau hetuśca).
And thus, it is not only because of the repetition of the word "Brahman";
rather, it is "because of the designation of its cause" (*taddhetuvyapadeśāt*).

In that section concerning the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), regarding Viṣṇu's state of being "consisting of bliss" through his fullness of bliss, there is indeed the designation of abundance (*prācurya*) itself.

And regarding the sense of the suffix *-maya*, because of the designation of its cause and the statement of the reason known as "being the mover of the world," it is Viṣṇu alone who is denoted by the word *ānandamaya* by virtue of being full of bliss; with this intention, following the commentary on the Sūtra, he shows that very designation of the cause [by asking]: "For who? (*ko hi*). "When" (*yat*) means when/if "this ether" (*eṣa ākāśaḥ*).

If Viṣṇu, who shines forth on all sides as bliss—that is, full bliss—were not [to exist], then he would not set the world in motion; this is the implied meaning. The sense is that without an overflow of bliss, there would be no impetus for activity due to the absence of any other cause.
This is the case if he were not to set the world in motion.
Then, who indeed would cause [the world] to breathe? Or what person would move about in the world? And who would live?
And who would set one forth in dharma and so on?
No one at all;
for another lacks independence—this is the meaning of the Śruti according to the method of the *Taittirīyabhāṣyaṭīkā*.

However, in the *Sudhā*, it is explained that because the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*) is included within [the meaning of the root], no one would engage in either worldly or Vedic activity;

thus, the word "iti" (thus) is connected with the phrase "iti taddhetuvyapadeśāt" (because of the designation of that as the cause). And it is sung as being based precisely on the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*). (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.15)

Having indicated this with the statement, "Through the knowledge of Brahman, one attains the Supreme," it is the Supreme Brahman itself— characterized by the words of the mantra, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"— that is celebrated through the contemplation of the word.
As for what was stated—that the term *brahman* establishes that the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) and the others are Viṣṇu—that is not correct.
This is because the word *brahman* can appropriately apply even to the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the lower *brahman*.

Furthermore, even if it has its primary sense in the supreme *brahman*, it must here have only a secondary meaning due to subverting evidence, such as the statement that Viṣṇu is a limb (*avayava*) of the one consisting of bliss.

He reads and explains the Sūtra— "māntravarṇikam"— while removing the doubt that [the term "self" might refer to something else] because its apprehension is possible, and stating another reason for the fact that that which is denoted by words such as "consisting of bliss" is Viṣṇu;
it is to be connected with the passage beginning with "yataḥ."
The phrase "not those" follows as the proposition (*pratijñā*).
And thus, because [it is stated] in the wording of the mantra: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1).

The meaning is this: in the syllables of the mantra—that is, in the specific sentence consisting of those very syllables—the Supreme Brahman alone is "unperceived" (alakṣitam) in the sense that it is described as possessing defining characteristics; it is not unperceived [in the sense of being non-existent], nor is it something other than the Supreme.
The construction is as follows: since they are "sung"— that is, propounded— by means of the words *annamaya* and so forth, the *ānandamaya* and the others are not something else,
but rather the supreme Brahman itself.

From where is it known that the reality characterized by the wording of the mantra is being presented by means of the terms "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and so forth? To this it is said: "from the coordination of words" (*śabdānusandhānāt*).

This means: from the "coordination" (*anusandhāna*)—that is, from the knowledge of their having a single referent—which arises from the coordination of the meanings of both the words such as "truth, knowledge, infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānamanantam*) and the words such as "consisting of food."

Since it is stated even in the wording of the mantra that "Brahman" alone [is meant], how can there be an understanding that the words *annamaya* and so forth—which denote its meanings—also have the Supreme Brahman as their referent? To this, he says: "The knower of Brahman" (*brahmavit*). The word "engaged" (*pravṛttaḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
This [word] is to be construed with the word from the mantra-text as distinguished by the intellect.

And so, having indicated the Supreme Brahman, the knowledge of it, and the attainment of it by the statement, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), and having stated them briefly, the Vedic verse proceeds to dispel any doubt that might have arisen regarding that attainment. Therefore, the "Supreme" characterized here—

The meaning is that it is known as "Brahman alone. In the Sūtra, the terms "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) and so forth, as well as "that [is] this," are carried over from the previous context. The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of "just as" (yathā), and for the purpose of joining together logical arguments.
And thus, it is not determined from the word "Brahman" alone that the one called Viṣṇu, consisting of bliss and so forth, is the supreme Brahman and not the subordinate Brahman; rather,

because that which is described by the Vedic statement "Truth, Knowledge" as possessing defining characteristics (lakṣaṇavat) is the supreme Brahman itself, it is that very [supreme Brahman] which is "sung" (gīyate) by the words beginning with "consisting of food" (annamaya).
And it is established [by scripture];
therefore, the meaning of the sūtra is that [the result] follows even from the implied designation (*samākhyāna*) of that [knowledge].
"Brahmavit" means one who knows the Supreme Brahman; "param" [means the supreme goal].

The meaning established by the scripture, "One who desires to attain the Supreme Brahman should know the Supreme Brahman," is that one attains the Supreme Brahman. When the doubt arises as to what that Brahman is, the passage beginning with "Truth" (satyam) proceeds.

In this context, that which was expressed by the word *satya* (Truth)—namely, the quality of bringing about [the attainment of] states of existence (*gati*), life (*jīvana*), and destruction (*nāśa*)—is expressed by the terms *annamaya* (consisting of food) and *prāṇamaya* (consisting of vital breath).

That which was expressed by the word *ananta* (Infinite)—namely, being undivided in terms of space, time, and substance—is established by the term *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss), since the Supreme Self is infinite because it is full bliss. Thus, one should understand that the words *satya* and so forth, as well as the words *annamaya* and so forth, have the same meaning.
In this context, "infinity of space" (deśānantya) means having an unlimited magnitude;
"infinity of time" (kālānantya) means having an uninterrupted existence;
and "infinity of substance" (vastvānantya) means possessing an unlimited number of qualities, actions, and forms.
And there is no contradiction with its being a composite whole:
"That is the head; that is the right wing; that is the left wing."
"He is the Self; He is the tail," because in the *Caturvedaśikha* it is stated that He is indeed a limb [of Brahman].
Now, one might object: "It is not logical for Viṣṇu to be composed of bliss (*ānandamaya*)."
Because that [bliss] is a part of it;
nor is there a lack of proof, since it is stated that "Brahman is the tail."
And because there is a contradiction between being a whole and being a part, he says "na ca" (not so).
The word "tasya" (of him) is drawn over from the previous context.
The meaning is that there is no contradiction in stating that Viṣṇu consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*) while simultaneously being its part.
The meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that there is no contradiction even between being a part (*avayavatva*) and being a whole (*avayavitva*).

Why is this so? With the intention that since the scripture itself declares that the possessor of parts (*avayavin*) is indeed the state of being a part and the state of being a whole, there is no difference between the whole and its parts, etc., he cites that scriptural passage with the word "saḥ":
"'Saḥ' refers to Nārāyaṇa; 'śiraḥ' means the head."
Or rather, "He is the head";
in this manner, it should also be explained in the subsequent cases.
The second and following instances of the word "tat" (that) refer to Pradyumna and the others, in accordance with the Smṛti.
The right wing is the arm; the left is the body, which is the middle part of the torso; and the tail is the hindquarters.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: in this *Caturvedaśikhā* passage beginning with "the two feet," it is stated that Viṣṇu—who is the very whole (*avayavin*)—is indeed a limb (*avayava*).
By the word "indeed" (*eva*), the distinction between the limb and the whole is negated.
Thus, regarding the fact that a limb is the whole, there is not only this scriptural statement (*śruti*).

However, the Śruti cited in the *Tattvapradīpa*—which is taken as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) in the Bhāṣya, namely, "The foot is the tail, the support; indeed, the Person"—should also be accepted as authoritative.
On this view, the word *avayava* occurring in the Bhāṣya ends in the suffix *ac* (added to the class beginning with *arśas*), and thus refers to the whole (*avayavin*).
Nārāyaṇa is the head; Pradyumna and Aniruddha are the right and left wings respectively; and Vāsudeva is the trunk.
Then Nārāyaṇa is the trunk, Vāsudeva is the head, and Saṅkarṣaṇa is said to be the tail; thus, though he is one alone, he is fivefold.
The Blessed One, the Supreme Person, sports by means of the relationship between limbs and the possessor of limbs.

No contradiction should be conceived regarding that Janārdana on account of his sovereignty; for how can there be logic concerning the inconceivable, and how can there be valid cognition concerning the immeasurable?
Thus, in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā.

Having dispelled the doubt that it is contradictory for a whole (avayavin) to possess the nature of being parts (avayavatva), he cites a scriptural authority and then states a traditional Smṛti text here, beginning with "The head.

Here, in a painting or similar work depicting the form of a young woman, the many women who constitute the parts are said to be parts of a single body; likewise, the five forms such as Nārāyaṇa and others are said to be parts of a single [divine] entity.
The first "ca" (and) serves to collect the various positions.
There are two [instances] for the mutual conjunction of the two forms.
The word "only" (eva) is connected as follows: Nārāyaṇa alone is the head;
likewise, Pradyumna alone is the right wing, the arm.
Aniruddha is the left [side];
Vāsudeva is the "Sandoha," meaning the middle body— this is the grammatical connection.
The compound particle *api vā* indicates an alternative position. In the former position, Nārāyaṇa constitutes the head, while Vāsudeva constitutes the middle part of the body.
In this view, however, there is a reversal regarding that portion; thus, the statement of different positions is made due to the difference in modes of meditation (*upāsanā*).
The syntactical connection is: "But Saṅkarṣaṇa is declared to be the 'tail' in both cases, [and] the feet."
By the word *tu*, a twofold nature or the specific form of Suparṇa is indicated.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "One.
Thus [is] "Puruṣottama."
The Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, who is superior to both the perishable and imperishable persons, is "one alone";
though divided fivefold, he remains one through his parts, being non-different rather than different.
This is by way of being the "limb" (aṅgatvena), that is, as a constituent part, and the "possessor of limbs" (aṅgitvena).
The meaning is that he plays, having attained that state by way of being a whole (*avayavin*). The third case ending is used here in the sense of a characteristic (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*).
[Objection: Even if this be so, the contradiction has not yet been resolved by that much alone; therefore, he says: "Because of his sovereignty" (*aiśvaryāt*).

When Janārdana has attained the state of being a whole and so forth, and when that which consists of those [parts]— namely, the state of being a part and so forth— is the object, there is no contradiction; that is to say,
a contradiction in the form of non-coexistence is not to be considered.
It cannot be conceptualized by anyone.
Why? Because of "sovereignty";

that is, due to the power of the Lord (Īśvara), the absence of contradiction in their coexistence in one place is established, for the meaning is that the power of the Lord accomplishes even the impossible.
Thus, there is no contradiction between that which is the part and that which is the whole.
Why? This should also be explained as being because each individual part possesses the nature of the Lord of all.

Likewise, there is no contradiction; this should also be explained as meaning that even the contradiction regarding the conventional usage of distinction—such as "this is the whole" and "this is the part"—does not exist when there is non-difference between the part and the whole.
In that regard, the reason is indicated by the word "ca" (and), namely: "by the power of the specific [attribute] (*viśeṣa*), due to the state of potentiality and manifestation."
For this very reason, the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of including what was not explicitly stated; it connects with the phrase "and because of sovereignty.

Furthermore: Is it contradictory for a whole (*avayavin*) to possess parts (*avayavatva*) and for a part (*avayava*) to possess wholeness (*avayavitva*), by means of another pramāṇa distinct from reasoning (*tarka*)? Or rather, is it that a whole is not a part because it possesses wholeness?
Or [is it argued] by means of the inference stated in the section on *tarka*: "The whole is not the possessor of parts because it possesses parts, like common worldly objects"?
It is not the first [alternative], because of its lack of proof (*asiddhatva*).
It is not the second either; thus he says: "uninferable" (*atarkya*).

"Indeed"; because [the Lord] is inconceivable, therefore "in the inconceivable"—that is, regarding the Blessed One who is beyond the scope of logic—there can be no "logical argument," such as the reason "He is a whole, not a part, because He possesses the nature of a whole," and so forth; whence [could such an argument arise]?
The meaning is that he is neither a benefactor nor a malefactor.

Furthermore, since in the world contradiction is observed only where there is limitation of power, and because Viṣṇu is devoid of the limited power that would give rise to contradiction, there is no contradiction even if one accepts his being an object of reasoning; thus he says, "immeasurable" (aprameya).

Regarding the term ‘aprameye’: in the Blessed One, who is undelimited by space, time, or qualities, there can be no ‘pramā’—that is, no delimitation of power such as "His capacity is only this much and not more than this. Why?
Because it is not so; this is the meaning.
And thus, the sense is that because the reasoning (tarka) stated by others is invalid due to being fallacious (sopādhika), it possesses no power of contradiction.
By this, it is stated that the meaning of the term "atarkya" is "that which is not within the scope of fallacious reasoning."
Thus, in the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā*, the word "iti" connects with the phrase "because it is stated to be a part of that very [Self]," which is supplied as an ellipsis.
By means of the qualification through the word "rasa," only pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which constitutes the essence of each respective thing, is expressed.
And the word "this" (*idam*) refers to that which is perceived as being proximate.

Now, as for the claim that in the sentence "or he who... there is a reference (*parāmarśa*) to this Supreme Self alone, and not to the body described in the passage "the person from food," that is incorrect;

for while the Self is distant, the body is present in the vicinity. Since there is no reason to abandon what is mentioned nearby and accept a reference to something distant, [the former interpretation is untenable].

Furthermore—since the word *puruṣa* refers only to that which has been introduced as the subject (*prakṛta*), and since the Self (*ātman*) has not been introduced [in this context], it is improper to refer to the Self by the word *puruṣa*. Nor can it be argued:
"Know both Nature (*prakṛti*) and the Person (*puruṣa*) to be indeed beginningless;
for the Person, situated in Nature, experiences the qualities born of Nature. [This does not apply here, because the context is different.]

It should not be argued that, just as in the two sentences cited above the term *puruṣa*—though of a single form—is accepted as denoting both the Supreme Self and the individual soul through a systematic distinction (*vyavasthā*), so too here the term *puruṣa*, though repeated with a single form, may be accepted as expressing two distinct meanings through such a systematic distinction. For in those cases, there exists a scriptural distinction (such as being the "experiencer of suffering") that differentiates them; whereas in the present case, there is no such differentiator, and thus in the phrase "from food, the person (*puruṣa*"), the word refers to the body.
Since it is untenable to maintain the established position that in this passage "sa vai" (he indeed) refers only to the Supreme Self, he says: "rasa... (the essence).
The phrase "sa vā eṣaḥ" (this indeed is that) continues; the word "tat" (that) recurs;
and the phrase "evam ucyate" (it is said thus) also recurs.
The phrase "having left aside anything else" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
And thus, by the sentence "Or rather, that," it is consciousness alone—pure consciousness, the very consciousness of Brahman—that is expressed and referred to, not the body.
Nor is there any contradiction with the statement regarding its being far away.

It should not be said that there is a contradiction with the subject matter [of the preceding context] regarding the word "puruṣa" (Person), because that which was described by the words beginning with "ether" and ending with "puruṣa"— in the passage, "From this Self, ether was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.2)— namely, Brahman as pure Consciousness, which is the essence and the most excellent reality among those entities such as ether, is what is referred to by the referential statement, "He indeed... (sa vā eṣa).
