If that is so, one should not say: "Since both are under discussion by means of the word *puruṣa*, let this [word] refer to both.

For, by the sentence of reference beginning with "he" (*saḥ*), it is stated that it is none other than Brahman—the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) which is the essence of that [body] and the essence of the *puruṣa*—having abandoned the other body and so forth.
Why? To this he says: "By the juice," etc. (*rasa-ityādi*).

The meaning is that by the qualification "consisting of the essence of food" (*annarasamaya*), which contains the word *rasa*, there is stated a specific qualification of the person (*puruṣa*) consisting of the essence of food. The word *mātra* is used for the purpose of awakening [the understanding of] Brahman, which is distinct from insentient matter and the individual soul (*jīva*).
Alternatively, it is because of the qualification by the primary sense of the word *rasa*—that is, by the referent of the word *rasa*—which serves as a qualification of the nature of being food.

Furthermore, in this context, the term *annarasa* (the essence of food) refers to that which is characterized by being the primary consumer among the meanings of the word "food," and it is abundant therein; thus says the *Sudhā*.

And in the *Ṭīkā*, the syntactical connection is: "Brahman alone, which is pure consciousness, [is the essence]. Now, one might object: in another section of the *Anuvāka*, it is said, "May the *annamaya*, *prāṇamaya*, *manomaya*, *vijñānamaya*, and *ānandamaya* [sheaths] be purified for me" (*Yājñikī* 66).
Thus has been stated the designation of the sheaths beginning with the *annamaya* (consisting of food), which have been purified through such prayers.
However, it is the Brahman-consciousness (*brahmacaitanya*) residing within them—which constitutes their respective essence and governs each sheath—that is truly meant.
Why? Because of the passage: "Now, this very one... (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1.3).

In passages beginning with "Thus, etc. and ending with "He is indeed the essence," the meaning is that [the Self] is qualified by the word *rasa* (essence) for the purpose of distinguishing it from the sheaths (*kośa*) such as the one consisting of food (*annamaya*), and for the purpose of showing its difference from them. "Being qualified at the beginning" means being included [in the initial statement].

Thus, the point is that, according to the principle of "differentiation by another term" (*śabdāntara-nyāya*), there is a distinction between those consisting of food (*annamaya*) and those consisting of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*), and so forth.

This is an elliptical indication; it should also be understood that [the term "this"] is qualified by the word "that" (tat), which refers to the Self as the cause of space and so forth, even though they are separated [from the body].
Now, if the visible body itself is not the "consisting of food" (annamaya), [how can it be called such]?

However, if there were a reflection such as "But Brahman alone is that, and he is that very one," then the direct designation "this [visible body] is his head" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.3) would not be tenable.
Nor should it be argued that the sage, the seer of the Upanishads, having realized Brahman through direct perception, points it out based on that perception;
for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of him likewise pointing out the "sheath of vital breath" (prāṇamaya) and the others, which he had also directly perceived.

Furthermore, since [Brahman] is known directly by himself, he has no need for words; and since the persons to be instructed are incapable of direct perception, such a pointing out would be useless. Therefore, the phrase "that of this" (tad asya) must also be explained [as follows].
And thus, because this head, wings, and so forth of the Lord consisting of food (annamaya) are in close proximity to the visible, perceptually established head, wings, and so forth of the body—
just like the joints and heroic limbs situated within the cloth and armor— and because they exist as perfect regulators,
it is appropriate to employ the term "this" (idam) with reference to the head of Brahman by way of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā); such is the construction.
To demonstrate the relationship between the primary meaning and the secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) based on capability, he says "dṛśyamāna" (being seen).

Thus, just as the conventional usage "this is a knee" is appropriate even when the knees are covered by a garment or enclosed within armor, this [present] usage is likewise logical; the point is that there is no contradiction with that [usage].
Even though it is not other, it is designated by the word "other"; likewise, though it is one, it possesses many forms.
The Blessed One Viṣṇu is called Puruṣottama because of his sovereign power.

Thus it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "But surely, the status of Brahman for the five [sheaths] beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*) is untenable, [as seen in the passage]: 'Now, different from this one consisting of the essence of food is another inner self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*')' (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.2.2)."

Since they have been described as distinct from one another in this way, the objection that there is no contradiction with the Śruti statement "one only" because Brahman alone possesses many forms is also untenable, as it lacks authoritative proof; therefore, he says: "ananya" (non-different).
The word *api* is used in the sense of "even though" (*yadyapi*);
the word *tathā* signifies conjunction (*samuccaye*).
Thus: "The Blessed One Viṣṇu is the Supreme Person."
"Even though non-different"; that is, even though it is not distinct, it is expressed by the word "different," meaning "distinct.
Likewise, although it is one, it nevertheless possesses many forms; such is the meaning.
To the question "How so?", he states that which constitutes both [reasons]: "Because of sovereignty" (aiśvaryāt);
this means because of inconceivable power (acintya-śakti).
This is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should also be understood that attributes such as distinctness and internality, which pertain to the five sheaths (*kośa*) beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*), are metaphorically attributed (*upacaryante*) to the forms of the Blessed One residing within them.
For this very reason, it is said in the third [chapter]: "Because of the difference in location and because of sovereignty."
Thus, in the *Bhāṣya*, another reason called "difference of location" (*sthānabheda*) has been stated.
However, in the *Taittirīyabhāṣya*, it is said that even in the absence of difference, there is a statement of distinctness because of being associated with specific numbers.
The syntactical connection is that there is no contradiction because [the statement] was made immediately after [the passage] in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*.
Nor is Viriñca or others referred to by the aforementioned attainment;
nor is it anyone else, because that would be untenable.
For liberation is not possible through the knowledge of another.
"For one who knows this thus becomes immortal here;
there is no other path for the journey," so it has been said (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12.7).

One might raise the following objection: "Since the word *brahman* is common to all [deities], since the designation of its cause (*taddhetuvyapadeśa*) clearly manifests as residing in Viṣṇu, and since the mention in the mantra-text (*mantravarṇa*) and the name (*samākhyā*) are weaker than other indicative marks (*liṅga*) and thus have room for another interpretation, and because there is no other cause that cannot be explained otherwise, it is possible that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) and the others are none other than Viriñca (Brahmā) and so forth. Anticipating this doubt, he introduces the sūtra with the words: "Not so" (*na ca*).
The word "eva" (only) functions as a restriction;
it connects with the phrase "Virinca and the others. And thus, by the aforementioned attainment;

It is not the case that Viriñca and others alone are denoted by the words *annamaya* and so forth—which convey the aforementioned states such as being the bliss of hundreds of Brahmas, having eight forms, and possessing manifold natures—but rather, Viṣṇu is also denoted by them.
Indeed, it is not so; on the contrary, [Viṣṇu is indeed denoted].
Viṣṇu alone is meant by those [names], not Viriñca (Brahmā) and others—this is the meaning.

When the question arises as to why it is not so, he presents the Sūtra; since the portion of the proposition (*pratijñā*) has already been explained by the commentary beginning with "And not" (*na ca*), he explains only the reason (*hetu*) from the Sūtra which cannot be established otherwise: "Not the other" (*netara*).
Thus; the word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the reason:
"from the knowledge of another."
This is due to the knowledge of Viṣṇu and others such as Viriñca.

Although this is not a logical reason (*hetu*) for the probandum (*sādhya*) stated as "this is not the other," nevertheless, the statement that it is a reason is made because it establishes that [the probandum] cannot be established otherwise.
The connection of this causal statement with the proposition "nor [is it anything else]" occurs by means of an implied causal statement.
By this, it is shown that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) and so forth is none other than Viṣṇu, not Viriñca or others; why?
Because of the scriptural passage: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1.1).
... "They indeed obtain all food" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.2.1) ... "They attain their full span of life" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.3.1);
because by such passages it is stated that the one consisting of bliss and the others are the objects of the knowledge that is the cause of liberation.
The meaning of the sūtra is thus stated: "because of its impossibility elsewhere," that is, because of its non-occurrence [elsewhere].
To the question, "Why is it that liberation comes from the knowledge of Viṣṇu alone and not from the knowledge of another? he says: "Him" (tam).
Indeed; because by the scripture stating "him thus," it is declared that there is no means for liberation other than the knowledge of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, the meaning is that liberation is not possible through the knowledge of anything other than Viṣṇu.
The meaning of the scriptural passage has already been stated.
Furthermore, because of the designation of difference:
"That which is a hundredfold the bliss of Prajāpati" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8).
"When he finds a foundation in that which is invisible, bodiless, inexpressible, and without abode, then he becomes free from fear" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7).
"And that which is in this person... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8).
Because of such designations of difference (*bhedavyapadeśa*).
Having cited and explained the Sūtra which refutes the blissful nature (*ānandamayatva*) of Brahmā and others by means of another reason, [the commentator] says "bhedeti.

Here, by the word *ca* (and), which serves to aggregate the preceding reasons, there is also an indication of the continuation of the proposition (*pratijñāvākya*) that "the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) and so forth is not the other."
Setting that aside, he shows the designation of distinction as stated in the Sūtra: "Those who are a hundred... and so forth.
The word "ādi" (etcetera) should also be applied after the word "ānandāḥ";
therein, by the first [phrase], "those which are a hundred... [is meant].
By this [statement], the preceding and following Taittirīya passages are understood.
By the second [passage]: "From which words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to reach it."
"Knowing Brahman as bliss," (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1), and so forth;
or rather, even when heard but once, [the word "Brahman"] is the comprehensive term for everything.
By this, the other Viriñca is not the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya); why?
Because of the designation of difference [from him], as in the case of Viriñca: "Those who are a hundred... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8.4).
Because it is stated [in such passages] that [the bliss of Rudra] is a hundredfold greater than that of Rudra,
and because it is stated that the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) possesses immeasurable bliss in passages such as "from which words turn back."
Thus, it is not Rudra,
because it is stated that his bliss is less than a hundredth part of that of Hiraṇyagarbha;
nor is it Prakṛti and the others.

In passages such as "in the invisible, bodiless," and so forth, there is the hearing of distinguishing attributes such as independence, which are incompatible with [the status of] primordial matter (prakṛti) and the like;
nor is the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) the collection of living beings beginning with Brahmā.

The meaning of the Sūtra is thus stated: because of the mention of distinguishing attributes—such as the state of being all-pervasive and so forth—in the passage "He who is this [person]," and because the aggregate of individual souls (jīvasamudāya) does not possess such characteristics;
furthermore, all these designations belong to the Taittirīya Śruti.

In this regard, according to the statement in the Śaiva Purāṇas, "Prajāpati is Śiva; the phallus is called the *liṅga*," the phrase "of Prajāpati" refers to Rudra, and "those hundred" [refers to his hundred forms].
The meaning of the first sentence is that "those joys multiplied a hundredfold belong to one who is not Brahmā," and that "the joy of the four-faced one (Caturmukha) is but a single [unit of] joy.
Regarding the terms "in the invisible" (*adṛśye*), it means that which cannot be known in its entirety; "in the bodiless" (*anātmye*).

"Belonging to the self" (*ātmya*) means belonging to the soul; those qualities of the living being (*jīva-guṇa*) do not exist in that which is "without the self" (*anātmya*). Thus, it refers to that which is devoid of the qualities of the living being.

Alternatively, "belonging to the self" (*ātmya*) means belonging to a master (*svāmin*), i.e., related to a master; that which does not have this is "without the self" (*anātmya*), meaning, in short, devoid of a master.
"In the indefinable" (*anirukte*): that which is beyond the scope of complete verbal definition.

"In the supportless" (*anilayane*): in Viṣṇu, who is denoted by the word *ānandamaya*, who has no other substratum, and who is the object of that [meditation]. The qualified seeker, so as to attain "fearlessness," attains a "firm foundation" (*pratiṣṭhām*) consisting of meditation in that manner.
"He finds stability" means he attains it, or rather, he establishes it;
"then," immediately thereafter, "he."
The meaning of the designation of the second division is that the lay follower (upāsaka) has "gone to" the Blessed One who is "fearless," meaning he has attained one who is free from fear.
"In the person": among the inferior living beings indicated by the word "person" (*puruṣa*), there is this Viṣṇu who consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*);
and "he who is in the sun."

The meaning of the designation of the third distinction is that Viṣṇu— who exists as "that" (saḥ) within the superior living beings characterized by the state of Āditya— is "one" (eka), meaning he is non-different, being present in both places.
The passage beginning with "from which speech turns back" has already been explained previously.
Nor [is there any contradiction] with such statements as "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8) and "I am Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.10).
This contradicts such scriptural passages as:
"All names enter into him" (Bhāllaveya Śruti).
This is because it has been stated that [the Self] is denotable by those various respective terms.
Now, one might object: "Granted that the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is the Supreme Brahman; nevertheless, how can a distinction between Brahman and the others be possible on that basis?"
Because such a distinction would contradict scriptural passages such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
The word "of" (*iti*) is to be understood as "of the designation of difference" (*bhedavyapadeśasya*).
The particle *ca* (and) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*),

because it is precisely the designation of difference— as conjoined with the removal of the doubt regarding contradiction with this [scriptural statement]— that serves to establish the intended meaning.
The same applies elsewhere as well;
"Thou art That, O Brahman" is the meaning of the first part of the Śruti according to the method of non-duality (advaita).
Regarding the second [maxim], however, it is "I am non-different from Brahman.
The first is the statement from the *Chāndogya* taught by Uddālaka to Śvetaketu;
the second is that spoken by Vāmadeva in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*.

In both these cases, since an identity between two qualified entities is impossible, what is expressed is the identity of the consciousness indicated (*lakṣita-caitanya*) by the terms *tat tvam* and *aham brahma*.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the texts] such as "That which I am, that he is; that which he is, that I am" (Ai. Ā.
2.2.4) and "That person who is yonder, I am he" (Ī. 26) are included.

The scriptural passage beginning with "ityādi" is thus understood. Why not? Because, in that context, these scriptural passages have the Supreme Brahman as their object and therefore lack the sense of non-duality (advaita). Intending to provide this logical refinement (*hetūpaskāra*), he states the proof for their having the Supreme Brahman as their object: by means of the scripture "Names," [it is shown] that of that Brahman, "by those respective words."
The meaning is that this is because [the Lord] is declared to be denotable by words such as "That" (*tat*).
And thus, since these [words] have Brahman as their ultimate purport through the syntactical connection of the words (*padasamanvaya*), there is no contradiction; this is the intended sense.
As for the manner of that [denotation]: it is "That" (*tat*) because of its pervasive nature (*tata-tvāt*).
He is called *tvam* because He is the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) understood by the word *tvam*, or because He is turned toward [the devotee].

He is *asi* because He withdraws the world (*asana*), or because He is the sword (*asi*). He is *aham* because He is not to be abandoned (*aheya*), or because He is distinct from the individual soul named *haṃ*.
It is Brahman because of its fullness;
it is "asmi" (I am) because of the roots *as* (to be) and *mī* (to diminish). Alternatively, the individual soul (*jīva*) is called "smi" because it is well-measured (*sumita*).
It is said that "I am that distinct, full Brahman.
Because it is of the nature of knowledge, because it is the ultimate controller,
because it is the refuge, and because it is the essence, it is so called.
The meaning of the *Aitareya Śruti* is that because [the Self] resides in such-and-such [places] and is beyond direct perception, it is denoted by the word "that" (*asau*).
The meaning of the *Īśāvāsya Śruti* is that the "Person" (*puruṣa*) residing in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is one who is complete in the six qualities.
For this entire universe is indeed the Lord, no other, since from him arise the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the world;
thus [the Upanishadic] scripture says, "He who is not-all is all.
Or rather, let it be that these scriptures have as their primary purport the oneness [of the Self], according to the method of syntactical connection (*vākya-anvaya*).
Nevertheless, one should not suspect that the scriptural texts concerning difference contradict the scriptural texts concerning oneness;

for the intention is that all scriptural texts regarding the oneness of the Blessed One are intended to signify oneness based on His being the Lord of all. With this in mind, he cites the Bhāgavata Smṛti as an authoritative proof for that point: "For this... and so forth.
The Blessed One, though being "other"— that is,
distinct from the world— is nevertheless said to be "this," the measured universe, in the statement "That thou art."
In such statements as "I am Brahman," it is as stated in the first *tātparya*: "The other Lord [Śiva] is also like the universe."

Why? "From whom" (yataḥ) means for what reason; "the origin, dissolution, and maintenance of the world" (jagatsthānanirodhasambhavaḥ): its maintenance is its persistence, dissolution is its destruction, and origin is its production; that from which these arise is so described.
Alternatively, it is so called because from it [the world] is established (*sthāpayati*), ceased (*nirodhayati*), or brought into being (*sambhāvayati*).
Or else, it is so called because the world abides in it (*tiṣṭhati*), is ceased within it (*niruddhyate*), dissolves into it (*pralīyate*), or is brought into being therein (*asmin sambhāvayati*);
thus, the meaning is that it is the creator of the creation and so forth of the world.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate that the differentiation of the world is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for one who is thus constituted.
However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, it is explained without using a *bahuvrīhi* compound: "This entire universe is like the Blessed Lord, because it is dependent upon Him."
But that other one is which?

"From whom" (*yataḥ*); from whom, as it has been said, comes "the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the world" (*jagat-sthāna-nirodha-sambhavaḥ*), meaning the creation and so forth of the universe.
And here in this commentary, the construction is "the Blessed One [is] like this universe.
He states precisely this—that there is a designation of identity by virtue of being the master—by saying "not-all" (*asarva*).
The word "but" (*tu*) is for the sake of the scriptural authority.
The meaning is that although the Blessed One is distinct from everything, he is called "all" without distinction in the Vedas and other texts because he is the master of all.
In the phrase "ityapi," the particle *api* found in the scripture serves as a conjunction;
the word "yataḥ" (since) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that for this reason as well, there is no contradiction. [This refers to the following: "In the self of knowledge (*vidyā*), there is the non-perception of difference; even by means of action that is free from attachment, [performed] with the conceit of the vision of difference."

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the cognition of difference is a false cognition, how can the scriptural texts concerning unity be interpreted in accordance with it? He dispels this doubt by means of a statement from the *Bhāgavata*: "Vidyā... and so forth.
And this speech, spoken by Kṛṣṇa in response to Uddhava’s question, "What is this knowledge?", is found in the eleventh book [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa]:

"'Abhidābodha' regarding the Self" means the cognition of difference from the Supreme Self (paramātman), that is, the knowledge of the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) [and the Self], or the knowledge of the distinction of the Lord (īśvara) from the individual soul.
The meaning is that this alone is knowledge (*vidyā*).
Nor should it be explained as "the non-cognition of difference," because ignorance (*ajñāna*) lacks the nature of knowledge.
Now, one might ask: since the cognition of difference is a cause for human goals (puruṣārtha), how can it be considered knowledge (vidyā)? To this he says: "The cognition of difference...
This is a statement from the third book of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*:
"He who is the first among all things moving and stationary, who contains the Vedas within himself, together with the sages..."
By the lords of yoga, such as Kumāra and others, who are perfected beings (siddhas) and initiators of yoga.
Thus, by the preceding statement, because of his agency, [he spoke of] Brahman with attributes as the Person, the bull among men; he,
having united again in due time with Time in the form of the Lord, [proceeded].
O Lord of Creatures, when the interchange of qualities has occurred, it is just as it was before.
This is to be construed together with the subsequent sentence.
Its specific manner is as follows: he who is the "first" (*ādya*) of the "stable and moving" (*sthiracara*), that is, of the stationary and the animate;

Hiraṇyagarbha, together with the sages— beginning from the best of men up to Garuḍa and Śeṣa, including those possessing knowledge, those perfected in yoga, and Sanatkumāra and others— [regarded him] "with a perception of difference," that is,
through the cognition of distinctions such as between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), and "with conceit."
Being liberated through devotion to Hari, through great reverence for the Supreme Lord, and through persistence— as well as by means of "disinterested action," that is,
by renounced action free from attachment to results— he [perceives] the "Qualified" [Lord] on account of "agency," meaning on account of His being the agent of the universe.

At the [proper] time, [he saw] the Brahman known as the Supreme Person— the "Puruṣa," the best among the perishable and the imperishable, the "Bull among Men" (Puruṣarṣabha) who is fully endowed with qualities such as omniscience.
"At the time of dissolution, having entered by way of non-attachment; again, by 'time'—
that is, by that which is called time, the form of the Lord."
"In form" means at a time other than the time of creation; "when not yet born" means when [the world] has arisen,
but while there is "no intermixture of the qualities."

In the *Sudhā*, it is stated that in the world of Viṣṇu— which is devoid of transformations such as the qualities of *sattva* and so forth— one is "born as before" (*ayathāpūrva*), meaning one is born as the sovereign of all liberated souls.
However, in the *Karmanirṇaya-ṭīkā*, it is said that not only is [the world] endowed with qualities (*saguṇa*),...
However,
the chanting of the Lord's name as "Brahman" and "the Full Puruṣa."
By the mention of "manhood" (puruṣatva), a similarity with ourselves and others is implied; to exclude that, he says "the bull among men" (puruṣarṣabha).
To establish that, the specific meaning was stated: that Brahman possesses qualities (saguṇa) because it is an agent.
In the *Tattvapradīpa*, however, having explained the word "abhimānena" as "by means of pervasive pride, that is,
by specific knowledge," and having split the word "guṇavyatikare," it says "he."

The multitude of living beings, beginning with Brahmā, having "joined" (asaṅgatya)— that is, having attained— Brahman, who possesses infinite qualities such as knowledge and sovereignty at the time of dissolution, [rejoin Him] "again at the time," meaning at the time of creation, "by means of time."

By means of His nature as knowledge, in the form of the Lord Viṣṇu, when there occurs a "disturbance of the qualities"— that is, an imbalance of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest— He is born "as characterized by that," without abandoning the previous gradations of qualities such as knowledge and their mutual distinctions.
It has been explained that [the quality] is manifested through excellence,
but it does not become non-different from that [substance]. This word-division is also accepted by the author of the commentary.
In that view, the phrase "at the time of the non-mixture of qualities" means at the time of creation;
in both cases, the expression "as before" means as in the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).

Or [it means] "as in a previous kalpa. Regarding this very point, he cites a statement from the Atharva Veda as authoritative: "When he perceives the Beloved, the other Lord, and His majesty, he is freed from sorrow" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.2). Thus: "The Beloved," etc.
When one perceives Him— the Lord who is cherished, served by all, and independent,
and therefore distinct from the individual soul (jīva) as Viṣṇu— and His majesty in the manner previously described through such passages as "This is the Truth" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.1).

The meaning is that when the individual soul (jīva) sees [the Lord], it then becomes free from sorrow; for in the *Tattvapradīpa*, however, it says: "When one sees the other, the Lord of this jīva, who is served by the gods, and His majesty consisting of majestic qualities, then and there the jīva becomes free from sorrow and is not touched by even a trace of suffering."

However, it has been explained that one does not become free from sorrow merely by beholding another who is devoid of the quality of majesty, who is not the Lord, and who is not served [by the world].

Even though this Śruti passage—under the Sūtra *viśeṣaṇabhedavyapadeśābhyām* (Brahma-sūtra 1.2.22)—states "another," just as the expression "this is another path" conveys a distinction from a well-known path, so too the expression "another Lord" conveys the perception of the one denoted by the word "Lord" (Brahman) as being distinct from the well-known Lord Rudra; thus, [it refers to] Brahman.
It was stated as a means of proof for [the self's] being other than Rudra,
but not for [the self's] being other than Brahman or the individual soul (jīva), nor was "lordship" (īśatva) made the reason for its being other [than these].
Nevertheless, since that [statement] is intended as referring to what follows immediately after the explanation, there is no contradiction with it.

For this very reason, in the *Dyubhvādi* section (*Brahma-sūtra* 1.3.5), this very passage is cited as an authority even regarding the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*).

"Though not the All, He appears as if He were the All; though He is indeed the Self, He appears as if He were the non-Self; though He is the inward-facing One, He appears as if He were turned away; though He is one, He is perceived as many.
"He is the Puruṣa"; "He is the Lord; He is Brahman.

Having thus explained the Śrutis intended by others to establish non-duality through the sense of His being the Master, he now explains those same Śruti and Smṛti passages as referring to Him as the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) by resorting to the harmony of the texts, beginning with the words "asarvaḥ."

Although the statement "asarvaḥ" (not all) was cited as an authority for the position that the word *ātman* signifies "lordship," and that the scriptural texts concerning oneness proceed by means of lordship as the underlying cause;

nevertheless, since it is possible for this same text to serve as an authority for both positions—namely, that the texts concerning oneness proceed not only by way of lordship but also by way of being the inner controller (*antaryāmitva*)—it is appropriate to cite it as an authority for both.

The intention of the authors of the *Tattvapradīpikā* is also that the scripture "asarvaḥ" serves as an authority for both [interpretations], namely that the texts concerning oneness proceed both by way of lordship and by way of being the inner controller.

Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction with the *Tattvapradīpa*—which states "He is the inner controller of all"—on the grounds that this passage is understood to intend a collective sense (samudāya) of the words.

For by the statement "even as their inner controller," it is shown that Viṣṇu is denoted by those respective words not merely by virtue of His names, but rather by virtue of being the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of those respective words, based on the authority of the Śruti text: "not only the names."

However, because there is only the cognition that [the Lord exists] also as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is not understood here in the syntactic connection (*padasamanvaya*) of the words;

for although each word such as "this" (*etad*) occurring in the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) denotes Viṣṇu by virtue of being the inner controller— based on the authority of the Smṛti stating that He is the inner controller of all— the syntactic connection of the sentence must be explained precisely by means of the other words having different referents.

When, by the force of the scriptural statement "names," one accepts that every word—which denotes all objects such as actions, agents, and so forth—is a denoter of Viṣṇu, only then does the syntactic coherence of words [occur].

It is not, however, that each individual word denotes Viṣṇu; thus there is no contradiction. Likewise, when words such as "I" (ahaṃ) occurring in sentences like "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) denote Viṣṇu on the basis of their being the inner controller (antaryāmin), then "you" (tvaṃ) refers to the inner controller of you—that is, Brahman.

The syntactical connection of the sentence should be understood as "I am the Inner Controller (antaryāmī), Brahman. Nor is there an inconsistency in connecting the verbal roots *asi* ("you are") and *asmi* ("I am") [with the subject], because the words *tvam* ("you") and so forth— which denote the Inner Controller as qualified by the individual soul (*jīva*)— have a primary application (*mukhyavṛtti*) toward the Inner Controller himself, just as the word "burner" has a primary application toward fire, even when applied to iron.

The use of words such as "asi" (you are) and "asmi" (I am) is justified by the intention to convey a non-primary meaning through the recourse to the secondary sense of "you live by my primary function. Although there is no syntactical connection for the three sentences beginning with "juṣṭam yadā" within the context of explaining the reasons [for the identification], nevertheless, since the Śruti and Smṛti have been cited to establish that the designation of oneness is based on the relationship of ownership, it is necessary to dispel the doubt that arises therein; thus, those three sentences are introduced by way of "contextual transition" (avasara-saṅgati).

The connection [of the words] "ityādeḥ" (from such [passages]) should be understood by drawing forward the word "iti" (thus) and by drawing forward the phrase "na virodhaḥ" (there is no contradiction).

As for the meaning of the scripture: Viṣṇu, although not the All (asarva), yet being the Self of all (sarvātmaka), is perceived as if he were the All (sarva), as if he were the Self of all (sarvātmaka), by virtue of being the Self of all.

To the question "Why?", with the intention of citing his state as the Inner Controller (antaryāmitva) as the reason, and having raised the doubt that this is unestablished due to the non-perception of his being the Inner Controller, he says: "He is indeed the Self. (ātmaiva).

Being indeed the Self and indeed the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmī*), He is perceived and known as if He were not the Self and not the Inner Ruler in forms such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa. Thus, the sense is that the perception of Him as not being the Inner Ruler is rooted in ignorance. Now, one might object: if Viṣṇu were the Inner Ruler, He would possess subjectivity (*pratyaktva*); and that is untenable.
To the objection that [the Lord] is perceived as being turned away (*parāktvena*), he says: "He is inward" (*pratyaṅ*).
Although the Blessed One is within the body, he is regarded as if turned away, as if his activity were restricted solely to the external.
Thus, the meaning is that the perception of him as being restricted solely to the external is an illusion.

Now, one might object: "If multiple contradictory attributes are admitted in Viṣṇu, then because of the resulting duality, there would be a contradiction with the Śruti text stating that He is 'one alone'. To this, he says: "He is one.
The meaning is that He, being truly one, is perceived in many ways through His manifold forms.
Thus, the point is that since He is a single entity possessing a multiplicity of forms, all [contradictory] attributes are logically consistent.
By the mention of "two," the connection with action in all instances is indicated.

However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, it is stated: "Though facing [all], as if turned away; though facing [them], as if not facing; being one alone, he is manifested, known, and attained as many. Is he omniscient, being designated as the self of all on account of his nature as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*)?
And where is he designated? To this he says: "He is the Puruṣa.
By this [it is meant] that "Puruṣa alone is all this" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12).
Thus he cites the Śruti.
The meaning is that he is designated as "Puruṣa" (the Person) because he possesses the six qualities in their entirety, or because he lies within the city called the body.
He states another scriptural passage with the word "sa" (he).
By this, he cites the scriptural passage: "All this, indeed, is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1).
The meaning is that the Blessed Lord, being designated as the self of all, is called "Brahman" because of His fullness everywhere.
Now, one might ask: how can it be possible for that which is internal to become external and so forth, since this is not seen elsewhere? To this he says: "He is the Lord.
Since He—Hari—is the Lord, endowed with inconceivable power (*acintya-śakti*), therefore everything, even that which is impossible elsewhere, is possible in Him.
Viṣṇu, the inner controller of all, is denoted by every name.
"I am this one," "you are that one"—but not in terms of the nature of all things.
"O scion of the Kuru lineage, they do not accept that there is but one person," and so forth;
furthermore, the suffix *kap* in this Smṛti text indicates the unknowability of Viṣṇu even though He is present within all bodies.
Alternatively, *yāma* means restraint (*niyamana*). In the sense of "that which exists therein," the suffix *ṭhak* is applied.
Since Viṣṇu is the inner controller (*antaryāmika*) of all and the restrainer within all, for this very reason he said, "This is the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.4), and "I am He" (Īśā Upaniṣad 16).
It is denoted by the pronoun *eṣaḥ* ("this one") in the sentence "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7),

by the pronoun *asau* ("that one") in the sentence "He who is that person over there" (Īśā Upaniṣad 16), by the plural pronoun *sarve* ("all") which is a term belonging to the class of all-encompassing pronouns, and by the name *sarva* ("the All").

The meaning is not, however, that [the Lord] is identical because He possesses the nature of everything. Furthermore, he explains the scriptural texts concerning identity through the Smṛti by way of the identity of purpose with the most excellent reality, stating "not this" (naitat).
For in the Mokṣadharma, Vaiśampāyana says to Brahmā: "O Brahmin, many Puruṣas are to be understood from the statements regarding difference."
Does the statement of unity refer to the Supreme Self and the individual self?
Or rather, does the statement of unity mean that there is only one self,
while the statement of duality refers to empirical distinctions?
Likewise— even if one accepts the plurality of persons on the grounds that a statement of unity refers to a preeminent [being]— are all selves equal,
or is one preeminent?
In the latter case, who among these persons is the preeminent one?
With the intention of asking how he is indeed the best, and that you ought to speak of him accordingly, Janamejaya posed a question to which Vaiśampāyana gave this reply:
"O scion of the Kuru lineage, they do not accept that there is a single Puruṣa."
For just as it is said that there is a single source for many persons, so too is this case.
In that same way, I shall describe to you that Universal Person, who is preeminent in qualities.
Thus [it is said]. The meaning of this is as follows: the wise do not accept this view.
To the question "What is this?", he explains it: "the one Puruṣa.
And so, the meaning is that the knowers do not accept the view that the Vedas speak of only one Puruṣa.
Alternatively, it may be that they do not accept a single Puruṣa in this world, but rather maintain that there are many Puruṣas;
in that case, one should not say that this contradicts the scriptural teachings on non-duality (advaita).
Since there is only one who is the best among many, that is the statement of supreme oneness. Who is the best among many?
How is He the most excellent? To this he gives the answer: "Of many.
O scion of the Kuru lineage, among these many persons (puruṣas), that source (yoni) which is the causal ground of the selves—[is the most excellent].

"Just as one is called 'the best' (*śreṣṭha*) because he is superior, so too, in that same manner, I shall declare—that is, explain—that Person (*puruṣa*), who is the universe, complete, and preeminent in qualities. This is the meaning of the *smṛti* according to the direction of Vyāsatīrtha in his *Prameyadīpikā*.
By this, it is shown that the statement regarding unity favored by others refers to the unity of the Supreme Reality.

And thus, since you are that one supreme reality which is Brahman, the meaning of the Śruti is stated as "you are lower than the lowest" (atyavaro 'si), repeated for emphasis as "I am lower than the lowest" (atyavaro 'smi).

This connects with the phrase "and there is no contradiction with such [teachings] as 'That thou art' (tattvamasi)," thereby establishing the attainment [of the goal]. Thus has the attainment been explained.
Even in the passage, "Being Brahman itself" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.5), the word "Brahman" refers to the individual soul (jīva) alone;
and this is appropriate given the context of non-difference.
[Objection: But if there were no scriptural statement of non-duality (*advaita*), how could non-duality be negated by means of scriptural statements concerning difference and so forth?
For, since it is not an object of perception, it cannot be established without scripture;
and what has not been established cannot be the object of a negation. To this, he says: "And it has been stated... (*uktā ca*).
The word *ca* (and) is used for the purpose of conjunction with the thesis (*sādhya*).

The meaning is that since the possibility of the identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)— which might arise from a failure to understand the meaning of the scriptures, such as "That thou art"— has already been stated [as a misconception],
there is no logical inconsistency in negating that [identity].

[Objection: Even if this does not contradict the Śrutis [regarding non-difference], there will still be a contradiction with the Śruti stating "being Brahman, he merges into Brahman" (brahmaiva san brahmāpyeti).

For here, by the word *eva* in "Brahman alone," the denial of the individual soul's non-Brahmanhood precludes the possibility of the interpretation you proposed—that the designation "Brahman" is applied to one who is not actually Brahman on the grounds of such factors as dependence upon Him.
To this, he says: "Brahman alone."
The word *api* (also/even) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

The meaning is that not only is [the teaching] such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) non-contradictory, but the statement from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, "Being Brahman itself... (*brahmaiva san*), is also [non-contradictory].
Why is this so? To this he says: "in the individual soul (jīva) alone. This locative case is used in the sense of the object (*viṣaya*).

Thus, because of the scriptural statement, "All individual souls are indeed Brahman," this first-occurring word "Brahman" heard in the sentence "being indeed Brahman" refers to the individual soul alone.
The meaning is that [the soul] is not [identical] with the supreme Brahman;
or alternatively, "jīva" is in the nominative case,
and thus, in the sentence, the one denoted by the word "Brahman" heard in scripture and so forth is indeed the individual soul (jīva).
The meaning is "not the supreme Brahman.
And thus, in the sentence, the one referred to by the word "Brahman" heard in the scripture is indeed the individual soul (jīva), not the supreme Brahman; this is the meaning.

And thus, that liberated soul, being Brahman itself while still remaining a living soul (jīva) and without abandoning its state as a living soul, attains the Supreme Brahman at the time of dissolution; for this is consistent with the meaning of the Śruti text, "Being concealed, he enters. Therefore, the intended sense is that the aforementioned designation of difference is not contradicted by this Śruti.
As it has been stated in the Bṛhadbhāṣya:
"The individual soul (jīva) is also denoted by the word Brahman, because it possesses many more qualities than the insentient [matter]."
One always attains the supreme Brahman at every dissolution. Thus it is said.
Although this scriptural passage was raised by the opponent regarding non-difference in liberation—
just as it is stated in the *Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya-ṭīkā*—
it should nevertheless have been stated as "in liberation" (*muktau*).
"But not dissolution" (pralaya).
Nevertheless, the term "dissolution" is used for the sake of its common application to all living beings (jīva).
Now, since the word "Brahman" is primarily applicable only to the Supreme Brahman (parabrahman) and is not fittingly applied to the individual soul (jīva), he says: "it is appropriate."
Whatever the meaning may be: the sense is that although the word *brahman* is primarily applied to the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*),

nevertheless, when there is a contradiction— either a contradiction with its own preceding or following statements, or a contradiction with other means of valid knowledge— it is applicable even to the individual soul (*jīva*).

And in the present context, the sense is that there is a contradiction with the subsequent statement "he attains Brahman," with the preceding statement "the highest equality," and with perception and other means of knowledge which apprehend difference.
Furthermore, since bondage consists of ignorance (*pramāda*), liberation is indeed possible.
[Objection: Even so, how can there be a designation of difference in the passage, "He who was already liberated is liberated again" (*Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 2.5.1)?
Thus, there is a contradiction with the Kaṭha Śruti.

Since the soul is described as being liberated even within this saṃsāra, the Supreme Brahman-hood of that soul is understood through the impossibility of it being otherwise; therefore, he says: "Through negligence... and so forth.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "api" (even/also) and denotes conjunction.
Thus, even in the absence of the individual soul's identity with the Supreme Brahman, its state of liberation and the scriptural declarations of liberation are appropriate.
Furthermore, the meaning is that it is not only the term "Brahman" that is applicable [to the soul].

How so? Because bondage—which consists of the egoistic conceit of being an agent and an enjoyer—is a form of transmigratory existence residing in the individual soul (*jīva*); and because it is rooted in ignorance, which is denoted by the term "negligence" (*pramāda*), it is merely a phenomenal appearance caused by that [ignorance], and thus not inherent. Since it is rooted in ignorance, as denoted by the term "negligence," it is merely a phenomenal appearance caused by that, and therefore not natural.
The meaning is that because the use of non-existent words is observed even in cases where things lack intrinsic nature (*asvābhāvika*).
Therefore, the intention is that there is no contradiction with that [scriptural authority]. Furthermore, the fact that bondage has ignorance as its root is as follows:
O Kṣatriya, both truths have been set forth today; delusion is the death that arises from attachment for the wise,
and I declare that heedlessness indeed is death.
"Likewise, I declare that through heedfulness one attains immortality"—

this statement by Sanatsujāta to Dhṛtarāṣṭra is established by the *Bhārata* passage cited in the *Tattvapradīpa* and the *Nyāyāmṛta*. O Kṣatriya, today both death, which is saṃsāra, and immortality, which is the absence of that [saṃsāra], are indeed real and operative.
Between these two, death is delusion (*moha*), which is dependent on ignorance and rooted therein.
If one were to ask, "In that case, would it be false? he says "no": "or rather, heedlessness.
I declare that death—that is, *saṃsāra*—is heedlessness, meaning it is not inherent to one's true nature.
The meaning is that I declare immortality and liberation to result from heedfulness (*apramāda*), through the removal of negligence (*pramāda*).
For it is said in the *Bhāgavata*: "Liberation is the abiding in one's own true nature after abandoning all other forms."
From what is it established that bondage is not inherent? To this, he says: "Liberation... [and so forth].
"Anyathārūpam": having abandoned (hitvā), that is, having relinquished, the non-intrinsic form (asvābhāvikam rūpam), [he remains] "in his own nature" (svarūpeṇa).

The meaning is that liberation is simply abiding in one's own true nature (*nijarūpa*). The phrase "in the Bhāgavata" is to be construed with the statement "because [the world] is said to consist of delusion.
Nor is there any contradiction with those respective inferences.

Now, even if there is no contradiction with scripture regarding the statement of difference, [one might argue]: "The individual soul (jīva) is non-different from Brahman because it is conscious, like Brahman;
difference is false because it is a difference, like the [apparent] difference in the moon;
and these bodies under dispute are the abodes of my enjoyment because they are bodies, like my own body."
Thinking that there might thus be a contradiction with inference, he says: "And not... (na ca).
The term "and" (ca) signifies non-contradictory conjunction.

Thus, the meaning is that not only is there an absence of contradiction with scripture, but furthermore, there is no contradiction between that statement of difference and the inference postulated by the proponents of non-duality (advaita).
By this, the word "and" (*ca*) in the Sūtra has been explained.
And because [the object] is according to one's desire, there is no need for inference (*anumāna*).
For it is possible to infer [it] exactly as one desires.
Therefore, a separate inference regarding reality is not required.
When there is a desire for the reason in that regard, he introduces and explains the Sūtra: "Because of desire," etc.

Indeed; because the "inference" (anumāna) propounded by the opponent for the purpose of establishing non-difference is "separate"— that is, contrary to perception and other means of knowledge and devoid of the support of scripture— therefore, regarding the "reality" (tattve):
This refers to that which characterizes knowledge regarding an object;
"it is not required" for the sake of the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) means that it does not serve as a cause for the knowledge of reality.
Nor is the argument inconclusive;
for "at will" means according to his desire, and God is not independent because he is conscious, like Devadatta.
An inference such as "the self is insentient because it is a real entity" cannot be established, whether with respect to reality or unreality.

Therefore, this constitutes a *bādhaka-tarka* (subverting argument) against the opposing view: if by this [inference] even that which contradicts perception and other means of knowledge were to attain the status of a valid means of proof (*pramāṇa*), then sentience, being a real entity, and so forth would also attain the status of a valid means of proof, since there is no distinction between them.
In the Sūtra, the word "akāmāt" [is used].

By the mention of a single part, "yathākāmāt" (at will), the word "samagra" (entirety) is indicated, just as the word "jyotis" indicates the "Jyotiṣṭoma" sacrifice; with this intention, it was stated as "yathākāmam.
By the word "hi," the ablative case is explained.
By the word "tattve," the attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*) or the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the word "asmin" (in this) is signaled.
By the term ‘anumānam’, [the compound] ‘nānumā’ is formed as a separate word; by the term ‘pṛthak’,
one relies on the negative particle (nañ) having a contradictory meaning, thus [forming] ‘nānumā’.
Thus, the reading as a single compound is indicated;
by the phrase "is not required" (*nāpekṣyate*), one accepts the compound containing the negative particle *na*, resulting in "non-requirement" (*nāpekṣā*).
This portion has been explained.

Following the *Smṛti*, in both the *Sūtra* and the *Bhāṣya*, there is a negation of [inference] being the object of the desire for proof regarding the scope of the means of knowledge, in order to demonstrate that it is not a means for attaining the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Thus, the meaning of this *sūtra* is: "Inference..."
The inference intended by others as a means of proving non-difference— [the inference] "in this reality"—
is such that there is "no dependence" (*nāpekṣā*) for the sake of knowing the truth; that is, it is so described because it does not serve as a cause for the knowledge of truth.
Why is this so? Because this inference is a "non-inference" (*anānumā*), meaning an inference contradicted by perception and other means of valid cognition.
Why could even that which is contradicted by them not be a valid inference? It could not.
Why? Because of the phrase "according to one's desire" (*yathākāmāt*); this [scripture] possesses an activity that follows its own desire or wish.

And thus, if validity were granted even to that which contradicts perception and other means of knowledge, then by the reasoning already stated, validity would also belong to inference when it functions regarding objects that are not the ultimate reality (*atattva*).
The meaning is that there is no distinction [between them].
Since this is so, there is no contradiction with inference even regarding the scriptural texts on duality.
And it has been stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Because it follows one's desire, therefore that [interpretation] never departs from the scripture;
for the sake of avoiding contradiction between what precedes and what follows, it is accepted, and not otherwise anywhere.
In this very context, he states the agreement of tradition (smṛti): "And it has been said," etc.
The word "ca" (and) signifies conjunction;
it means that this was stated not only by the author of the Sūtra, but also in the Skanda [Purāṇa].
To address the question "What was said?", he recites the verse beginning with "yathā" (as).
This word "yathā" has the sense of not exceeding the meaning of the term.
The [use of the] neuter gender is archaic.
Alternatively, this is not an *avyayībhāva* compound;
rather, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that by which desire has not been transcended. The word "proceeds" (*pravartate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: that whose movement (*gamanam*) has turned away (*apavṛttam*) or is contrary (*viruddham*) is *apagā*; one who is not *apagā* is *anapagā*.
And thus, because [it is] "inference" (*anumā*).
The separate inference that contradicts scripture and other authorities is "according to desire" (*yathākāmā*);
it functions without overstepping desire.
That is to say, it proceeds in accordance with human will.
Therefore, [the Smṛti] "is not departing from Śruti";

it is in accordance with Śruti and indeed not in contradiction with it. It "is desired" for the sake of avoiding contradiction between preceding and succeeding [scriptural] statements—that is, for the purpose of removing the conflict between earlier and later passages of Śruti; it is accepted.
The meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) is that [this scripture] serves not only for the ascertainment of the reality of supersensuous objects;

furthermore, in some cases it may be otherwise: where there is conformity with the Vedas (*śruti*) and so forth, that constitutes non-contradiction, and it is accepted as the cause for ensuring consistency between what precedes and what follows, as well as for the ascertainment of reality.
It is not otherwise, nor is there any other separate inference anywhere even in a sentence.

Why? Because that inference is "mere inference" (*kevalānumā*), which is to be construed as "according to one's whim" (*yathākāmā*); or alternatively, *yathākāmānumā* may be taken as a single compound word.
The analysis of the compound is: "and she follows according to one's desire.
In that case—because this [faith] is never departing, it does not depend upon the aforementioned result for its own sake.
The word "otherwise" (anyathā) connects by way of repetition with the phrase "not without reasoning" (yuktiṃ vinā na).
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Sudhā* that "the phrase ‘the knowledge of everything as appropriate’ (*yathāyogyākhilajñatā*) is a single compound word.
The word "iti" is to be construed with the word "Skānda."
And also: "This wisdom is not to be attained by means of reasoning" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.9).
Having first presented the Smṛti because of its clear expression, he states the agreement with Śruti regarding this very point: "naiṣā...
In the word *āpaneyā*, the division is *ā* and *apeti*.
There is a sequential connection with the two prefixes (*upasarga*) of contrary meaning.
And thus, this "cognition" regarding the supreme Brahman is not to be attained by means of dry logic.
The meaning is that it is neither something to be produced nor something to be removed, nor is it something to be discarded;
"it has been declared by another for the sake of easy understanding, O dearest one."
This is the completion of the sentence. "O Beloved" (*preṣṭha*) is Yama’s mode of address to Naciketas.

"By another" (*anyena*) means by one who possesses knowledge of otherness—that is, by one who knows the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśvara*), and so forth, and who possesses devotion to the Blessed One (*bhagavad-bhakti*) and the like.
The meaning is that it has been "proclaimed" by the Teacher; [it is said] so that, through his instruction, there may arise "good knowledge."
The word *ca* [in the phrase] *iti ca* signifies conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Thus, the connection is: "And likewise, it is stated in the Kaṭha-Śruti. Furthermore, the sūtra states: "And in this [world], it teaches his union with that" (BBs 1.1.19).
The word "ca" (and) serves to collect [the following] arguments regarding this living self (*jīva*): "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1).
"He finds fearlessness, a firm foundation, in the supportless" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7);
"He attains this Self consisting of bliss" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8), and so forth. // 6 //

Granted that there may be a difference between the Brahman consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) and individual souls such as Hiraṇyagarbha; nevertheless, that difference exists only within the empirical realm of saṃsāra,
and not as an ultimate reality even in liberation.
Anticipating the objection that the cited scriptural passages can be reasonably interpreted as referring to the distinctions within saṃsāra, he recites the sūtra—*asmin*—to dispel that doubt.
Here, the word *asya* does not refer to the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*);
rather, he states *asya* refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), as previously mentioned in the phrase "not the other" (*netaraḥ*).
To refute the notion that this [liberation] belongs to something else, he explains the word "ca" (and) with the word "yukti" (reasoning);
the word "asti" (exists) is to be supplied.
To the question "What is that teaching on yoga?", he says: "He attains it."
This is an adverbial expression;
or, it is a presentation in which the case ending has been elided.
And thus: "He teaches [this] and so forth."
Or, the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that [the text] teaches by means of these and other such statements.
By this, it is established that the difference between the individual souls (*jīva*) and the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is not proven merely through the designation of their difference;
rather, what is it? Because in this context, there is [a teaching regarding] this individual soul together with this one consisting of bliss, and [the phrase] "in this."
Even with regard to liberation, scripture teaches "union" (yoga), meaning connection; therefore,
there is neither identity of the individual souls (jīvas) nor is their difference merely worldly.
Nor is the distinction established by this much alone, because a relation depends upon a distinction [between its terms].
Or rather: because of the word "in this" (*asmin*).
In both sections, it "teaches" the "connection"— that is, the relationship— of this individual soul (jīva) with those [sheaths] beginning with the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya).
The scripture teaches [this] as being the fruit; this is the implied sense.
Therefore, it has been stated that the meaning of the Sūtra is that the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is not the individual soul (jīva), the sheaths (kośa), or the like.
"He" refers to the knower of Brahman; "by the wise one" (vipaścitā).
Together with the "Supreme Brahman," known as the Omniscient One,
and with the Four-faced One (Brahmā),
he "attains" all his own appropriate desires.
The meaning of the Vedic scripture is that one attains liberation;
as for the passage "in the invisible, bodiless," it has already been explained previously.
The individual soul (jīva), having departed from the body,
"approaches" this "consisting of bliss," the Supreme Self who is full bliss.
The meaning of the third sentence within that other section is: "He reaches its vicinity."
Thus concludes the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-adhikaraṇa*).
// 7. The Section on Being Situated Within //
"It is said, 'in the invisible, in the bodiless'";
and that invisibility [is described as] "this agent who has entered within,
moving within the moon by means of the mind."
"The gods do not recognize him while he exists together [with them]" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.11)— this refers to someone residing within;
and he is "Indra, the King."...
From such passages as "Seven yoke [the chariot]" (Tai.
Ā. 3.11.6) and others, another [Self] is understood;
therefore, one should not think that this [Self] alone is the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya).

In this section, the connection with the scripture (*śāstra*), the chapter (*adhyāya*), and the sub-section (*pāda*) is established by the intention that the reconciliation of the characteristic mark (*liṅga*)— consisting in abiding within the body— is performed for the sake of establishing the reconciliation of names such as Indra, which are well-known elsewhere but belong to the divine realm (*adhidaiva*). With this intent,
he demonstrates the connection with the preceding section and its subject matter through the words "The Invisible One" (*adṛśya*).

The meaning is that in the sentence "invisible, bodiless," cited in the preceding section, the invisibility of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is stated in the form of its being entirely unknowable.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And that... (*tacceti*).
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "eva" (only).

Thus, that very invisibility which was previously mentioned is what is referred to by the phrase "na vijānanti" (they do not know) in the statement "antaḥpraviṣṭam" (entered within), signifying someone residing within.
The meaning is that [the fact of being] the Self of all is established by way of *kaimutya* (a fortiori), because it is not to be known even by the gods.

By this, through the aspect of "abiding within," the connection (*saṅgati*) of this section with the preceding one is stated as being by way of a challenge (*ākṣepikī*), since the qualities of being invisible and consisting of bliss are suggested to belong to something else.

The gods—the presiding deities of the principles—do not know in their entirety this very one who has entered the cave of the heart, the creator of the world, who moves at will within the moon with his mind, dwelling together [with it].
This is the meaning of the scripture.
However, in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), this [scriptural passage] has another purpose.
He states that prima facie view, along with its reasoning, beginning with "And he... (sa ca).
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis.
The word "anya" (other) is repeated;
thus, that internal [self] is "other than Viṣṇu."

"He must be someone else; why? Because he is perceived as being within [the body] through such statements as 'Indra is the king'—this is the construction [of the sentence], since he is understood from these to be another.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi),...
The leader of the waters, the guardian of the world,
Tvaṣṭṛ who transforms forms,
the wise one— Brahman, Indra, Agni, the foundation of the moving world, the soul of heaven, Savitṛ, Bṛhaspati.
"He discovered the four-faced one, fashioned according to the quarters, the potency of speech through austerity"—
such passages from the Taittirīya, which contain various scriptural indications (*śruti-liṅga*) regarding Varuṇa, Tvaṣṭṛ, Agni, and others as the creator, are to be understood here.
He states the result of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
And this [consequence] recurs;
the word "it follows" (prasajyate) is to be supplied as the remainder.
And thus, "therefore" (tasmāt).
Since the one within [the heart] is distinct from Viṣṇu,
it would follow that "he" is someone else who is invisible;
therefore, because another is invisible, "he" must indeed be someone else.
The construction is as follows: [the opponent argues that] one of those beginning with Indra would necessarily be the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), and not Viṣṇu.
"The king" refers to Indra; "who rules the world" means he exists as the lord of the world by virtue of being its sovereign.
Because he rules (*īṣṭe*) over the Lord (*īśe*), he is therefore called the "King of the World.

Regarding the subsequent term "Saptahotṛ": he is the Saptahotṛ because he offers (*juhoti*) the seven faculties of perception (*buddhīndriya*) to their objects by means of the individual soul (*jīva*).
The meaning is "by means of the objects, the senses, and the individual soul (jīva).
Regarding the phrase "seven yoke," the word "seven" refers to the first half-verse.
The Vedic meters, beginning with the Gāyatrī,
take the form of horses; they "yoke themselves" to the sun's chariot, which has a single wheel— the meaning is that they become harnessed to the chariot.

According to the *Tattvapradīpa*, there is one principal horse named Saptacchandas, who possesses the conceit of the seven meters (*chandas*) and the conceit of the individual Vedas; that is, among the seven [horses], there is one named Saptacchandas who possesses the conceit of the seven meters and the conceit of the individual Vedas.
For this very reason, there is no contradiction between these two [Vedic passages]: "Seven yoke [the chariot]... and "One horse, having seven names, draws [it].
He describes the stability of the sun's chariot wheel with the word "trinābhi" (having three naves).

The meaning is that the chariot of the Sun possesses a wheel that is "unaging"—meaning it is eternally firm—and "without rival" (*anarva*), because it remains far removed from the "horses" (*arva*) denoted by the word *arvan*.

This is logical because the wheel revolves around the perimeter of the crest of Mount Mānasottara, while the horses travel through the space between Meru and Mānasottara; thus, their distance from the wheel is appropriate.

The meaning of the second half-verse is: "upon which" (yena) [wheel], "wherein" (yatra), "these" (cakre)— that is, "these" (imā)— all these (viśvāni) worlds (bhuvanāni) "stand" (tasthuḥ), that is, they are established.
The "support" (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the world—that is, its substratum; the "fourfold offerer" (*caturhotā*), who offers objects to the fourfold internal organ; and the "directions" (*pradiśaḥ*).
"Arranged in every direction" means established; "of speech" means of the Veda; "the vigor" [is its power].
The essence, the primary meaning, is "Indra and Agni";
[the word] "from heaven" refers to the "Self" of the Goddess.
The Lord Vāyu— [namely] Savitṛ, Bṛhaspati,
and Brahmā— Hiraṇyagarbha, discovered [him] through austerity.
The meaning is that he has obtained [it].
He establishes his own position (siddhānta) with the words "iti" (thus).
[The Self is] within, because of the teaching of its attributes. (BBs 1.1.20)
"He who is heard within is Viṣṇu alone":
"Brahmā, the ten-hotṛ priest, found him moving within the ocean with his mind, the Lord of the flood" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.11.1).
"Within the ocean, the wise perceive; the ordainers seek the station of the rays" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.11.11);
"Whose egg-shell they call the vital heat" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.11.4)—because of such teachings regarding His attributes.
For he indeed dwells in the Ocean of Milk;
why should this not be considered? To address this, he introduces and explains a Sūtra as the reason for it, beginning with the word "antar" (within).
Having supplied the word required by the portion of the sūtra intended as the subject (*uddeśya*), he shows it with the words "being heard" (*śrūyamāṇa*).
This means being expressed by the sacred text (*śruti*) as being situated within. As for that which follows and provides the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*):
He states the meaning of this [verse] as "Viṣṇu alone.
He explains the portion concerning the reason (*hetvaṃśa*) by first citing various distinct passages from the *Taittirīya Upaniṣad*, beginning with "within" (*antar*).
The phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*) refers to these.

"Dharmas of that" (taddharmāḥ) means those [specific] dharmas; "instruction regarding those dharmas" (taddharmopadeśaḥ) refers to the teaching or verbal expression concerning them, and so forth—and this is what is meant by "from that instruction regarding those dharmas.
Alternatively, this is a grammatical reference with an elided case-ending;
thus, it means "from the instruction beginning with 'and likewise' (tathā ca)," and so on.
This is a singular expression for a collective; by this [term], in the sentence "entered within" (*antaḥpraviṣṭam*),
[the meaning is] "that which is heard within."
Viṣṇu alone, and no other, is the one spoken of in the Śruti as residing within the heart. Why?

Because the attributes of that Viṣṇu—such as abiding in the ocean of milk at the time of dissolution, being knowable by Brahmā, being attainable through the austerity of Brahmā, and being the support of the cosmic egg—are [found] "in him."
By the phrase "because of the teaching" (*upadeśāt*), starting with "by him [the Self] within" (*tenāntaḥ*), the meaning of the sūtra is stated as being because it has been so declared.
The connection of the sūtra ending with "because of the teaching" is with the statement: "therefore, it should not be thought that [the inner ruler] is someone other than that."

"Brahmā" refers to the present four-faced one; "in the ocean" means in the ocean of dissolution (*pralaya*) and in the Ocean of Milk (*kṣīrābdhi*); "within the water" means within the waters and within the milk; and "with the mind."

He discovered—that is, he came to know—Viṣṇu, who moves according to his own will as the "Daśahotṛ," the offerer of objects among the ten organs known as knowledge and action, who establishes those respective objects, or who causes the ten organs to offer themselves to the objects through the individual soul (jīva).
The "seers" (kavayaḥ) are the wise ones; [he discovered him] "in the ocean."

The "creators" (vedhasaḥ)—meaning the Brahmās of the past and the future—perceive and know that which resides within the milk-ocean and the dissolution-ocean; for it is stated in the *Chāndogya-bhāṣya*: "Marīci is so called because his light is measured."

On account of the reason stated [in the previous verse], those who are "seers" (*kavaya�*)— meaning "wise ones" (*vedhasaḥ*) according to the *Tattvapradīpa*— desire and pray for the "station," that is, the refuge, of Viṣṇu, who is designated by the word "mirage" (*marīci*) because he is measured [as the source].
The wise, desiring Viṣṇu—the station of the rays—perceive him for the sake of discerning knowledge; this may be construed as a single sentence. The seers [perceive] the "egg-shell."
The meaning of the Vedic text is that they declare the place called the Brahmāṇḍa to be the "śuṣma"— the virility— of Viṣṇu, having him as its material cause.
The remainder of this statement by Viriñci is: "Prāṇa is the womb; by that immortal [principle] I am fashioned.
Of that [remainder], the word is "ulbam" (the womb).
The *jarāyu* is the "vital breath" (*prāṇa*), the inner covering with which one is born; by means of that "immortal" [element], I [am].
The meaning "I am prepared" is stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*.
To the question, "Why is residing in the Ocean of Milk a characteristic (*liṅga*) of Viṣṇu?", he says: "For he...
The word "he" refers to Viṣṇu; by the word "for" (*hi*), the reason is indicated, namely, because it is well-known in the world.
And his was the seed-vessel of vigor;
desiring to emit various creatures from his own body,
he first created the waters alone, and into them he cast his vigor.
Then there appeared a golden egg, radiant as the thousand-rayed sun,
in which Brahmā himself was born, the grandfather of all the worlds. Water is called *nārāḥ*, for water is indeed the offspring of Nara.
"Because they were his original abode (ayana), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa"—
so says the Vyāsa-smṛti.
Let it be that residing in the Ocean of Milk is a characteristic mark (liṅga) of Viṣṇu, because it is well-known.

Nevertheless, one might ask: how can the state of residing in the ocean of dissolution and the state of being the potency of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) belong to Viṣṇu? To this, he makes a formal declaration in order to state the evidence for those two being attributes of Viṣṇu: "Of that...
The phrase "the shell of the egg" refers to the place known as the cosmic egg;
"of that" means it is the potency (*vīrya*) of Viṣṇu.
By the word "ca" (and), the proposition that he is the one reclining upon the ocean of dissolution is indicated;
or, the word "ca" serves as an emphasis on "of him alone.
If it were so, another proposition should be understood as implied.

For this very reason, regarding the state of lying upon the ocean of dissolution, the scriptural authority "āpo nārāḥ" is cited later; even though the word *aṇḍakośa* (egg-shell) is heard in the Śruti, because the suffix there has its own primary sense (*svārthika*), it was restated as *aṇḍakośa* itself by abandoning that [suffix].
Or rather, there is a similar elision (*cheda*) even in the Śruti.
"He," Viṣṇu, born from Vāsudeva, "desiring to create" (sisṛkṣuḥ)— that is, wishing to bring forth— various creatures "from his own" (svāt), that is, from his own body, "meditated" (abhidhyāya).
Having reflected, "in the beginning," even prior to the creation of the cosmic egg, he created the "waters" which serve as its covering.
"In those waters he deposited his seed"—
the remainder of the sense being that he placed it by means of Māyā;
"golden" means consisting of gold, "possessing a splendor equal to the thousand-rayed sun."
That energy, possessing a radiance equal to the sun, became what is called the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*),
within which [resides] the Grandfather of all the worlds.
The four-faced Brahmā was born "himself" (svayam) from Hari directly; that is to say, he was born from the independent Lord.
For water is the offspring of Nara.
They are the sons of Nara and Viṣṇu,
according to the statement in the *Bhāgavata-tātparya*: "Viṣṇu is called Nara because he is beyond destruction."

Therefore, they are called *nārāḥ* for this reason: because in the beginning, at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), those waters (*āpaḥ*) were the abode (*ayana*) of that Viṣṇu; "for that reason, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa."

The meaning is that he is mentioned in the Smṛti by virtue of being denoted by that word [‘puruṣa’]. Although it is said: “When the Puruṣa first emerged after piercing through the egg, seeking a path for himself, the pure one emitted the pure waters.”
Thus it is stated in the Bhāgavata:
"Viṣṇu, who had entered the cosmic egg, burst through the egg and became manifest;
he then created the waters, from which [he is called] Nārāyaṇa..."
Thus, in the *Bhāgavata-tātparya*, the creation of the waters (*apsṛṣṭi*) is described immediately after the creation of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍasṛṣṭi*).
Nevertheless, there is no contradiction, because that [creation of the waters] is an internal creation distinct from the external creation.
This refers to the phrase "iti," which signifies: "And his seed was the shell of the cosmic egg."
"For he indeed lies upon the ocean of dissolution"—this connects with what precedes it.
"I [am] those rays of light; Nārāyaṇa, the Puruṣa, was born first."
"From the Puruṣa arises Prakṛti, the cosmic egg";
thus it is stated in the Caturvedaśikhā. // 20 //

Furthermore, he states "I am" to show that its status as the seed-virility (vīryatva) that generates the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and its state of abiding during dissolution are known to belong to that very [Self] alone;
the completion of the sentence is: "The triple-personality (tripuruṣa) was born from the seed of Māyā."
The word *tat* is a non-pronominal term expressing pervasion (*vyāpti*); or rather, it is a pronominal term,
and for this very reason, the reversal of word order was made in the commentary as *tad-ahēyam*.
And thus, that which is well-known as "I" is pervaded by it;

"raśmi" refers to the individual soul (jīva), for it is measured by delight (rati) and bliss (śam). It is called "raśmīn" because it impels or urges that [soul]—the word "rayati" meaning "it impels"—derived from the root *inda* in the sense of "impelling"; this word ends in the letter *d*.

In the section concerning imitation (*anukṛtyadhikaraṇa*), however, based on the etymological explanation of the verbal root *indh* as "to shine," it is explained that [the term] refers to the illuminator of the minor lights such as the sun and others, which are rays in relation to the Blessed Lord; in this regard, this word should be understood as ending in the letter *dh*, like the word *agni*.
[The text speaks of] the "light" (*tejaḥ*) which is the "Person" (*puruṣa*) who illumines the world.
"Nārāyaṇa," who is endowed with the six perfections in their fullness, is that which is called Brahman or *tejas*.
"In front" (*agrataḥ*) means that at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), it remained "unborn" (*ajātam*);
therefore, [it existed] "in front" of that person known as Nārāyaṇa.
First, "prakṛtiḥ";
[then] "cetanā jāyate" (consciousness is born); "jagat" means the collection of living beings (jīvasamudāya), which moves; the word "jātam" (born) is to be connected appropriately with both [terms].
And the birth should be accepted according to what is appropriate;
subsequently, [the terms] "the egg" and "the three persons" [are mentioned].

The meaning of the Śruti, according to the *Tattvapradīpa*, is that [the universe] was born from the "seed of Māyā" (*māyābīja*), which has *prakṛti* as its material cause (*upādāna*) and is joined with the triad of persons known as Brahmā, Vāyu, and Rudra.
