The phrase "in the *Caturvedaśikhā*" is to be construed with the word "of that" (*tasya*) by supplying the word "from the statement" (*vacanāt*).
"And because there is a designation of difference, [the Self] is other [than the individual soul]:
'The Self of Indra is deposited as the five Hotṛ-priests'... 'The sages have discerned the Self of Vāyu'."
...because of the designation of difference in such passages as, "Brahmā discovered the heart of the gods, which moves within the sun by means of the mind" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.11). // 21 //
If, on the basis of such marks as residing within the ocean and so forth, Viṣṇu is the one who dwells within,
then let it be intended here that there is non-difference between that Viṣṇu dwelling within and Indra and the other deities;
for there also exists scriptural testimony and other evidence that establishes Indra and the others.

Since the indicative mark (*liṅga*) derived from the nature of the Vedic texts and other sources is stronger due to its being without alternative application (*niravakāśatva*), it is impossible to determine one side by subverting the other; thus,

when both the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the final (*uttara-pakṣa*) positions are devoid of a mutual relationship of sublated and sublater, the Sūtra is recited and explained— beginning with "bhedeti"— to dispel the doubt that Viṣṇu, residing within, might be non-different from Indra and the others because such a conclusion would otherwise be untenable.
In the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], there is one designation of difference: "of Indra";
and another: "of Vāyu."
"End," says one;
"of the gods," says another. By the word "etcetera," [one includes]: "The nectar of the gods, the life-span of creatures, King Indra, Savitṛ."
Such [passages] as these are understood.
The word "anya" (another) is construed with the sūtra's proposition "vyapadeśāt" (because of designation).
By this, through the transposition of the word "ca" (and)—which serves to aggregate the things to be enjoined in the sūtra—it follows that not only is Viṣṇu heard at the end [of the passage], but...
However, [the Self] is other than Indra and the rest.
Why? Because it is stated to be distinct from them by describing it as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) and as abiding within them; this is the meaning of the Sūtra.
In this scriptural passage, the word "Indra" refers to something else.
Because of the hearing of the genitive case [in such passages as "the Lord of the six"].
However, in cases such as "Indra is the king," words like "Indra" refer exclusively to Viṣṇu in their primary, most direct sense,
since there is no subverting evidence to the contrary.
And thus, having set aside the mind, it becomes the experiencer of objects such as sound through the five sense organs;
it is the self of Indra, the inner controller, or the agent of grasping and so forth,
"established" within all hearts.
The "seers," that is,
the wise ones, being present, "perceived the self of the wind"; they beheld it within the sun by means of the mind.
The wise poets discovered Viṣṇu as he was wandering at his own will.

The meaning of the Śruti is that "Brahmā"— the four-faced one— discovered (anvavindat), that is, saw, Viṣṇu as the "Heart" (hṛdayam), because [Viṣṇu] abides in the hearts of the gods or because he is the impeller [of them].
Thus ends the section concerning abiding within [the heart]. // 7 //
8. The Section on Space (Ākāśādhikaraṇa)
"For who indeed could breathe, or who could live, if this Ākāśa were not bliss? (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7). Thus, the reason for Ākāśa being composed of bliss is stated, but not for Viṣṇu.

In this section (*adhikaraṇa*), the reconciliation of all words pertaining to the physical realm—indicated by the term "ether" (*ākāśa*), which is well-known elsewhere than [in the sense of Brahman]—is carried out.
With the intention that the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is indicated by the statement of the result, he states the result of the prima facie view: "For who indeed... (*ko hi...*) and so forth.

The word "iti" means "by the passage cited in the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya-adhikaraṇa). The particle "tu" is to be connected with the phrase "of the ether" (ākāśasya tu).
And thus, the meaning is that it refers specifically to the ether that is non-different from the ether mentioned in the Chāndogya Śruti.
Regarding the phrase "in the state of being composed of bliss" (*ānandamayatve*),
the "reason" is the designation by the term "composed of bliss" based on the cause of being full bliss (*pūrṇānandatva*).
[The nature of the subject] is that of being the agent of the world's activity.
He states what is excluded by the particle *tu* (but) and the restrictive particle *eva* (only)—namely, "not" (*na*).

By this, he addresses the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) mentioned in the Chāndogya Śruti refers only to the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) distinct from Viṣṇu; [the sūtra begins with] "For who indeed... (*ko hi*).

Thus, even though that [Self] is mentioned in the Taittirīya Śruti as being "that very one," it is established by the reason stated therein that He alone is the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), and not Viṣṇu; this is the result that has been stated. As for the connection with the preceding section, it should be understood as an extension (ātideśika), since the previous reasoning is extended here after raising a further doubt.
This should not be so thought; for it is said: "Space [is the cause], because of its characteristic mark" (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.22).
As it is stated in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (1.9): "'What is the goal of this world? 'Space,' he replied."
In this context, there would be the attainment of the elemental ether;
however, that is not tenable,
for [the referent] is Viṣṇu alone.
"This very Udgītha is higher than the high; it is infinite"— from such indicative marks as these [the author] establishes the final conclusion with the word "iti" (thus).
In response to the doubt as to why it should not be so considered, he cites the Sūtra as the reason for that [conclusion], beginning with the words "Since... This [word] is also repeated.
In that context, regarding the first [verse], the meaning of "from what" (*kutaḥ*) is like [the phrase] "from whence it rises" (*yataścodeti*);
for it is said that "the word *yat* is used both for reference (*parāmarśa*) and for the purpose of a question."
This is because it is stated thus in the *Bhāgavata-tātparya*.
The particle "tu" (but), however, indicates that the meaning of the Sūtra serves as the reason for the proposition "it should not be so considered.

Although the subject matter and so forth were indicated by stating the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the resulting conclusion, they were not explicitly mentioned; therefore, he explains the Sūtra following that restatement with the words "of this" (*asya*).
In this sentence, the word "iti" implies that [the property of] being the object of exposition is the remainder [of the sense]. The particle "ca" has the sense of "even though.
It means "although it is so, nevertheless."

The word "asau" (that) refers here to space; this is the sense to be understood as the ellipsis. Furthermore, the meaning of the term "tat tu" (but that), which is carried over from the preceding sūtra, is Viṣṇu alone.

Regarding the phrase "ityādi" (and so forth): this is a reference in which the case-ending has been elided. By the word "ādi" (etcetera), sentences establishing [Brahman] as the cause of the world, such as "all beings," are included.
As stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "By the words 'all beings' and so forth, one should understand from the word 'etc. [the qualities] such as being the creator of the world that are being proclaimed.
Here, the term *liṅga* (mark) is indicative of the *śruti* (scriptural authority).

And thus, the application here is as follows: although the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) is established as the subject to be taught in the Chāndogya passage "of this world" by the force of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and other means,
nevertheless, it is not appropriate for that [ether] to be denoted by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) in this present sentence.
But [it is] Viṣṇu alone. Why? Because of the characteristic mark (liṅga) of that [Viṣṇu] in the passage beginning with "He is this," and so forth.
The characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of that Viṣṇu is His unique attribute, such as being "higher than the high" (*parovarīyastva*);
because that mark is heard—that is, mentioned—in that space (*ākāśa*).
Since this is so, by virtue of that characteristic mark, He [is meant].
The ether mentioned in the *Chāndogya* śruti is indeed Viṣṇu;

for that very reason, it is He alone who is taught even in the Taittirīya passage beginning with "For who [else]? Thus, the reason stated is for His being the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), and not for the elemental ether.
Therefore, one should not think that the reason stated for being "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) refers to the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) and not to Viṣṇu;
by this, the application of the sūtra has been demonstrated.
The meaning of the passage beginning with "asya" is as follows: "Of this"— that is,
of the world of earth established by perception and of its presiding deity, the four-faced Brahmā— "what is the destination?"
When Śilaka asked about the "substratum" (*āśraya*), King Pravāhaṇa replied that it is Viṣṇu, who is named Ākāśa because he is all-pervading.

To explain how this is so, in response to the inquiry as to why, he describes the greatness of that Ākāśa: "Verily, all these beings arise from Ākāśa alone; they merge back into Ākāśa; for Ākāśa is indeed greater than these; Ākāśa is [the substratum]."
"He is the ultimate resort; he is that supreme, most excellent Udgītha; he is infinite. Here, the word *vai*, which indicates well-knownness, connects with all the nearby beings; for it is said:
"'*syuḥ*, *evaṃ*, *tu*, *punaḥ*, *vai*, and *vā* are words expressing certainty (*avadhāraṇa*)."
Or rather, because of this statement, it should be understood as having the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the word "element" (*bhūta*) refers only to the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*);
however, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it refers to all elements.
Or, he is the one who transcends the entire world beginning with Brahmā.
And thus, as measured by valid cognition, all these elements such as space, or the world beginning with Brahmā, arise from space alone.
It is well known that they go to the "dissolution" (pratyasta), which is the disappearance into space (ākāśa).
In that very [ether], they become dissolved during dissolution and in liberation.
Why? Because "hi"—that is, since—space alone is "greater than these," namely, greater than Brahmā and the others.
He is the supreme-most. Why is this so? Because space is the "final resort" (parāyaṇa), the highest refuge; with the intention that no entity superior to this can be suspected, he says: "He."
"This very one"—the Blessed One named Ākāśa—is "higher than the high" (*parovarīyān*). Herein:
that which is superior to the highest is called *para*;
higher than that is *parovara*; and what is higher than even that is called *pārovarīyaka*.

According to this statement from the Sāmasaṃhitā, one should understand that the meaning "the most excellent of the excellent" (*uttamottamottama*) is derived as follows: first, by the insertion (*āvāpa*) of the word *para* at the beginning and the word *vara* in the middle;

then, in the resulting sentence, by the substitution of *su* for the nominative case-ending (*sU*), followed by the elision of *sU* (*ulopa*), and then the application of *rutva*, *utva*, and *guṇa* since the following sound is identical; finally, by the elision of both instances of the word *opta*. Thus, the sense is established.
"Udgītha" is said by the Veda to be that which is sung with elevation;
the letter *tha* is used for the letter *ta* due to metrical transposition. "This very one" refers to space (*ākāśa*), which is "infinite."
"Unrestricted by the qualities of place and time.
However, in the *Chāndogyabhāṣya*, it is explained as: "The Blessed One is the Udgītha because of his loftiness, because he is the object of song (*gītha*), and because he abides in all places."
"Of Viṣṇu indeed shall I proclaim the heroic deeds, he who measured out the earthly realms" (Ṛgveda 1.154.1);
"Increasing beyond measure in his body" (Ṛgveda 7.99.1)—
by such passages as these, this very mark belongs to him alone.
To the question, "How is it known that the infinity and immeasurability mentioned in the phrase 'He is this infinite' reside in Viṣṇu?", he says: "Of Viṣṇu"—
referring to the heroic powers (*vīryāṇi*) of Viṣṇu as "Kaṃ".
"Who has declared it? Or who indeed has proclaimed it?"—no one has proclaimed it in its entirety.
"Who"—which seer or Brahmā [knows] "the earthly realms"?
"He measured," that is, he counted, the earthly atoms;
yet even he does not declare [the limit]—this is the meaning of the Vedic text.
"Higher than the high" (parovarīyān).
To the question, "Why is this state of being the supreme among all, as thus stated, a quality of Viṣṇu?", he says: "The Supreme.

He shows the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) along with its reasoning: "And that," etc.

the word "and" (ca) is used for emphasis;

Furthermore, since the primary cause for the application of the word "breath"—namely, being the cause of life and so forth—exists in the body, [the term applies] primarily to the functions of living and so on.

The construction is as follows: because it is observed that [the term "wind"] is established only for the primary wind (mukhyavāyu) through its connection with the modifications of the air within one's own body, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—namely, that [the effect] occurs when [the primary wind] exists and does not occur when it is absent.
And yet, this is not the case.
Since Viṣṇu alone is the vital breath (prāṇa), for that very reason it is said: "Śrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives;

This is because of such indicative marks as these.
He establishes the final conclusion: "And not so."

The meaning is that, in this way, it is not logical for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to possess the nature of air (*vāyu*) or to consist of bliss (*ānandamaya*). To the doubt as to why this is so, he explains the Sūtra as the reason for that, beginning with the word "yataḥ" (since).
This word "yataḥ" indicates that the meaning of the Sūtra serves as the reason.
The meaning of the word "tat" (that) which follows in the Sūtra is Viṣṇu alone.
Thus, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Since this Prāṇa belongs to Viṣṇu alone, it is not so [as previously argued].
To the question, "Why is this Prāṇa Viṣṇu alone?", he explains by restating the reason given in the Sūtra: "For this very reason."
The phrase "ityādi" means "precisely because of that which has been stated by [the words] beginning with 'iti' as a mark (liṅga) of Viṣṇu.

As for how there can be a determination by means of a mark when the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) was established by means of scripture (śruti), the particle "eva" (precisely) is used to indicate that the mark is without any other possible application (niravakāśatva).

And thus, the meaning is that a scriptural statement which has room for another interpretation (*sāvakāśa-śruti*) is sublated by an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that admits of no other interpretation (*niravakāśa*).
"O Viṣṇu, *te*"; you have two wives, Śrī and Lakṣmī.

// 10. The Section on Light //
It has been stated: "He who knows [Brahman] hidden in the cave" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
And that [Brahman] is hidden in the cave.
"My ears fly apart, my vision [reaches] far, this light which is placed within the heart;
my mind wanders far with its thoughts. What indeed shall I speak? And what now shall I perceive?
(Ṛgveda 6.9.6). Thus, "light" (jyotis) is mentioned.

In this section, the reconciliation with Brahman is established for the name "Jyotis" (Light), which—though well-known elsewhere—is here used as an indicator for all the words occurring in the respective hymns.

He demonstrates the connection between this section and its subject matter with the preceding section, and presents the subject matter and the doubt, preceded by the citation of the scriptural passage: "He who knows... etc.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And that" (*tacceti*).
The particle *ca* is used here for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
And thus, that which was previously mentioned as being conveyed by the words of the mantra-text (*māntravarṇika*) through the phrase "he who knows" (*yo veda*) found within the mantra;
By the statement "thus," it is said that the reality hidden in the cave is that very same thing designated as the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) and so forth;
that same reality is what is called "light" in the passage "these two ears."
The meaning is that it is expressed by the word "jyotis.

By this, through an examination of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) to be stated hereafter—which establishes that *jyotis* is other than Viṣṇu—there is an implication that the state of being "consisting of bliss" (ānandamayatva) resides in something else; thus, the connection between this [section] and the section on the "Consisting of Bliss" (Ānandamayādhikaraṇa) as one of "implication" (ākṣepikī saṅgatiḥ) is indicated.
A doubt is also indicated as to whether the subject of the light is Agni or Viṣṇu.
In the Ṛgvedic mantra "vi me," the prepositions beginning with "vi" are construed with the verbal action;
therein, the verbal root itself denotes the act of moving apart or spreading.
Prefixes (*upasarga*), however, are indicators (*dyotaka*) and not denoters (*vācaka*).
For this very reason, it is stated in the Sūtra simply as "because of the mention of *caraṇa*";
but in the Bhāṣya, it is stated as "because of the mention of *vicaraṇa*."
Thus, the meaning has been stated clearly.
For this very reason, it is said in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "Because [the commentary] is called a *vicaraṇā* for the sake of clarity.
By the word "me" (*mama*), the seer (*ṛṣi*) who perceived the mantra is denoted.
Although the word *dūrādhīḥ* consists of a single compound, because an *avagraha* (word division) is observed, it is divided into two parts and analyzed accordingly.
The prefix *āṅ* conveys both the senses of "slight" (*īṣat*) and "pervasion" (*abhivyāpti*).
The verb "exists" (*vartate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

And likewise: "Since my two ears fall [down], flying against the light"—the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used in the sense of the direct object (*svārthe*). The connection is made by changing the word order to: "and my eye falls, flying against [it]."
Just as the light is far from the ear and other sense organs, so too the light is far from the ear and other sense organs; thus he says, "vīdam" (far indeed).
The word "kampa" means "extremely.
And so it is said: "that which is placed within the heart."
The light that stands all around exists in absolute contradiction to the ears and other senses;

likewise, my mind wanders far from that light and acts in extreme opposition to its perception. The contradiction between the movement of the mind and the state of abiding in reality is expressed as: "For the mind is restless, O Kṛṣṇa."
Thus it is stated in the Gītā.
For this reason, "ādhīḥ" means either "I am of slight intellect" or "I am of all-pervading intellect," or "what indeed [am I]?"
"What indeed shall I say?
Or rather, what indeed shall I now reflect upon?"— this is the meaning of the mantra.
In the *Tattvapradīpa*, however, it is explained that "I" (aham) is a single continuous cognition extending everywhere, including those situated at a distance.
And since that light is from the *Agni-sūkta* and because of its well-known character, it follows that it is indeed Agni.
Now, he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) along with its reasoning, beginning with the words "And that... (*tac ca*).
In the *Cassamuccaya*,
the word "that" (*tad*) is repeated;
the word "fire" (*agni*) refers to the actual element and its corresponding deity.
The second word "ca" (and) is displaced [in its logical position].
Thus, it follows that this light hidden in the cave must be fire itself; why?
Because of its "well-known status" (prasiddheḥ).
Because the term "light" (jyotis) is well-known and conventionally established as referring to that very fire,
and because this light is not only so according to scripture but also because "that light is the subject of the Agni-sūkta."
The construction [of the argument] is: "and because it occurs within the context (prakaraṇa) of Agni.

For this very reason, in the commentary on the conclusion of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the word "Śruti" is mentioned first—characterized by its well-known usage—in the phrase "because of the greater strength of Śruti and context.
For this same reason, it is stated in the *Candrikā* that the word "ca" (and) is employed in the Bhāṣya [in the phrase] "and because it is situated in the Agni-sūkta."

And thus, since the mere indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being "hidden in the cave" is set aside by both the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*), the sense is that this light is indeed fire, as in: "This light is hidden in the cave.
To this, he says: "The light [is Brahman], because of the mention of its feet. (BS 1.1.24)
Viṣṇu alone is the light,
because of the mention of the movement [of the soul] through the ears and other [senses].
He introduces the aphorism that establishes this conclusion with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ).
Since the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been reached, the meaning is that the Blessed Lord Bādarāyaṇa states the subsequent sūtra.
He recites that very sūtra: "Light" (*jyotiḥ*).

Intending both the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) and the modification (*vipariṇāma*) of the word "that" (*tat*) from the previous sūtra, he explains the part of the proposition (*pratijñā*) as: "Viṣṇu alone."
The construction is as follows: "Light" must indeed be Viṣṇu, who is denoted by that word.

To the question "Why?", he explains—taking into account the logical reason "because of the mention of feet" and the intended supply of the words "of the ears, etc. and the sense of the word "feet" as meaning "moving"—with the words "of the ears, etc. (karṇādīnām).

The meaning here is that in this passage, because it is stated that Karna and the others act in opposition toward this light, there is the hearing of a mark (liṅga) indicating distance from Karna and the rest.
In this context, "distance from Karna and the rest" refers to possessing a majesty that cannot be delimited by them as being "this much," and not merely being distant from Karna and the rest.
Because that [reason] is impossible with respect to that [subject].
It should be understood that the pursuit of the limit of verbal expression is for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of the unestablished reason (*hetvasiddhi*).
For it is said: "He indeed increased by a measure through his body" (Ṛgveda 7.99.1).
By these and other such statements, [the Self] is distant from the ears and other sense organs. // 10 //
Granted that there is the statement regarding the light being distant from the ears and so forth;

however, on what basis does that establish its identity as Viṣṇu? To this, he makes the formal proposition, citing scripture to show that being distant from the ears and so forth is a unique characteristic (liṅga) of Viṣṇu alone, saying: "For He... (sa hi).
The word "evam" (thus) is supplied [from the previous context].
By the word "ādi" (etcetera), passages such as "na te viṣṇo" and so forth are included.
And thus, because "he"—

namely Viṣṇu alone— is established by such scriptural passages as "beyond measure" (*paro mātrayā*) as being remote from the ears and other sense organs, there is no lack of logical necessity (*aprayojakatā*).
Alternatively, the construction is made by supplying the words "nor is there a failure to establish the qualification of the reason" (*na vā hetuviśeṣaṇāsiddhiḥ*).
By this, it is shown that "light" (*jyotiḥ*) is indeed Brahman, which is denoted by the word "That" (*tat*).
Why? Because here, with respect to this light, there is the mention of the "non-performance" (acaraṇa) by the ears and other senses in its entirety, which is contradictory [to their functioning];

for the scriptural mark (liṅga) of being remote from the ears and so forth is heard. Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is stated through both repetition (āvṛtti) and ellipsis (adhyāhāra). Alternatively, *mātrā* refers to the group of sense organs—either that which measures (māpayati) or makes known objects, or that by which objects are measured (*mīyante*)—and you are "beyond" (*para*) that.

Regarding the phrase "dūro 'si" (You are far), O Viṣṇu, no one can reach the furthest limit—the boundary of Your greatness—by means of the ears or other senses; thus the Śruti should be explained in accordance with the context.

Here, the authors of the *Tattvapradīpa* and the *Sannyāyaratnāvalī* intend that the four-sūtra section beginning with "jyotiḥ" constitutes a single topical discussion (*adhikaraṇa*) concerning internal distinctions.
The difference between these two [interpretations] arises from the difference in the subject sentences (*viṣayavākya*) found in the *Agnisūkta* and the *Chāndogya*.

However, according to the author of the commentary (Ṭīkākṛt), it should be understood that the single *jyotiḥ-sūtra* constitutes one topic (*adhikaraṇa*), while the triad of sūtras beginning with "chandaḥ" constitutes another topic. // 10 //
Thus ends the section concerning light (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa), [10].
11. The Section on the Designation of Metre (Chanda-abhidhāna-adhikaraṇa)

"If it be argued that [the word *gāyatrī*] does not refer to Brahman because it denotes a meter (*chandas*), we say no; for there is a teaching on the fixing of the mind (*ceto'rpaṇa*) in that manner, and such is the scriptural vision.
(BBs 1.25) In this section (*adhikaraṇa*), the reconciliation of all terms—such as *gāyatrī* and others found in the Vedas—is carried out.
To generate an inquiry regarding the connection and so forth, he first recites the very Sūtra: "Meter" (*chandaḥ*).
Here, the term "intention" (chanda) recurs;
and that [intention] is both separate and combined.
Thus, it is said: "Because of the mention of intention."

Because the word "Gāyatrī" in the sentence "The Gāyatrī indeed is this [universe]" denotes the specific meter consisting of a mantra of twenty-four syllables, as that word is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that sense.
That which is denoted by the word "Gāyatrī" is not Viṣṇu, but rather the meter itself;
for Gāyatrī is not Viṣṇu.
Rather, it is *chandas*;
therefore, even the light is not Viṣṇu, but *chandas*. Why? Because of the mention of *chandas*.
If it is argued that because the term "light" (*jyotis*) is used with the *gāyatrī* meter in the sense of their identity, [Viṣṇu is meant] on account of the introductory statement—[we reply:
no, Viṣṇu alone is the light. Why? Because of the explicit declaration (*nigada*).

Because Viṣṇu alone is denoted by the word "Gāyatrī," and because words such as "Gāyatrī" and so forth denote Viṣṇu alone for the purpose of enjoining non-difference with Him, he says "tathā" (thus), meaning that [one should meditate] with the mind upon Him as having the nature and qualities of the referents of the words "Gāyatrī" and so on. Thus, it is solely for the purpose of such meditation. "Tathā": with the mind, [regarding Him] as the essence and qualities of the meanings of the words "Gāyatrī" and so forth.
The meaning is that [the name] Viṣṇu is mentioned for the purpose of "fixing" the mind— that is, for the sake of meditation by placing [the mind] upon Brahman.
This is stated without explicitly using the word "meditation."
The expression "the offering of the mind" (*cetorpaṇā*) is intended to explain the nature of *upāsanā* (meditative worship).
By this, the objection that it is redundant to designate Viṣṇu by means of well-known terms such as *Gāyatrī* is refuted.

Now, one might argue that while it may be possible to establish that Viṣṇu is denoted by the word "light" (*jyotis*) on the grounds that he is denoted by the word "Gāyatrī," [the same cannot be said for other terms].
If it were established that Viṣṇu is denoted by the word *gāyatrī*, then from what [source] would that be known? To this he says: "For thus" (*tathā hi*).
"For" (*hi*) means because; "thus" (*tathā*)—[the rest follows].

The "darśana" (scriptural vision) that establishes Viṣṇu’s designation by the term *gāyatrī* on the basis of his being the agent of singing (*gāna*) and protecting (*trāṇa*)— derived from the etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) "that by which the meaning is seen (*dṛśyate*) and known (*jñāyate*)"— is expressed in another recension as: "He sings and he protects" (*gāyati ca trāyati ca*).
The meaning of the Sūtra is that there exists Śruti of such a form as this; therefore [the conclusion follows].

Regarding the light mentioned in the passage, "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.7), [it is identified with] the Gāyatrī in the passage, "Gāyatrī indeed is all this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.1).
Thus, the commencement was made with the Gāyatrī.
If it is argued that, therefore, he is not Viṣṇu—no; for he is indeed designated by such names for the purpose of directing the mind.
That is to say, he is designated by the names of Agni, Gāyatrī, and so forth, which are the referents of those words, solely for the purpose of directing the mind toward him.

Indicating the connection with the scriptures and so forth, the subject matter of the passage, the doubt regarding that subject, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view, and its result, he explains the portion concerning the prima facie view in the Sūtra, beginning with "atha" (now).
The word "of what was said" (uktasya) is repeated.
And thus, it refers to that very "light" which was described as being situated in the cave by the statement, "that which is placed in the heart."

Furthermore, regarding that which is stated even in the *Chāndogya*: "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven, on the backs of all, on the backs of everything, in the worlds that are unsurpassed and supreme— this indeed is that light which is within this person," [it refers to] the *Gāyatrī*.
The third case ending is used here in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*). "Commencement as the Gāyatrī" means that the recitation was performed in the form of the Gāyatrī.
From where is this understood?
From the statement: "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this; the Gāyatrī is speech; speech indeed is all this," [where it is said] "of the Gāyatrī."
The construction is as follows: "Therefore" means that the "commencement"—that is, the beginning—was made with the word *gāyatrī* with the intent of its identity [with Brahman].
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therefore."
And this [phrase] recurs; "the Jyotis Gāyatrī" is the remainder, and the word "metre" (chandas) is also supplied.
And so, since the commencement was made with the Gāyatrī,
and since that [commencement] is stronger because its contradiction has not yet arisen,
therefore this light must be the Gāyatrī itself.
And that Gāyatrī must be the metre itself, whose nature consists of mantras characterized by the entrance of Viṣṇu, and not Viṣṇu himself.
Why? Because the word "Gāyatrī" is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as referring only to the metre, and because it is designated as speech (*vāk*). This is the construction [of the argument].
By this, [the passage] "The Gāyatrī is indeed all this... [is explained].

Thus, if the word *gāyatrī* occurring in the preceding passage were to refer to something other than Viṣṇu, then by that very fact the *jyotis* (light) mentioned in the subsequent passage would also necessarily be something other than Viṣṇu; and for that same reason, even the *ānandamayatva* (the state of consisting of bliss) would belong to another and not to Viṣṇu. It is precisely because this section arises as a rebuttal to such an objection raised against what was previously stated that there is an "objection-based" (*ākṣepikī*) connection between the preceding and the present section.
Thus, regarding the subject of the Gāyatrī, there is a doubt: is it a particular type of meter, or is it Viṣṇu? In that case, the Gāyatrī would indeed be merely a particular type of meter.
This constitutes the reasoned prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), based on the fact that the word "that" (*tat*) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that sense.

Likewise, it indicates the conclusion of the prima facie argument: therefore, the "light" (*jyotis*) is also indeed a *chandas*, and it is precisely this that resides in the cave and consists of bliss.
In this prima facie view, words such as "Gāyatrī" refer to the *mantras*.
Every statement should be interpreted as being directed toward His majesty.

However, according to our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the meaning of "atha" and so forth at the beginning is this: the word "atha" occurs at the commencement of another section concerning the majesty of the Blessed One; "yat" [refers to that].

The three forms known as Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, and Vaikuṇṭha, which reside in Śvetadvīpa, Anantāsana, and Vaikuṇṭha respectively— those [forms] are "beyond this heaven" (divaḥ paraḥ); that is to say, they abide in a higher place in relation to this intended object present in the mind.
"Jyotiḥ" (light) means consisting of pure luster;

such is that [abode] which is considered to have three types of dwellings: on the earth, in the Brahma-loka, on Mount Meru, and in Vaijayanta; in the intermediate space; and in Satyaloka as the third.

According to this statement, [the worlds] are "higher than all" (*sarvataḥ pṛṣṭheṣu*) in the sense that they are successively higher than the celestial abodes of Brahmā located in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), the Vaijayanta palace, Mount Meru, and Satyaloka; and they are "unsurpassed" (*anuttameṣu*) in the sense that they are successively higher than the worlds consisting of the intermediate space, the earth, and the heavenly spheres (*svarātma-ka-loka*), or alternatively, because there is no world superior to them, they are "not lower" (*pratyavareṣu*).

"In the highest"; that is, in the "highest worlds" themselves—namely, Śvetadvīpa, Anantāsana, and Vaikuṇṭha—it "shines," meaning it is manifest. That shining splendor is indeed "this very thing"; that is, this [very light] indeed.
And what is this? "That which is the light within this person" in the heart; the meaning is that Brahman, denoted by that word, exists and has become one with it.

With the intention that this first form is the Lord known as Hayaśīrṣa, who is named Gāyatrī, whose conclusion is the Gāyatrī, and who has a female form, the sentence beginning with "Gāyatrī" is introduced in order to describe His second form:
"Whatever being there is here..."
That which is the full form consisting of the incarnations such as the Fish and others, and that form which abides within all— “all” (sarvam)— all that is “Gāyatrī”;
the Lord himself is indeed named Gāyatrī.
This is well known.
He states the third form of that very [Bhagavān] as "Speech" (vāk);
the Blessed One, whose name is Gāyatrī, is indeed "Speech."
That which is called speech is indeed Viṣṇu.

To the question, "On what basis does he possess the nature of Viṣṇu?", [the text] says that it is because of the possession of his defining characteristics: "Speech, verily... and "All this being... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3).
"The class of living beings is indeed speech"; this means that [living beings] are dependent solely upon the Lord named Speech. Therefore, because He is the master of all, Speech is Viṣṇu.
It follows the portion of the Siddhāntasūtra with the word "no" (na).
The verb "is declared" (nigadyate) is also connected here.
Thus, the meaning is that Viṣṇu alone is indeed declared by the word "light" (jyotis).
He provides the reason for this with the phrase "because he is called so" (*nigadāt*), connecting it as follows: "for [he] is called" (*hi nigadyate*).
The remainder of the sentence is "by the word *gāyatrī*.
And thus: "for" (*hi*) means because Viṣṇu alone is indeed "called" (*nigadyate*) even by the word *gāyatrī*.
The meaning is that it is "designated" (abhīdhīyate) as such.

Furthermore, the designation of Viṣṇu by means of words such as *gāyatrī* is not for the purpose of enjoining identity with them, but rather solely for the purpose of meditating upon Him in that manner; thus he says, "so."

The purpose of the statement "ceto 'rpaṇā" (the offering of the mind) is as previously explained. To indicate that this is a commentary (*bhāṣya*), he explains his own words beginning with "tathā" by expounding upon the meaning of the word "tathā": "agnīti.
Here, the word "agni," which indicates the term "jyotis," [is used] elsewhere in the view that the *Jyotiḥ-sūtra* constitutes a separate section (*adhikaraṇa*).

By stating here the purpose for employing the well-known term *gāyatrī* in reference to Viṣṇu, the author of the Sūtras indicates that the purpose for employing terms such as *agni* in reference to Viṣṇu has been shown both previously and subsequently.

Nor should it be argued that the word *agni* is redundant, since it might be possible to indicate the result of the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the term *gāyatrī* through the words *gāyatrī* and so on themselves, as well as the result of the concordance stated previously and subsequently.
Since this [sūtra] must necessarily be accepted as having for its object the connection that has reached fruition, and since the word "etc.
(ādi) is also necessary because it includes speech and the other organs mentioned in the same context, both are indispensable;

for by means of both these necessarily required elements, it is possible to indicate the purpose already stated in the sections concerning the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) and so forth, as well as in subsequent passages.

However, under the view that the four aphorisms beginning with "jyotiḥ" constitute a single topical section (adhikaraṇa), the two words are cited solely because they are terms whose meanings must be directly reconciled, and not because they are the results [of the meditation]; furthermore, the indication of this principle for other sections is done by the word "ādi" alone, and not by both words.
The phrase beginning with "two words" (*śabdadvayottara*) is intended for the purpose of grasping multiple words of different classes.

For this very reason, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, it is stated: "of the fire-words such as *agni* and so forth, and of the meter-words such as *gāyatrī* and so forth," having intended that the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) applies to both [groups], and that the first "and so forth" refers to the fire-words while the second refers to the meter-words.
However, some say that the word "hi" (for) occurring in the commentary indicates the establishment of the means of knowledge, such as for the sake of knowledge or for the sake of meditation,
and serves to inform us that this same principle is to be applied in other sections as well;
whereas the phrase "for the purpose of fixing the mind" (*ceto 'rpaṇārtham*) is restrictive.
And thus, "this" Blessed One is the very nature and essence of the qualities denoted by the words "Agni," "Gāyatrī," and so forth; in that regard,
it is for the purpose of fixing the mind.
The meaning is that [the identity] is stated solely for the purpose of bringing about awakening and for the purpose of meditation, not for the purpose of enjoining non-difference with that [Brahman].
By the word "iti" (thus), the meaning of the term "tathā" (so) has been explained.

By this phrase "the unestablished Gāyatrī, etc.," the suspicion that the designation of Viṣṇu would be redundant is dispelled; for there is indeed scriptural evidence [to this effect], such as: "He sings and protects" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.1).

Now, one might object: "The proof that Viṣṇu is denoted by the word 'light' (jyotis) would indeed be valid if this Gāyatrī were Viṣṇu; but how is that so? To address this, with the intention of showing that the [opponent's] reason—namely, the mark (*liṅga*) of being the agent of singing and protecting—is established, the remainder of the Sūtra begins with "For thus" (*tathā hi*).
Having imitated [the previous], he shows the scriptural statement mentioned in the section on "vision" with the words: "Thus."
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: because there is a scriptural statement (*śruti*) beginning with "for [it is] thus seen" (*iti hi darśanam*).
Although it is said that "[it] sings and protects" (*gāyati trāyate ca*), [the meaning is established].
Such is the reading of the Chāndogyas;
nevertheless, there is no fault, as this is simply another recensional branch (*śākhā*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the text includes]: "That which is Gāyatrī is indeed this very earth, for upon her all beings are established, and nothing exceeds her" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.2).
This and other such passages are included.
As for the meaning of the scripture: because the Blessed One, who is denoted by the word *gāyatrī*, "sings" (*gāyati*) the Vedas—that is to say, he emits them from his mouth as the first speaker.
And because she "protects" (trāyate) everything—
"everything," being the understood remainder—
therefore she is called by the word *gāyatrī*.
"That which is well-known as Gāyatrī is indeed Viṣṇu by that name; she is this very one.
What is this? "That which is this earth" is the Blessed Lord by that name.
How is it that the earth is Viṣṇu? To this he says: "Because of the possession of his characteristics," namely, "for in her (asyām) this (idam) [is supported].
That is to say, the "beings" (bhūtam)—the entire multitude of living creatures—are supported "in her," which is the earth.
In the *Sudhā*, however, in accordance with the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is explained that the Gāyatrī "sings" (*gāyati*) and "protects" (*trāyate*) the students.
"He protects" means he guards one from evil; this has been stated.
For he is designated by all the Vedic meters, he is designated by all the gods, and he is designated by all the worlds, because of the metaphorical application of those [names] to him.
Thus it is stated in the Vāmana [Purāṇa].

Now, one might object: "Since words such as *gāyatrī* are conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in other senses, how can Viṣṇu be determined [as the referent] by a mere indicative mark (*liṅga*) alone?

To this, with the intention that the scriptural mention of *gāyatrī* and so forth has other possible applications, [the author] states a traditional text (*smṛti*) regarding that point—beginning with "All"—with the underlying thought that words such as *gāyatrī*, *agni*, and *pṛthivī* have application for Viṣṇu not only through the etymological derivation (*yoga*) stated in scripture, but also because, according to the conventional usage of the Purāṇas, even *gāyatrī* is dependent upon the Blessed Lord.
‘This’ Viṣṇu is ‘designated by all the meters’ (*sarvacchando'bhidhaḥ*); this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning “he whose designation (*abhidhā*) is the same as the designation of all the meters.
He is denotable by all words that express meters, such as *gāyatrī* and so forth.
"In this way, He"—that is, Viṣṇu—is denoted by words such as "Agni" and others which denote all deities;
likewise, "this"—that is, Viṣṇu—is denoted by words such as "Earth" and others which denote all worlds. This is the meaning.
Why is this so? Because the Vedas (*chandas*) and so forth are dependent upon the Blessed Lord; thus, three instances of the word *hi* (for/indeed) are used to indicate three reasons respectively.
Or, it is for the purpose of making known the Vedic tradition.
Because the Vedas (*chandas*) and the worlds (*lokas*) are perceptible, whereas the gods (*devas*) are imperceptible, there is this diverse expression: "This is that.
To the question, "How then is there conventional usage [regarding them] elsewhere?", he says: "Of those..."
The meaning is "of the worlds of the gods of desire" (*chandodevalokānām*).
"That" (*tat*) refers to being understood by that word; "figuratively" (*upacārataḥ*) means that it is only in a non-primary sense, because [the worlds] move near Viṣṇu and are dependent upon him.

Because there is a "vision"—that is, a presentation—of the term *vāmana* in the sense of "Vāmana," the Śruti has its scope primarily in Viṣṇu alone; whereas the indicative mark (*liṅga*) has no scope elsewhere even in a secondary sense. Therefore, by that [Śruti]...

The connection with the *upaskara* (the commentary) is as follows: "Because that [contrary view] is sublated, this determination indeed arises by means of the mere indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being the agent of singing and protection.
And: "Also because the designation of the quarters beginning with the elements is thus possible" (BBs 1.1.26).
Having introduced the sūtra which establishes the identity of Gāyatrī with Viṣṇu through another reason, he cites the scriptural passage grasped therein: "The elements, etc. (bhūtādīti).
The word *iti* is connected with the phrase *bhūtādi*.
In the Sūtra, those things among which the "existent" (*bhūta*)—meaning the universe—is the "beginning," i.e., first mentioned, are called *bhūtādi*;
that object of the Gāyatrī which has these as its feet is the *bhūtādipāda*.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "designation" (*vyapadeśa*) refers to the statement that establishes it; "on account of its establishment" (*upapatteḥ*) means because it is logical (*yuktatvāt*).
The word *pāda* has the state [of being a foot] as its primary meaning.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Ṭīkā*: "of the state of having the elements (*bhūta*) and so forth as its feet."
The word "evam" (thus) connects with both [parts of the verse]; and so it is said:
"All beings are one quarter of Him;
His three quarters are the immortal in heaven."

Thus, because the Gāyatrī is taught to possess four parts called "immortal" (amṛta), which are comprised by the words "beings" (bhūta) and so forth, and because that [possession of such parts] is possible only in Viṣṇu and impossible elsewhere, the meaning is that the one denoted by the word "Gāyatrī" must indeed be Viṣṇu.

Furthermore, when the word "ca" (and) is construed with the word "vyapadeśa" (designation), it serves to combine— within the proof that the Gāyatrī is Viṣṇu— the reason stated in the previous sūtra by the word "darśana" (perception) with the two reasons stated in this sūtra.

However, it should be understood that the term "sa" [in the commentary] is used to indicate a conjunction of reasons: that the status of being the four-footed *bhūta* and so forth as a mark of Viṣṇu is established not only because it is logically appropriate for Viṣṇu alone, but also because it is stated in the *Puruṣasūkta*.
For in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, it is said: "This very Gāyatrī is four-footed and sixfold" (*Chāndogya* 3.12.5).

By this statement, having restated the sixfold nature of the Lord named Gāyatrī— consisting of the previously mentioned Gāyatrī-mantra, the earth, the body, and the heart— and having enjoined His four-footedness in the form of possessing four parts, the Brāhmaṇa has cited the Puruṣasūkta mantra as an illustrative designation for the very point he himself has stated.
"This very thing has been declared by a Ṛg-verse" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.5). Thus,
"this very thing" refers to the Lord's fourfold nature as expressed in the Ṛg-verse.
By the *ṛc* mantra,
[the word] "abhi" means "fearlessly," "clearly," and "in accordance";
thus, it means it was spoken favorably.
"Such is His greatness, and yet the Puruṣa is greater than that; all beings constitute one quarter of Him, while His three quarters are the immortal in heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.6).
To the question "What has been said?", he recites that mantra: "Such is His... and so forth.
Although the reading in the Ṛgveda is "etāvān" and "viśvā," respectively;
Nevertheless, there is no fault, as this is a reading from another Vedic branch (*śākhā*).
By the verse, "Of this Person, all this is indeed the Person" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 3.12), that greatness consisting of universal sovereignty and so forth has been declared.
Not only this much, but the person [is also characterized] "therefrom."
"Greater even than the previously mentioned majesty" means endowed with a superior greatness.
He demonstrates this very superiority with the words beginning "A foot of Him," and so forth.
"All beings" refers to the entire universe; "of him," that is, of Viṣṇu, this constitutes "one foot."
The term *pādavat* means "having a foot" or "divided into parts.

Although in the *Tattvapradīpa* it appears as *viśvabhū-vidhiḥ*, nevertheless, in the *Ṭīkā* one observes the definition of a "foot" in the statement: "all beings (*sarvāṇi bhūtāni*) are his single foot."

Furthermore, since it is stated in the *Candrikā* that "just as in the case of the single animal (*paśvekatva*), the singularity of the foot is intended because it resides in that which is to be enjoined," the *Tattvapradīpa* should also be interpreted in exactly this way.
His "immortal" [nature] is devoid of destruction; for that very reason, it is his essential nature, consisting of "three quarters"—

the aggregate of three parts known as Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, and Vaikuṇṭha— and because it shines by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) in the three realms denoted by the word *dyu*, namely Śvetadvīpa, Anantāsana, and Vaikuṇṭha.
The meaning is that it is stated in the *Ṛgveda* that "He stands.

Although the word *bhūta* was explained in the *Chāndogya-bhāṣya* as referring to the individual soul (*jīva*) in the passage "all living beings are non-different from the quarters," [here it refers to Brahman].
Nevertheless, in accordance with the Vedic revelation "suvarṇam," it should be explained here as having the meaning of the universe:
"The golden vessel enveloped by dust."
"Of the gods, they regard that one-sixteenth part as the Virāj, the supporter of wealth, which is full of immortality;
yet one has certainly not found even a quarter of the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ," so says the Śruti (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.11).
The term *pāda* (foot) refers to a portion measured as a fourth part, as in the expression "the strength of a quarter," and thus it is distinct [from the whole].
Now, one might object: "Is not the description of Viṣṇu as having 'feet' consisting of the elements (*bhūta*) and so forth untenable, even as it is in the case of the *gāyatrī* meter?
For He is distinct from the elements. To this, he says: "Suvarṇam," etc.
The passage beginning with "gold" and ending with "and distinct" should be explained as a single syntactical unit according to the sequence of its meanings.
[This refers to] Yajñadatta’s...
It is called Devadatta,
and "the universe" is the understood remainder.
The word "pāda" (quarter) recurs;
the particle "ca" (and) has the sense of "only" (eva) and also indicates a reason (hetu).
The phrase "measured by a single part" (ekadeśaparimita), which contains the reason within it, must be repeated.

And likewise, the word "and" (ca) [is used] because the term "foot" (pāda) found in the scripture does not express that the elements possess the nature of being constituent parts of the immortal like the three feet; for if it did, there would be an inconsistency.
Rather, as in the expression "Devadatta has a strength that is one-fourth that of Yajñadatta," the universe is indeed distinct [from Brahman].
The meaning is that because [the capacity] is "limited"—that is, its power is limited by the foot of Viṣṇu—it is therefore called a "foot" (pāda) by virtue of being a foot of Viṣṇu.
Thus, the connection with the preceding [sūtra] is: "And because this designation of the quarters as beginning with the elements is possible in Viṣṇu, it is so."
In that case, it would follow that Hari is equal to the fourfold universe; therefore, he says "it is called a 'quarter'" (pāda).
Thus, by the word "śrautapāda," it is not meant—as in the expression "one whose strength is a fourth part"—that the universe is limited to a fourth portion of Viṣṇu’s power;
rather, it means "limited to a single part."

The meaning is that since [the power of the individual soul] is limited to only a single portion of Viṣṇu’s capacity, the aforementioned defect does not apply. To show how this is known, he says: "The golden treasure," which refers to the Taittirīya Śruti.
In the scripture, the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental,
and this is a singular form denoting a collective whole;
for this very reason, it says, "full of those who are liberated."
Thus it is stated in the *Ṭīkā*;
and so, by virtue of the syntactic unity of the *Tattvapradīpa* and the *Ṭīkā*,
the word "pādam" (the quarter) is understood to recur.
Among these, one is a derivation based on the state of being (*bhāvasādhana*).
The long vowel in *na kila* is due to *saṃhitā*-sandhi.
And likewise, [it is said] "not gold" (*asuvarṇa*) in the case of a single potsherd.

Consisting of that [unmanifest], "enveloped by rajas" means surrounded by the qualities of fire, air, ether, ego, and the great principle (mahat)— that is, the three qualities (guṇas); "the Virāj" is the body of Brahmā.

According to the method of the *Tattvapradīpa*, there is that which is called the "egg of Brahmā" (*brahmāṇḍa*), which shines forth preeminently like a "treasury" (*kośa*); here, there is a change in gender (from masculine to neuter).
[He saw] that "treasure-chest" (*avasudhānī*) of the gods— a casket for the storage of wealth— which was filled with "nectars," meaning liberated beings, [and which belonged] to the "Ṣaḍḍhotṛ."
Either one who offers the objects into the six senses,
or one who offers the six senses into the objects by means of the vital breath (jīva), or one who performs the act of eating with the six senses.
Regarding Viṣṇu’s "kalās," meaning those limited to a single part, the *pāda*; the remainder of the sentence is: "the Puruṣasūkta and other scriptures call it, speak of it, by the word 'pāda'."
It is said that here the word *pāda* does not refer to a foot, nor does it mean a fourth part.
Why? Because that chest (*mañjūṣā*) is [described as] "a *pāda*."
The meaning of the Vedic text is that he "did not obtain" (*na vivitse*) a state of being a "foot"—that is, equality with a fourth part;
as it says in the *Sattarkadīpāvali*: "He did not obtain a foot."
It has been stated that metrical symmetry was not achieved;
in both of these two positions, the transposition of the person (puruṣa) is equal,
and in the position of the commentator (ṭīkākṛt), there is also a transposition of the verbal suffix (lakāra).

Alternatively, by accepting that the change of gender is Vedic and that *kośam* ends in the accusative case, there is a single syntactic connection wherein even the feminine nouns function as qualifiers of *kośa*.
For He is indeed the one denoted by the *Puruṣasūkta*:
"With sacrifice they sacrificed to the Sacrifice" (*yajñena yajñamayajanta*; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12).
Thus, from the word "sacrifice" [it follows that] Viṣṇu is the deity; so says another Śruti passage: "Viṣṇu is the sacrifice, he is the deity."
For such is the Vedic revelation (śruti). This might be so if there were authoritative evidence that Viṣṇu is denoted by the word "so great" (tāvān) in this verse.
That very thing does not exist;

therefore, the indicative mark (liṅga) must belong to something else. Anticipating the objection that the inference indicated by the word "ca" in the Sūtra—namely, that the state of being a foot of the Bhūta-hymn and so forth is an indicative mark of Viṣṇu because it is mentioned in the Puruṣasūkta—is non-conclusive (aprayojaka), he refutes it with the words "sa hi" (for he...).

The construction is as follows: "For" (*hi*); because "He"—Viṣṇu alone—"is the one denoted by the Puruṣasūkta," that is, he is its subject matter; therefore, He alone is also the one whose feet consist of the elements and so forth, as stated in the Puruṣasūkta.
The sense is that, otherwise, if the state of having the elements (bhūta) and so forth as its feet were not an attribute of Viṣṇu, it would not be the subject matter of the *Puruṣasūkta*.

Alternatively, while proving that Gāyatrī is Viṣṇu, he states another supporting argument indicated by the word "ca" (and), which is construed with a different order in the Sūtra, beginning with "sa hi":
this connects with the main thesis statement, "Therefore, Gāyatrī is indeed Viṣṇu."

The sense is as follows: since the four-footed nature of the *gāyatrī* mentioned in the phrase "four-footed" is established by the *Puruṣasūkta* mantra, if that [mantra] is what is being expounded, then the referent of the word *gāyatrī*—which is established therein—must also belong to Him alone.
To the question, "On what basis is that which is spoken of in the *Puruṣasūkta* Viṣṇu?", he says: "By sacrifice," [referring to] the gods. "By sacrifice."
The meaning of the Vedic text is that they "worshipped" (ayajanta)— that is, they adored— Viṣṇu by means of a sacrifice consisting of knowledge and action, performed by the animal known as Rudra.
"From the word 'sacrifice' (yajña)" means because the word "sacrifice" is heard in the sentence.
To the question, "How does the word 'sacrifice' determine that [the Lord] is Viṣṇu?", he says "as sacrifice" (yajña), meaning by way of the conventional usage of the learned.
Indeed; for the meaning is that by the word "sacrifice" (yajña), the deity named Viṣṇu is denoted.
Although there is a Śruti of the Adhvaryus stating, "Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice."
Nevertheless, there is no fault, as this is another scriptural passage [of the same purport].
O Great King, at that time it is Rāma alone who is designated;
just as in the Puruṣa-sūkta, it is Viṣṇu alone who is designated.
And thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Now, it may be argued that the Puruṣasūkta does not belong to the context of Viṣṇu, but rather constitutes a different context altogether;
nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural mention of sacrifice.
It should not be argued that because there is no mention of Viṣṇu other than the one in the context of the "form of the sacrificial animal" (*paśurūpa*), [Viṣṇu] cannot be intended;
for it is possible that such a mention is merely incidental (*prāsaṅgika*).
Nor can the status of being a foot consisting of the elements (*bhūtādi*) be determined as a characteristic mark of Viṣṇu solely on that basis.
Nevertheless, [the argument] remains unproven;

for in the Śruti passage, "All beings are one foot of Him," there is no mention of sacrifice (yajña) in the foot consisting of the elements and so forth. Therefore, he cites Smṛti to establish that what is described in the Puruṣasūkta is indeed Viṣṇu, stating: "In that... etc.
"Mahārāja" is either an address to someone or an epithet of Rāma;
if it were the latter, it would be long [in vowel],
and thus [the form] would be "he mahārāja tasmin."
The meaning is that in the Tretā Yuga, Rāma alone is designated by all the names of Puruṣa.
For this very reason, in the Aṃśādhikaraṇa [it is said]:
"The calculation of the measure of the stars consists of thirteen thousand."
He made everything equal to the world of Brahmā, and that state then came to be for all.
At that time, the name "Rāma, Rāma" was on everyone's lips;
indeed, the entire world became permeated with Rāma when Rāma protected it.
Thus it is stated in the *Tattvapradīpa* on the authority of the *Skanda-purāṇa*. Here he provides an illustration with the words "just as" (*yathā*):
just as in the entire *Puruṣasūkta*, Viṣṇu alone is meant and no other.
The meaning is that the "animal" (paśu) is mentioned incidentally as a "man" (nara).

By this, since only something already established can serve as an illustration, the intention is that the *Puruṣasūkta* is proven to have Viṣṇu as its subject. The word "in the Skanda [Purāṇa]" is followed by the ellipsis "this was stated."
The phrase "for that [is] his" is to be construed with the preceding sentence.

"If it be argued that [the two teachings] are not identical because of a difference in instruction, we say no, for there is no contradiction in either case. (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.27) "The three-quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.6).
Thus is the prior instruction;
"beyond the sky" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.7), ending in the ablative case, is the latter.
If it is argued that, therefore, a single entity is not being spoken of here— no,
for there is no contradiction in either case when considering the three and seven worlds respectively.
Having raised an objection to what was stated, he presents the sūtra as a resolution: "Upadeśa... and so forth.
"In the two teachings" refers to the two statements containing the locative and ablative cases;

"by the teaching" means because of the difference [between them] due to the mention of contradictory attributes— namely, being situated in heaven and being beyond heaven— pertaining to Gāyatrī and Jyotis respectively.
If it is argued that, due to contradiction, a single entity called Viṣṇu cannot be the subject taught by both [texts], but rather they must refer to distinct entities— no; rather, it is "in both."
In both instructions, there is only one thing to be established;
how so? Because there is no contradiction.

Since the seventh and fifth [stages] have the same meaning in relation to the twenty-one worlds, there is an absence of contradiction—intending this application of the Sūtra, he first explains the portion of the objection with the words "tripād" (three-quarters).
‘Pūrvopadeśaḥ’ means a prior statement; ‘paścimaḥ’ means a subsequent one. The ellipsis is that there exists a later instruction distinct from that [prior one].
The statement beginning with “ending in the fifth case” (pañcamyanta) and so forth is for the purpose of highlighting the contradiction.
The statement "previously" is made to establish the superiority of that which is subject to the initial approach.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therefore.
Since there are thus two distinct teachings, therefore, in these two teachings, a single entity named Viṣṇu is not denoted by the two words *gāyatrī* and *jyotis*.
Why? Because here the word "not one" (*anaikam*) refers to two properties—namely, being situated in heaven and being beyond the sky—which constitute multiple entities;
however, in this context, "not one" [refers to something else].
The construction is: "it is said that there are two distinct entities. He explains the portion of the sūtra establishing the final position with the word "no" (na).
The meaning is: "in this context, two distinct entities are not being spoken of."
The word "but" (*kiṃ tu*) is the ellipsis; it is connected with the phrase "one thing is stated.
The term "in both" (*ubhayasmin*) is included within the probandum (*sādhya*).
The word "api" (also/even) is used for the purpose of conjunction, meaning that it is not only in one case, but in both cases as well.
Thus, the construction is: "And so, in both teachings, it is the very same entity called Viṣṇu that is being spoken of."
To the question, "How is this consistent given the contradiction? he says: "with reference to the three and seven worlds.

The meaning is that there is "no contradiction" because there is no conflict in designating a single entity in both cases—namely, with the intention of referring to the three worlds and with the intention of referring to the seven worlds.

The intended meaning is as follows: when there is a desire to express the three worlds as *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*, then everything situated above the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*)—which is called *bhuvaḥ* and rises to a height of one hundred thousand *yojanas*—is designated as *dyu*.

Since Śvetadvīpa, Anantasana, and Vaikuṇṭha are all situated above this intermediate space, that which resides therein—namely, what is called Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, and Vaikuṇṭha—is expressed by the term "three-quarters" (*tripād*).

It is said that the three forms abide in heaven; thus, there is no contradiction with the instruction ending in the locative case. Furthermore, among those situated on earth, the highest world consists of Anantāsana; and Hari, residing in Śvetadvīpa, is higher than those whose nature is the intermediate space (antarikṣa).
It should not be suspected that, because of this statement, the seat of Ananta is not situated above the atmosphere;
for even though it is located on the earth, its height of many hundred thousand yojanas makes it logically possible for it to be above the atmosphere, which is only one hundred thousand yojanas high.
Furthermore, by stating that it is higher than everything situated on the earth, the possibility of other things situated on the earth being higher is not excluded.
However, there is no possibility of [Vaikuṇṭha] being situated above the earth.
But when the seven worlds— Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Mahaḥ, Janaḥ, Tapaḥ, and Satyam— are intended, then,
since Indra’s abode (Svarga) is the heaven (*div*), and because Vaikuṇṭha, which is of the same class as that, is situated even higher than what is above it, it is "beyond the heaven" (*divaḥ para*).
On the earth is the great Mount Meru, in the sky is the solar disc, and in heaven is the abode of Indra; yet beyond that is what lies even further than heaven.

According to this traditional teaching (*smṛti*), since even Mount Meru is celestial (*div*), that which is higher than it—namely the Anantāsana, which belongs to the same category—is beyond heaven (*divaḥ paratā*).

Likewise, since the solar orb (*sūryamaṇḍala*) is also celestial, that which is situated above it—the Śvetadvīpa, which is slightly separated from the earth, equal in height to the entire universe, and belongs to the same category—is likewise beyond heaven. Thus, there is no contradiction with the instruction involving the ablative case ending (*pañcamyantopadeśa*).

Furthermore, "being beyond heaven" (*dyuparatva*) means being beyond a heaven that is possible as belonging to its own class; thus, there is no room for criticism on the grounds of [the definition being] either too narrow or too broad.

Although the status of being beyond heaven is established for Vaikuṇṭha simply by its being beyond the heavenly world (*svargaloka*), since that point has already been stated by the phrase "in all regions beyond," the term "heaven" (*div*) here refers specifically to Indra’s abode (*indrasadana*) to the exclusion of the [general] heavenly world.

Nor should it be argued that the reference to the seven worlds is redundant, since even the infinite seats and so forth—by virtue of being beyond Meru and other such peaks—are established as being "beyond heaven" (divaḥ paratva) through the intention of referring to the three worlds alone;

for if that were the case, Vaikuṇṭha would also be included within the meaning of the word "heaven," and its status as being beyond all heavens would fail to be established, thereby contradicting the authoritative testimony: "And Vaikuṇṭha is said to be higher than all those things consisting of the two [lower] worlds."
In the *Chāndogyabhāṣya*, however, it is stated:
"Because Ananta’s bed and likewise Ananta’s seat of Hari are situated in an eternal celestial chariot (*vimāna*) that rises many hundreds of thousands of leagues."

Since it is stated in the Śruti, "In the heaven (divi) within the Self whose nature is consciousness," by the force of this authority, the word *dyu* ending in the locative case is etymological (*yaugika*)—based on the reason of being luminous—in the three locations known as Śvetadvīpa and Vaikuṇṭha, which have the infinite seat whose nature is consciousness as their essence; whereas in [the context of] heaven (*svarga*) and so forth, it is conventional (*rūḍha*). Thus, there is no contradiction between the two teachings. In this manner, an alternative resolution of the contradiction has been made. // 11 //
Thus concludes the section concerning the designation of the meters. 11.
12. The Section on the Vital Breath at the End of the Foot.
It has been stated that Prāṇa is Viṣṇu.
However, in the passage, "These indeed are the glories resting upon the head: sight, hearing, mind, speech, and breath" (Ai. Ā.
2.1.4), the status of Prāṇa as Viṣṇu is not evident.
Because it is mentioned together with the sense organs (*indriya*), he says:
"In this section, the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the name 'Prāṇa'—which is well-known in common usage for something other than [Viṣṇu]—is established as referring to Viṣṇu.

He demonstrates the introductory statement (*saṅgati*), the subject sentence (*viṣayavākya*), the doubt (*saṃśaya*), and the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) supported by reasoning, beginning with the word "Prāṇa."
The meaning is that in the *Ādyaprāṇādhikaraṇa*, it was stated that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) mentioned in the passage "That indeed art thou" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 3.14) is Viṣṇu.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "In that [context]."
The word "stated" (uktam) is to be supplied [from the previous context]. "Its non-repetition and transformation" (tasyāvṛttivipariṇāmau)—
in this way, the phrase "there too" (tatra) is also to be repeated.

And likewise, in that passage, "That indeed you are," the status of Viṣṇu does not belong to, nor is it appropriate for, the prāṇa mentioned in that sentence. Why? Because in that context, [it says] "That indeed you are."

The construction is as follows: "the state of being Viṣṇu does not exist" for the Prāṇa who is "spoken of"—that is, mentioned—in the statement of the sentence [of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad], and who is "heard"—that is, mentioned—as heard in the Aitareya statement, "Now these [channels]... (Tā vā etāḥ).
To the question "Why does it not exist?", he says: "Because it is mentioned together with the sense organs.
This means that because it is recited along with the sense organs, it is enumerated within the group of sense organs.

By this, through the refutation of the *aitareya-prāṇa* being other than Viṣṇu, the refutation of the *prāṇa* mentioned in the earlier Taittirīya [text] is also implied; thus, its "suggestive connection" (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*) is stated.
The subject matter is the one called *prāṇa* in the *Aitareya* [Upaniṣad];

the doubt is indicated as to whether this *prāṇa* is something other than Viṣṇu, or indeed Viṣṇu himself. Likewise, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is simply something else, such as the wind (*vāyu*).
By the phrase "being enumerated among the group of faculties," the probative mark (*liṅga*) that establishes that [the head] is indicated.
Furthermore, the statement "these indeed" (*tā vā etāḥ*) is intended to explain the ground for applying the word "head" (*śiras*) to the heads of the Four-faced One (*Caturmukha*).
The word *vai* signifies well-known tradition (*prasiddhi*).
And thus, since "these"— namely,
those deities presiding over [the functions] denoted by the words "eye," "ear," "mind," "speech," and "vital breath"—
are "in the head"; that is, they are situated in the head, which is designated as the "skull" (*śīrṣan*).
Therefore, according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), the meaning of the scriptural passage is "the Śris because they resort [to it].
By this, it is stated that being resorted to by the eyes and so forth is the ground for the application of the term "head" (śiras).
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin), however, considers the word "prāṇa" to refer to something other than the vital breath alone.
He introduces the sūtra that establishes the final conclusion with the words "ataḥ" (therefore).
The meaning is: since the prima facie position has been reached, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa states the subsequent sūtra.
*Prāṇas tathānugamāt* (The vital breath [is Brahman], because of the corresponding agreement). 1.1.28.
"The gods breathed him forth" (AiĀ 2.1.5);
"He is this breath, he is this vital air" (AiĀ 2.1.5); "One should know that the *ṛc* is the vital air" (AiĀ 2.2.2).
"Because this breath presides over it" (Ai. Ā. 2.3.8);
having recited the Sūtra, he explains the logical portion "because of the concordance therein" by citing the scriptural passage—namely, "the breath."
The phrase "and so forth" means that the marks— such as being taught by a deity— which are stated in such sentences as these, are found "in many places" (*anugamāt*) within this very section;
that is to say, because they recur and are repeated.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the statement establishing that [the Self] resides within the solar orb—namely, "For this which shines yonder is indeed the vital breath" (*prāṇo hy evaiṣa ya eṣa tapati*)—is included.
Likewise, [there is the statement]: "All beings, down to the ants, are pervaded by the great vital breath" (*sarvāṇi bhūtāny āpipīlikābhyaḥ prāṇena bṛhatyā viṣṭabdhāni*).
And such statements as these are also included.
Here too, Prāṇa is indeed Viṣṇu. He explains the word "tathā" from the Sūtra with the words: "atrāpi" (here too).

The word "heard" (śruta) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. The particle "api" (also/even) is used for the purpose of conjunction, indicating that this is not only found in the passage "That indeed you are," but also in the Aitareya [Upaniṣad].
He states the meaning of the word "that" (tat) as it occurs in the Sūtra: "Viṣṇu alone. By this, [it is shown that] just as in the phrase "That indeed is Thou" (tattvamasi);
Thus, the Prāṇa mentioned in the Śruti is Viṣṇu; likewise, the one mentioned in the Aitareya [Upaniṣad] is also Viṣṇu alone, and not anyone else.

Why? Because the marks of Viṣṇu—such as being the deity to be taught and so forth—are found to "follow" (anugama) this context; that is to say, they persist through repetition. This is the meaning of the Sūtra as stated.
In the *Aitareya*, there is a statement within a single section: "The gods breathed that [being] into life.
Therein, "that" refers to Nārāyaṇa and Vāyu, whom the gods "breathed into life."
The meaning is that they have led [the teaching] to its highest excellence among disciples, grand-disciples, and others;
by this, it is stated that Viṣṇu is the object of worship for all the gods.
"He is this breath, he is this vital force, he is this prosperity."
This and other such statements are found in another section [of the scripture].

By this, the status of being an object of worship for the gods and others is expressed through [the attributes of] *bhūti* (prosperity) and so forth. "He, this very one" refers to the Blessed Lord: he is *asu* because he dispels the wicked; he is *prāṇa* because his nature is supreme bliss; and he is the bestower of sovereignty—consisting of knowledge and other powers denoted by the word *bhūti*—to the gods, while [he is the destroyer] of the asuras.
The meaning is that because it is the cause of ignorance, lack of sovereignty, and so forth, it is denoted by the words "prosperity" (*bhūti*) and "non-prosperity" (*abhūti*).
In that very context [the scripture] says: "All these *ṛg* verses, all the Vedas, and all sounds are indeed one single *vyāhṛti*;
one should know that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone is the *ṛg*, the *prāṇa*."
This is another statement;
here it is declared that the Prāṇa is described in all the Vedas.
Of all those Ṛg-verses, there is "but one single Vyāhṛti."
Only one thing must be spoken and established;
and what is that? It is Viṣṇu alone who is Prāṇa.
Furthermore, Prāṇa alone is the subject to be established even by all the Vedas.
Moreover, this applies even to the sounds of the ocean and the like, let alone those of the Vedas.
Among these, the *ṛc* verses, in particular, reveal the qualities of Viṣṇu— who possesses names such as Indra and others— even to those of limited knowledge.

The meaning is that one should know that [the mantras] have Nārāyaṇa as their object— that is, they refer to Him alone— since He is the Prāṇa. However, in the Aitareya Bhāṣya, even the first word "prāṇe" is interpreted as a locative denoting the object, and the word "vyāhṛti" is likewise treated.

Having explained [the passage] by focusing on the act of utterance, it is stated that "name" (*nāma*) refers to a single utterance which is of one kind because it expresses the perfection of faultless qualities;
this very point is also stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*.

Now, another passage— “Of that [chariot], speech is the pole, the ears are the side-pieces, the eyes are the yoke-horses, the mind is the reins, and this vital breath (prāṇa) mounts it”— states here that the vital breath is the charioteer of the body.
The word "atha" (now) serves to introduce the discussion of a different object of knowledge.
The word "is said" (*ucyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

Thus, the meaning is that the chariot of the Lord Viṣṇu—or of Vāyu—is described both with respect to the internal self (*adhyātma*) and with respect to the deity (*adhidaivata*). Regarding its internal aspect, [the component] called the body is "speech" (*vāk*).

Umā, known as Speech, is the ocean in the form of the rope for mooring; in the case of the well-known chariot of Viṣṇu, Umā in the form of a serpent is the "ocean. The moon and his wife, situated on the right and left sides, are the "two wings";
elsewhere, the two horses in the form of horses yoked to the sides are the "two eyes."
The sun and his wife situated on both sides are "yoked";
the two horses yoked in front are "the mind";
Rudra, who presides over the mind, is "the holder."
Thus, with respect to the divine, Rudra is the charioteer even of the well-known chariot;
and "he" (sa) and "this" (ayam) together form the single compound "tad-ayam," according to the method of the *Tattvapradīpa*.
Even though the words are split, the word "that" (tat) refers back to the body described as a chariot;
or, by a change of gender, it refers to "that chariot.
The meaning is that this Prāṇa—namely Viṣṇu and Vāyu—presides over it.

The mention of the multiplicity of indicative marks (*liṅga*) is intended to prevent the doubt as to how the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) can be established by that very same mark which was used to formulate the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
"The gods brought Viṣṇu alone; they worship Viṣṇu as prosperity (*bhūti*);
he alone is declared in all the Vedas; his chariot is said to be the body."
Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.

Now, one might object: even more than a Siddhāntin’s mark (liṅga), which is frequent, the mark adduced by the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvavādī) is indeed stronger, because it is inherently stronger due to its being without any other scope for application (niravakāśatva).
Nor is there a definitive conclusion without distinction, because even that which is strong by virtue of its abundance may be overridden by that which is stronger by its very nature. As they say:
"Strength is of two kinds: that arising from abundance and that arising from intrinsic nature."
Between those two, its own nature is stronger, as it is that which must be relied upon and so forth.
