Thus [it is asked]: "How, then, can there be a certainty regarding Viṣṇu by means of those [signs]? To this, he establishes through Smṛti that the signs—such as being taught by the gods (devatopadeśyatva)—are also without any other possible application, stating:
"Viṣṇum. The gods "brought forth" (ānayan) Viṣṇu alone by primarily initiating the tradition of knowledge among disciples and others;
they worship Viṣṇu alone for the sake of prosperity (bhūti).
"Bhūtim" may also be understood as a qualifying attribute of the object to be enjoined (*vidheya-viśeṣaṇa*).
Thus, the meaning is that they worship Viṣṇu as *bhūti*—where *bhūti* consists of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) such as knowledge and so forth.
The word "he" (*saḥ*) refers to Viṣṇu as the primary denotation (*mukhya-vācyatayā*); this is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*).
The application of the particle *eva* is precisely by that [same word].
In the phrase "his chariot" (*tadrathaḥ*), it means the chariot of Viṣṇu alone.
Here, because the particle *eva* is repeated twice, it is indicated that it is to be supplied everywhere.
By this, it is stated that all the [opposing] marks (liṅgas) are rendered without scope.
The ellipsis of the sentence following "In the Skanda" is: "the non-otherwise-establishability of the marks has been stated.

Thus, the sense is that while the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) mark is strong in one way, the conclusive (siddhānta) mark is stronger even in two ways; therefore, the determination [of the truth] is logically established by its superiority.
This has been stated as a concession;
however, in reality, the prima facie indicator (pūrvapakṣaliṅga) does not possess strength even by virtue of being without scope,
because being enumerated together with the vital breaths (prāṇas) can possibly reside in the Inner Controller (antaryāmin).
And because it follows from the word "Brahman."

When the status of Prāṇa as Viṣṇu is established by that very [reasoning], since the weaker indicative mark (liṅga) can be sublated in both ways by the stronger indicative mark through two modes—namely, its being numerous and its having no other scope—then what need is there to mention [the case] based on the repetition of the term "Brahman," which has no other scope? With this intention, he explains the word "anugama" (conformity) in another way: "Brahman... [and so forth].
In this context, [the following passages occur]: "This is Brahman" (AiĀ 2.1.1), "The world of Brahman" (AiĀ 2.1.3),
and "Brahman [leads] this person" (AiĀ 2.1.4).

The meaning is that this is also because of the repeated use of the term "Brahman" in its exclusive sense, as in: "They call the belly Brahman" (AiĀ 2.1.4) and "A is Brahman" (AiĀ 2.3.8), and so forth.
This is the nature of Viṣṇu, the Brahman complete with all attributes.
This individual soul (jīva) is the locus of the Supreme Brahman.
He entered this four-faced Puruṣa, the Supreme Brahman.
The meaning is that the place where the wind is situated—just as one might utter a roar or a song—is the stomach; it has entered therein.

"If it be argued that [the Self taught here] is not the speaker's own Self because of the instruction [of another], we reply: no, for there is an abundance of references to the inner self (*adhyātma*) in this [text]. [For example:
'O Seer, I am indeed Prāṇa' (Ai. Ā. 2.2.3)."
If it is argued that Indra alone is meant because of this instruction by the speaker himself, we say no;
for [the text continues]: "You are Prāṇa; Prāṇa is all beings."
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.3) Thus, many connections with the inner self (adhyātma) are indeed found here. // 29 //
Having raised an objection to what was stated, he provides a resolution; first, having recited the sūtra, he explains the portion containing the objection: "No."
The term "Prāṇa" is understood to carry over [from the previous context].
Thus, it is not tenable that Prāṇa is Viṣṇu. Why? Because [it is said]: "O Sage, I am indeed Prāṇa."
The meaning of this statement is that, by means of this sentence, Indra instructed Viśvāmitra—the reciter of a thousand *bṛhatī* verses—regarding his own self as being the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The statement of the result is that the vital breath is indeed Indra;
it is not, however, a statement of the probandum (the thesis) based on the reason already stated.
Regarding the statement, "O Sage, I am indeed Prāṇa," Indra said to him: "O Sage, you have come to a dear abode of mine; I shall grant you a boon.
He replied, "May I know you alone."
Indra said to him;
this should be explained together with the preceding sentence.
As for its manner: "To him."
To Viśvāmitra, [addressed as] "Indra," the Blessed One dwelling within him spoke. What did he say? "O Sage, you have come to my beloved abode; attain it!"
"I grant you a boon.
The word *vai* is used here for emphasis or to indicate what is well-known.

Thus, by proclaiming this three times, he "attained" the grace of the Lord—which is the means for attaining the state called *sālokya* (residing in the same world) and reaching the city of the Lord—by means of such praise. "He" refers to the one who has thus attained it.
Being addressed again by Indra with the words, "I shall grant you a boon," Viśvāmitra said:
"What is it? [He meant: "Previously I knew you only in a general sense;
now I wish to know you specifically—what you truly are."
Thus addressed, Indra—that is, Hari dwelling within him—replied to the seer.
What did he say? "O seer, because I am of the nature of supreme bliss, I am denoted by the word 'Prāṇa'."

In this view, which maintains the syntactical connection (*vākyasamanvaya*), since it is easy for forms such as *asmi* (I am) and other verbal endings prescribed with *asmad* and so forth as upapadas to function therein, the use of the first person (*uttamapuruṣa*) in the word *asmi* is justified by the fact that Hari, abiding within Indra, refers to His own self as "I" (*aham*), according to the method of the *Tattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā*.
The meaning of the scriptural passage according to the view of the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) is clear.

However, it should be understood that there is no inconsistency in the view of concordance (samanvaya) with the Lord—based on the grounds of being the one who cannot be abandoned, supreme bliss, the withdrawer, and the knower—regarding the words "I am the Prāṇa.
He explains the portion of the final conclusion (siddhānta) by supplying the negative particle (nañ): "Not so."
The term "because of following" (anugamāt) is understood to carry over [from the previous context]. The word "not" (na) is repeated. The word "hi" has the sense of "since" (yataḥ).
The word "said" (*uktam*) is to be supplied [at the end of the previous sentence].
Thus, the interpretation stated in the *Tattvapradīpa-ṭīkā* is as follows: "This Prāṇa is not Indra, but Viṣṇu alone."

Why? "Because of the accompaniment," that is, because of the previously mentioned strongest inferential marks (*liṅga*) and so forth. If that were the case, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural instruction (*upadeśa*).
If this is argued—no; why?
Because in this context, Indra first declared his own status as the Supreme Self to one established in himself with the statement: "O Sage, I am indeed Prāṇa."
Nor is there a contradiction with the statement of identity;
for here, that very Supreme Self called Prāṇa possesses "many connections with the adhyātma" through such statements as, "You are Prāṇa; all beings are Prāṇa."

The connection with many bodies in the form of individual souls (jīvas), such as Indra and others, is indeed omnipresence; this was stated by Indra to the seer (ṛṣi) in the words "it exists" (vidyate), meaning it is present, but not that there is identity (aikya).
This is said with the intention that the multiplicity of connections mentioned in the Sūtra ultimately resides in the connected entity itself.
It has been stated that [the term] is "much" (*bahu*).

Although the word *bhūman* denotes a state (*bhāva*), it is used with reference to the possessor of the state (*bhavitṛ*) because there is no distinction between the state and the possessor of the state.
In the Sūtra, however, the final member of the compound is placed first (*paranipāta*), which is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*).

Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is as follows: *adhyātma* is that which is both "excessive" (*adhika*) and "self" (*ātman*); its connection is *adhyātmasambandha*, and this is "many" (*bahu*), hence the term *bahvadhyātmasambandha*.
And thus, because "here," in Indra, there is "much."

The meaning is that there exists an abundant and specific proximity with the Supreme Self. Immediately after the word "exists," the ellipsis is: "this instruction is in relation to that [proximity], not in relation to oneself.
Thus, Indra's statement, "I am indeed Prāṇa," is intended to refer to a specific, temporary proximity to the Lord.
The meaning is that there is no contradiction with the instruction because [the statement] is not made from one's own perspective.

To the question "Why is it not from one's own perspective?", he says, "Because it is a praise of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)," and so forth. The construction is as follows: for (*hi*) because [it is said], "You are the vital breath."
By such statements as these, it is declared that this *prāṇa* has "an extensive connection with the inner self" (*adhyātma*);

that is, by way of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), it possesses a connection with many bodies in the form of Indra and others, and its omnipresence is thus established. This [omnipresence] does not exist nor is it appropriate for a particular individual soul (*jīva*) such as Indra; therefore, according to the first position, [the text says] "of whom the self is the body."

The term "adhyātma" is used to indicate that the scriptural statement "Mādhyandina" refers to Indra and others being designated as one with Viṣṇu on the basis of the relationship between body and embodied soul, since they are the bodies of Viṣṇu.
By this [statement], it is shown that because Indra taught himself to Viśvāmitra— the speaker of the thousand Bṛhatīs— as the vital breath (prāṇa), this prāṇa is not Viṣṇu.
If it be argued that this is indeed Indra—[we reply: this vital breath (prāṇa) is not Indra, but Viṣṇu alone.
Why? Because of the continuity [of attributes], such as the previously mentioned mark of being the strongest.
Nor is there any contradiction with the traditional instruction (upadeśa), because this [text] concerns precisely the internal subject matter pertaining to Indra.
Why? Because in this context, there is an abundance of references related to the internal self.

Here, by the term "internal connection" (*adhyātma-sambandha*), it is meant that which exists within the domain of the Self (*ātman*). "Adhyātman" refers to both the body and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Thus, because a connection between the internal Self, Viṣṇu, and the bodies of Indra, Viśvāmitra, and others is stated to exist, [the term is used].

Alternatively— the sense is that because in this Indra there is an abundance (*bhūmā*) of connection with the internal self— that is, since there exists an abundance or preponderance of the connection and absorption of the "higher" Self, the Supreme Self— therefore it is appropriate for the teaching to have the proximate Supreme Self as its object. Why is that so?
For because in this context the stage of internal connection has been taught, therefore the meaning of the Sūtra is stated as "therefore.
However, according to the perspective of the Śāstra, the instruction is like that of Vāmadeva;
the Śāstra is the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī).

Now, one might raise the objection: "If Viṣṇu alone is indeed denoted by the word 'prāṇa' even when used for Indra due to His all-pervading nature as one's own self and so forth, then the designation should have been 'prāṇa is in me,' and not 'I am [the prāṇa],' because it is inappropriate to teach Viṣṇu in the form of 'I am,' etc. To dispel this doubt, the author recites the sūtra: "Because of the teaching... (Śāstra).
The word *tu* also has the sense of "also" (*api*),
and it indicates a traditional authority (*smṛti*) in the sense of "just as" (*yathā*).
The word "is appropriate" (*yujyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
And thus, since even when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is Viṣṇu, an instruction such as "I am indeed the vital breath" is appropriate, there is no inconsistency therein. How is this appropriate?
For this instruction is given "from the perspective of the Teacher" (*śāstradṛṣṭyā*);
the "Teacher" (*śāstṛ*) is the Lord who dwells within (*antaryāmī*), for he teaches everything.
It proceeds from his perspective and with reference to him alone, but not through identity.
Nor is it incorrect [to apply the term "I"] to the inner controller (antaryāmin), because we do not observe the use of "I" and so forth in reference to him;
for [the sūtra] says "as in the case of Vāmadeva," meaning as in the usage made by him.

Just as the sage named Vāmadeva, with the intention of expressing the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), employed words such as "I" and "Manu" in reference to himself—saying, "I was Manu"—so too is this instruction appropriate; intending thus to provide the construction of the Sūtra, he explains the word *śāstra* from the Sūtra itself: "The scripture (*śāstra*)."
The word "Viṣṇu" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
Thus, the meaning is that Viṣṇu, as the inner controller (antaryāmī), is denoted here by the term of the scripture. The term "inner controller" is used with reference to the subject under discussion.

Alternatively, by the etymological derivation that "it instructs" (śāsti) or "impels" (prerayati) all beings, the term *antaryāmī* itself becomes the explanation of the word *śāstra*; thus, there is no room for the suspicion that it is a non-existent referent (*apadārtha*).
For this very reason, in the *Bhāgavata*, the word *śāstra* is applied specifically to the *antaryāmī*, who is the object of meditation.

Even when the word *śāstṛ* (teacher/governor) is taken as the basis for the commentary in the *Aitareyabhāṣya* which states "of the Teacher, the Inner Controller," and even when the *Tattvapradīpa* explains it accordingly as "of Viṣṇu, the Teacher, the Inner Controller," one should not suspect that this [current work] contradicts that.
With the intention that the word *śāstra* (treatise) is explained by the very explanation of its synonymous term, the synonymous word *śāstṛ* (teacher/instructor) is now explained.

Alternatively, having intended the division of the word *śāstra* into the parts *śāstṛ* and *a*, the portion *śāstṛ* has been explained by the term *antaryāmī* (the inner controller), and the syllable *a* by the term *viṣṇoḥ* (of Viṣṇu).

However, here, without intending such a division of parts, the single, indivisible word *śāstram* is explained as *antaryāmī*; accordingly, it is stated that "consciousness (*saṃvit*) is the treatise."
And because of this citation, there is no contradiction;
for it is said in the *Bhāgavata*: "The scripture of consciousness is the supreme state."
He states the proof for Viṣṇu, the inner controller, being denoted by the words of the scriptures: "Consciousness," etc.
In the first book, these words were spoken by Nārada to Vyāsa:
"The dream is the grasp of illusion, the bed is the appearance of waking for the Self;
name, form, and activity are its functions; consciousness is the scripture, the supreme state."

The meaning of this is as follows: Dream (*svapna*) is the cognition of objects arising from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) known as the tendencies of *māyā* belonging to the self, which is the individual soul (*jīva*). Deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is the state of non-perception (*agraha*), being a state of rest devoid of the cognitions of objects belonging to either the waking or the dreaming states. Waking (*jāgrat*) is the manifestation (*ābhāsa*), the cognitive representation (*pratyaya*), which consists of the engagement with and withdrawal from names, forms, and actions—that is, words, their referents, and activities—as well as the cognition of objects such as designations and the like.
Since this triad of states arises from the Self, which is the Supreme Brahman,
that consciousness is omniscient, consisting of the knowledge of all objects as they truly are.
I reflected: "The Śāstra is the controller of all; I am the Supreme, the Highest State, the Brahman to be attained by the virtuous.
After the word "Bhāgavata," the word "because of its usage" (*prayogāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
The word "of this" is to be construed with the term "inner controller" (*antaryāmī*).
Viṣṇu is designated by various names because he is the cause of all instruction;
there is no name whatsoever that exists anywhere apart from that Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*).
Thus it is stated in the Padma Purāṇa.

Anticipating the objection as to how the use of terms such as "I" (aham) can possibly apply to the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), he states the traditional authority (smṛti) indicated by the word "tu" (but/rather): "That very [Self]," etc.
Viṣṇu is called by names such as "I," which are otherwise well-known to refer to something else.

By this, it is shown that there is both learned consensus (*viddhi*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) regarding Viṣṇu as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*); [the phrase] "on account of the cause of being the teacher of all" means by reason of being the controller of all.

By this, Mahāyoga is demonstrated, because its independence is stated therein. By this, [the objection that] our position, like the views of others, is merely conventional (lākṣaṇika) is also refuted; [this is shown by the term] "Puruṣottama."
"Except for" (ṛte) Viṣṇu, the inner controller;
"anywhere else" (anyatra kvāpi);
[namely] "anything at all" (kiṃcit) among the individual soul and so forth.
The term "name" refers to the form of the "I" (the ego); it does not exist as a denoter [of Hari].
By this, it is stated that [the word] has the highest primary sense in Hari, while elsewhere it possesses only a secondary primary sense.
Otherwise, since it would be impossible to deny [the existence of] the universal [term] altogether— stating that "it does not exist anywhere"—
in this context, words such as "I" (aham) are well-known to denote the inner self (pratyagātman), and the inner selves and so forth are always found in a unified state.
The ignorant, lacking discrimination, apply [words] such as "I" to the individual soul alone, just as one might apply the word "fire" to wood.

However, the wise, possessing the discrimination between the primary and the secondary, disregard the secondary meaning and apply them to the primary referent, Hari; this should be understood as stated in the *Tattvanirṇaya*.

Following the mention of the *Padma Purāṇa*, [it says]: "Since it is stated that words such as 'I' have their primary sense in the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), the teaching of 'I' and so forth is indeed appropriate from the perspective of the scriptural vision."
This is the completion of the sentence, as in [the Vedic passage]:
"I was Manu and I was the Sun" (Ṛgveda 4.26.1), and so forth. // 30 //

He dispels the doubt that the application of [words] such as "I" is inappropriate with respect to the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) because such usage is not observed there—by explaining the example mentioned in the Sūtra: "I... (aham).
The meaning of the Ṛgvedic mantra is: "I," the seer named Vāmadeva, who am the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), became Manu and Sūrya by virtue of being their respective inner controllers.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), passages such as "I am the seer Kakṣīvān, the sage; I am Kutsa" (Ṛgveda 4.26.1) are included.

The phrase "like this and so forth" (*ityādivat*)—meaning "like such examples of usage"—is connected with the statement "the teaching is by means of the vision of the scripture" (*śāstradṛṣṭyopadeśaḥ*). "If it be argued that [the Self spoken of here] is not [the Supreme Self] because of the marks of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), we say no; because there is a threefold nature of meditation, and because that [threefold nature] is applicable here due to its being resorted to. (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.31)
"If there are so many thousands of days in a hundred years," (Ai. Ā.

2.2.4)—thus [it is argued that] there is a mark of the individual soul (*jīva*) and a mark of the chief vital air (*mukhya-prāṇa*) in the dialogue of the vital airs and so forth; therefore, [the Self taught here is not Brahman].
Having raised this objection—which is a repetition of a previous point—the author presents the Sūtra and explains the part concerning the objection first: "The individual soul... and so on.
The word "is explained" (anusandhīyate) is also to be understood as the ellipsis for "what was said.
The analysis of the compound is: "the dialogue of the vital breath with the vital breaths," namely, agreement, dispute, and quarrel.
And likewise, because in this context it is stated, "He worshipped him for a hundred years; therefore, the lifespan of man is a hundred years" (Ai. Ā.

2.2.1), that characteristic of living beings—namely, having a lifespan of a hundred years, which is caused by the Prāṇa's abiding in the living body for a period of one hundred years—is connected in many places by such passages as, "There are so many thousands of days in a hundred-year period," and so forth.
And because, by the statement, "Not harming them, [he said], 'I am the hymn, I am the hymn'" (Ai. Ā.
2.1.4), a characteristic mark of the principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*)—namely, its dialogue with the vital breaths, i.e., the sense organs—is stated;
and because, as included under the word "etcetera," the statement "The vital breath is the roof-beam," [as said by] the elder Śākalya—"just as all [the rafters] in a house-roof beam... is found.
"Just as the reeds are held together, so too in this prāṇa are the eye, the ear, the mind, the organs of speech, the body, and the entire self held together" (Ai.

Ā. 3.2.1.1). By this statement, the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) consisting of being the sustainer of all living beings, sense organs, and the body is also stated; therefore, this prāṇa is not Viṣṇu.
However, the construction is that [the passage refers] to the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) alone.

Although the statement "Therefore, the lifespan of a person is one hundred years" (Ai. Ā. 2.2.1), which establishes the mark of a hundred-year life, would have been the appropriate example to cite, [this other passage is used].
However, the phrase "not that many" is not [the intended meaning].

Nevertheless, the illustrative sentence was cited specifically to demonstrate that there is a concordance of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in many places, and to show that the Upaniṣad intends to convey that these are the marks of the individual soul (*jīva*).

According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the meaning of the scriptural passage is as follows: the thousands of days of a hundred-year human lifespan are those very forms of the Lord’s Person residing in the Sun, who governs the days contained within the hundred-year period.
How many thousands? There are as many thousands of male forms as there are syllables contained within a thousand *bṛhatī* verses;
thus, they amount to thirty-six thousand.
"Those," namely the deities of the eye and so forth, "did not harm one another";
that is, they did not engage in dispute.
But what [was the cause]? [Each thought]: "I am the *uktha*, the arouser of this four-faced body."
No; because there is a threefold mode of meditation—namely, as being within, as being without, and as being all-pervading—and because [the Lord] is the support here.
He explains the part of the refutation with the word "no."
The meaning is that it is not the case that "Prāṇa is Viṣṇu," but rather that this is indeed Viṣṇu himself, and not the individual soul (jīva) or any other.

To the question "Why not?", there is the connection (*anuṣaṅga*) of the previously stated reason for the concordance (*anugama*); and to the objection that this contradicts the previously mentioned marks (*liṅga*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), there is the connection of the reason: "Because this instruction is [given] from the perspective of the scripture" (*śāstradṛṣṭyā*).

Intending the answer to the question "For what purpose is the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*)?"—namely, "for the sake of internal meditation" (*antar-upāsti*)—and addressing the objection that "there is no distinction in meditation," the Sūtra begins with the word "meditation" (*upāsā*).
He explains this portion of the Sūtra with the word "antar" (within).
The term "by way of having gone to" (*gatatvena*) is to be connected individually with each of the words "internal," "external," and "all.
The particle "iti" has the sense of "manner" or "kind."

And thus, because there is a threefold mode of meditation—namely, as being within the body, as being outside the body, and as being all-pervading—the meaning is that the meditation on the Blessed One is of three kinds, due to this "threefoldness of meditation" (*upāsātraividhyāt*).

Now, one might object: even so, this statement is useless, because the actual threefold nature of the meditation, which is not explicitly stated here, cannot serve as a reason for mentioning the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*). To this, [the author] proceeds with the phrase: "Because it is based upon" (*āśritatvāt*).
He explains the portion beginning with "iti" by supplying the word "ca" (and), saying "iha" (here).
The meaning is: because it has been stated in this very context.
The term "upāsātraividhyasya" (of the threefold nature of meditation) is to be construed here by changing its case-ending [to the genitive]. And... [the particle] "ca".
In the context of the collection of causes that bring about origination, the point is this:
it is logical to speak of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) for the purpose of meditating upon that which is included within the threefold categories mentioned here. [As it is said:
"He, having split open this very suture, entered by means of this door" (AiĀ 2.4.3).
"He beheld this very Person as the most pervasive Brahman" (AiĀ 2.4.3); "Knowing this, indeed, Mahidāsa Aitareya used to say" (AiĀ 2.1.8),
and so forth.
To the question, "What is the indicative mark (liṅga) here that the threefold nature of worship is being stated? he says:
"He. Vāsudeva, the Blessed Lord, having indeed split open this very boundary—the middle of the head—by means of this door;
"He entered by means of the *suṣumnā* channel" means he reached it; the remainder of the sense is "the heart of the Four-faced One.

Since this describes the Lord's entry into the interior of the body, and because such descriptions are intended for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*), internal worship (*antar-upāsti*) is thereby described.

"He"— Nārāyaṇa, who had previously entered from the two forefeet into the body of the four-faced one— [perceives] "this very Puruṣa," that is, the Self in the form of Vyāsa, Kṛṣṇa, Kapila, and so forth, whose qualities are expanded, who is His own essential nature, and who is the agent of creation and the rest;
[the word *tataṃ* becomes *taṃ* by the rule] "there is elision when the same vowel follows."

Thus, by the rule *sūtra*, there is the elision of the suffix *tal*; or alternatively, the suffix *map* is used in the sense of the superlative suffix *tamap*. Consequently, "Brahman" refers to that which is most pervaded—that is, possessing limitless pervasion.
"He saw [him] as full of qualities" means that he beheld him as having that form by virtue of possessing those qualities.
However, some say that the letter *ta* itself denotes pervasion (*vyāpti*).

By this, its omnipresence has been stated for the purpose of worship. "That which is this"— referring to everything under discussion— the "knower" (vidvān), namely Aitareya, the son of Itarā, born from the sage named Viśāla, is Aitareya.
‘Mahidāsa’: the meaning is that the Blessed One said this, he for whom the great-souled gods (mahinaḥ) have become servants (dāsabhūtāḥ).
The particles *ha*, *sma*, and *vai* indicate well-known tradition (*prasiddhi*).
Here, because it is stated that “Mahidāsa said,” an external form of worship (*bahirupāsti*) is expressed for the purpose of external meditation.
Nor should it be said here that only the essential nature is being stated,
and not for the purpose of meditation; for without meditation, there would be no purpose for the statement.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: because the threefold nature of meditation (*upāsanā*) is resorted to by the phrase beginning with "ityādinā," it is [thereby] stated by implication (*arthāt*).
By the word "ādi" (etcetera), passages such as "He entered him through his two feet; this Brahman, this Person, in this [Person]" (*Ai. Ā. 2.1.4*) are included.
If it is argued that Mahidāsa should also be mentioned as a seer (*ṛṣi*), just as it is said, "Knowing this, Hiraṇyadan Vaida said... (*Ai. Ā. 2.1.5*), we say no.
For the seerhood of Mahidāsa, the son of Itarā, is already established by the very name of this *Upaniṣad*, namely "Aitareya"; therefore, such a statement would be redundant.
By the power of her asceticism, Itarā gave birth to one named Mahīdāsa;
he was the Lord Viṣṇu himself, who composed the Vaiṣṇava Tantra.
Thus it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*.
Nevertheless, one might ask: "How is it known that Mahidāsa is Viṣṇu? To this, he says: "Mahidāsa."
"He was born" means he became manifest.
"And he" refers to Mahidāsa— Mahidāsa Aitareya, who appears in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* of the Ṛgveda.
That Lord Viṣṇu himself became a certain sage by that name.

Thus, in the *Chāndogyabhāṣya*, the sage mentioned immediately prior— who is other than the Lord and whose son was named after Him— is not intended here; rather, it refers to "that which is non-Vaiṣṇava," namely,
a system (*tantra*) concerning Viṣṇu.
He "composed" (avyadhāt) the "text" (grantha); that is, he composed it. Or else, he "composed" the "Tantra," namely the Pañcarātra, and explained it to Nārada and others.
And he who is Viṣṇu, the Lord himself, directly possessing perfect knowledge and other such qualities.
He states "directly" (*sākṣāt*) to indicate that the very one previously mentioned as his incarnation is intended here.
This connects with the phrase "because it is based on the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*.
The meaning is that Mahīdāsa is declared to be Viṣṇu.
And by that [word], there is a connection with the word "ca" (and).
Furthermore, [it refers] to the fitness of persons for those respective meditations.

Now, one might ask: since direct realization of Brahman is possible for all through a single type of meditation, what is the purpose of this threefold classification of meditation? To this, the text proceeds with the phrase "tadyogāt" (due to connection with that).
Thus he explains the remainder of the Sūtra with the words "tattad" (that and that).
By the words "upāsana" (meditation) and "puruṣāṇām" (of persons), the repetition of the word "tat" (that) is indicated.
The particle "ca" (and) is used for conjunction.
Thus, it refers to those three kinds of meditations belonging to those persons—namely, the qualified practitioners known as humans, sages, gandharvas, and gods.

"In the middle" means that, according to the sequence, through the fitness [of the aspirant], there is the worship of each one individually in the form of external and internal pervasion; this is the meaning.
This connects with the phrase "because of this threefold nature of worship.

Thus, the sense is that for qualified aspirants who possess the fitness for various kinds of worship, the knowledge of Brahman does not arise through a single kind of worship alone; therefore, this threefold nature is necessary.
"For some, Hari is to be worshipped as being omnipresent; for some, in the heart; and for others, that Supreme Person is to be worshipped only externally. Thus it is stated in the Brāhma [Purāṇa].

From what is it known that men possess the fitness for the various kinds of worship mentioned? To this, he cites a Smṛti passage which establishes the threefold nature of worshippers in general, without specifying particular agents: "Of some," etc.;
Hari is the "Supreme Person" (Puruṣottama) "of some."
He is to be worshipped by the gods through the mode of being all-pervading;
he is to be worshipped "in the hearts" of some— such as the ṛṣis, gandharvas, and others— within the space of their own respective hearts.
"For some," however, [the meaning is] that for certain supreme humans, [the Brahman] is to be worshipped only externally; this statement is made because of their predominance.

Thus, the connection with the preceding [text] is as follows: because those persons are supported by [the Brahman] as qualified by that [Brahman], due to its suitability for various forms of worship, it is described as "belonging to the Brahman" (*brāhma*).
Viṣṇu is in the fire for those who perform ritual acts; Hari is in the heart of yogis; He is in idols for the unawakened; and for those who have realized the Self, He is everywhere.
And thus it is said. // 31 //
Thus ends the section concerning the vital breath at the end of the quarters.
Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter in the *Brahmasūtrabhāṣya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
In this very section, he states a specific authority that establishes the particular agent: "In fire," etc.
Viṣṇu states: "For those who perform rituals" (kriyāvatām),
that is, for those who carry out rites such as sacrifices, Hari is to be worshipped "in the fire," namely in the Gārhapatya and other sacred fires.
He is to be worshipped in the hearts of yogis and sages;
[he is to be worshipped] in the images of those best among men who are unawakened, of dull intellect, and of very limited insight.
He is to be worshipped in the forms of Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and others; however,
for the gods who have "known the Self"— that is, those who specifically know the forms of the Lord but whose inspired intuition has not yet been awakened— he is present "everywhere."
The meaning is that he is to be worshipped in all places.
Here, by the two phrases "in the fire" and "in the images," worship consisting solely of external forms is indicated;
for this very reason, only two locations are mentioned.
Otherwise, according to the literal sense, the worship of Viṣṇu in the sun and other objects would not constitute external worship;
by the phrase "of the yogins," internal worship is indicated.
"Because of the Śruti text, 'The sages have internal illumination,' it should be understood that the phrase 'everywhere' refers to meditation on [the Lord] as omnipresent.

Nor does this contradict the *Bṛhadbhāṣya*, which states, "Even for those who attain liberation through external worship, some form of worship within the heart must certainly be performed," nor the *Nyāyavivaraṇa*, which says, "The Blessed Lord liberates him solely by means of the vision of His image."*
Nor should a contradiction be suspected;

for in the passage beginning with "in the fire" (*agnau*), since there is no negation of other [meditations], it is accepted by all that meditation upon one's own self—designated as the *bimba* (archetype) and appropriate to oneself—for the sake of direct realization (*aparokṣa*), must also be performed within the heart.

Furthermore, it is because the various specific meditations, which serve as the means for the direct realization of incarnations (*avatāra*) and so forth that act as gateways to the direct realization of the liberating [Self], are predominantly established by those respective authorities through systematic arrangement in the context of the passage beginning with "in the fire."
Regarding "iti ca":
the particle *ca* denotes conjunction (*samuccaye*).
Since both statements establish the same point, this [second statement] is also connected with the preceding one by virtue of its being based on the *brāhma* [state].
The meaning of that [statement] is that specific individuals have been described as possessing the fitness for various respective forms of worship;
therefore, the intention is that one should not suspect the unestablished nature (*asiddhi*) of the reason "because of connection with that.
By this, it is shown that the Prāṇa mentioned here is not Viṣṇu.

But [the opponent may argue] that it refers only to the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa). Why? Because of the "indicative marks (liṅga) of the individual soul and the chief vital breath";

for here we hear the indicative mark of the individual soul in the form of having a lifespan of a hundred years, and the indicative mark of the chief vital breath in the form of the dialogue with the vital breaths and so forth—if this is argued, we say: no.

This vital breath (prāṇa) is Viṣṇu alone, not the individual soul (jīva) or others. Why? Because of the "concordance" (anugama); for this very reason, there is no contradiction with other scriptural texts or indicatory marks.
This is because, according to the method stated,
those [passages] are appropriately understood as referring to the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin),
or because this teaching is given from the perspective of the scripture (śāstra-dṛṣṭyā).

If it is asked, "For what purpose is the mention of the Antaryāmin here?", we reply: it is for the sake of internal meditation (*antar-upāsti*). Furthermore, there is no absence of intermediate distinctions within meditation.
"Because of the threefoldness of meditation";
for the meditation upon the Blessed One is threefold according to the distinctions of "within" and so forth.
Nor is it improper to speak thus even so.
It should not be argued that there is no purpose in stating the threefold nature of reality here because it has not been mentioned;
for that threefold nature is both relied upon and stated "here" in this context.
Nor should it be argued: "Since the direct realization of Brahman is possible for all through a single mode of worship, what is the use of a threefold worship?"

The meaning of the sūtra is stated as follows: "Because of their connection to that" (*tadyogāt*), meaning because those persons are fit for that very meditation; and since it is impossible for persons who possess fitness for various kinds of worship to attain immediate realization through a single kind of worship, the threefold nature of worship is necessary due to the difference in their respective fitness.

Furthermore, if the mark of being an agent of dispute were intended to refer to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), [it would contradict the statement]: "Both Keśava and the Lotus-born remained indifferent."
Thus, the contradiction of the scriptural statements should not be suspected;
for those [statements] have as their object external forms distinct from the inner controller (antaryāmin).
Therefore, since it is logical that those possessing various gender-markers refer to their respective inner controllers, there is no contradiction with them.
It is established that this Prāṇa is indeed Viṣṇu, consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), and thus it is proper to desire to know Him.
Thus ends the section on Prāṇa at the end of the [first] chapter.

Thus [ends] the work composed by the illustrious ascetic Jagannātha, disciple of the venerable feet of the holy Raghunāthatīrtha, the revered teacher of the Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka order and independent master of all philosophical systems.
In the *Śrīmad-Brahmasūtra-Bhāṣya-Dīpikā*,
the first quarter of the first chapter.
Om.
